From here on, the ritual for cultivation and study is clarified. Within this, first the characteristics of receiving and upholding [the precepts] are explained. Regarding the transgressions committed by a Bodhisattva, there is no "remainder" (i.e., no minor offense) that is not grave;
furthermore, the meaning of upholding and violating these precepts is analyzed. In the preceding section, there are four parts. First, receiving them from the source.

Second, "making this reflection" and below clarifies the exclusive protection and maintenance. Third, "if there is anything transgressed, repenting according to the Dharma" means being able to repent after having committed a transgression.

Fourth, "if there is no one according to the Dharma, receiving it with a well-purified mind" is still the accomplishment of the four virtues within the previously mentioned natural precepts (*svabhāva-śīla*);
however, whereas the second [virtue] therein was "receiving with a well-purified mind," it is now the fourth. Among the former...
Furthermore, there are four parts: first, the preliminary preparation (*pūrvakalpa*); second, "I desire [to receive] from the Master... which clearly explains the actual reception of the precepts;

third, "The wise person recites it three times to bestow the precepts upon him," which clarifies the subsequent preparation (*paścimakalpa*); and fourth, "Among other disciplines, this is the most supreme," which is a comparative evaluation to manifest its excellence.
Within the preliminary preparation, there are both distant and proximate stages. From the beginning up to the granting of permission is the distant preparation. Thus:

The following is the proximate preparatory practice (*upāya*). Within the remote preparatory practice, there should be two aspects: first, the preparatory practice of the recipient, which consists of requesting the precepts from the teacher;
second, the preparatory practice of the bestower, which consists of examining whether the person is a fit candidate and explaining to them the rules of observance and transgression.
Now, we shall clarify only the skillful means (*upāya*) of the recipient; the skillful means of the bestower will be omitted for brevity.

Within these skillful means of the recipient, one first distinguishes the training to be undertaken by designating the restraint of wholesome conduct (*kuśala-saṃgraha*) and the gathering of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha*). Next, one determines whether the recipient is a layperson or an ordained monastic.
The aspiration for *bodhicitta* is the cause for obtaining the precepts; therefore, one must first generate this aspiration as the skillful means for receiving the precepts. Thus it is said.

It is taught that the aspirational mind (*praṇidhicitta*) serves as the cause for the vow of ethical discipline (*śīla*). From "those of equal dharma" (*samānadharma*) onwards, these are the conditions for obtaining the vow. "Bodhisattva of equal dharma" identifies the preceptor (*ācārya*);
they are called "of equal dharma" because they practice the Mahāyāna together. The following reveals the virtues of the preceptor:

"one who has already made the aspiration" indicates the establishment of the preceptor’s resolve. "That aspiration having first arisen" refers to its initial generation. "Possessing wisdom" and so forth indicate the full possession of the preceptor’s virtues. Thus it is said:

One who possesses wisdom is able to know the Dharma of the precepts. One who possesses power is able to expound the Dharma of the precepts. "Excellent speech" and "excellent meaning" clarify what was previously termed "wisdom":
being able to penetrate the holy teachings is called excellent speech; clearly elucidating the Dharma of the precepts is called excellent meaning.

Being able to recite and uphold [the teachings] clarifies what was previously termed "power": because the body and mind possess power, one is able to recite and uphold them; by means of such recitation and upholding, one becomes capable.

He is able to explain it. This is the preliminary method for the Bodhisattva to prostrate at the feet [of the preceptor] and request the precepts. First, he requests by means of the body through prostration;

then, he requests by means of speech through verbal expression. Within this, the preceptor employs two methods: first, the mental method, which is to observe whether the person is capable or incapable [of receiving the precepts];
second, the verbal method, which is to fully proclaim the characteristics of upholding and violating the precepts, so that the recipient may [understand them] for themselves.

To assess whether one’s own mind is capable or incapable [of receiving the precepts] is a skillful means (*upāya*) of this teacher, as explained later in the section on the skillful means for maintaining the precepts;

therefore, it is not discussed here. The passage beginning with "Having made this request" (*evaṃ yācitvā*) refers to the proximate skillful means. The initial section clarifies the skillful means for the recipient to receive the precepts.

The passage beginning with "At that time, the wise one" (*atha khalu jñānī*) clarifies the skillful means for the precept-teacher (*śīlācārya*) to bestow the precepts. The preceding statement regarding "having requested" serves to recapitulate what has gone before and introduce what follows.

Next is the formal seeking of the precepts. Within this, there are three parts: first, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one respectfully performs prostrations and pays homage to that which is to be studied;

second, one recollects their merits and gives rise to soft, medium, and superior pure minds, thereby recollecting that which is sought; and third, by recollecting those merits, one gives rise to a mind of aspiration and seeking.
When this mind of seeking increases further, it is termed soft, medium, and superior. Being unmixed with other thoughts is called "purity."
Purify the mind; this mind is the very cause for obtaining the precepts. Third, regarding "before the wise one," this clearly explains the ritual for receiving [the precepts].
One kneels in a humble and respectful manner before the wise one; this is the expedient means of bodily action (*kāyakarman*). The wise one is the teacher, and it is fitting to pay homage to them;
the Buddha image represents the witness, and in principle, one must face it. Regarding the phrase "uttering these words," this is the expedient means of vocal action (*vākkarman*). The speech...

Having already reflected upon the preparatory application of mental karma, there are three stages therein. Once speech has ceased, one who dwells in mindfulness cultivates the mind by generating a resolute intention (*pranidhāna-citta*).
This resolute intention to sever evil, embrace the wholesome, and sustain sentient beings is called "nurturing the pure mind.

Thinking, "I have now lowered [my pride] and attained the perception of having received the precepts; the Preceptor has conferred them upon me, and I have immediately obtained them," one realizes that their attainment is not far off; therefore, it is said: "It shall not be long before..."
One attains the precept of the inexhaustible discipline (*vinaya-saṃvara*). One shall attain the immeasurable precept of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

One shall attain the unsurpassed precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). These three are collectively termed the "Great Accumulation of Merit. Having reflected thus, one remains silent and arouses the intention to receive the explanation.

The above constitutes the first section: the preparatory methods for the recipient. Below is clarified the preparatory method for the preceptor (*śīla-ācārya*) and the recipient. Without giving rise to distraction—
The mind and intention constitute the skillful means (*upāya*). To single-mindedly transmit the Dharma without any divergent thoughts is called "an undisturbed mind.

Whether sitting or standing constitutes the physical skillful means. Speaking these words constitutes the verbal skillful means. First one says, "Dharma-brother, are you a Bodhisattva? This is to question the person.
To respond that the Buddha is one's teacher—this is the general designation for all Bodhisattvas who study the Buddha-Dharma together.

"Brothers. Those who have previously studied are called "elder brothers" (brothers in meaning) by way of their teaching; those who receive [the teachings] later are termed "younger brothers" (brothers in meaning).

Because they are younger brothers in the reception of the Dharma, they are called "Dharma-brothers. If one does not refer to the Buddha, but regards them in relation to one another, the one who bestows [the teachings] is the teacher and the one who receives is the disciple.
One calls them "brothers" because, in receiving that person, one causes their mind to rejoice. This Bodhisattva does not inquire [of others].

That person [thinks], "Since this dharma of the precepts applies only to bodhisattvas, I now ask whether or not he is a bodhisattva. The recipient should respond within that context by saying, "I am. The question regarding whether the vow has been made concerns the mind;

one is only designated a bodhisattva once they have generated the resolve (*cittotpāda*). Since it was previously stated that the bodhisattva already possesses the vow, why labor to ask again whether the vow has been made? To explain: [The text continues: "If one has already generated the resolve, one is called a bodhisattva. The previous statement that the bodhisattva already possesses the vow implies that the resolve has been generated. Why, then, is there a need for a redundant inquiry as to whether the vow has been made or not? [This] is explained as follows: [The text continues: "One who has already generated the resolve is indeed a bodhisattva, yet there remains a distinction between those who have merely generated the resolve and those who have fully perfected the vow. Thus, the question is asked to distinguish between these two stages. Furthermore, since the term "bodhisattva" is applied to anyone who aspires to enlightenment, even if they have not yet formally received the precepts, the question serves to clarify their specific status and commitment. Therefore, the inquiry into whether the vow has been made is both necessary and appropriate.

The virtues of a bodhisattva’s practice are not limited to one; even possessing a heart of compassion alone entitles one to be called a bodhisattva, though it does not necessarily imply the presence of a vow.

Therefore, it is necessary to inquire about this. The response below states that they do possess it. From the preceding section up to this point, the preliminary preparations (*pūrvaprayoga*) have been received. Below, the precepts are formally conferred.

Within this, first, the threefold aggregate of precepts (*triskandhaka-śīla*) sought by the candidate is restated. Following these various precepts, their excellence is praised so as to encourage their reception throughout the three periods of time.
Together they dwell and receive the precepts; throughout the three periods of time, they study together in learning and upholding the precepts.

"Can you receive them? clearly indicates the act of receiving the precepts. "I can receive them" is the response. The second and third repetitions clarify the ritual of bestowal. Why are there three recitations?
Fewer would lack sufficient earnestness, while more would be cumbersome and prolix. Therefore, the elaborate is omitted and the concise is adopted; the ritual consists of three [recitations] alone.
From here below is the third section, clarifying the subsequent ritual procedures (*paścātkarman*). This contains six parts: first, the preceptor performs the formal announcement;

second, because of this announcement, signs appear before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; third, through the appearance of these signs, all are simultaneously awakened to the knowledge [of the candidate’s attainment].
Fourth, by perceiving [the precepts], one gives rise to a mind of affectionate regard. Fifth, through this affectionate regard, one increases their merit.

Sixth, once the task is completed, both perform a prostration together before departing. Regarding the initial announcement: it is for the sake of letting the recipient know that the Buddha and Bodhisattvas are all fully aware [of the transgression], so that they may feel shame and uphold [the precepts] firmly.
Having recited the threefold bestowal, one reiterates what preceded to introduce what follows. As for the recipient, they do not rise; this is the ritual for the recipient.
This is the ritual for the one of wisdom who bestows [the precepts] below. At that time, the one of wisdom raises their hands and makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

First, they announce to the Bodhisattvas because they are fellow students; afterwards, they announce to the Buddhas because they are the original teachers. Within the announcement to the Bodhisattvas:

First, one performs a physical prostration; then, one makes a verbal declaration. Within this verbal declaration to the Buddha, one identifies the person being informed as "the foremost Great Teacher among those who know and see, O Buddhas of the ten directions.
Following the phrase "in all matters," one must state the reason for the declaration. Because [the Buddha] is able to know and see, one must offer this report.
Regarding the one who manifests knowledge, vision, and awakening toward all sentient beings and receives this [teaching], concerning all phenomena...

One presently knows, sees, perceives, and cognizes the dharmas received. This "threefold confession" (*tri-śaraṇa*) is precisely the white [virtuous] words; it is threefold for the purpose of increasing the mind.

In the second section, having thus completed the reception, the preceding is concluded and the subsequent is initiated. From the phrase "in sequence" (*kramaśas*) below, the actual manifestation of signs is clearly explained.
As for the presence of signs in the dharmas, by the power of the merit of the precepts, there may be a fragrant terrace before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
There may be exquisite flowers, or sounds may emerge, and various signs appear. At that time, throughout the ten directions, [one considers] from whom one has received the bodhisattva precepts;
this is the third section, "Awakening through Signs. From "giving rise to the thought of them as children" below is the fourth section, "Knowing and Cherishing.
From "causing goodness to increase" below is the fifth section, "Increasing Goodness through Affection. Thus, "the white [light]" below...
This concludes the sixth section; having paid homage, one departs. These six sections together constitute the subsequent preparatory application (*pūrvaprayoga*).

From here below is the fourth part, which is the comparative evaluation that reveals superiority. Within this, it is shown that the higher [levels] can surpass the lower; from the point of *mokṣa* (liberation) downward, the lower is shown to be inferior to the higher.
The previous statement—that the ethical discipline (*saṃvara*) received by a bodhisattva is the most supreme among all others—was a general comparison to reveal its superiority.

This is the general name for the threefold aggregate of vows (*trisaṃvara*) received by Bodhisattvas; because they equally refrain from evil, this is the most supreme when compared to the vows of ordinary persons and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
It will be explained specifically below. It is superior because it encompasses immeasurable virtuous qualities and is vast.
The three clusters being perfectly complete is called the encompassing of immeasurable and boundless virtues. Arising from the true mind and relying upon the true, it is supreme.
The bodhicitta can shatter the marks of deluded emotion and return to the ultimate reality of the self; this is called the "true mind. Precepts arise in dependence upon this.
Therefore, it is most excellent. It is superior because it extensively remedies all evils. The morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) can remedy all faults such as killing;
the morality of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) can remedy all faults of not gathering wholesome qualities;

and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*) can remedy all faults of not benefiting sentient beings. All sentient beings and all evil conduct are not outside these three.
It is able to counteract all [defilements] and is therefore supreme; the inferior, superior, and middling forms of *vinaya* cannot equal it.
It clarifies that the small is inferior to the great, and its inclusion of all virtues is beyond the reach of the *śīla*.

The preceding section was the first: receiving the precepts from another. From here on is the second: guarding and maintaining them with single-minded diligence. Within this, the initial portion clarifies the skillful means for upholding the precepts.

Having received them from another, one maintains them with an extremely pure mind; this correctly clarifies the preliminary skillful means for upholding the precepts. Among these, there are those that are proximate and those that are remote.
Arising the intention to guard and maintain [the precepts] after having already received them is called "proximate. That which occurs before receiving the precepts—
One must employ skillful means to subsequently give rise to and maintain the precepts; this is called "distant. Now, first clarify the "near. The wise do not accept [precepts] from everyone;
this clarifies the skillful means of the distant. Within the near, one contemplates those who act according to the Dharma and does not follow those who do not.

This refers to the mind that upholds the precepts. Regarding "the increase of merit," this is a praise of its benefits and an exhortation to uphold them; because the merit of upholding the precepts surpasses what was previously received, it is said to "increase further.
As for the statement in the *Sūtra* and *Mātṛkā* that "one should uphold [them]," this is a formal exhortation to protect and maintain them.

From here below, within the second section on the remote preparatory practices (*pūrvaprayoga*), there are two distinct parts: first, clarifying the internal mental preparation of the preceptor, which involves observing whether the candidate is capable or incapable of receiving the vows;
second, clarifying the verbal activity of the preceptor, which consists of explaining the observance and transgression of the precepts.
This causes the recipient to personally weigh their own mind to determine whether they are capable or incapable.
Within the first section, it is stated in general that a wise person does not receive precepts from everyone;
this refers to the preceptor as a "wise one," who must not hastily grant the precepts to every petitioner. Below, this is explained in detail. Among these, the first concerns conduct based on merit.

This clarifies what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. Regarding the practice of wisdom that follows from not drinking alcohol, it first clarifies what is inappropriate and subsequently clarifies what is appropriate.
Within the preceding section on merit, the former clarifies the inappropriate and the latter clarifies the appropriate.

Within the eight distinct phrases concerning the inappropriate, the first three concern the absence of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), while the latter five concern the absence of the practice itself (*caryā*). Among these, the phrase "one who lacks faith" refers to the first case.
What is it that is not believed? It refers to being unable to believe in the teachings on the precepts upon hearing them. "Not requiring the second" means there is no desire for it;
"not contemplating the third" means there is no deliberation. Within the absence of right practice, these are distinguished as obstacles in relation to the five perfections.

First, the obstacles to *dāna* (generosity) are clarified. That which is called "miserliness" (*mātsarya*) is the begrudging attachment to one's own possessions. "Greed" (*lobha*) refers to the desire to seek the wealth of others;

initial attachment to wealth is considered greed, while seeking wealth without satiety is termed "excessive desire" (*bahukāmatā*), and taking it without limit is termed "lack of contentment" (*asamtuṣṭi*).

Next, the obstacles to *śīla* (ethical discipline) are clarified. Regarding those who speak of "breaking precepts," this refers to unwholesome karma. Since [the precepts] have not yet been received, how [can there be breaking]?

It has already been established that there are precepts that can be violated. The commentary explains that although one may not yet have received the bodhisattva precepts, if one has previously received the disciplinary laws of the seven classes of practitioners (*saptanikāya*) and violates them therein, this is called "breaking the precepts.
If one breaks those [monastic] precepts, it is clear that one will also be unable to protect the bodhisattva precepts;

therefore, they are excluded here. To be negligent and fail to maintain [the precepts] such that one commits transgressions, while having no sense of moral dread or aversion, is termed [non-vigilance].

Arrogance and laxity; failing to avoid conditions for transgression is called "lack of restraint" (*anārakṣā*). Next, the obstacle to patience (*kṣānti*) is explained: intolerance within the inner mind is termed "resentment" (*upanāha*).
"Anger" (*krodha*) refers to the immediate moment, while "resentment" refers to what follows. Sudden outbursts of violence through body and speech are termed "intolerance" (*akṣamā*).
Next, the obstacle to diligence (*vīrya*): consistently failing to practice is termed "laziness" (*kausīdya*). This obstacle to diligence is described as abandoning one's practice midway.
Laziness is a defilement of this diligence. Next, the obstacles to dhyāna are clarified: sleep and mental sinking (*laya*), and talkativeness and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
One should not receive [the precepts] from such persons; this concludes the section on those from whom one should not receive them. Below, the appropriate recipients are clarified.

Regarding the phrase "practicing virtue for even as long as it takes to milk a cow": this is stated according to a minimum duration; more is always better, but if the minimum is reached at this point, one may receive [the precepts]. How long does this duration last?

The duration of milking a cow once with the hand is called a "cow-milking moment" (*gopālakṣaṇa*). This does not mean that one must finish milking a single cow before it is designated as a "cow-milking moment.

How can such an extremely brief period of merit be said to proceed from formal undertaking? Nevertheless, since he was already able to spontaneously give rise to such a virtuous mind even before undertaking [the precepts], it is clear that he is also capable of maintaining them once the undertaking is complete; therefore, he may receive [the precepts]. This is explained in terms of his capacity.

Regarding virtue, the following section addresses wisdom by clarifying what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. First, the appropriateness is clarified because it follows naturally from the preceding context;

subsequently, the inappropriateness is clarified. Within the clarification of what is appropriate: "not drinking alcohol" clarifies the distancing from the conditions for delusion (*moha*); "not being foolish" clarifies the absence of the essence of delusion. This distinguishes [the practitioner] from ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

The subsequent passage distinguishes [him] from those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Being able to enter into the profound meaning is called "not being timid"; being able to [master] the extensive teachings...
That they "hear not a little" clarifies that there is understanding. That they "do not slander the Bodhisattva Sūtras" clarifies that there is faith.
Furthermore, they do not slander the Bodhisattva Vinaya or Mātṛkā; however, since the Sūtra-piṭaka is the foremost of the three piṭakas, it is mentioned first.
The following lines constitute the summary of what should be done. Below, what should not be done is clarified; therein, at the beginning—
To speak of slandering and opposing means: not explaining, not teaching, and failing to clearly elucidate what is improper; slandering and lacking faith, opposing and being unwilling;
not speaking toward the speaker, and not explaining the teachings; not teaching the meaning, and not teaching the methods of practice.
Why is this? It is clarified by the following question and answer. Why is it asked? Because a bodhisattva should properly transform and gather sentient beings; why then [does he not do so]?
The statement "Furthermore, it is not taught for the sake of meaning" serves to clarify its intent. This section contains three points:

first, it explains that because such persons lack both faith and wisdom, being shrouded by these two obscurations, they slander upon hearing [the teaching]; therefore, it must not be taught to them. Second, from "In this way" onwards, it clarifies that slandering [the Dharma] entails harm and incurs immeasurable demerit;
therefore, it must not be taught. Since the gravity of the offense of slandering is vast and manifold, it cannot be stated directly; thus, the text mentions the "reception" [of the fruit].
This merit is revealed by way of contrast. For the Bodhisattva precepts involve abandoning every evil, cultivating every good, and delivering all sentient beings.
Therefore, the merit of one who receives them is immeasurable; conversely, for one who slanders them, how could their sin not be even greater?

Third, from "even down to" [the end of the section], it clarifies the limits of the offense incurred by the slanderer: from the moment after having slandered, until they have abandoned their evil words and evil views.
Since the onset of evil thoughts, one constantly incurs these transgressions. Evil speech and evil words, as well as evil views and evil thoughts, constitute the mind’s slander.
When the slandering mind penetrates deeply, it is called an "evil view"; when the initial mind begins to deliberate, it is called an "evil thought.

One must make a firm resolve and vow to sever these various evils; only then can one distance oneself from such great sins. Even without a conscious intent to sever them, they arise incessantly and continuously.
The above constitutes the mental expedient (*upāya*) of the Preceptor. Below this follows the verbal expedient of the Preceptor, which consists of three parts:

first, instructing the Preceptor to explain the characteristics of upholding and violating the precepts to the candidate for ordination; second, extensively clarifying the four *pārājika* offenses and other matters of upholding and violating the precepts for Bodhisattvas;
third, concluding with a eulogy and citation of evidence from the section beginning "When these matters arise" regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, exhorting all beings to practice them.
Regarding the study: within the first section, one first teaches by explaining the characteristics of upholding and violating the *Mātṛkā*.
Since this treatise fully contains the characteristics of upholding and violating, it specifically teaches the *Mātṛkā*. Next, the intention behind the teaching is clarified:
it is to enable the recipient to advance or retreat according to their own mind. Thus, for such a person, the conclusion is that they should receive [the precepts].

In the second section, the heavy [offenses] are explained first, followed by the light ones. Within the preceding discussion of the heavy offenses, there is first a general overview, followed by a specific analysis, and finally a detailed classification.
Regarding the four *pārājika* offenses that constitute the initial general overview, they will be briefly analyzed here according to three gates.
First, regarding the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*), one must determine their respective locations; specifically, within which aggregate do these four heavy offenses belong?

[Included in the] Compendium. It should be known that these four are subsumed under the "virtuous precepts" (*śīla*). How is it known that this is not included within the "restraint precepts" (*saṃvara-śīla*)?

The preceding text explains that the "restraint precepts" are like the precepts of the seven classes [of practitioners]. Within the dharma of the seven classes, this has never been stated to be a *pārājika* offense;

thus, it is clearly understood that it is not subsumed under the restraint precepts. How is it known that this is not subsumed under the "precepts for benefiting beings" (*upapatti-śīla*)? According to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*...

The Sūtra clearly shows that this is not what is explained at the beginning of that [text]. It states that not giving rise to a mind of transgression regarding the precepts one has received constitutes the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint morality).

Next are the four [precepts] that gather wholesome qualities (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and finally the four that gather sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). Among these, the four faults prevented within the *kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* are identical to these four grave offenses.
Therefore, it is known that these four belong to the *kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*, not the *sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*. What are their characteristics? Among those, the first...
First, not being arrogant toward the Honored One. That which is eliminated by this [precept] is equivalent to the offense of the fourth type of mind, namely arrogance born of delusion;
the only difference is that the former is directed toward a person, while here it is directed toward the Dharma. Second, not being angry toward living beings.
That which is eliminated by this [precept] is equivalent to the offense of the third type of mind, namely hatred. Third, not being deluded regarding others. That which is eliminated by this...

Delusion is like this first transgression of the mind of greed and delusion. Among those [transgressions], the fourth—non-stinginess regarding internal and external things—is like the second transgression of the mind of stinginess and parsimony, which is excluded there.
By inferring from that, one can certainly know that these four constitute the precept of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

Second, regarding the three categories of ethical discipline (*tri-śīla*), we shall examine their presence or absence. Question: For what reason are the objects prevented by the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) not included in the precept of gathering virtuous qualities?

All evils possess grave consequences; among these, there is none that does not encompass the welfare of living beings. The commentary explains that in the cultivation of conduct, there are both the inclusive and the primary.

When analyzed from the perspective of the mind, the inclusion of the welfare of living beings is the primary [practice], while the other two are the inclusive. This is because the intention of a Bodhisattva is primarily directed toward living beings. When analyzed from the perspective of conduct:

the restraint (*saṃvara*) and the gathering of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*) constitute the primary practice, while the inclusion of the welfare of living beings is the inclusive. Now, analyzing from the perspective of conduct, the restraint...

Because virtue is right conduct, its violation carries deep faults; therefore, it is said to be "heavy. Because the vows that encompass beings involve concurrent practice, their violation carries lighter faults;
therefore, they are not called "heavy. Such is the distinction between existence and non-existence [of gravity]. These three explanations clarify the text.

Now, when it says that a bodhisattva "abides in the restraint" (*saṃvara*), this refers to the vow of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) as the restraint. However, in the subsequent text, the dharma of the three clusters of vows (*tri-skandha-śīla*) is collectively termed "restraint."
[This refers to] the *vinaya*. It is not that only those precepts of the *vinaya* discipline are called "discipline" (*vinaya*).
Why is this so? Discipline has the meaning of "preventing transgressions. Since all three [aggregates] prevent transgressions, all three aggregates are collectively termed "discipline.

Because discipline applies universally, it is now designated as "discipline" by virtue of its inclusion of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka*). As for *pārājika*, this is translated as "without remainder. One who commits this offense [is irredeemable].
Such a person, within the Buddha-dharma, is like one who is already dead; they possess no further goodness, hence it is called "without remainder.

What are these four? [This is] the second section, which provides a detailed analysis. First is the question, next is the explanation, and finally is the summary. Among the four, the first is an offense committed with a mind of greed and delusion;

the second is an offense of stinginess (*mātsarya*). Within this, there are two types: first, stinginess regarding material wealth; second, [stinginess regarding the Dharma], as indicated by the phrase "desiring to hear" and so forth.

This is the transgression of stinginess regarding the Dharma. The third is the transgression of anger: harsh speech is that of the mouth; striking with the hand is that of the body; and harboring resentment is that of the mind.
The fourth is the transgression of the deluded and arrogant mind: slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is to slander the True Dharma;
preaching what is counterfeit and inferior is to establish what is false.
The following is a further detailed analysis of the four [categories] below. Within this, there are five parts: first, clarifying the limits of transgression;

second, explaining the meaning of "inexorable" (*anavaśeṣa*) regarding the *pārājika* offenses through the inability to increase or decrease them; third, clarifying the gravity of transgressions—whether they constitute a loss or not—by means of the categories of weak, medium, and inferior;

fourth, clarifying the limits of loss through the absence of suddenness; and fifth, demonstrating that even if a Bodhisattva has incurred such a loss, they are capable of receiving [the precepts] once again.

The following section contrasts [the present text] with other sources to highlight its distinctiveness. Within the first part, the statement, "If one commits even a single offense, it is called a *pārājika*, how much more so for four," clarifies the scope of the transgression.
If one commits even one of the four, it is already termed "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*); how much more so if all four are committed?
This is similar in wording to the Vinaya, which states that committing even a single rule constitutes a *pārājika*. Below this, the second section explains the term *pārājika*.
The meaning of "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) is as follows: because one cannot increase or expand the adornments of the present life, there is no practice in the present;

this clarifies the absence of aspiration (*apraṇihita*). Furthermore, because one commits these four transgressions, one cannot in the present increase or expand the merit and wisdom that adorn the bodhisattva conduct, nor does one possess a pure mind.
Since both the mind and its activities are absent, it is called "without remainder. From here on, the next...

The three knowledges (*vidyā*) clarify whether there is a loss or non-loss of the precepts regarding the gravity of transgressions. The first knowledge clarifies that although one commits a light offense, the precept is not lost.

The latter two clarify superior offenses; having committed such, the precept is lost. Within this, first the loss of the precept through superior offenses is clarified, followed by an analysis of their characteristics:

namely, frequent violation constitutes a superior offense. Furthermore, there are four types of transgression: first, transgression with a slight or minor mind; second, [transgression with a medium mind]...
There are four types of transgressions: first, those committed with a deliberate mind; second, those committed with a heavy mind; third, those committed with a mind of divergent views;

and fourth, those where one repeatedly violates the precepts through these first three states of mind without shame or remorse, even taking pleasure in them and claiming they are meritorious. Among these four types of transgressions, the first is not a *pārājika*;
it is subsumed under the subsequent forty-two rules. The second is classified as minor (*hīna*), and the third as middling (*madhya*).
The fourth is the superior [position]. From here below, the fourth section clarifies the limits of what constitutes a transgression.

There is no such thing as suddenly committing a transgression and thereby abandoning the bodhisattva precepts, as is the case with a bhikṣu. This clarifies that regarding the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), if a bodhisattva commits even a single one through the force of predominant afflictions (*adhimātra-kleśa*), they immediately lose the precepts;
this is similar to how a bhikṣu abandons the precepts at the time of renouncing the path. There is no sudden [abandonment].

One loses the precepts only after having committed the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*). For example, when a bhikṣu abandons the path and abandons the precepts—this is the fifth section below, which clarifies differences through contrast.

First, it clarifies the difference in receiving [the precepts]; later, it clarifies the difference in abandoning them. A bodhisattva who loses the precepts is capable of receiving them again, unlike a bhikṣu;
this is the difference in receiving. If a bhikṣu commits a grave offense and yet does not lose his prohibitive precepts, why would he need to [receive them again]?

One may receive [the precepts] but say that they cannot be obtained. Although a bhikṣu’s transgression of the precepts does not cause their loss, if he later encounters other conditions and relinquishes this discipline, and then wishes to receive it again, the prior transgression constitutes an obstacle; therefore, they cannot be obtained. When a bodhisattva transgresses, although he may lose the precepts, he can obtain them again upon receiving them later.
Why is this so? Because a śrāvaka aims for the fruit within a single lifetime and must rely on his own body.

One attains it only when the vessel is utterly pure. If one has previously committed a grave offense, then even if they later wish to receive it, because their karmic obstructions are deep and heavy, they cannot attain it.

A bodhisattva, desiring to seek the fruit through many bodies, sets aside even minor virtues; therefore, they do attain it. Furthermore, the bodhicitta is a superior remedy that extinguishes transgressions;
when this mind arises, grave offenses are eliminated, and thus one can generate the precepts. As for the mind of the two vehicles...

Inferior. Because it cannot extinguish transgressions, the precepts are not generated. There are two conditions for the subsequent clarification of the differences regarding relinquishment (*prahāṇa*).

Within this, first the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is clarified, followed by an explanation of the text itself. Regarding the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: there are two in the Mahāyāna and four in the Hīnayāna. The two in the Mahāyāna are:
first, the abandonment of the vow for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); second, the commission of a grave afflictive offense (*kleśa-āpatti*). The four in the Hīnayāna are: first...

There is relinquishment through abandoning the path, relinquishment through death, relinquishment through the severance of the roots of goodness, and relinquishment through the emergence of both sexual organs.

Why does a bodhisattva not have relinquishment through abandoning the path? Because they universally receive the dharmas of the seven classes of followers. Why does a bodhisattva not have relinquishment through death?

At the time of originally receiving the precepts, one made a vow to continue until the attainment of Bodhi; therefore, the severing of the roots of goodness constitutes the abandonment of the bodhisattva, which is equivalent to this [case].
It is still a transgression caused by predominant afflictions (*kleśa*). Why does a bodhisattva not abandon the precepts through the appearance of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*)?

Because that which was received universally protects against all physical forms. Why does a śrāvaka not abandon the precepts through a regressive mind? Because the śrāvaka’s disciplinary dharma is intended for ordinary, inferior beings.

Ordinary beings of inferior capacity have not yet established a wholesome mind; their progress and retreat are difficult to rely upon. For this reason, one cannot speak of relinquishing [the precepts] according to the state of the mind.

Why, then, is there no relinquishing of the supreme afflictions? The śrāvaka precepts are established based on formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); they are all equal in that they constitute the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*).

One cannot relinquish them according to the mind—that is, by saying that the superior [affliction] causes relinquishment while the middling and inferior do not—because such is the nature of what has been established.
Because it does not follow the mind, its specific characteristics are thus. Next, I shall explain the text. Within this, first the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s relinquishment are clarified;

following "there is no relinquishing of the body," the differences are distinguished through contrast. In the preceding section, the initial statement regarding the two conditions for losing the precepts serves as a general heading.

The following provides a detailed explanation. One abandons [the precepts] because abandoning the bodhicitta vow destroys their root; since the precepts arise dependent upon the vow—just as grass depends upon the earth—by now abandoning the root, one loses the precepts.
Furthermore, they are lost due to "excessive transgression" because the obstruction is heavy.

Regarding the analysis of abandonment, this text clarifies only that a Bodhisattva does not abandon them at the end of life, while other cases are omitted for brevity. There is no instance of losing them through the discarding of one body and taking up another.

The distinct forms are not lost; even across different locations in the ten directions, they are not abandoned. This means that the vows are not discarded and the fundamental clarity is not newly acquired but remains intact.

Above, the heavy [offenses] were explained; next, the light [offenses] will be discussed. Within the light offenses, there are two parts: first, a general enumeration of the precepts so that people may recognize them.

This refers to offenses and non-offenses, defiled and undefiled states, and so forth. Among the forty-two cases explained below, each first clarifies what constitutes an offense and subsequently clarifies what constitutes a non-offense.
Furthermore, within the category of offenses, there are those that are defiled and those that are undefiled; therefore, these are now presented collectively so that people may understand them.
To act with an evil mind in violation of the Dharma is called an offense (*āpatti*). To act with a virtuous mind in accordance with the Dharma is called non-offense (*anāpatti*).
Offenses vary in degree of gravity. Those that are grave arise from a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) and are termed "defiled offenses. Those that are light do not arise from a defiled mind.

It is called "unstained. Since there are gradations of defilement, it is therefore described as weak, middling, and superior. Second, the detailed classification: within this detailed exposition, there are forty-two precepts in total.
The first thirteen are the precepts for gathering wholesome qualities (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*); the latter eleven are the precepts for gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

Within the former category of gathering wholesome qualities, the initial seven are the precepts of generosity (*dāna-śīla*), and the subsequent six are the precepts of ethical discipline (*śīla-śīla*).
Next are the four precepts of patience; next, three are the precepts of diligence; next, three are the precepts of meditative concentration; and finally, eight are the precepts of wisdom.

Within the precept of giving (*dāna*), the first one is paired with those above to clarify the giving of respect, while the subsequent six are paired with those below to clarify the giving of gathering.

The preceding section clarifies what constitutes an offense, while the subsequent section clarifies what does not constitute an offense. Within the discussion of offenses, there are two parts: first, the characteristics of the offense;

second, a comparative analysis of the gravity of the offense—distinguishing between light and heavy, as well as those with and without defilement—based on whether one fails to show respect. Regarding the characteristics of the offense, the period of one day and night is specified to clarify the time of the transgression.
A duration longer than this would be excessive, while shorter would be insufficient; therefore, one day and one night is established as the limit. If [the Buddha has already]...
The following clarifies the objects of transgression. "Objects" refers to the Three Jewels. Whether it be the Buddha remaining in the world or a stupa and temple, these are the Jewel of the Buddha.
That which is below the Buddha is the Jewel of the Dharma. The Dharma and its scriptures constitute the minor Dharma;

the principles and the treasury of practice are termed the [minor] Dharma, while the teachings themselves are called the scriptures. The *sūtras* and their virtues constitute the great Dharma. If a bhikṣu...
The following refers to the Jewel of the Saṃgha. The assembly of bhikṣus, śrāvakas, and great bodhisattvas constitutes the Bodhisattva Saṃgha.
To fail to show even the slightest respect clarifies the nature of one’s transgression. Not making offerings, even down to a single prostration, is a transgression of body.
Not offering praise with even a single verse is a transgression of speech. Failing to maintain even a single moment of pure mind is a transgression of mind. This is what is called...

Regarding those who commit many offenses (*anekāpatti*), their characteristics of offense are established. When a single offense arises, many offenses arise in succession; this is called "committing many offenses. What is the meaning of this?
When one offense arises, offenses are produced continuously as a stream of similar types. Furthermore, when there is the obstruction of concealing this [initial offense], another offense arises;
and when there is successive concealment, yet another offense arises. Therefore, it is called "many offenses. The above clarifies the commission of offenses.

[The preceding] explains the characteristics. Below, the meaning of heavy versus light, and defiled versus non-defiled, is clarified. A mind that lacks respect, is indolent, or is negligent, thereby violating superior offerings, is termed "defiled.
An offense committed based on such a state is termed a "defiled" offense. A mind that forgets or errs, characterized by lightness [of intent], is termed "non-defiled.
An offense committed based on such a state is termed a "non-defiled" offense. The above has explained offenses; below, the cases of non-offense are clarified. Entering the pure mind...
As for this, from the first bhūmi upward, one never again commits such transgressions. Regarding "like the unbreakable purity" (akṣayyaprasāda):

in the Hīnayāna teachings, that which is attained above the realization of the truths is called unbreakable purity. Therein, one attains indestructible faith in the Triple Gem and is always able to make offerings to the Triple Gem in accordance with the Dharma.
By using that category as an analogy to clarify the Bodhisattva of Pure Mind, it is said "like. The Bodhisattva of Pure Mind has indeed transcended [the stages].
In that regard, because they are roughly similar in their general characteristics, they are said to be "like" [the preceding].

Among the six items below, the first is the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*); the second is the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*); and the following two concern the gathering of others through the gift of material wealth by means of ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Below are two sets of precepts concerning the gathering [of beings] through material gifts and the Dharma-gift. In the first, regarding material gifts, one first clarifies what constitutes an offense and subsequently clarifies what does not constitute an offense.

Within the offenses, one clarifies those that are defiled but not those that are undefiled. In the second, regarding the Dharma-gift, one likewise first clarifies what constitutes an offense and subsequently clarifies what does not constitute an offense.

Among the offenses, the first involves defilement while the latter clarifies non-defilement. Regarding the first instance of defilement, it states that one should respectfully inquire about the Dharma from a senior (*sthavira*) who possesses virtue;

this establishes the conditions for the offense. One is called a "senior" (*sthavira*) by virtue of having many years of summer retreats (*varṣa*), and is called "possessing virtue" when their wisdom and merit have surpassed others.
These two types of persons are equally termed "those who should be revered. To speak of those who share the same Dharma refers to those of inferior status.

They are called "those who share the same Dharma" because they practice the Buddha-Dharma together. Arrogance and resentment constitute the transgressive mind. These correspond to the two aforementioned categories:

being disrespectful toward those of superior status is termed arrogance; being angry toward those of inferior status is termed resentment. Generally speaking, their meaning is equivalent. [From this point on,] one should not give rise to them.
This clarifies the characteristics of offenses (*āpatti*). "Not rising and not yielding" refers to an offense committed in relation to a superior;

when one does not rise to show respect nor yield a seat before a superior person, an offense is thereby established. "Questioning and not answering" refers to an offense committed in relation to an inferior;

when one does not respond to the greetings of an inferior person nor answer their request for the Dharma, an offense is thereby established. This is called the "concluding summary of the lower. The following clarifies non-defilement.
A state of mind characterized by indolence, neutrality, forgetfulness, or error is not defiled, as it differs from anger or pride;

because it does not involve deliberate intent, it constitutes an offense [of non-defilement]. However, among the various precepts where diligence is paramount, an offense committed through laziness is termed "defiled."

If one’s primary aim is to protect, guide, and transform others, then an offense committed through laziness is to be understood as non-defiled. Thus far has the explanation of offenses been clarified;

hereafter follows the explanation of non-offenses. If one is seriously ill—that is, personally afflicted by a grave illness—or if one’s mind is distracted by other matters such that one does not perceive the person before asking for greetings or requesting the Dharma, or if one who is asleep perceives it as waking—these constitute non-offenses for a Bodhisattva who is truly asleep.

The preceding section refers to "awakening. These inquiries and requests not being answered constitute no offense; this clarifies that within the context of offenses regarding inquiries and requests, there is no offense [in such cases].
Furthermore, if one remains seated when another is rising, or does not rise or yield their seat when facing someone who has committed an offense, this clarifies that there is no offense.
Among these seven points, the first three concern the Dharma; not paying homage in these cases does not constitute an offense. The latter four concern persons. Regarding the first three points:

first, seeing a senior monk (upādhyāya) expounding the Dharma or discussing doctrine, not paying homage does not constitute an offense. Second, while one is oneself expounding the Dharma or listening to the Dharma and discussing doctrine.

Even if one does not pay homage upon seeing a senior elder (sthavira), there is no offense. Third, among others, when preaching the Dharma, during a formal assembly, or during a definitive discussion, not paying homage constitutes no offense.
Regarding the latter four points: first, to protect the mind of the speaker; second, to bring about the subduing [of others]; third, to protect the sentiments of the many;
and fourth, to protect the monastic regulations (*saṃgha-vidhi*). Their characteristics are manifest and thus easily understood.

Next, regarding the two precepts concerning the inclusion of material giving (*āmiṣa-dāna*): first, it clarifies that when a donor offers a respectful gift, if one refuses it out of anger or pride while disregarding the material value, thereby ruining the donor’s merit, it constitutes an offense;
subsequently, it clarifies that when a donor presents precious treasures, if one refuses them out of anger or pride, one loses the donor’s wholesome roots, and thus it constitutes an offense.
Within the former [section], the first part explains the offense and the latter part explains the non-offense. Within the explanation of the offense, the defilement is clarified.

Briefly stated, there is no [offense] that is not stained. When a donor invites one, even down to the preparation of the necessary requisites, these constitute the conditions for the arising of an offense.

A mind of anger or pride constitutes the mental state that gives rise to the offense. Not accepting [the gift] and not remaining [in the invitation] are the characteristics of the offense. Because one does not accept the gift when it is offered and does not go when invited, the offense is established.
This is called the "conclusion of the name. Regarding the section on non-offenses below, there are twelve distinct points. The third concerns the insane.

This means that one who gives while insane does not incur [the offense of] receiving [what is forbidden]. The rest may be understood accordingly. Within the second category, it clarifies what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as defiled and non-defiled [transgressions].
Regarding the defiled, when a donor offers gold, silver, and so forth, these serve as the conditions for the offense; the mind of anger or pride constitutes the transgressive intent.

The state of not accepting constitutes a transgression; this is termed the "lower bond. It should be understood that one is not defiled [by it]. There are eight cases where there is no transgression. First, regarding the "insane":

if a donor gives while insane and one does not accept, there is no transgression. Second, regarding those who have already accepted but then developed craving and attachment: if one refuses out of a desire to protect oneself from afflictions, there is no transgression.
Third, if the donor develops regret and one does not accept, there is no transgression. Fourth, if the donor develops confusion and one does not accept...
There is no offense. Because one doubts that there is no karmic retribution, it is said that "delusion arises. The rest may be understood accordingly.
Within the section on the inclusion of dharmas, first it clarifies why a virtuous person seeking the Dharma fails to bestow it, thereby constituting an offense;

subsequently, it clarifies why an evil person abandons others and fails to transform them, thereby constituting an offense. Within the first inclusion, it clarifies both offenses and non-offenses, as well as those that are defiled and those that are undefiled.
Regarding the preceding section on defilements (*saṃkleśa*): when sentient beings desire to hear [the teaching], this constitutes the condition for the offense (*āpatti-pratyaya*).

To harbor hatred and resentment while lacking envy is the mental state of the offense (*citta*). To fail to explain it to them is the manifestation of the offense (*ākāra*). This is termed the "concluding summary" (*nigamana*). The "non-defiled" cases can be understood accordingly.

In the subsequent section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*), there are ten distinct items. The second concerns the sick: if one is personally ill and incapable of explaining [the teaching]. The third concerns the insane: if one is deranged.

It should not be explained to those who are deranged; all other cases may be understood accordingly. Regarding the section on the wicked person to clarify what should be included, it explains both transgressions and non-transgressions.

Within the explanation of transgressions, there is first a formal analysis followed by a detailed exposition. In the analysis, there is first that which is defiled, followed by that which is undefiled.
Within the section on defilements, the initial mention of "viciousness" and "violation of precepts" refers to the conditions for transgression.

Those who are exclusively sinful are termed "vicious," while sentient beings who possess mixed evils are termed "violators of precepts. To harbor resentment and a transgressive mind, thereby abandoning oneself and obstructing others, constitutes the characteristic of transgression.

This is called the "lower fetters"; it can be understood as being undefiled. Why? Because the subsequent explanation establishes what constitutes an offense, while what does not constitute an offense is easily understood.

Next, the following six sections concern the *śīla* precepts. Among them, the first four pertain to the personal cultivation of ethical conduct, while the latter two concern the gathering of sentient beings by relying upon that ethical discipline.
Within the first four, the first clarifies right morality (*samyak-śīla*), the second right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), and the third right deportment (*samyak-īryāpatha*).

The fourth is Right View. Within the context of Right Precepts, this section exclusively clarifies transgressions while omitting non-transgressions. The text is divided into three parts: first, it clarifies those points where the Bodhisattva should be the same as the Śrāvaka;
second, it clarifies those points where they should differ by prohibiting what follows for the Śrāvaka but not for the Bodhisattva;

third, it clarifies why one incurs a transgression when one is consistently the same [as the Śrāvaka] due to resentment and malice. Regarding the first point on being the same, the text first presents an example.

The same applies to the *dharmas*. The subsequent formulation [of the precepts] should be understood as identical. The subsequent explanation is of the same intent. From the beginning up to the phrase "for the increase and expansion of those with faith," this cites the *dharmas* that are common [to all].
In the Tathāgata’s *Prātimokṣa*, the places where the regulations were established are clarified;

that is to say, within the Tathāgata’s *Śīla-sūtra*. The Vinaya establishes prohibitions and correctly sets forth the methods of regulation. This is for the sake of protecting sentient beings, and so on, up to the increase and expansion of the clarification of these establishments.
The intention behind the establishment of the rules: The Buddha originally established the disciplinary laws (*vinaya*) in order to protect sentient beings from lack of faith.

He did so so that those who have not yet developed faith might gain it through these means, and those who already possess faith might increase and expand it. Such is the intention behind the establishment of the rules.

For example, as stated in the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, the World-Honored One formulated the precepts for the sake of ten benefits; this present case corresponds to two of those ten. Because the disciplinary laws were established, the bhikṣus rely upon them, and thus people see [the results].
Out of respect, those in the world who have not yet developed faith now develop it, and those who already possess faith see it increase and expand.

This cites a parallel case; the formal conclusion should be identical to that of the śrāvakas. The subsequent explanation expresses agreement. Why is this asked? Because the Great and Small Vehicles should differ, why do they study together?

The subsequent explanation expresses agreement. First, the Small Vehicle is cited; later, it will be used as a comparison for the Great Vehicle. Within the initial citation of the Small Vehicle, it first says:
The śrāvakas, up to and including those who save themselves alone, surpass others by exalting their own excellence and disparaging the inferior.

They surpass those bodhisattvas who save both themselves and others, because they exceed and elevate the merit of the śrāvakas who save themselves alone; hence the phrase "up to and including. Furthermore, they do not fail to protect others, causing those without faith to believe and those with faith to increase and expand.
They surpass themselves by exalting others; for although they have saved themselves, the practice they cultivate does not stop at saving themselves alone.
Protection. This extends even to not abandoning the protection of sentient beings, so that those without faith may develop it upon seeing [this], and those with faith may increase and expand it.
This refers to the minor [level]. How much more so for those below this—using the minor to illustrate the major—it is evident that they must necessarily be the same.

They merely seek their own liberation, yet they still protect others and act in accordance with the established laws; how much more so for a Bodhisattva who seeks the ultimate liberation? How could they possibly fail to provide protection?

He. Regarding the method of universal deliverance (*sahāya-dharma*), the meaning is as follows: "The deliverance of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-tāraṇa*) refers to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Because the Bodhisattva delivers all beings simultaneously, and this deliverance is the most supreme among all forms of deliverance, it is therefore called the "deliverance of the ultimate truth."
From here below is the second section, which clarifies their differences. This contains three parts. First, it clarifies how Bodhisattvas who possess little benefit and little skillful means differ.
They are unable to extensively accept and practice abundant giving or bestow many gifts so as to bring about the merit of generosity; this is termed "little benefit."
Being unable to extensively beg for the sake of others is called "doing little. Being unable to accumulate wealth to extensively gather in sentient beings is called "having few skillful means.
Regarding the second point, "For what reason? and so forth, this is the question and answer that provides an explanation. Why is it asked? One might ask:

since having few desires and being content is the proper principle, why is it not the same [as the Bodhisattva path]? The following section answers this by explaining: the Śrāvaka, seeking only his own liberation, should abide in having few desires.
The term "those" distinguishes the small from the great; "non-Bodhisattvas" distinguish the great from the small. Therefore, they should not be treated as identical.
This passage remains obscure. If expressed fully, it should state: "A Bodhisattva, who delivers both self and others, should not abide in little benefit, little activity, or little skillful means.
Since one knows this, the measure [of the Bodhisattva] does not precede [the non-Bodhisattva]. To draw it out further to complete the text, one may also say: "It is likewise permissible..."

[The author] explains: Regarding the three [points] "for the sake of generating [the distinction]," the following section extensively clarifies the differences. First, the specific instances are cited; subsequently, the differences are summarized.
Among the five categories of precepts (*pañca-nikāya-śīla*), only thirty matters have both similarities and differences;

the remainder are all identical. Within those thirty, eleven are different, while the rest are studied in common. What are the eleven? First, requesting robes from a householder who is not a relative. Second, [not a...]
1. A layperson personally offers robes at the invitation for self-indulgence (*pravāraṇā*). 2. Three kings and their ministers send precious gems;

because the Bodhisattva may personally accept and store them, there is no fault of pressuring them to give by demanding gems. 3. A bedding made entirely of black wool. 4. A bedding made entirely of white wool. 5.
A bedding that has not been used for less than six years. 6. A sitting mat that is not patched. 7. Personally accepting precious objects. 8. Begging for a bowl. 9. [The tenth item.]
Soliciting thread oneself and having a weaver who is not a relative weave it; requesting a rain-bath robe eleven times before [the proper time];
these cases are all different. The others are all the same. Why are the initial "staying apart from one's robes" and the "six-night robe" the same?

Because the Bodhisattva also has the method for relinquishing robes. The long robe, the long bowl, the robe for the full and new moon, the robe offered during the rainy season retreat, and the seventh...
Why are the cases of the "Sun-medicine" (divyauṣadhi) the same? Because the Bodhisattva also speaks of the dharma of purification.
Why are the cases of having a nun who is not a relative wash, dye, or card woolen cloth the same? Because it increases the fault of attachment and gives rise to public censure.

Why are the cases of exhorting one householder and praising two householders the same? Because it protects against the world's reproach. Why is the case of the bedding for wild insects [the same]? [Because it is for the sake of non-injury.]
Why are these cases the same? Because they cause much distress to sentient beings and give rise to worldly resentment. Why is it the same when one carries wool oneself?
Because one must conform to proper decorum (*īryāpatha*) so as to inspire respect in others. Why is it the same when buying and selling jewels? Because it serves to quell worldly resentment.
Why is it the same when encouraging or hiring weavers? Because it increases one’s own fault of greed and gives rise to worldly resentment. Why is it the same when taking a bhikṣu’s robe? [Because...]

Regarding "the same": because it distresses sentient beings, the transgression of diverting property donated to the Saṃgha is profound and grave; logically, it must be treated as the same. This has been fully explained in such detail.
Now, to briefly clarify the nine kinds of differences: begging for robes from a householder who is not a relative is the first difference;
and giving at one's own discretion is the second difference. One should observe whether the donor is capable or incapable [of giving]. [This applies to] the Śrāvakas.
Within the Dharma there are two kinds of contentment: first, the donor’s contentment; second, the recipient’s contentment. However, nowadays there is no recipient’s contentment;
one merely observes whether the donor is capable or incapable of giving, and must not exceed the donor’s own sense of contentment.
The alms bowl is also like this; these are the three differences. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva may accept many [offerings].
Regarding the statement "begging for thread oneself and having a weaver weave it," this is the fourth difference. There are four types of bedding and sitting mats made of *kauśeya* silk.
There are sleeping mats that are purely black, sleeping mats that are purely white, sleeping mats not kept for less than six years, and sitting cloths that are not patched;
these together constitute eight items. Gold and silver may also be accepted, which together with the preceding constitute nine. The above has extensively enumerated various differing matters;
such as these, the following concludes by clarifying these differences. This is the second clarification of the points where the Bodhisattva differs [from the Śrāvaka].

From here below is the third section, clarifying why being in agreement constitutes an offense. Within this, first it is explained that one commits an offense through malice and hatred, which is defiled;
subsequently, it is explained that one commits an offense through indolence, which is non-defiled.

Regarding the correct exposition of the precepts, this section first clarifies what constitutes an offense and subsequently clarifies what does not constitute an offense. Within the offenses, it clarifies those that are defiled; for brevity’s sake, it omits those that are undefiled.

The deceitfulness of body and speech is explained collectively as the characteristics of an offense, which will be specifically detailed below. If one manifests signs [of desire], this is the deceit of the body.
Displaying deceitful deportment is called "hinting" (*nimitta*). Seeking profit through disparagement is "verbal deceit.
To praise others while disparaging this [person] in hopes of obtaining profit from them is called "disparagement.

Because of greed for profit, one says that one has already obtained great gains and offerings from another donor, hoping that this donor will emulate that donor and give; this is called "seeking profit by means of profit" (*lābhena lābha-niścikīrṣā*).
That which was previously called "arising of what has not yet arisen" refers to abiding in wrong livelihood; being unable to abandon what has already arisen is termed the "lower fetter.
It should be understood that this does not constitute an offense.

Within the context of correct deportment, this clarifies what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as whether it is defiled or undefiled. Restlessness, lack of tranquility, and loud laughter or playfulness are the characteristics of an offense.
"Restlessness" refers to the body; "lack of tranquility" refers to the mind; and "loudness" refers to speech. Causing others to experience joy and amusement is the act that constitutes an offense.
Having established these conditions, they are subsequently cited and concluded: by creating such causes and conditions for causing others to experience joy and amusement, an offense is committed.

Thus, an offense is established; it may be understood that there is no defilement [in the following cases]. There are seven instances of non-offense. Regarding the fourth, "one who is fond of [gathering others]":
there may be someone who is fond of play; the Bodhisattva engages with them so as to cause them to find joy and to gather them through the Path.

Regarding the fifth, "for the purpose of severing that [habit]": there may be someone who indulges excessively in play; the Bodhisattva first conforms to them and later demonstrates its faults so as to cause them to abandon it.

The rest may be understood as before. Within the section on right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), the characteristics of transgressions are explained exclusively; there is no mention of non-transgressions. Among the transgressions, only those that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) are clarified, while those that are undefiled (*akliṣṭa*) are not.

Within the defiled category, there are four parts: first, clarifying the transgressive mind; second, clarifying the characteristics of the transgression; third, restating the preceding points and concluding them; and fourth, explaining the transgression.
The ritual format is as follows: "Forming such a view" refers to the transgressive mind; "making such a statement" below refers to the characteristics of the transgression.
Within this, the initial statement, "A Bodhisattva should not delight in Nirvana," etc., sets forth one's own view. "For what reason? below explains that view.
"Making such a statement" below restates it to conclude the point. "For what reason? below explains the grounds for the transgression. "Why? is the question.

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas constantly vow to remain within the various realms of existence (*bhava*). Now, returning to this point, why is the violation [of precepts] explained? There are three parts to the subsequent explanation:
first, it briefly clarifies that the mind of the Śrāvaka’s aversion to worldly pleasure does not equal that of the Bodhisattva; second, it explains the reason why the Śrāvaka falls short;

third, it states that the Śrāvaka seeks only self-benefit, whereas the Bodhisattva acts for the sake of all universally. Thus, the Śrāvaka does not equal the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva acts universally for all.
He considers himself superior because he acts for the sake of all. He swiftly vows to abandon faults and rapidly seeks Bodhi to benefit sentient beings.
Third, regarding the inferiority of that practice, this clarifies the characteristic of being surpassed. That practice is undefiled and superior to that of the Arhats;

by comparing the inferior to the superior, it is shown that Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are merely beginning their practice of non-defilement, whereas from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, they have already accomplished non-defilement. However, those prior to the stages are merely at the beginning...
Their habits are undefiled; they are already able to ensure that transgressions never arise, surpassing even the Arhats, let alone reaching ultimate perfection.

Therefore, it is said that Śrāvakas do not equal Bodhisattvas. Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the contaminated while being free from afflictions": this explains and clarifies their prior superiority.

As for the two wheels, although they have not yet severed the afflictions prior to the stage of the grounds (*bhūmi*), they are called "accomplishing the contaminated. Their suppression of defilements so that they do not arise is called "being free from afflictions. [End of fragment] *Luo* (羅).
Although Han [the Arhat] had severed the three poisons, they still persisted; therefore, the Bodhisattva surpasses that Arhat. As it is said in the sutras:
"Nanda practiced greed, while Śāriputra practiced anger," and so forth.

The first four [cases] concern one's own conduct; the latter two concern the gathering of others. In the former, one commits an offense because one fails to gather virtuous persons in accordance with the Dharma when they are unable to abandon their faults.
In the latter, one commits an offense because one fails to subdue and gather wicked persons through harsh and urgent measures.

Regarding the first precept, it clarifies what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as defiled and non-defiled transgressions. Within the defiled category, from the beginning up to "nor even eliminate it," refers to the characteristics of an offense.
Failing to maintain restraint and lacking faith are verbal faults; failing to maintain restraint against derision and disparagement are physical faults.
These two clarifications concern those who have not yet given rise to non-restraint and have not yet abandoned [faults] because they previously committed offenses without repentance.

Regarding the case where there is actually a fault, it is cited below to conclude the offense. As for the "unafflicted" category: if there is actually no fault and one does not abandon what is non-afflicted, although one has no personal transgression oneself...
To purify the minds of others, one must repent and eliminate [the offense], yet if one does not eliminate it, it constitutes a transgression.

Because there is actually no fault and the mind is unobscured, it is not defiled; thus, it can be understood that there is no violation. In the following section on "Subsuming Evil," the transgressions and non-transgressions are clarified.

Regarding the offenses arising from the Middle Way, the condition for an offense is the use of harsh words. Even if one fears causing distress, if it does not result in such an outcome, it constitutes an offense.
This is termed the "conclusion of the name. Because there was no malicious intent, it is called "non-defiled. That it is non-offensive can be understood [from this].

Next are the four types of patience and precepts. The first is an offense committed because one retaliates against the provocation of others; the second is an offense committed because one does not confess when another has offended;

the third is an offense committed because one does not accept an apology from another who has confessed; the fourth is an offense committed because one harbors a long-standing grudge and does not relinquish it.

Regarding the first [of these], it clarifies that the offense alone constitutes defilement. Retaliating with verbal abuse refers to the mouth; retaliating with anger refers to the mind; and retaliating with slander refers again to the mouth. How does this differ from mere verbal abuse?

When one is reviled with evil names and slandered for one's transgressions and faults, this is called the "lower fetter" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the second [fetter] may be understood in the same way.

Thirdly, within the precepts, it clarifies the distinction between transgression and non-transgression, defilement and non-defilement, the conditions for another’s confession of a transgression, the mind of malice that constitutes a transgression, and the characteristics of not accepting a transgression.
This is called the "lower fetters"; the rest can all be understood. The fourth [category] is easy to explain.
The next three precepts constitute the precept of diligence; among them, the first clarifies the practice of benefiting others, the characteristics of which are manifest and thus easily known.
The latter two concern self-benefit. The first clarifies that an offense occurs due to sleep and lethargy; the latter explains that an offense occurs due to agitation caused by worldly affairs.
Their characteristics are manifest and thus easily known.

Next, regarding the precepts of the third dhyāna, they are divided into three types according to the beginning and end of their cultivation. The first is based on the beginning and clarifies [offenses] through anger and pride.

The first constitutes an offense because one does not receive the teacher’s instruction. The second constitutes an offense because, while practicing, the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) shroud the mind so that it cannot open to learning.
The third constitutes an offense because, having achieved the practice, one grasps at its flavor as a virtue; this is called "savoring dhyāna" (*āsvādita-dhyāna*).
Here, one takes the afflictions and false views to be virtues, and thus an offense is committed. These three points should be understood.
