Next, the following eight precepts constitute the prajñā-precepts. Among them, the first five clarify transgressions in relation to the Dharma, while the latter three clarify transgressions in relation to persons.
Within the former group, the initial four concern the loss of decorum during study and practice, while the final one concerns slandering the profound upon hearing it.
Regarding the first four [precepts], the initial two pairs contrast the Great and Small Vehicles to clarify the loss of proper conduct in study;

the latter two pairs contrast the heterodox and the orthodox to manifest the loss of proper conduct in study. Within the former two, the first is a partial study of the Great Vehicle, while the latter is a partial practice of the Small Vehicle.

In studying the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, one clarifies what constitutes an offense and what does not among offenses; within offenses, one clarifies those that are defiled while omitting those that are undefiled.

"Seeing" refers to the mind of offense, and "speaking" refers to the characteristics of the offense. "That which should not be listened to" means it should not be heard; "that which should not be received" means it should not be contemplated.

"One should not study it; one should not cultivate it. Why should a bodhisattva employ the dharmas of the śrāvakas? This explains the reasons why the aforementioned three types [of views] should not be studied.
This is called the "concluding summary" (nigamana). Because they hold divergent views, stating that [the śrāvaka path] should not be studied constitutes defilement.

Why is this? The following explains the reason for the transgression; the cases of non-transgression are readily understood. In the second precept, it clarifies that a transgression does not constitute defilement; the rest is omitted without discussion.

Regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, "not applying skillful means" refers to the mind of one who has no more to learn (aśaikṣa). "Abandoning and failing to study" refers to the conduct of one who has no more to learn.
This clarifies the abandonment of the Great [Vehicle]. To "study the Śrāvaka-dharma" clarifies the exclusive practice of the Small [Vehicle]. These are the characteristics of the transgression.

This is called the "minor bond" (*kṣudra-bandhana*). Why is it that in the former case, studying the Great [Vehicle] while abandoning the Small [Vehicle] constitutes an offense that is defiled (*kliṣṭa*), whereas in this present case, practicing the Small [Vehicle] while not at all studying the Great [Vehicle] constitutes an offense that is non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*)?
In the former instance, it was due to a view-based mind that it was proclaimed that a bodhisattva should not study the Small [Vehicle]; therefore, it was defiled.
In this present precept, however, one commits an offense because of losing proper decorum by studying [the Small Vehicle], as there is no such divergent view.
Therefore, it is not defiled. Why is it that the former [set of precepts] specifically contains the mind of views (*dṛṣṭi-citta*), while this one does not?
It is because many people in the world say that a bodhisattva should not study the dharmas of the śrāvakas; therefore, the former contains views.

There is no such saying in the world that a bodhisattva should not study the dharmas of a bodhisattva; therefore, this one lacks views. Regarding the next two sets of precepts, in the first set, one abandons the internal and practices the external.

Thus, one incurs an offense. Regarding the latter precept, one incurs an offense because of practicing external paths and generating attachment. Within the first precept, the offenses and non-offenses are clarified.

Within the offenses, there are three cases where one is not guilty of an offense despite being defiled: first, one is able to receive [the teachings] quickly; second, one has long studied the Buddha-dharma and deeply understands that practicing external paths does not constitute an offense;

and third, having studied for a long time, one does not forget—this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). If one knows the meaning through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), [one likewise incurs no offense].

This is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). To possess comprehensive observation of phenomena is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). To attain immovable knowledge is the wisdom of realization (*adhigama-jñāna*).

On the third day, one avoids transgression by delighting in study through proper ritual conduct. For a Bodhisattva, to be well-disposed toward external objects, to delight in them, not to abandon them, and not to regard them as poison—this is called a transgression;
this is the second gate. Because one gives rise to attachment in accordance with what is known, it constitutes a transgression.
The above four sections have explained the loss of propriety in training and study. Next, we address one precept regarding deep slander.

Within this precept, the nature of transgression and non-transgression is clarified; within the section on transgression, the defiled aspect is clarified. There are four distinct textual parts: first, the clarification of the conditions for transgression, namely, the Triple Gem.
The initial arrival at the ultimate reality is the Jewel of the Dharma. The Bodhisattva’s treasury of teachings is the Jewel of the Dharma of the Doctrine.

Profound meaning and ultimate meaning are the Jewel of the Dharma of Principle; the principle of emptiness is called "profound," and the possession of principle is called "ultimate. The immeasurable spiritual powers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constitute the Jewel of the Sangha.
Second, from the section on "slandering" onwards, the characteristics of transgressions are clarified. First, the slandering of the Dharma is clarified: to slander is to refuse to accept it.

This section generally clarifies the slander of the Dharma. To say that it is not beneficial is to specifically slander the Dharma of Principle (理法). To say it is not spoken by the Tathāgata is to specifically slander the Dharma of Teaching (教法).
This also fails to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings; it slanders the immeasurable power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. "The third" concludes the names [of the offenses].
"The fourth, 'or by one's own mind,'" clarifies the causes for committing the offense—whether through one's own reflection or by following others in slandering. Below this is not... [text ends].
Within the section on offenses, there are three distinct parts: first, exhorting one to abandon the mind of understanding and to give rise to the mind of faith;

second, instructing those who are not deceitful to abandon the mind of understanding and to give rise to the mind of faith; third, personally taking a lower position to restate what was taught and conclude that no offense has been committed. Regarding the first part:
for one who hears profound meanings but does not produce understanding, it is exhorted that they should abandon such understanding; it is further exhorted that they should give rise to faith.
This gives rise to faith. In the second section, with a mind free from flattery and crookedness, one trains thus: "I am greatly at fault; I am blind and lack the eye of wisdom.
One abandons the conceptualizing mind and, within the mind of reality (*bhūtacitta*), gives rise to this intention; therefore, it is called "non-flattery.

The Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom teaches in accordance with [the disciples' capacities], providing the instructions that give rise to faith. Within this, first, one looks up to and places faith in the Tathāgata. All...
The Tathāgata’s wisdom that illuminates principle is called the "eye of wisdom" (*prajñā-cakṣus*). To give teachings in accordance with that principle is called "teaching in conformity.
This teaching is termed "incomplete teaching" (*sopadeśa*) because it exists outside of other sūtras. How does one eliminate slander by means of one's own subsequent consciousness?
In the third section, regarding one's own lack of knowledge, the preceding passage cites the teaching to abandon the conceptualizing mind. Having reflected, this is called being "without eyes."
Abiding in non-cognition, the Tathāgata perceives the Dharma with right contemplation and right orientation. This reiterates the instruction in the preceding text to give rise to faith;
this principle is what is seen by the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom, and is thus called "the Dharma known and seen by the Tathāgata.

Contemplating this Dharma as previously described is what is called "right contemplation. As for the previous self-admonition, "How could one give rise to slander?"—this is called "right orientation. Because...
Because of faith and compliance, one does not transgress the precepts. Due to the abandonment of [wrong] views, there is no slander arising from lack of understanding.

Regarding the three subsequent precepts, the transgressions are clarified in relation to other persons. In the first case, a transgression is established because of greed and anger, whereby one praises oneself and disparages others.

The second [offense] constitutes a transgression because one refuses to listen when hearing [the teaching] out of anger and pride. The third constitutes a transgression because one treats others with contempt and derision out of arrogance.
The first precept is clear. Within the second precept, it clarifies what constitutes a transgression and what does not, as well as the defiled and non-defiled [states].

Upon first hearing the discourse on the determination of the locus, the conditions for committing an offense arise at that locus. Anger and pride constitute the mental state of the offense; not listening constitutes the characteristic of the offense.
This is termed the "concluding summary. It should be understood that these are not defiled. Regarding the section on non-offenses, there are eleven distinct points.

First, "not understanding" refers to either the speaker’s own lack of comprehension or the fact that the person being addressed lacks knowledge and understanding. "Illness" and "lack of strength" [are further cases].
"He guides himself. Regarding "that person who speaks erroneously": he speaks incorrectly and thus does not attain [the goal]. "One who guards the mind of the speaker":
the speaker fears himself and does not depart [from the teaching]. "Having heard repeatedly, having received it, and having known the meaning":
this clarifies that one has already previously known the meaning within those teachings spoken. "If there are many," then below it clarifies that one further [studies] other sūtras.
If one has no leisure for study, one cannot go [to hear the Dharma]. If a person of much learning listens extensively to other teachings, this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

If one who maintains what they have heard relies on that hearing to give rise to reflection (*cintā*), and if one who acts according to the teaching relies on the Dharma to give rise to cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—that is, relying on the Dharma to give rise to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)—this is called "acting according to the teaching.
To advance in the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*) is called "cultivating meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-samādhi*). If one is of dull faculties, it is because of one's own dull faculties.

If it is difficult to approach and of no benefit, one should not go; if it is difficult to uphold, because one already finds it arduous to uphold other dharmas, there is no room for further effort and thus one should not go.
The characteristics of the final precept are manifest and can be understood.

Within the eleven precepts for gathering and sustaining beings that follow below, the first two concern *samānārthatā* (common purpose); the next one concerns *priyavāditā* (affectionate speech); the next four concern *dāna* (generosity);
and the final four concern *arthacaryā* (beneficial conduct). Regarding *samānārthatā*, the first precept clarifies commonality in matters of pleasure. Within this specific precept:

This clarifies the distinction between transgression and non-transgression, as well as defilement and non-defilement. For one who abides in the *saṃvara* (restraint), that which encompasses the welfare of sentient beings is called the "precept of gathering living beings" (*saṃgraha-śīla*), which constitutes the restraint itself.

To perceive the actions of sentient beings as the conditions for transgression is a case of transgressing through a mind of resentment; this differs from the characteristics of other forms of transgression, which will be explained separately below.

Deliberating on various matters constitutes the beginning of affairs. The subsequent discussion of traveling on roads and so forth clearly elucidates what is to be done: traveling on roads refers to matters of dignified deportment;
engaging in agriculture, profit-seeking, and animal husbandry refers to matters of laboring for one's livelihood; and reconciling disputes and litigation refers to matters of mutual benefit.
Auspicious assemblies refer to matters that conform to worldly customs; meritorious deeds refer to matters of cultivating goodness. The rest may be understood by extension.

Regarding the second [category], the precepts, they are the same as in the section on suffering; within them, there are likewise transgressions and non-transgressions, as well as those with defilement and those without defilement.

Seeing the conditions for transgression, harboring a mind of resentment toward the transgression, and failing to approach the signs of transgression—this is termed the "inferior bond. Within the section on non-transgression, there are eleven distinct points.
Regarding those of dull faculties who find it difficult to awaken and difficult to uphold: for such individuals of dull faculties themselves, the task of upholding [the precepts] is arduous.

Regarding one's own actions, they require much exertion and cannot be overlooked; thus, one does not go [astray] and does not transgress. Next is the first of the four types of loving speech (*priyavāditā*), which can be understood from its manifest characteristics.

Next, among the four kinds of giving (*dāna*): the first is the giving of gratitude (*anurakṣaṇādāna*), the second is the giving of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), and the third is the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).
The fourth is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*); its characteristics are manifest and thus easily known.

Regarding the four types of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), the first—restraining those of no virtue through skillful means that accord with them—is manifest and thus easily known. The second involves praising those of virtue to bring them joy;

herein, both transgression and non-transgression, as well as defilement and non-defilement, are clarified. Within the context of non-transgression, regarding those who cause provocation, it is explained that by praising [the virtuous], one may give rise to craving.
Alternatively, one may give rise to anger and so forth. Hearing praise for others' faults is called "overflowing joy. Hearing praise for oneself and becoming haughty is called "giving rise to pride.

Because such praise leads to negligence and the commission of unwholesome karma, it is called "giving rise to what is non-beneficial. All these cases result in not receiving the praise [one might expect].

To say that a real virtue appears to be a non-virtue is, for example, as when it is said that the bodhisattva's practice is not a common path; while it is in fact a supreme virtue, it resembles a non-virtue.
If one were to praise them, it would cause many sentient beings to habitually give rise to unwholesome states; therefore, they are not praised.
To say that what is actually well-spoken appears to be otherwise is as the Sūtra proclaims: "Lust is a path, and so too are hatred and delusion.
All such instances are truly well-spoken, yet appear to be otherwise. If one were to praise them, it would increase the confusion of people; therefore, they are not praised.

The third section concerns the single precept for easily taming wicked people by punishing them according to their transgressions. First, the nature of the offense is clarified so that it may be clearly understood.

Below, the non-offenses are explained. Regarding those who "cannot be disciplined," this refers to those who possess such power that they cannot be subdued. Regarding those who "cannot be spoken to," [this refers to those who are incorrigible].
That person’s nature is radiant yet perverse, and their speech only increases further; they are incorrigible. Being devoid of shame and remorse, they do not change even when spoken to.
One who gives rise to resentment hears this and increases their anger. As for "observing the time," it means observing when one has no virtuous companions oneself.
Fearing that those who incite strife might, while being punished for it, raise other matters as pretexts, all else may be understood accordingly.

From this point downward, regarding the precept on the difficult-to-tame and evil person being gathered through spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), first the transgression is clarified; its characteristics are manifest and thus easily known.

The following clarifies non-offenses. As for one who again gives rise to defilement: because they perceive their committed transgression as being in accordance with reason through the observation of supernatural transformations, they again give rise to attachment and refuse to relinquish it;
such a person does not incur [the full offense]. The rest may be understood accordingly.
From the four *pārājika* dharmas mentioned above until this point, the second major section—the detailed explanation of observance and violation—is concluded.

From here below is the third section, which concludes with praise and cites evidence to exhort beings to practice and study. The initial statement, "This matter gives rise to the Bodhisattva precepts," constitutes the conclusion and praise.
The matters of observance and transgression clarified above are that, by relying upon them, one can generate the conduct of the Bodhisattva precepts.
This is called the "arising of morality. The Buddha provides citations from various places to establish this through proof.

When the Buddha speaks in various places of the morality that encompasses wholesome conduct and the generation of beings, this clarifies how the Sūtras accord with the Śāstras. When Maudgalyāyana speaks of their harmonious integration, this demonstrates how the Śāstras support the Sūtras.

The treatise is identical to the sūtra; it is called the "Exposition of Concordant Discourse. Below, there is an exhortation to practice and study: "One should diligently receive and uphold [the teachings]" is the exhortation to practice and study.

"Arousing reverence and studying with single-minded devotion" refers to the cultivation of practice and study. The above constitutes the first section: the preparatory means for upholding the precepts. From here below is the second section:

the explicit clarification of protective maintenance. This refers to the dharmas that have been received from others and are now being maintained. It concerns those who wish to study bodhi and possess the mind to benefit sentient beings.

The mind of upholding the precepts is the mind that seeks to train in the purest manner in maintaining the vows of discipline. The bodhicitta is the mind that maintains the gathering of wholesome qualities;
seeking the fruit through the gathering of wholesome qualities is called bodhicitta. The mind that benefits sentient beings is the mind that maintains the gathering of sentient beings;
it is the practice of upholding the precepts with single-minded diligence.
The preceding section was the second, on diligent protection and maintenance. From here below is the third, on being able to repent after having committed an offense.

If one has committed an offense and repents according to the Dharma, this is a general exhortation to repent. This section identifies the names of the offenses, subsuming all such transgressions under *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
*Duṭiguhu* is a term from the Hu language; here it is translated as "evil action" (*duṣkṛta*). One should perform a detailed confession as explained below.

Among these, first is the method of confession before another person; if no such person is available, there is the method of mental remorse. Within the confession before another person, there are both general and specific types.
To repent according to the Dharma before both the great and the small is the general rule. Although they differ in status as great or small, they are equally practitioners;

therefore, one may confess before them. As for those who can understand speech, there must be comprehension; only when one understands the meaning of the person's words may the confession be accepted.
One who is able to receive a confession must possess moral conduct and be capable of receiving another's repentance before they may face one another.

This distinction is based on the gradations of "superior," "intermediate," and "inferior. Within these distinctions: first, it clarifies that a superior offense results in the loss of precepts and cannot be expiated;

second, it clarifies that an intermediate offense requires repentance before many people; and third, it clarifies that an inferior offense requires repentance before a single person. Regarding the intermediate offenses, there are those committed through intermediate afflictions.
This identifies those to whom the confession is addressed. Regarding the number of people: it should be at least three, though more is better.

One kneels with palms joined and confesses a *duṣkṛta* offense. Reciting the name of the previous offense constitutes the ritual for confession. The phrase "Venerable Sir" (*bhadanta*) and what follows is the formula for the confession. As for "abandoning the *vinaya*":
to turn one's back on the Dharma and give rise to transgressions is called abandoning the *vinaya*; it does not mean completely relinquishing the precepts.

The remainder is as in the *pāyattika* confession for a bhikṣu. As for the wording of the confession, it is not fully set forth here; it is identical to what is stated elsewhere. Within the bhikṣu’s confessions:
"Now, before the Venerable One, I reveal and confess [this offense], not daring to conceal it. Through confession there is peace and happiness; without confession there is no peace and happiness.
Recalling my transgression, I reveal it; knowing it, I do not conceal it. May the Venerable One bear in mind that my body of precepts is complete."
Regarding the pure *poṣadha*: the one receiving the confession asks, "Do you recognize your offense? The one confessing replies, "I recognize it.
The one receiving the confession says, "You should reproach yourself and not commit it again. Because these words are currently omitted, they are being referred to here. Question:
Among the *duṣkṛta* offenses of a bhikṣu, which ones involve the method of repentance before another person? Is it now referring to those? It refers to [the case of] schism in the Saṃgha.

The offenses involving skillful means (*upāya*) and so forth are confessed before others. Regarding the methods of repentance for minor infractions (*avara-āpatti*), they are the same as those mentioned previously.

As for "other offenses," this refers to the remaining forty-two light precepts (*laghu-śīla*). The method of repentance through self-reproach (*citta-vinodana*) is clear and can be understood from its description. Question: Self-reproach is used only for repenting minor infractions, yet it also applies to repenting medium-grade offenses.

This is based on the principle that while receiving the medium grade [of ordination], one obtains the precepts without a teacher; now, regarding this method of repentance: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available.]

It merely causes the mind of remorse to be extinguished as well. If there is no person possessing such qualities, the following is the fourth section on receiving [the precepts] with a thoroughly pure mind.
Within this, the initial statement that one "should receive them oneself when no person possessing qualities is available" summarizes the method of self-reception.

As stated in the sūtra: "One may receive [the precepts] for oneself only when there is no one within a thousand li. The section beginning with "Next, he instructs him separately" refers to the preliminary preparations, such as adjusting one's robes.
The section beginning with "He speaks these words" clearly explains the formal words of reception. The remainder, as previously mentioned, constitutes the subsequent procedures.
This refers to the formal announcement made by others as previously described.

Above, the characteristics of receiving and upholding [the precepts] have been extensively analyzed. Below, the meaning of maintaining and violating them will be further distinguished. First, the violations shall be clarified.

Next, the meaning of upholding [the precepts] is discussed. Regarding transgressions, there are two parts: first, clarifying that a bodhisattva’s transgression is not such that they are incapable of receiving [the vows] again;
second, clarifying the lightness and gravity of transgressions through the categories of weak, medium, and superior.

Within the first section, it is explained that there is no "remainderless" (anupadhiśeṣa) transgression for a bodhisattva, which precisely clarifies that a bodhisattva’s transgression is not such that they are incapable of receiving [the vows] again. A śrāvaka who commits a grave offense cannot receive them again.
The name for this is "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*). Because the Bodhisattva receives this [vow], there is no such thing as a transgression without remainder for him.

As the World-Honored One explained below to clarify the limits that must be received by a Bodhisattva: regarding transgressions of anger, one must receive [the vow] again; regarding transgressions of greed, it is not necessary.

As the World-Honored One said, "Transgressions of anger require receiving [the vow] again, whereas those of desire do not. This is cited to distinguish between them. Question: It was previously stated that there are four grave rules (*caturmahāpatti*).

Within this [category], there is also the transgression of greed. Previously it was stated that one loses the precepts; why then is it now said that it is not a transgression of greed? Greed is of two kinds:
first, the transgression of greed for wealth, which causes one to lose the precepts; second, the transgression of greed for sensual form, which does not cause one to lose them.

The former refers to greed for wealth, while this refers to greed for sensual form; thus, the two statements do not contradict each other. Question: Greed for wealth is also a loss of the precepts. For what reason, then, does the world...

The Venerable One spoke specifically of the offense of *dveṣa* (hatred). The commentator explains that while one may covet wealth, if there is no other perception of benefit for living beings, one will inevitably feel hatred;
therefore, it is still termed an offense of *dveṣa*. One should know that from this point downward, the Master of the Treatise explains the sūtra to clarify the limits of what must be accepted.
One should know that this intention is intended as a general exhortation to understand, which will be explained in detail below. Attachment gives rise to everything that can be produced.

Therefore, the Buddha proclaimed that it is not an offense of desire. Bringing benefit to sentient beings is the task of a bodhisattva; because they are able to do so through their attachment to [sentient] beings, it is called "capable of acting.

The phrase "not acting" and what follows explains the previous offense of anger, which should be received [as a vow] anew. "Not acting, yet receiving [the vow] anew" establishes the underlying principle.
From "anger toward sentient beings" downward, he clarifies this by means of its faults: if one does not deliver oneself and others, there will be no end [to suffering].
Furthermore, one does not perform what should be done, manifesting a lack of mutual benefit. Thus, it is concluded without further elaboration.

From here below is the second section, clarifying the gravity of transgressions. Regarding soft, medium, and superior transgressions as explained in the "Chapter on the Four Means of Gathering" (*Catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*):

in the preceding text, while expounding the characteristics of observance and violation, the author raised the cases of violating and not violating, as well as those involving defilement and non-defilement. These soft, medium, and superior transgressions are urged so that beings may understand them; however, regarding these violations—

The offenses involving defilement and those not involving defilement have already been fully explained above. The distinctions between weak, medium, and superior offenses have not yet been clarified; therefore, they are now restated here.

Although this refers to the "Chapter on the Four Means of Integration" (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*), even when referring to it, these characteristics are entirely absent from the section concerning the "inferior seekers.

One should therefore further refer to other sūtras or śāstras that contain a "Chapter on the Four Means of Integration. Alternatively, this term may refer to the four means of integration previously discussed.
This constitutes the Chapter on the Four Means of Integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). Within the preceding text, the four practices of integration were divided into eleven sections;
in the tenth section, the gravity of transgressions was clarified, detailing the nine grades of disciplinary measures for Bodhisattvas. This present passage refers back to that.

The following clarifies the maintenance [of the precepts], first explaining dwelling in happiness and subsequently explaining dwelling in suffering. Within the section on happiness, there are four parts: first, the enumeration; second, the names; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion.
"Possessing the three dwellings in happiness" is the enumeration. Next, the three names are listed: the perfection of practice and cultivation is called the "equipment of skillful means";
the purity of the mind that guards the precepts is called the "equipment of a pure mind"; and the present attainment of superior retribution through the cultivation of virtuous causes is [the third].

The conditions that assist the precepts are called the "complete primary causes. Next, this is explained in detail. Within the complete means (*upāya*), "the precepts being without breach" refers to the integrity of the essence of the vow;
"purity of body and speech" refers to the purity of conduct; and "purifying body, speech, and mind" clarifies the inclusion of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
Not transgressing and revealing [one's faults] clearly sets one apart from all errors. Not committing what has not yet arisen is called "not repeatedly transgressing";
being able to eliminate what has already arisen is called "revealing evil. This is the concluding summary. Regarding the pure mind, first one seeks purity of mind;

through non-laxity, one clarifies the purity of the mind in practice. Within the initial seeking of purity, there are three stages from beginning to end: leaving home for the sake of the Dharma, and not for the sake of body or life.

The beginning is the purity of mind (*citta-śuddhi*). Simply seeking the Buddha-dharma without regard for body or life constitutes this. From the phrase "for the sake of the Dharma" (*ārthāya*) onwards, it clarifies the purity of conduct (*śīla-śuddhi*).

Because the precepts can provide benefit and profit, they are termed "the Dharma" (*artha*). Having already left the household life, one acts for the sake of the Dharma and for the sake of meditation (*dhyāna*), not for the sake of wealth.
"Acting as a śramaṇa" concludes with "purity of mind. This is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*). The essence of a śramaṇa is wisdom; nirvāṇa is the fruit of wisdom.
One acts solely for the sake of this fruit and not for that which is non-beneficial. The five desires of Māra and the devas are what is non-beneficial; the bodhisattva does not seek them.
Within the purity of the mind during practice, "not being indolent" and "not regressing" clarify the gathering of what is wholesome.

"Not being indolent" regarding one's own level and "not regressing" from superior progress clarify the abandonment of evil. "Not being mixed with various evils and unwholesome dharmas" clarifies the abandonment of karma.

"Being unmixed with afflictions means being free from afflictions. 'Experiencing existence' and below refer to being free from the fruits of suffering. Future suffering is called 'experiencing existence.
The blazing retribution of suffering refers to the sufferings of the three miserable realms. Birth, old age, sickness, and death refer to the sufferings of humans and devas."
The severance of causes and the departure from fruits is termed "non-confusion. The term "non-confusion" encompasses all these phrases; this constitutes the conclusion of the name.
The original causes can be understood. Possessing the three correct [factors], the following section cites them to provide a final summary.
The opposite of this is explained as pleasure being suffering. The preceding section concludes the extensive explanation of all precepts;
this is called the "concluding summary," which summarizes what was previously stated both briefly and extensively. Within the preceding text, there were both concise and detailed expositions.
The first section, concerning the householder and the renunciant, is divided into two parts and termed "concise. The subsequent section is divided into three clusters and termed "extensive.
The phrase "this is called a concise exposition" concludes the preceding concise section; the phrase "this is called an extensive exposition" concludes the preceding extensive section.

The statement "all these precepts are divided into [the categories of] difficult and so forth" introduces what follows; that is to say, the six gates below are all categorized according to their respective meanings based on the entirety [of the precepts].
Regarding the section on the difficulty of the precepts, first the number is cited and introduced. In the preceding section, it was divided into two; here, three are added.

In the subsequent sections that follow, the numbers gradually increase, which will be explained individually below. Among these, in the first section, the reason why renouncing pleasure and single-mindedly upholding the precepts is difficult is presented.
Second, it is difficult because one must endure suffering and maintain [the precepts] with persistence. Third, it is difficult because one must always be able to fully maintain them.
All "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to practicing wholesome dharmas; all "right reception" (*samyak-samādāna*) refers to ceasing unwholesome dharmas.

These two receptions clarify the maintenance of conduct below. "Mindfulness without distraction" follows the aforementioned wholesome dharmas; "for as long as life lasts" and following follow the aforementioned dharma of cessation. All...
Within this section, first the number is cited; next, four names are listed. The first three pertain to self-benefit, while the last one pertains to benefiting others.

"Right reception" refers to the initial arousal [of the precepts] in response to conditions. "Natural morality" (dharmatā-śīla) refers to that which was perfected through past habituation, such as the accomplishment of natural morality by a *srotāpanna*.
"Habitual morality" (*abhyasta-śīla*) refers to that which can be further aroused now because of prior cultivation. "Skillful means" refers to the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
This is the practice. The subsequent explanation is as can be understood. Within the precepts for virtuous persons, first the number is cited, and subsequently their characteristics are analyzed.
Of the former four, the first is exclusively for one’s own benefit, while the latter three benefit others.
Among all the practices, first the number is cited; the six types and seven types are explained concisely, while the thirteen types belong to the preceding section.

Originally five were taught; now they are increased to six. Increasing them by six, seven are taught. Because the six and the seven are discussed together, there are thirteen. Regarding the term "exclusive" (*ekānta*):

the first six are the factors of cultivation (*bhāvanā-aṅga*), and the latter seven are the factors of accomplishment (*niṣpatti-aṅga*). Because one proceeds from cultivation toward accomplishment, they are called "exclusive.

Below, these are specifically elucidated. First, the former six are clarified. Among these six, the first three are distinguished according to cultivation, while the latter three gates are distinguished according to practice.
Analysis. Among the three preceding cultivations, the first clarifies that the initial mind is vast and expansive; the second clarifies that the actual cultivation is free from fault.

Regarding "being free from both sensual pleasure and asceticism": attachment to the five desires is called sensual pleasure, while the asceticism of self-mortification based on wrong views is called asceticism.
Because correct cultivation is free from these two, it is said to be "without fault. The third clarifies its final accomplishment.
Firmness. Within this, there are four aspects: first, not being moved by the five desires of the household life; that is, never returning the precepts even when faced with objects of pleasure.
Objects that satisfy the senses are called "objects of pleasure"; because one perceives their faults and feels deep revulsion, one does not return the precepts.
Second, not being moved by the gain and offerings of the renunciant life. Third, not being moved by the heterodox arguments of non-Buddhists. Fourth, not being moved by...
It cannot be moved by the various entanglements of affliction (*kleśa-paryavasthāna*), nor can it be deceived or even slightly damaged; nor can it be stripped away or entirely lost.

Among these four, the first constitutes "firmness in reception" (*pratigraha-dṛḍhatā*), while the latter three constitute "firmness in maintenance" (*dhāraṇa-dṛḍhatā*). This is called the "lower fetter.

Within the latter three modes of conduct, there is the distinction of the three aggregates of precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*); when combined with the preceding six, they comprise [the ten types of firmness].
Within the context of the vows (*saṃvara*), this constitutes a comprehensive summary. It should be understood that the "vows as armor" (*śīla-saṃnāha*) generally reveals their characteristics.

That is to say, regarding the Śrāvakas, it refers specifically to individuals of lower capacity; the vows received by Bodhisattvas are similar to theirs. This is the fourth section, which concludes the nomenclature of the vows.

The fifth is the gathering of wholesome qualities; the sixth is the gathering of sentient beings. Regarding the latter seven [perfections], the first three are distinguished by their essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the latter four are distinguished by way of their results (*phala*).

As for "conforming to morality" (*śīla-anuloma*), this refers to conforming to virtuous morality (*kuśala-śīla*). "Not conforming to morality" refers to abstaining from unwholesome morality (*akuśala-śīla*).

These two constitute the morality of undertaking and maintaining protection (*samādāna-saṃvara-śīla*). "Guarding prohibitions" (*saṃvara*) is termed "protection"; this protection follows upon what was previously undertaken.
Therefore, it is called "protecting accordingly. Regarding the latter four [categories], the "retribution of a great person" refers to the fruit of restraint (*saṃvara*).

Because one abandons evil, one attains the retribution of the marks and signs of a Buddha-Tathāgata; thus, the text below states that the thirty-two marks have no cause other than the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Therefore, the present passage cites the fruit to distinguish its cause. Next follow two phrases concerning the fruit of the "precept for gathering wholesome qualities" (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

Increased intention is concentration (*samādhi*); the "good destination" (*sugati*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). The supramundane noble path is what is called the "good destination," not the mundane good destinations of the three realms—humans and devas.

One attains this by gathering wholesome qualities; therefore, the fruit is cited here to distinguish its cause. "The retribution of benefiting sentient beings" refers to the gathering of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Regarding the removal of affliction (*vighāta*), first the number is stated, then it is explained, and finally it is concluded. Within the explanation, there are five parts.

First, one reflects for oneself that one does not wish to cause others to be afflicted by the eight matters. As for these "eight matters," they consist of the three actions of the body and the four of speech, plus the hands, stones, and so forth, which together constitute the eight.
Second, [the text says] "add me" and below, using one's own skillful means, one considers: "What he does not desire, I do not desire. At the very beginning...
This refers to desire. Regarding the statement "not rejoicing," it means that when the eight things manifest before one, the mind does not rejoice.

As it is with me, so it is with others. Third, from "How so? below, he uses reasoning to refute [the objection] himself. Fourth, from "For this reason" below, he concludes his resolve not to engage in [such actions].
Fifth, from "Thinking thus" below, he describes how he abandons them through reflection. This is called the conclusion.

Regarding the exposition of happiness in this world and the next, there are three parts: first, the enumeration; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Below, the meaning of happiness in this world and the next is interpreted.
Within the explanation, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is divided into four categories, while each of the remaining five perfections (*pāramitā*) is treated individually as one.
Thus, there are nine [categories]. This is because the primary principle here is the precepts (*śīla*); therefore, within the precepts, they are specifically divided into four.

The first two pertain to one's own practice (*svārtha*), while the latter two pertain to benefiting others (*parārtha*). Alternatively, the first two may be distinguished according to the phenomena (*dharma*): namely, the prohibition of unwholesome phenomena.
Wholesome dharmas are thereby opened. The latter two gates distinguish between persons: those who are wholesome are gathered in, while those who are unwholesome are subdued.
Within the final five [gates], "generosity combined with precepts" refers to being free from the fault of non-giving; the others follow this same pattern. Thus concludes the section below.

The following explains the meaning of happiness in this world and the next. During the time of present practice, attaining the savor of conduct is called "happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*).

Attaining superior renown in the future is called "happiness in future lives" (*sāmparāyikasukha*). Within the section on pure precepts, first the number is introduced, then explained, and finally concluded.
In this explanation, the first nine [stages] concern the means of cultivating ethical discipline (*śīla*), while the final one concerns the perfection of purity through the removal of faults.

Within the first nine, the initial five constitute the stage of self-maintenance (*svabhāga*), and the subsequent four constitute the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*). Within the stage of self-maintenance, the first is right aspiration (*samyakpraṇidhāna*), and the next two are right cultivation (*samyakbhāvanā*).
The latter two constitute correct practice. First, properly receiving the precepts as a śramaṇa and so forth—not for the sake of body or life—is called "right aspiration.
Seeking the fruit of training is termed being a "śramaṇa," while seeking the fruit of Buddhahood is termed "bodhi.

Regarding the next two [aspects] within cultivation: the first avoids deficiency, and the latter avoids excess. Not regressing and not giving rise to doubt is avoiding deficiency; regretting what one has cultivated is avoiding excess.

This is called the arising of doubt and regret. It does not exceed the violation of the precepts, but rather refers to the arising of doubt regarding what is improper (*apravṛtti*). To be free from excess:

once one has cultivated [the path] beyond measure, the mind becomes agitated and cannot enter into the Dharma, whereby divergent thoughts arise. To say that there is no Noble Path is called doubt regarding what is improper.

Within the latter two lines, the first concerns one who gathers wholesome qualities and abandons laziness; that is, being free from the defilement of lack of diligence and not delighting in sleep, thereby abandoning the obstacles to diligence.
"Diligence by day and night" clarifies the aforementioned abandonment of laziness, while "accomplishing wholesome dharmas" clarifies the aforementioned statement regarding not delighting in sleep.
The latter [line] concerns the abandonment of faults, namely, the abandonment of the fault of negligence (*pramāda*). As previously stated:
As in the previous section on maintaining the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of restraint, one accomplishes five kinds of heedfulness (*apramāda*).

Within the subsequent section on superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*), there is first right aspiration (*samyakpraṇidhāna*), next right practice (*samyakkarmānta*), next right cultivation (*samyagbhāvanā*), and finally right understanding (*samyagjñāna*), which is also called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Right aspiration may be understood as previously explained.
Within right conduct (*samyak-pratipatti*), there are three distinctions: first, right deportment (*samyag-īryāpatha*); second, right action (*samyak-karmānta*);
and third, right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). Regarding deportment: "maintaining deportment" marks its commencement; "being skilled in deportment" marks its completion.

Regarding right action (*samyak-karmānta*): the various activities performed through skillful means constitute the beginning of the practice; "skillfully and in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the completion of the activity.
Regarding right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*): the full possession of right livelihood comprises the antidotes;

it involves being entirely free from flattery and so forth, and abandoning all faults. Regarding right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*): "abandoning the two extremes" refers to the cultivation that attains the middle way, which is free from both pleasure and suffering.

This clarifies the preceding avoidance of extremes: both worldly sensual pleasures and the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists are entirely abandoned by the Bodhisattva; this can be understood through correct interpretation.

The above nine sections concern the skillful means for cultivating ethical discipline (*śīla*). The tenth section, "that which is received without deficiency," signifies the perfection of the practice of ethical discipline.

These ten are the concluding summary of the preceding section, which has been explained in detail above. From here on, the third section consists of a concluding praise that reveals its excellence. "This is called the aggregate of precepts" is the final summary.
"Attaining Bodhi," and so forth, constitutes the praise of its excellence. Within this, there are four parts: first, attaining Bodhi in the distant future; second, and so on...
In the lower [section], one immediately obtains five benefits. Three are as previously stated; the lower [section] is further able to perform three functions.

Fourth, regarding what is performed below, there is a general praise that reveals its excellence, causing beings to desire and seek it. Within the first section, "attaining enlightenment" generally clarifies the attainment of the fruit.

"Fulfilling this ethical discipline (śīla) leads to the attainment of enlightenment" explains the cause by which it is attained. In the second section, up until the point where it is not yet accomplished, one obtains the five benefits.
The former [term] serves as a general heading; the following sections explain it in detail. The first three refer to the benefits resulting from the maturation of practice:

"being mindful of the Buddha" means that during the present period of cultivation, the Buddha constantly protects and remembers one; "joy at the end" means being without regret at the time of death; and "having cast off the body" refers to the excellence of future retribution.
The latter two clarify the benefits resulting from the virtues of practice: "the perfection of the precept-pāramitā" means the completion of virtuous conduct.

Furthermore, the perfection of the nature-precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) refers to the perfection of the mind of precept. Within the third section, there are three distinct parts: first, subsuming the nine [precepts] into three;

second, clarifying that the three clusters (*tri-skandha*) can perform three functions; and third, concluding both together. Regarding the first part, it first cites the previous nine and subsequently subsumes them into three.
In the second part, the three types are first presented as a general heading for the three, followed by their specific [explanation].
This clarifies the statement that the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint) causes the mind to abide. Since restraint prevents what is non-virtuous, the mind does not follow evil;

training in the precepts without abandoning them is called "the mind abiding. The other two [categories of precepts] may be understood accordingly. This is termed the "concluding summary" (*adhara-nigamana*).

The phrase "this is called all matters of a bodhisattva" is the general conclusion, while the following section provides the specific details. It concludes the preceding discussion on how the *saṃvara-śīla* causes the mind to abide in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*).
"Abiding" means that those whose bodies and minds are untiring and who possess the Buddha-dharma fulfill the previous [precept] of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

"Accomplishing birth" means fulfilling the previous [precept] of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). These three are called the "three clusters" (*tri-skandha*) as the three matters. Below, these are concluded together:
"This is called the Bodhisattva’s all-encompassing precepts" concludes the nine types [of precepts] into the three clusters. This is called...
The merit of the precepts concludes with the summary of the three clusters as the three matters. From here below, the fourth section concludes by praising and manifesting their excellence:
"without remainder" refers to its extensiveness; "unsurpassed" refers to its supremacy; and "studied together throughout the three periods of time" praises its essentiality.
The Eleventh Chapter of the Main Treatise:
The Chapter on Patience (Kṣānti-varga).

Regarding this "Chapter on Patience": because one does not afflict sentient beings by virtue of maintaining ethical discipline (śīla), patience is explained immediately thereafter; it is for the purpose of extensively analyzing the meaning of patience.
This is the Chapter on Patience (*Kṣānti-varga*).
Within this chapter, there is first the inquiry, second the explanation, and finally the concluding summary and praise. What is the inquiry?

In the explanation, there is first the opening enumeration of the topical headings (*mukha*), followed by the extensive analysis and exposition. Within the preceding opening of the headings, there are nine points: first, the citation of the number; second, the sequential listing of the names.

"Self-nature" refers to the essential nature of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*). "All" refers to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the practice of patience; because the characteristics of patience are not singular, they are called "all.
"Difficult to endure" refers to the excellence of the practice of patience; because the mind of patience is resolute and is able to endure what is difficult to endure, it is called "difficult.
"All gates" refers to the vastness of the encompassing practices; all practices of patience are subsumed within these gates.

It is called "the gateway of all. One who is called a "virtuous person" (satpuruṣa) is one whose practice of patience is purely wholesome; because they cultivate patience with a virtuous mind, they are named a "virtuous person.
One who is a "practitioner of all" is one who is fully endowed with the practice of patience; because they accomplish the practice of patience amidst all objects of perception, they are named "all."

"Removing affliction" refers to the functional capacity of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*). When one cultivates this patience, it is able to remove the afflictions of others; thus, it is called "patience that removes affliction.

"Happiness in this world and the next" refers to the benefit of the practice of patience. By cultivating this practice of patience, one enables oneself and others to attain joy in both the present and the future;
therefore, it is called "happiness in this world and the next. "Pure patience" refers to the practice of patience being free from faults. When cultivated, it is without...

Because it is free from fault, it is called "pure. The following provides a detailed explanation. Regarding the explanation of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is first the question, then the explanation, and finally the summary.
Within the explanation, there are four phrases. "Relying on the power of reflection" means being able to endure by relying on the power of present reflection.
"If it is endurance by nature" means that because of long-term cultivation in the past, one is now able to endure.
The nature of these two types of patience serves as the cause for the latter two types of patience. Regarding the statement that "all forms of patience rely on non-attachment":
because one who is attached to their own body becomes angry when encountering adversity, patience relies on non-attachment. Regarding "pure and singular compassion":

because one who lacks compassion for sentient beings becomes enraged upon meeting with adversity, patience relies on compassion. Among all forms of patience, this consists of: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation; and finally, the summary.

The commentary explains this in two sections: first, dividing it according to persons; second, dividing it according to practice. Each of these two sections further divides into three parts, restating what precedes and opening the way for what follows.
Next, the three names are listed: "endurance of harm by others" means being able to endure the injuries inflicted by others;

"endurance of suffering" means being able to endure the afflictions resulting from spiritual cultivation; "endurance through reflection on the Dharma" refers to endurance within the principles [of reality]. Regarding the eight...

The thorough observation of the locus of understanding is called "reflection" (*vitarka*). When the mind of reflection dwells upon the Dharma, it is called "receptivity to reflection on the Dharma" (*dharmavitarkakṣānti*).

This will be explained extensively below. Within the explanation of the first gate, there is first a restatement (*uddeśa*) and subsequently an exposition (*nirdeśa*). In the exposition, one first clarifies the non-beneficial actions of others;

then, with the words "one trains in this way," one explains the cultivation of patience (*kṣānti*) in response to them. Within the former [section], the initial statement "suffering has long been great" clarifies that one's own nature is suffering. Because of this nature of suffering...

He clarifies this because others cause provocation and distress. Regarding "long-lasting, profound suffering" and "suffering from not hearing [the Dharma]," these clarify the actual harm inflicted by others when they are present and pressing.

In the subsequent cultivation of patience (*kṣānti*), one first cultivates three contemplations to discipline one's own mind, and subsequently practices five perceptions to be able to endure in the face of conditions. What are the three contemplations? First, by means of karma... [self-...]
1. Reprimanding oneself; 2. Furthermore, from "I [should] below," opening oneself through wisdom; 3. Furthermore, from "The śrāvakas below," liberating oneself through the Great [Vehicle].

Within the first [section], the initial statement, "One should train thus," etc., involves reprimanding one's past karma to eliminate anger. How does one eliminate anger? Suffering relies upon causes and conditions:
past karma acts as the cause, and the provocation of others acts as the condition. When the cause is strong and the condition weak, [the thought arises]: "This was my own doing; it cannot..."
Self-reproach: Why do I selectively direct my anger toward others who are weak? One who trains in this manner will find it difficult to achieve a patient mind; therefore, one must practice.
"This is the result of my own past karma and evil deeds" briefly clarifies that present suffering arises from causes in the past.

Having originally created the causes for transgression, one now undergoes heavy suffering today; this is further made manifest. If, from this point on, one fears the increase of future suffering, one should give rise to...
Patience. In the second section, it is shown that both my own body and those others are equally subject to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*);

this is the direct principle [of practice]. Below, the cultivation of patience is explained: regarding "those who lack wisdom," one should empathize with their ignorance and failings, rather than giving rise to anger.

Regarding "I possess wisdom," one uses wisdom to open oneself up and generate the mind of patience. In the third section, the self-interest of the *śrāvaka* is cited as a small example to illustrate the great; one should abandon...
As for the mind of anger, how much more so for a Bodhisattva, who gives rise to a mind of patience through great self-liberation.

This section, the second [of the chapter], further cultivates five perceptions regarding sentient beings because the mind is difficult to tame. Within this, there are three parts: first, the brief; second, the extensive;

and third, the explanation of the meaning of patience. Regarding the first part: having reflected in this way, the preceding is restated to introduce what follows. To cultivate the five perceptions is, briefly stated:
The heading: Briefly explaining the benefits of cultivation regarding enemies and kin; the distinction between those who oppose and those who comply;
the distinction between inferior, middling, and superior qualities; the distinction based on retribution as either suffering or pleasure;

and the distinction based on conduct regarding virtue or its absence—thus, the ability to endure summarizes the benefits of cultivation. In the second section, the extensive explanation, first the inquiry is raised, followed by the enumeration.

There are five types of perception. Among these five, the first is a perception shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). The middle three are perceptions shared with those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

The last one is the unique perception of a Bodhisattva. Regarding the "perception of original kinship": by contemplating that all beings are one's original kin, one is able to practice patience (*kṣānti*). Regarding the "perception of phenomena as mere enumerations":

by contemplating that beings are merely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and nothing more, there is no person toward whom one can feel anger. Regarding the "perception of impermanence": by contemplating beings... [text ends]
The nature of the categories of phenomena (*dharmasaṃkhyā*) is impermanent. Since that which causes affliction has already passed away, there is currently nothing toward which one can feel anger.

Regarding the "notion of suffering": one contemplates that the essence of these produced categories of phenomena is great suffering; they are only fit for compassion and should not be objects of anger. Regarding the "notion of gathering":

one contemplates that those who are produced are worthy of pity and should be gathered in, rather than being objects of anger. This will be explained extensively below. The first [point] is restated here as the basis; the following provides the explanation.

There are three [points]. First, the cultivation of the skillful means of perception (*saṃjñā-upāya*). Second, the accomplishment of the perception of endearment toward those who are hateful or hostile. Third, the accomplishment of the capacity for patience by relying on the perception of them as being like one's own original kin.
Within the second section, the categories of the Dharma restate what preceded; the subsequent explanation has three parts: first, the cultivation of the skillful means of perception; second, thus...
One achieves the contemplation of lower phenomena. Third, by relying on the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), one achieves the ability to endure through the perception of the lower.
Within the first section, one first contemplates all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). The practitioner observes that arising is without intrinsic nature;

it is merely that which is gathered and named from the causal conditions of past karma, hence it is called "conditioned formation. Because one observes that arising is subsumed solely within conditioned formations, it is referred to as the "counting of formations" (*saṃskāragaṇanā*). Counting...

This refers to the principle of analogy. For example, one who has left the household life is counted among the number of the Saṃgha; this case is likewise. Regarding the term "dharma-number" (*dharmagaṇanā*):
because those currently seeking [enlightenment] as sentient beings consist solely of the number of the various dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), it is called the "dharma-number.
This clarifies what exists; below, one contemplates what does not exist. The first character "wu" (non-/without) applies throughout all the subsequent phrases. That is to say: non-self, non-...
There is no life, up to and including no contention.
In the third section, impermanence is restated from what precedes; the subsequent explanation also has three parts: first, the application of the cultivation of perception;

second, from "thinking thus" onwards, the perfection of the perception of impermanence; third, based on impermanence, the perfection of the perception that enables endurance. There are two types of impermanence. First...
First, one correctly cultivates the perception of impermanence. Regarding what is called "that which arises," all that is produced is entirely impermanent.
As for "death," it refers to the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as being impermanent. That which is designated by the arising of characteristics is called "that which arises.

Within this, there are also the perceptions of duration, change, and so forth; however, here "arising" is mentioned first. Because its nature is impermanent and a phenomenon subject to exhaustion and destruction, it is called a "dharma of death. Regarding...

Furthermore, regarding matters that do not bring benefit, one contemplates the impermanence of those matters. For the two types of wise persons, they use reasoning to restrain themselves from below and should not cause distress to others.
In the fourth section, the characteristic of suffering is restated; the subsequent explanation has three parts: first, the skillful means of cultivating perception; second, correct reflection.

One achieves the contemplation of suffering as inferior. Third, based on the characteristic of suffering, through the inferior contemplation and the contemplation of inferiority, one becomes able to endure.

Within the former [section], there are two parts: first, contemplating that sentient beings equally possess the three types of suffering; first, one contemplates those who possess power, and subsequently, by contrast, those who lack it.

The spiritual transformations and mastery of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles are called "great power. That even they do not escape [suffering] generally clarifies that all possess suffering; this marks the superior to illustrate the inferior.

Therefore, it is said to be "superior. Because the three types of suffering constantly follow [the conditioned], they are called "inseparable" (*avinirbhāga*). Because they are the essential nature and characteristics of the three sufferings, they are called the "three marks" (*trilakṣaṇa*).

These are what are specifically distinguished below. The names and meanings of the three sufferings are as extensive as those in the separate chapter. As for "change" (*vipariṇāma*), it is simply the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).
"Transformation and destruction" is what is meant by "change. How much more so for those who are incomplete? Ordinary beings are called "incomplete" because they lack power;

if even the noble ones cannot avoid [such change], how much less can these inferior ordinary beings? Second, regarding the training mentioned below, one uses reason to restrain oneself and does not cause affliction to others.

In the fifth section, the "conception of inclusion" (*saṃgraha-saṃjñā*) is introduced by referring back to what preceded. The subsequent explanation has three parts: first, the arousal of the conception of inclusion; second, from "thinking thus" onwards, the accomplishment of the conception of inclusion;

third, from "relying on the conception of inclusion" onwards, the attainment of forbearance through the perfection of that conception. Within the first part, there are two sentences: the first is the arousal of the conception of inclusion;
the second, from "it should not be so," uses reasoning to internally restrain oneself from causing harm to others.
From here below is the third section, a general explanation of the meaning of patience (*kṣānti*). What is the question? "Not being angry" means that the internal mind does not feel anger.
"Not retaliating" means that one does not retaliate through body or speech; this refers to the immediate moment. "Not harboring resentment" means that there is no lingering grudge afterward.
This is called the "concluding summary.

Within the section on the patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), there is first the restatement of the preceding section, followed by the explanation, and finally the conclusion. The explanation consists of three parts: first, the preparatory means for cultivating contemplation;

second, from "contemplating in this way" onwards, the accomplishment of the contemplation of patience; and third, from "all suffering" onwards, the capacity for patience resulting from the completion of contemplation. The former...

Within this, first, one cites the pointlessness of suffering that has been endured in vain for a long time to admonish oneself; subsequently, one cites the necessity of enduring that which is beneficial according to principle.

Regarding the pointlessness: the statement that "seeking desires has, from of old, served as the cause of all sufferings and gives rise to great suffering" generally clarifies that seeking desires can produce great suffering.
Because one brings about affliction through such seeking, it is termed "seeking desires" as the cause of suffering. As for the cause...

This can give rise to immeasurable great suffering, namely the various lower realms; all of these are "lower fetters. This demonstrates that because such great suffering arises entirely from delusion, one remains for a long time in unawareness.
The following clarifies that since there is benefit in principle, one must certainly endure it. Now, while cultivating the causes of happiness, one must endure immeasurable things;

if one can endure even those of heavy weight, how much more so minor sufferings? By using the heavy to illustrate the light, it is shown that one will certainly be able to do so. [End of] Upper Section.

One comes to practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). When one reflects in this way, for one who possesses *saṃprajanya* (clear comprehension), the contemplation of patience (*kṣānti-vipaśyanā*) is accomplished.

To be aware of the suffering that has previously been of no benefit is called possessing *saṃprajanya*. To know that the principle of suffering that is beneficial must necessarily be accepted is called possessing *prajñā* (wisdom).

Regarding all sufferings, the ability to endure them when facing conditions is the general summary at the beginning; the eight types [of patience] below are the specific details. Although one must undergo various sufferings...
The conclusion summarizes and praises [the preceding] as a whole; the first part may be understood generally. In the second part, regarding the specific details, eight types are enumerated.
"Basis" (*niśraya*) refers to the four bases of reliance, such as alms-food and so forth. "Worldly phenomena" (*lokadharma*) refers to matters of decline and affliction;

because such things necessarily exist within the world, they are termed "worldly phenomena. "Dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*) refers to the four modes of conduct, such as walking, standing, and so forth.

This is the practice of ritual propriety (*li*). The station of gathering the Dharma is the practice of seeking the Dharma. The station of following the precepts is the practice of upholding the precepts.
The station of skillful means (*upāya*) is the practice of cultivating goodness; it is called "skillful means" because it gives rise to the cultivation of goodness with dexterity.

The station of benefiting sentient beings is the practice of transforming others. All that is performed refers to worldly occupations. All of these are the domain of the patience of birth (*janma-kṣānti*). Thus, they are all...
This is the section on "Names and Bases. Below, this will be extensively elucidated. Regarding the middle [section], it first restates [the topic], then explains it, and finally concludes it.

Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, clarifying the bases; second, clarifying the capacity for patience. Regarding the clarification of the bases, the four bases are presented as a general heading:
begging for food for as long as one lives, wearing rag-robes, sitting at the foot of a tree, and taking discarded medicine when ill. These four constitute the commencement of practice.
It is called "dependence" (*niśraya*) because it serves as a basis; this will be explained in detail below. "Dependence on the Dharma for going forth" refers to relying upon a person [as a teacher].
"Obtaining the portion of a bhikṣu" refers to relying upon the essence of practice. "Precepts" are the cause of being a bhikṣu, and thus they are termed the "portion of a bhikṣu.

From the words "if one obtains" onwards, the characteristics of dependence are correctly analyzed; however, this specifically clarifies the practice of begging for food. If one obtains coarse [food], it is wretched, evil, and painful, and constitutes a lack of respect.

"Respect" refers to the suffering of being treated with contempt. "Obstacles and untimely hindrances" refer to the suffering of being obstructed and hindered at improper times. The following clarifies the capacity for endurance.

Within the context of worldly phenomena, it first restates the preceding section, then provides an explanation, and finally concludes. In the explanation, it first elucidates the nature of worldly dharmas.
The following clarifies the capacity for endurance (*kṣānti*). Within the worldly dharmas (*lokadharma*), nine categories are enumerated. Next, the names of these nine are listed.

Of these, the first four arise from the convergence of adverse conditions (*pratikūla-pratyaya*), while the latter five arise from the separation from favorable conditions (*anukūla-pratyaya*). The former four are identical to the four unwholesome worldly dharmas among the eight worldly dharmas (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*).

These eight worldly dharmas are: first, gain (*lābha*); second, loss (*alābha*); third, defamation (*nindā*); fourth, praise (*praśaṃsā*); fifth, fame (*yaśas*); and sixth, infamy (*ayaśas*). [The remaining two are pleasure and pain.]
There are seven types of suffering and eight types of pleasure. Regarding the first four of the eight neutral states, the first two pertain to the body:

the flourishing of wealth that benefits oneself is termed "gain" (lābha), while matters such as being beaten or bound are termed "loss" (alābha). The next four pertain to speech: speaking well and appropriately is termed "praise" (yaśas).
To speak of what is evil as if it were true is to mock; to praise what is good beyond its measure is to flatter; and to speak of evil beyond its measure is to slander.
Regarding these latter two types of mental factors (*manodharma*), they are not discussed here because, among these eight kinds [of speech], they accord with the Dharma and are easily endured.

The sufferings of decline, censure, and defamation are difficult for the mind to endure; therefore, they are singled out here. Within the latter five [sufferings], the first two concern the suffering arising from the total destruction of the fruits of reliance (*niśraya-phala*);
the latter three concern the suffering arising from the decay and extinction of the primary retribution (*pratyupabhoga*). Regarding "the nature of things that are subject to destruction":

the means of subsistence and articles of pleasure are by nature subject to destruction, yet they meet with conditions that cause their destruction. Regarding "the nature of things that are subject to exhaustion": what previously existed as a substantial entity is now entirely exhausted.

Regarding "the aging of the dharma of aging within the subsequent primary retribution": the nature of the internal retribution is the dharma of decay and senescence; when the time arrives, it becomes old, which is termed "the aging of the dharma of aging.
The same applies to sickness and death. This concludes the section below.

Regarding the section on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), first the preceding section is cited, then it is explained, and finally it is concluded. In the explanation, first the distinctions of dignified conduct are clarified, followed by the clarification of what can be endured.
Within the clarification of dignified conduct, there are four enumerations; next, the four names are listed, and below, their characteristics are defined.

Whether walking or sitting, one removes the hindrances of the aggregates and does not lie down at improper times. By mentioning "walking" and "sitting," the suffering of extreme exhaustion is clarified;
by mentioning "lying on a bed," "sitting on a bench," or "spreading out grass and leaves," the suffering of the coarseness and inferiority of one's physical support is clarified.
The dwelling is not explained in detail. From here below, its capacity for endurance is clarified; this is termed the "concluding summary.

The "inclusion of dharmas" restates what preceded, which will be explained extensively below. There are seven enumerations; next, their names are listed: making offerings to the jewels constitutes the first.

Virtuous offerings constitute the second; inquiring about the Dharma is the third; extensive exposition is the fourth; sublime praise is the fifth; solitary seclusion and those following it constitute the sixth;
mindfulness and those following it constitute the seventh. The first one subsumes merit (*puṇya*); the latter six subsume wisdom (*jñāna*).

Making offerings to the Three Jewels is called "offering to the jewels. Among the latter six types of knowledge, the first four encompass hearing (*śruta*), the next one encompasses reflection (*cintā*), and the last one encompasses cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Within the wisdom of hearing, making offerings to those of virtue and seeking the Dharma from them is called "offering to virtue."
This first is the expedient means for seeking the Dharma: consulting and receiving the true Dharma, which is the correct hearing of the Dharma.

These two [points] concern self-benefit; the following two concern the benefit of others. "Extensively explaining" refers to the initial explanation; "praising with wondrous sounds" refers to praising so that they will accept [the teaching].

Within the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), "solitary and quiet contemplation" is the beginning of the wisdom born of reflection; "weighing and measuring" is its sequence; and "investigative observation" is its completion.

Within the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), "recollection and grasping" refers to the practitioner of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* training in concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

These seven types of dharmas collectively conclude [the section]. As for the practitioner who cultivates through skillful means (*upāya*), this is the sixth stage of skillful means, which gives rise to clear understanding (*vidyā*). This is based upon the aforementioned seven dharmas.

The practice undertaken in advancing one's study is called "cultivation through skillful means" (*upāya-bhāvanā*). Regarding the phrase "being able to endure all the various sufferings that arise," this generally clarifies that one is able to endure all the aforementioned sufferings.

Within the section on "following the robes" (*cīvara-anuvartana*), there is first a restatement of the topic and subsequently an explanation. In the explanation, there is first a clarification of the distinctions among the precepts (*śīla*) and, following that, a clarification of the capacity for endurance.
Within the precepts for following [the training], there are seven enumerations, which will be explained individually below.
Third, regarding "abandoning unwholesome conduct through right mindfulness," this refers to refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth; the rest may be understood accordingly.

Such passages as these conclude the section on the capacity for patience. The phrase "benefiting sentient beings" reiterates what was stated previously, briefly explaining eleven points to manifest their characteristics. As described before...
