As explained in the Chapter on Precepts (*Śīla-varga*), there are two types of *samānārthatā* (common purpose), one type of *priyavāditā* (affectionate speech), four types of *dāna* (giving), and four types of *arthacaryā* (beneficial conduct).

Combined, these total eleven. The following section concludes based on these [categories]. The preceding [section] restates what was previously established, while the subsequent portion provides the explanation, which is clear to understand. From the words "Although having received...
onwards, there is a general concluding eulogy. From the words "This is called... onwards, there is a summary conclusion regarding the alleviation of suffering.

Within the patience of reflection on the Dharma (*dharmānvayakṣānti*), there is first a restatement of the subject and subsequently an explanation. In the explanation, the initial statement regarding the Dharma is the formal exposition.

"Skillfully observing and awakening" is the general explanation. The formal exposition refers to the beginning; because it involves the observation of the Dharma to distinguish the correct from the erroneous, it is called the formal exposition.
"Thorough observation" (*sudarśana*) is the second; knowing through illumination in accordance with the Dharma is called thorough observation. "Awakening" (*vibodha*) is the conclusion;

because one opens up understanding and awakens within all phenomena, it is called awakening. Regarding the eight [sections], they are distinguished individually. Within these distinctions, the initial statement regarding the "eight bases" (*aṣṭasthāna*) is a brief summary of deep reflection.
What follows below is the detailed exposition. First, the eight bases are expanded upon: the Three Jewels constitute three [bases], and the meaning of the Jewels constitutes four.

Supernatural power constitutes the fifth; cause and effect constitute the sixth; the attainment of meaning constitutes the seventh; skillful means constitutes the eighth; and the sphere of what is to be known summarizes the preceding eight.

These are all called "the knowable" because they are objects of knowledge for the mind of understanding (*parijñā-citta*). The sphere of practice for the mind of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-citta*) is called the "sphere of practice.

Furthermore, following the section on understanding, this extensively elaborates upon the previously mentioned profound mindfulness. There are two [sections], which state the number; [this refers to] long-term cultivation and swift purification.
Their two names are listed: "Long-cultivated Worldly Understanding" refers to mundane knowledge; "Attained Pure and Clear Transcendental Wisdom" refers to supramundane knowledge.
Alternatively, long-term cultivation may be understood as the teaching (*śāsana*), while pure wisdom is the realization (*adhigama*).
The preceding section has provided a detailed explanation. From here on, the third part is the summary of all [points]. "This is called 'all'" refers back to what preceded;

"distinguishing two as difficult-to-endure and so forth" opens up what follows. That is to say, within the two categories of the laity and the ordained, they are opened up into "difficult" and so forth.
Regarding the first gate among these difficulties, there are three enumerations; whereas the previous gate spoke of two, here we speak of adding three.
In the subsequent sections, the items gradually increase in number. Below, the names are listed individually. First, regarding "inferiority," it encompasses several types:
(1) inferiority in status; (2) inferiority in virtue and deeds; (3) inferiority in years or summer retreats; (4) inferiority of station, referring to wives, children, and so forth;

and (5) inferiority of birth, referring to commoners and the like. The remaining two types may be understood by analogy. In all these sections, the initial question states the number of categories, followed by a detailed exposition.

Analysis: Regarding the first three pairs, they have been analyzed according to their opposition or conformity; regarding the final pair, they have been analyzed according to their hierarchical gradation.

As for the categories of inferior, middling, and superior, they encompass many types: (1) classification by position into inferior, middling, and superior; (2) classification by virtue and activity into inferior, middling, and superior;
(3) classification by years of seniority (*varṣa*) into inferior, middling, and superior; (4) classification by rank of honor into inferior, middling, and superior; and (5) as for...
The categories of noble and base are divided into low, middle, and high. The six types of afflictive matters are likewise divided into low, middle, and high.

Regarding patience, the first question among the virtuous presents the enumeration, followed by a detailed analysis. Of these, the first two concern self-benefit, while the latter three concern the benefit of others.

Within the section on self-benefit, the first explains the benefits and merit of seeing patience; this consists of an initial summary, followed by a detailed exposition, and finally a conclusion. The "great benefit of seeing patience" is the initial summary, which refers to cultivation.

The distinctions below are as follows: in future lives, one will not harbor much resentment, nor suffer from enmity or hatred; one will not experience much separation, but rather possess a mind full of joy and happiness, free from the suffering of being parted from loved ones;
at the time of death, there will be no regret, and upon rebirth in a happy realm, there will be no suffering of failing to obtain what one seeks.
Because there are no unwholesome dharmas to be abandoned that one cannot escape, there is no remorse; because there are no wholesome fruits that one seeks but fails to obtain, there is no regret.
One is born in the happy realms and the heavens. The happy realms consist of the human path; the heavens consist of the celestial path. Thus, the following serves as a general conclusion.
This concludes the first section.

From here below is the second [section], "Patience for the Benefit of Others. Within this, teaching others constitutes one [aspect], praising patience constitutes two, and sympathetic joy constitutes three;

these together comprise the first five [categories]. Among all the practices, the initial inquiry enumerates the number: the first six are the factors of cultivation (*bhāvanā-aṅga*), and the latter seven are the factors of completion (*niṣpatti-aṅga*).

Taken together, there are thirteen. The following provides a detailed analysis. First, the first six are explained in detail. Among these six, the first involves enduring [suffering] out of fear of it.
Next, there is one gate involving endurance because of mindfulness of rebirth. Bestowing happiness is called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*); extracting from suffering is termed "compassion" (*karuṇā*).

"Intimacy" (*praṇaya*) reveals the depth of the preceding loving-kindness and compassion; "affection" (*preman*) reveals the culmination of the preceding intimacy. The final four gates involve the endurance sought for the sake of attaining *bodhi*.

Among these, the first two stages of patience (*kṣānti*) on the grounds of the happy destinies involve the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and the desire to fulfill patience (*kṣānti*), thereby connecting with a virtuous mind.
The aspiration for enlightenment is the mind that seeks the fruit; the desire to fulfill patience is the mind that seeks the cause.

The second stage is the practice of receiving the Dharma and remaining free from faults. Through the power of patience, one leaves the household life to receive the Dharma as a skillful means, constantly maintaining and correctly upholding the received Dharma.

From here below, they are bound together. This is the patience of renunciation (naiṣkramya-kṣānti), which binds one to renunciation; it is called the patience of receiving the Dharma (dharma-kṣānti), which binds one to the full reception of the precepts.

Next, the patience of the single nature (ekajātīya-kṣānti) pertains to the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotrabhūmi). When the spiritual lineage is complete, this constitutes the fulfillment of the stage of the spiritual lineage.

That which is previously cultivated and currently abiding is the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukticaryābhūmi). Furthermore, when its nature and seeds are fully possessed, that which is previously cultivated and currently abiding constitutes the stage of the developmental seed (parikarma-gotra).

This is called the concluding summary. Next, "right mindfulness" refers to the realization on the first bhūmi that phenomena are unarisen; this is the contemplation of the emptiness of arising (*anutpattika-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

"Seeing the ineffable dharma" refers to the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). This is called the concluding summary. Being in accord with principle is termed "right mindfulness-patience" (*samyak-smṛti-kṣānti*).
Next, the latter seven [patiences] are explained. "Patience with what is not beneficial" is still the aforementioned patience toward that which is not beneficial from others.

"Patience with everything" is still the aforementioned patience in accepting suffering. These two gates are distinguished according to their objects. The next two are distinguished according to time and place:
"patience in all places" is explained in terms of place, while "patience at all times" is analyzed in terms of time.
Below, there are three sections that provide a detailed analysis; their characteristics are clear and can be understood.

Within the patience of removing affliction (*āghātavinodana-kṣānti*), first the number of questions is raised, then they are explained in detail, and finally they are concluded. Below follows the explanation of removing affliction. Within the detailed section, the first three pairs are distinguished according to the person:
"those who seek through suffering" refers to the bodhisattva’s ability to endure when those who are suffering come to him for help. The latter two concern evil persons.
The Bodhisattva is able to endure. Those called "violent" are exclusively evil persons; those who have left the household life and violated the precepts are persons of mixed evil.
The five subsequent phrases distinguish the benefits of transformation and edification. The five types of endurance are presented as a general heading, which are then individually elucidated below.

These five [categories] further clarify the benefits of transformation by contrasting them with the first three types of sentient beings. "Suffering beings" refers to those who seek to eliminate suffering, as opposed to the previous [category of those who] seek to eliminate suffering itself.
The latter four categories generally contrast with the violent and the various evil ones in order to eliminate such evil. As for the term "those who seek the Dharma":

From the very beginning of seeking the Dharma, one proceeds toward the Dharma through the Dharma; one personally relies upon and practices the Dharma—these two are the skillful means for benefiting others.
Extensively explaining verbal benefit and providing assistance through physical benefit—these two constitute the direct transformation [of others]. Diligence and capability summarize these five.

This is called the eighth [category], which concludes the section by way of generalization. Below is the general explanation of the meaning of "removing affliction" (*nir-√bādh*). That which is suffered is "affliction"; it refers to the suffering of being oppressed by adverse conditions.
This is precisely what was previously described as "suffering due to seeking" (*pari-eṣaṇā-duḥkha*), which consists in the capacity for benefit through the removal of what is lacking.

This is for the purpose of eliminating the suffering caused by a deficiency in favorable conditions. This is precisely what was previously described as providing assistance to unwholesome sentient beings.

Regarding the exposition of happiness in this world and the next, first the number of questions is raised; second, there is an extensive analysis and explanation; third, the meaning of happiness in this world and the next is interpreted;
and finally, it is summarized below. The first section is self-evident. Within the second, extensive section, one should abide in heedfulness (*apramāda*).
The practice of patience (*kṣānti*) is the basis [of the path]. Prajñā, which is true wisdom, is non-negligence (*apramāda*). Because a bodhisattva abides in this, they are able to endure.

Having established endurance, the following clarifies patience with respect to its objects. There are five types of one's own suffering and four types of others' suffering; together these constitute nine.

Regarding the five types of endurance toward one's own [circumstances]: first, enduring cold and heat; second, enduring hunger and thirst; third, enduring mosquitoes and gadflies; fourth, enduring contact with wind, sun, and various poisons;
fifth, enduring the suffering of physical and mental exhaustion. Regarding the four types of endurance toward others:
these are the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death. One benefits others by being able to endure these various sufferings. Thus, through such endurance, one explains this world.

Regarding the meaning of happiness in future lives: first it is explained from one’s own perspective, and subsequently from the perspective of others; this continuity may be understood. This is termed the "concluding summary.

Within the section on pure patience (*śuddhakṣānti*), first the number is cited, then it is explained, and finally it is concluded. In the explanation, the first eight items concern the cultivation of the practice of patience.
Next is the cause of patience; finally is the removal of hindrances. Within the first eight [categories], the first six concern one's own patience, while the latter two assist others.
Regarding one's own patience: "not retaliating" means not repaying [an injury] at that very moment; "not giving rise to anger" means having no resentment later on.

One who is free from thoughts of enmity forever severs all other thoughts. As for the statement, "constantly benefiting others as one did originally," this is not merely the absence of thought while desiring to benefit them;
this phrasing is inverted. If the text were correct, it should read: "constantly benefiting [others] as was the original intention."

"Directing the finger toward its source" means that although a bodhisattva’s original intention is to benefit sentient beings, even when encountering harm or affliction, they still give rise to a beneficial mind;

this is like directing the finger back toward its source. Regarding "offering soft words of apology to those who do not benefit one," this refers to apologizing with gentle speech to others who have not been helpful to oneself.
One must apologize because, due to my own lack of skill, I caused them distress.
When that person comes to offer an apology, the Bodhisattva endures it. Within the context of assisting others, one must feel compassion because they are unable to endure their own suffering;

yet, because they possess the virtue of practicing patience, one must respect them. One respects the Buddha all the more because he is free from afflictions, making it no difficulty for him to give rise to patience.
Because he possesses afflictions yet is able to endure with a power that surpasses even that of a Buddha, he is to be revered all the more.

The ninth section is a single chapter on the causes for cultivating patience; because his compassion is profound, he is able to give rise to patience. The final section clarifies the characteristics of being free from hindrances, which can be understood accordingly.
These ten types [of practices] are thus summarized.

The preceding section provided a detailed explanation. Below follows the third part: the concluding summary and praise that reveals their excellence. From "nature" up to "purity," the vastness and immeasurability [of these practices] are praised as the breadth of their application.
That the cause of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is necessarily attained based on [correct] vision is praised as the efficacy of their application.
Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Diligence (*Vīrya-varga*).

Regarding the Chapter on Diligence: because one is able to exert oneself in the uninterrupted cultivation of wholesome dharmas by means of enduring patience (*kṣānti*), diligence is explained immediately after patience.
The extensive exposition of this meaning is called the Chapter on Diligence.

Within this chapter, there is first the question, followed by the explanation, and finally the concluding summary and praise. In the explanation, there are first nine headings enumerated, followed by a detailed analysis and exposition.
Within the initial enumeration of the headings, the number nine is raised, and the names are listed according to their respective natures; these names are the same as those explained previously.

The following provides a detailed explanation. Regarding the nature [of the bodhicitta], there is first the question, second the explanation, and third the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are four parts: first, clarifying its essence; second, distinguishing its capacity;
third, clarifying what it is free from; and fourth, clarifying what it gives rise to. That which is the mind of the bodhisattva is its essence.
In essence, this refers to the mental factor of diligence (*vīrya*), which is generally termed "mind. From "capable" (*samartha*) onwards, up to "uninterrupted," these constitute its capacity.
Within this, there are four phrases: "capable" is subsumed as one, which is the practice for one's own benefit; "benefiting and pacifying" is the second.

This is the practice of benefiting others. These two constitute one pair, distinguished according to their application (*prayoga*). "Blazing" is the third, clarifying that they are practiced simultaneously. "Uninterrupted" is the fourth, clarifying that they are practiced continuously.
These two constitute another pair, distinguished according to their cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Furthermore, "non-perversion" refers to what is to be abandoned;
it is clarified as non-perverted because diligence (*vīrya*) initiates joy (*prīti*) so that one does not enter into error. It is accompanied by right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
It is not inverted. That which is initiated consists of the actions of body, speech, and mind; that is to say, the mind of diligence initiates the activities of the body and so forth.

Regarding all [these], first there is the question and subsequently the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, the division according to form, and second, the division according to practice.
Each of these two is further divided into three; having thus stated the number by citing them, their names are then listed. Among the three [divisions], the first involves the arousal of the vow.
Vigor (*vīrya*). "Great" (*mahā*) means vast. "Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) means aspiration. Based on the mind of vigor, one gives rise to a great vow;
this is called "vast-vowed vigor. The latter two are the vigor of undertaking practice. "Gathering wholesome dharmas" refers to initiating practices for one's own benefit.

"Gathering sentient beings" refers to initiating practices for the benefit of others. These will be explained extensively below. Regarding the explanation of the "vast vow," first there is the citation [of the term], then the explanation, and finally—

[The section on] "Vows" (kṣānti). [The following] lamentation has its initial summary readily understood. In the explanation, first arises the mental factor of diligence (*vīrya*), which is the essence of diligence.

Below, the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) arises; it is capable of donning the armor of the vow, briefly clarifying the great vow. Because the mind of the vow is difficult to destroy, it is like donning armor;
therefore, it is metaphorically termed "donning armor. From "I, for the sake of one... below, the great vow is explained extensively. For the sake of a single sentient being...
It is extremely brief; a hundred thousand great kalpas constitute a single day and night, which is the longest duration of time.

The suffering within the hells is the most intense. Reaching the state of Buddhahood is an exceedingly distant goal. This is the Bodhisattva’s solemn vow made despite the gravity of his transgressions;

how much more so for those below him, who use the heavy to illustrate the light, demonstrating their certain capacity to act. This is called the "concluding summary. The following section is a praise of similar types. Praise.

Within this, there are two parts: first, praising the beginning by way of illustrating the end; second, praising the capacity of the vow. Regarding the former praise, the "bodhisattva-like" (*pratirūpaka-bodhisattva*) refers to the person who has undertaken the great vows.
Although they have initially given rise to the aspirational mind and do not yet possess true practice, they are already similar to a bodhisattva; hence, they are called "bodhisattva-like."

The "Vigor of the Great Vow" (mahāpraṇidhāna-vīrya) refers back to the previously mentioned vow-mind. From "arising with slight understanding" (*alpa-adhimukti*) below, it praises the beginning and, by implication, the end.

Even with slight understanding and slight faith, one is already able to nurture an immeasurable nature of diligence; this is the praise of the beginning. Having only coarse faith and subtle understanding regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma is called "slight faith and understanding.
Based on this faith and understanding, one gives rise to the mind of the great vow; this is called "nurturing the great vow. It is able to provide...
Taking immeasurable supreme wisdom as its basis, it is called the nature of immeasurable awakening.

Being able to serve as the basis for immeasurable supreme cultivation, it is called the nature of immeasurable diligent application. How much more so for those who achieve it, and how much more so for those who bring it to completion?

Within the Mahāyāna, even those with slight understanding and slight faith are already able to thus nurture the immeasurable natures of awakening and diligence; how much more so [for those with greater realization]?

The ultimate accomplishment of faith and understanding. The following praises the capacity for the vow. Thus, the bodhisattva of great resolve and diligence cites the person who previously took the vow;
for the sake of awakening, he does not find it difficult to benefit sentient beings—this is a formal praise of the capacity for the vow.

The section on "Vigor for Gathering Virtue" (śubhasaṃgrāhakavīrya) follows the second gate. The subsequent explanation has two parts: first, clarifying that vigor serves to gather all the perfections (pāramitās), which is evident from its characteristics;
second, following the stages of cultivation, it is divided into seven types. First, the number is stated in general; next, they are analyzed in detail; finally, their excellence is praised.
However, these seven modes of practice are actually simultaneous; they are distinguished according to their characteristics and are not without a sequential gradation. Among them, the first...
Regarding the virtues of the three types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*): first is the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*);

next is the first stage (*bhūmi*); next pertains to the second stage and above; and the final one pertains to the eighth stage and above. Among these three types of lineages, the first is characterized by the abandonment of evil, while the latter two involve the gathering of virtue.
Within the category of abandoning evil, "immovability" (*akampya*) is listed as its name; this will be explained individually below. There are three distinct types: first, afflictions (*kleśa*).

Unshakable: first, unshakable by heterodox doctrines; second, unshakable by all sufferings. Among the virtues subsumed under the lower category of "gathering wholesome qualities," the first is merit and the last is wisdom.

Regarding the attainment of the fields of knowledge within wisdom, this means that because the knowledge of the dharmas of the immeasurable five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) is gathered within the mind, it is called "attainment.
This is the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of abiding in right mindfulness, as well as the ultimate knowledge (*paramārthajñāna*).

The "endowment of skillful means" refers to the practice of understanding and conduct (*adhimukti-caryā*). Because this practice of understanding and conduct can serve as the ultimate skillful means for transcending the world, it is called the "endowment of skillful means.
The following explains its characteristics: "That which is to be attained is the meaning; the path that accords with attainment is non-perverted.

Unsurpassed *bodhi* is the meaning of "that which is to be attained," and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the path belonging to that which is to be attained. Within this path, being non-deviant is termed "non-perverted."
Perversion. The stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) that grasps the meaning of the path of the noble ones is called "conformity" (*anuloma*).

Right effort (*samyag-vīrya*) is the practice of the first stage (*bhūmi*). To be in accord with and realize the true path is termed "right" (*samyak*); to give rise to the vow and advance toward the fruit is termed "effort" (*vīrya*). Below, its characteristics are explained.

"Beneficial meaning" (*artha-hita*) refers to one's own level of practice (*svabhūmi-pratipatti*). When true practice moistens oneself, it is called "beneficial meaning. That which is to be... [text ends]
"Attaining the fulfillment of the goal" refers to the aspiration for diligence; "unsurpassed bodhi" is the goal to be attained.

The aspiration sought at the first stage (*bhūmi*) is called the "fulfillment of the aspiration. Regarding the term "blazing," this refers to the practice of the path from the second stage upward. It is called "blazing" because the cultivation of the path is uninterrupted.
The phrase "constantly diligent in skillful means" explains and clarifies its characteristics. The term "free from pride" refers to the eighth stage.
The above constitutes the practice of accomplishment. Being free from effort and having the discursive mind stilled is called "freedom from pride.
The phrase "the mind does not exalt itself" explains its characteristics.

What has preceded is a detailed explanation; what follows is a praise that reveals its excellence. Within this, there are four lines: first, it clarifies how diligence swiftly fulfills all the perfections (*pāramitās*).
One is able to attain *bodhi*. Second, from "all" onwards, it clarifies that the practice for *bodhi* is accomplished through diligence; *bodhi* is the fruit, while practice is the cause.

Third, from "therefore" onwards, it concludes by praising and manifesting its excellence. Fourth, from "World-Honored One" onwards, it cites scriptural teachings to provide proof and establish the point.

Regarding the diligence for benefiting sentient beings, the enumeration is listed as before. Within the section on difficult diligence, first the number is raised by way of a question, followed by the explanation, and finally the praise.

In the explanation, the first [point] is difficult because it involves exclusive cultivation; the second category is difficult because it involves constant cultivation; the third category is difficult because it involves skillful cultivation.
This is first explained and then concluded. Within the explanation, there are six phrases: equanimity constitutes one, and through the cultivation of the mind, one attains the middle way.

Discrimination constitutes the second. Right knowledge, free from error and endowed with virtue, constitutes the third. The perfection of conduct and virtue, being neither lax nor hasty, constitutes the fourth gate, which reveals the aforementioned equanimity.
Non-perversion constitutes the fifth, revealing the aforementioned discrimination. Benefit through meaning constitutes the sixth.

The preceding section reveals the possession of virtues; the following section praises and manifests their excellence. Based on this diligence, one is able to benefit sentient beings, and thus it serves as the cause for compassion (*karuṇā*);

one is able to enter into the true meaning (*tattvārtha*), and thus it serves as the cause for wisdom (*prajñā*). Within each of the gates, the first question sets forth the number, followed by the enumeration of the four names.
Abandoning defilement and departing from evil; giving rise to purity and cultivating goodness—these two constitute a pair concerning the classification of practice (*caryā*).

Cultivating pure karma and accumulating merit; increasing knowledge and giving rise to wisdom—these two constitute a pair concerning the classification of virtue (*guṇa*). The details of these may be understood from the extensive explanation below.

Regarding the category of virtuous persons, first the number is stated, and subsequently there is an extensive classification. Of these, the first four pertain to the mundane world (*laukika*), while the last one pertains to the supramundane stages (*bhūmi*). Within the mundane category:
They are divided into four types according to the beginning and end of their cultivation. Among these, the first involves the vastness of the aspiration;
the statement "there is nothing one does not do for all desires" refers to the vastness of desire (*chanda*). This means that within all vast desires, there is nothing that is not undertaken.
The non-ceasing of skillful means is constant desire. Next, the first [category] is not inferior; it initiates the cultivation of superior application. The following clarifies its characteristics:

practice is not accomplished instantaneously, which is why it is like the middle; gradual study becomes increasingly lofty, which is why it is like the superior. Thus, one proceeds from the middle to the superior.
Therefore, it is called "nurturing. Next, the first [category] is the non-laxity of gathering practice without falling back. Within this, there are eight phrases;

non-laxity constitutes one [aspect], while self-exertion and diligence constitute two, and heroic valor constitutes three—these two together correspond to the one [of non-laxity]. This represents the non-retrogression of superior progress. As for "blazing," it is the third.

"Clarifying their exclusive cultivation" constitutes four [aspects], clarifying that they practice for a long duration. "Clarifying their constant cultivation" constitutes two [aspects], forming a pair with the former.

The following section further elucidates these: "Vigor" constitutes five [aspects], clarifying the absence of indolence mentioned previously; "non-retrogression" constitutes the sixth, clarifying the aforementioned courage and ferocity; and "unremittingness" constitutes the seventh.
The first [verse] reveals blazing intensity; the second, indestructibility—these two constitute eight [qualities]. The third reveals long duration.

The next one concerns non-erroneous skillful observation for seeking liberation. The first three are precisely the practices of the world; this clarifies the skillful means for entering the path leading out [of saṃsāra].

The phrase "non-erroneous and beneficial in meaning" refers to that which is sought. The correct realization of the supramundane is called "non-erroneous"; it is the accomplishment of practicing for the benefit [of others].

The benefit of names and meanings refers to the practice of seeking through skillful means. Understanding, practice, and the arousal of cultivation directed toward those meanings and names constitute being encompassed by skillful means.
Diligent skillful means refers to supramundane practice. Proceeding without interval toward Buddhahood is called diligent skillful means.
"Swift awakening" reveals its characteristic.

Among all the practices, first the number is raised by way of a question, then it is explained, and finally it is concluded. Regarding the explanation of the preceding six [points], first the previous [topic] is restated.
Next is the explanation, followed by the praise. Within the explanation, the first two sections distinguish the meaning of cultivation: the first concerns the constant, and the second the sudden.

Next, there are two gates that distinguish [cultivation] in relation to causes: the first relates to past causes, and the second relates to present causes. Below these, there are two gates that distinguish the divisions of cultivation.
The first is self-maintenance (*svabhāva*), and the latter is superior progress (*viśeṣa*). Immovable diligence is firmness in self-maintenance. This is explained in detail below:

being unmoved by painful contact is immovability in practice; not turning toward other goals is immovability in aspiration. "Other goals" refers to humans, devas, and the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*);
the bodhisattva does not turn toward these. One who is not content possesses superior progress without satiety; one who is limited does not rejoice [in this].

The commentary explains their characteristics. The following section cites the praise of excellence; it consists of six parts that cite what preceded. From "earnestly" (*yinqin*) onwards is the praise of excellence:

because the initial mind is single-minded and focused, it is called "earnest"; because one is immovable during right cultivation, it is named "capable and firm"; and because one ultimately achieves non-retrogression, it is said to be "indestructible regarding all dharmas.
Regarding the explanation of the latter seven [verses], first there is the citation, next the explanation, and finally the conclusion.

In this commentary, the first [verse] explains the preliminary application for generating desire, while the subsequent six explain the actual cultivation. "Accompanied by desire" means that the mind of diligence is accompanied by desire.
The following explains their characteristics: "diligent" refers to the mind of diligence, and "wishing for bodhi" refers to the mind of aspiration.
Because these two accompany one another, they are said to be "accompanied. Within the latter six cultivations, they are subsumed into three pairs.
The first two pairs are distinguished according to their cultivation: the former is "one's own level" (*svabhāga*), and the latter is "progressive advancement" (*viśeṣa*).

"Fully endowed" refers to being fully endowed with one's own level. The following explains their characteristics. Among all other afflictions, dwelling in a mind that is defiled is designated as "dwelling in an inferior state" to highlight the excellence [of the Bodhisattva's state].

Dwelling in a defiled mind refers to all other sentient beings whose mental states are accompanied by afflictions; this is contrasted with the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in a virtuous and so forth mind. This is the explanation.
"Surpassing the inferior" means that because one abides in wholesome states and so forth, one excels other births. "Excellence and progress" refers to seeking superior practice.

The following explains its characteristics: among the various remaining afflictions (*kleśa*), those that abide as higher-order afflictions (*upakleśa*) are used to highlight the inferior by revealing the superior.
Those whose nature is to bind are simply called "afflictions," while those delusions that arise coarsely are called "higher-order afflictions. Other sentient beings are not devoid of those delusions.
The desire of the mind to sever [afflictions] is called "abiding of the mind. Severing those afflictions is like saving one's head from fire; this distinguishes the superior from the inferior.

One should infer other cases according to the preceding examples, though the text here is slightly insufficient. If it were complete, it should state: "The Bodhisattva’s diligence in severing those afflictions is like saving one's head from fire.
The next two pairs are distinguished by their stages of understanding (*adhimukti*) and practice (*pratipatti*): first understanding, then practice. "Seeking diligence" means seeking...
The Dharma gives rise to understanding. Because it is sought within the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), its characteristics are explained and revealed;

that is to say, those who seek the five fields of knowledge and practice with diligence initiate their conduct in accordance with the Dharma. The following explains its characteristics: "That such Dharma" refers to the *adhyātma-vidyā* (inner science) among the five fields of knowledge.
"Arising the sequence of the Dharma as appropriate" means initiating the practice according to what is suitable for oneself. These two are as previously described regarding power.

The *Śīlapaṭala* (Chapter on Ethics) explains that the latter two pairs are distinguished by their application to the benefit of others and the benefit of oneself. The former [pair] is for the benefit of others; its characteristics are manifest and thus easily known. The latter [pair] is for one's own benefit:
it consists of the practice of gathering wholesome deeds through correct personal means, and the practice of avoiding faults through the protection of diligence.

This concludes the summary of the names. The preceding explanation is finished. Having thus explained these thirteen [categories], they are summarized as "the removal of affliction and the attainment of happiness. This refers to...

This is explained as the same as the previous patience. Within that former patience, there are eight types of non-affliction: first, non-affliction despite seeking [the Dharma] with hardship; second, enduring and not being disturbed by wicked people;
third, enduring and not being disturbed by those who are corrupt; fourth, for the sake of eliminating suffering; fifth, for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
Sixth is the practice directed toward the higher dharma; seventh is the extensive exposition; eighth is the performance of assistance—these are the same as those [previously mentioned].

Furthermore, regarding the nine kinds of happiness in this world and the next as elucidated in the preceding section on patience: first is enduring cold and heat; second is enduring hunger and thirst;
third is enduring mosquitoes and gadflies; fourth is enduring wind and sun; fifth is enduring extreme exhaustion—these constitute the first five. Following these, there are further...
Regarding those four types of sentient beings—those subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death—he endures and gathers them through conversion, making four;
together with the previous [five], nine are spoken of. Now, it is explained in the same manner as that.
Within the section on purification, first the number is raised by means of a question, followed by the listing of their names. Among the ten, the first three are mundane practices.

The latter seven pertain to the supramundane. Regarding the former three, they constitute the beginning of practice that accords with reality; because one cultivates and remedies transgressions in accordance with them, they are called "accordant.
As for the sequence of cultivation in practice, when one desires to enter the path of transcendence, one diligently practices according to the dharmas of instruction and admonition.

The section on "exclusive attachment" concludes here. Because of previous cultivation, supramundane signs appear; yet, by following these signs and giving rise to seeking, one's emotional state lacks reality and becomes lax—hence it is called "exclusive attachment.

Within the subsequent seven [categories], the first three pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the next three to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the last one to the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhogamārga*).
Regarding the term "skillfully grasping" within the path of seeing, it refers to skillfully cultivating the correspondence with supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, it is called "skillfully gathering. Regarding "endowment at the time": this refers to practicing fully during the aforementioned stage of gathering. Regarding "discerning characteristics":
this refers to discerning and knowing during the aforementioned stage of practice. Next, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), "non-retrogression" means that the initial mind is not timid.
"Non-destruction" refers to immovability in correct cultivation. "Equanimity" refers to ultimately attaining the Middle Way. Regarding "dedication" within the context of effortlessness:
because one proceeds toward and accords with Bodhi within the water of the Dharma, it is called dedication. This will be explained extensively below.

Within the first section, in order to sever the afflictions, one should cultivate purification as appropriate; this is a general explanation of "conformity," which teaches cultivation according to the specific ailments that arise.

This is the treatment. As with the distinction regarding "affection for the lower," so too is the conclusion of the section below. Within the second gate, first there is the exclusion of the preceding gate, followed by the explanation, and finally the conclusion.

"Not establishing the initial practice" is the exclusion of the preceding [gate]. To cultivate the practices of the five perfections at the beginning is called "initial"; this is not that [initial stage].

Rather, it refers to the mind abiding in the lower [stage] through correct understanding and cultivation. Abiding in the mind by practicing in accordance with the Dharma is what is meant by "mind-abiding. This is the instruction.

The phrase "instruction" (*avavāda*) is the general heading; what follows below explains it specifically. "The means of cultivation" refers to the accumulation of virtuous conduct through the aforementioned instruction.
"The means of discipline" refers to the abandonment of unwholesome conduct through the aforementioned instruction. This concludes the summary of the names.

Within the third section, the phrase "the mind abiding in the means of non-cultivation of diligence" serves to distinguish this from the preceding [categories]. "Cultivating diligence" refers to the former.

This is a general clarification. From "having already been instructed" onwards constitutes the explanation of the preceding characteristics. "Instruction and admonition" refers to the instruction and admonition within the preceding section.
The term "skillful means" (*upāya*) refers to the skillful means of cultivation and the skillful means of subduing within the preceding section.

The term "abiding of the mind" (*cittasthiti*) refers to the state where the mind has already become settled within the preceding section. This [present case] is not that [previous one]; rather, it is intended to manifest the initial stage and its distinctiveness.

Subsequently, the mind of one at the end of the mundane stage is focused on their practice, which serves as the initial expedient for the supramundane; therefore, it is called "initial practice" (*ādikarmika*).
From this point downward, the meaning of "focus" is correctly explained. Understanding and practice constitute the expedient for the supramundane.

A bodhisattva’s diligent cultivation of these supramundane expedients is termed "focus. Constant training is called "perpetual," and simultaneous study is termed "sudden. This concludes the section below.

Regarding the first [section], it is called "exclusive attachment" because of its binding nature. In the fourth section, it refers to the conditions for gathering the Dharma based on those who are honored.
The power of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) is the cause for gathering the Dharma. From "without error" (*aviparyāsa*) onwards, the gathering of the Dharma is correctly explained:

initially observing without deviation is called "non-inverted" (*aviparyasta*); attaining correct realization in accordance with reality is called "the mind abiding in peace. This is the concluding summary. In the fifth section:

In this way, by citing what precedes to initiate what follows without error, one clearly manifests the characteristics [of the practice]: cultivating calm (*śamatha*) at the time of calming, cultivating exertion (*pragraha*) at the time of exerting, and cultivating equanimity (*upekṣā*) at the time of equanimity.
This is called the "concluding summary" (*nigamana*) of the sixth section, wherein the characteristics of calming, exertion, and equanimity cite what precedes to initiate what follows.

The phrase "one who constantly observes well during the abiding and arising from samādhi" precisely clarifies its characteristics. Stopping (*śamatha*), uplifting (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are designated as samādhi.
The moment of entering [samādhi] is called "abiding," and the moment of emerging is called "arising. One thoroughly knows these states of abiding and arising and discerns them without error.
This is called the "lower bond. It is the first of the seven categories: the sublime and wondrous Dharma of non-abiding.

The first, the profound and inconceivable, refers to the Dharma of the realized path (*adhigama-mārga*). That which is called "immeasurable" refers to the Dharma of the auxiliary path (*sambhāra-mārga*).

When it says that the Bodhisattva’s skillful means do not involve self-deprecation, this refers to not deprecating oneself regarding the aforementioned sublime and wondrous [Dharma]. "Not being timid or weak" refers to the aforementioned profound [Dharma].
It is not timid. One who does not conceive a sense of sufficiency regarding their slight progress can extensively cultivate the immeasurable [virtues] before them.

This is called the concluding summary. In the first explanation within the eighth section, there is first the exposition and later the conclusion. Within the exposition, there are four phrases; the first is guarding the gates of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Second, knowing the proper measure in eating. Third, practicing with diligence and fewness of sleep. Fourth, abiding in the mind through right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*).

Right wisdom is insight (*vipaśyanā*), and abiding of the mind is calm (*śamatha*). Among these four, the first three comprise the means of cultivation, while the last one is the perfection of cultivation.

Below, this is summarized and concluded: *samādhi-sambhāra* (the equipment for concentration) restates the preceding three phrases. The causes of the first three concentrations are termed the "equipment for concentration," which is accomplished through diligence.

This concludes the three preceding phrases, establishing the causal basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The section on "Righteous Benefit" cites and concludes the fourth point, the abiding of the mind in right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*);
this is termed the concluding summary of the name. Within the ninth gate, "cultivating with neither laxity nor haste, but with equanimity," refers to the balancing and harmonizing [of the practice].
"Cultivating all phenomena with evenness" refers to their uniform and complete possession; this is termed the concluding summary of the name. The tenth [gate]... [reversal].

The preceding sections have extensively explained how the characteristics [of the stages] are manifested and can be known. From this point onward is the third section, which concludes the explanation with a summary praise.

Regarding the phrase "attaining bodhi from nature to purity," it refers to attaining the fruit in a brief period of time. Based on this fulfillment, the following section explains the reasons for attaining it.
Chapter Thirteen: On Dhyāna. Regarding the "Chapter on Dhyāna":
because the mind is made one-pointed through diligence, the section on meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) is elucidated immediately following diligence.
It is called the "Chapter on Dhyāna" because it provides an extensive explanation of the definition of dhyāna.

Within this chapter, there is first the question, next the explanation, and finally the praise that reveals its excellence. In the explanation, there is first the opening enumeration of nine gates, followed by a detailed analysis and exposition.

Within the preceding opening of the gates, there are nine points: the citation of the number, the sequential listing of the names such as "nature" (prakṛti), and so forth, which are also explained as above.

The explanation will be given next. Regarding the nature [of meditation], there is first the question, second the explanation, and finally the conclusion. Within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, this is the dharma of *dhyāna*.

Hearing and reflection (*śruta* and *cintā*) as preceding stages are the causes of *dhyāna*. *Dhyāna-samādhi* is cultivation; hearing and reflection are called "preceding stages" because they precede cultivation through their function of understanding.
The section beginning with "mundane and supramundane" precisely defines the essence of *dhyāna*. Mundane and supramundane are distinguished by way of their respective stages. Mundane...
The eight mundane dhyānas are called "worldly. Outflow-free (anāsrava) meditative concentration based on principle is called "transcendent" (lokottara).

One should distinguish their essence by abiding with a single mind within their respective characteristics. Alternatively, one may distinguish their essence by focusing on the lower stage of the cessation aspect (śamatha-bhāga). "Cessation" refers to the cultivation of śamatha; "insight" (vipaśyanā) refers to the cultivation of vipaśyanā. These two are of a similar nature.

Regarding the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, or that which belongs to both parts: this refers to dwelling joyfully in śamatha and vipaśyanā. This meaning is as previously explained regarding power (bala).

The *Śīla-paṭala* (Chapter on Nature) explains that among all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), there is first the inquiry, then the explanation, and finally the concluding summary and praise. Within the explanation, there are two parts. The first follows the stages (*bhūmi*) and is divided into two:

that which is prior to the stages, which is mundane (*laukika*); and that which is upon the stages, which is supramundane (*lokottara*). If distinguished according to their specific meanings, pure worldly concentrations are termed mundane, while those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) are termed supramundane.
Question: Why are ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), and diligence (*vīrya*) each divided into two categories according to their respective forms?
Dhyāna is not like this. [The author] explains that because the cultivation and arising of the precepts and so forth reside in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they follow the distinctions of form.

Since meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is accomplished within and its distinctions of form are difficult to differentiate, it follows the stages (*avasthā*). The subsequent wisdom (*prajñā*) is likewise. Second, regarding the division by way of practice, there are three;

first, the number is stated, and next, the three names are listed. "Bliss in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*): the Dharma being manifest in the mind is called "present life. Realizing the Dharma brings immediate...

The name of the deity is "Delight in the Present Dharma" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*). It may also be called "Delight in the Present Dharma" because one realizes the dharma and experiences delight in the present life.
According to the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā), the first dhyāna is specifically named "delight in the present" because it is the first stage where one abandons the pleasures of the five desires.

In the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, however, it is only from the second dhyāna upward that it is termed "delight in the present," because it is free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). This is as explained in detail in the section on the four types of cultivated concentration (*catvāri dhyānāni*) in that same *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

[The previous section was] explained; now it is clarified. "Producing one's own virtues" means producing virtues for oneself. "Benefiting sentient beings" means producing virtues for the benefit of others.
This will be explained extensively below.

In the explanation of the first gate: "Leaving behind all delusions, body and mind come to rest; abandoning signs, one proceeds toward tranquility. Because one cultivates meditative concentration on principles (*li-ting*), one leaves behind all delusions.

Because one cultivates meditative concentration on phenomena (*shi-ting*), body and mind come to rest. Abandoning the discursive agitation that follows after objects within the five consciousnesses is called the coming to rest of the body.
Abandoning the confusion of grasping at dharmas within the mental consciousness is called the coming to rest of the mind. Below this is the section on the primary tranquility.

One realizes the mark of quiescence; this constitutes the accomplishment of the essence of the foremost meditative concentration of quiescence (*śamatha*). In principle, the removal of delusion is called "stopping the mind" (*cittasthāpana*);
in practice, the removal of distraction is called "abandoning attachment to flavors. Furthermore, abandoning attachment to all marks means remaining far removed from defiled obstructions.

This refers to being free from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages, as well as being detached from all signs that obstruct cultivation—namely, speech, discursive thought (*vitarka*), and investigation (*vicāra*).
This is called the "lower fetter" (*adhaḥ-saṃyojana*).

In the first part of the second section, the arising of the merits of the Mahāyāna is explained; subsequently, the Hīnayāna is addressed. Within the Mahāyāna, that which arises in great abundance is termed "various" (*vicitra*);
that which arises in subtle detail is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*); that which is profound in its origin is designated as "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*);
and because its locus is vast and expansive, it is called "boundless" (*ananta*). Thus far has been the praise of excellence regarding the lineage of the ten powers (*daśabala-gotra*).
The samādhis included therein produce what is praised. The immeasurable samādhis accomplished by a bodhisattva can serve as the causal basis for power;

this is termed the nature of the ten powers (*daśabala*). Regarding the samādhis included therein, those lower samādhis are contrasted to manifest their superiority, and the subsequent section clarifies the production of the merits of the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*).
This, too, represents the bodhisattva’s merit being identical to that of the two vehicles.
Therefore, these are called the merits of the two vehicles. What is termed "liberation" refers to the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).

What is termed "bases of mastery" refers to the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*). The "totalities" refer to the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*). What is termed "unimpeded wisdom" refers to the four unimpeded knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).

These various meanings are explained extensively in other chapters; they should be discussed in full detail here. Regarding the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-jñāna*): one who possesses this knowledge constantly observes the minds of others so as not to provoke their awareness.
As for the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), it is swift knowledge; because one can know things according to one's wish, it is called the knowledge of aspiration.
"Victorious and Sublime Virtue" summarizes [the preceding] as a whole; this is called the "concluding summary.

Regarding "the dhyāna for benefiting sentient beings," it refers to the third section, which consists of eleven types, as previously explained—that is, as explained in the "Chapter on Precepts" (Śīla-paṭala).
Based on the lower category of giving, eleven types are specifically clarified within the section on giving; the same applies to the others. A question is raised:

since patience (*kṣānti*) and vigor (*vīrya*) have already been addressed previously, why are the eleven types again discussed under meditation (*dhyāna*)? It is because meditation is the fundamental source for generating virtuous qualities (*guṇa*).

Question: Why is it that these eleven [perfections] are specifically elucidated within the context of giving (*dāna*)? Answer: Because within giving, all three types—material wealth, the Dharma, and fearlessness—are fully present;

its modes of practice are vast and expansive, and its manifestations are clearly complete. That which relies upon giving is subsumed under the category of giving. Sentient beings constitute the "recipient" (*pratigrahaka*).
Regarding the aforementioned generosity, it is explained as possessing eleven aspects. The first two are *sāṃbhoga* (common purpose):
sharing the same joyful activities and sharing the same suffering activities for the sake of removing the sufferer's pain. Speaking appropriately is *priyavāditā* (loving speech).

The next four are *dāna* (giving): knowing gratitude and repaying kindness is *dāna*; protecting against all fears and sorrows is *abhayadāna* (the gift of fearlessness); [and] providing [material gifts].
That which is required is the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*). To maintain a community in accordance with the Dharma is the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

Regarding the four subsequent bases of sympathetic conduct (*saṃgrahavastu*): one who can act in accordance is a virtuous person capable of compliance; one who praises true virtue is a virtuous person capable of extolling virtue;
one who subdues with an impartial mind is one capable of taming those who are difficult to discipline.
"Prostration. "Terror through supernormal power" refers to the supernormal power used to terrify those difficult-to-tame evil persons. This is called the concluding summary.

Regarding the section on the difficulty of dhyāna, first the number is raised by means of a question, and subsequently its characteristics are explained. First, it is difficult because one possesses mastery over the essence of dhyāna.
Second, it is difficult because it gives rise to vast merit; third, it is difficult because the attainment of its fruit is vast.
Within all the sections, first the number is stated in response to the question, and subsequently their names are enumerated. That which possesses vitarka and vicāra is the first dhyāna.

The second dhyāna is accompanied by joy (*prīti*). Joy is common to the first two [dhyānas]. Having already distinguished the first dhyāna by its function of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the present statement that it is "accompanied by joy" serves to distinguish it from the subsequent [stages].
As for the essence of the single-mindedness of dhyāna: because this essence of single-mindedness is associated with joy, it is said to be "accompanied by joy."
The same applies to all subsequent cases. "Accompanied by pleasure" (*sukha-sahagata*) refers to the third dhyāna; "pleasure" (*sukha*) generally applies to the first three [dhyānas].

Having already distinguished between applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and joy (*prīti*) within the first two dhyānas, the present mention of "accompanied by pleasure" serves to distinguish it from what follows. From the fourth dhyāna upward, they are all uniformly termed "accompanied by equanimity" (*upekṣā-sahagata*).
This is the equanimity of feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), not the equanimity of formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*). The meaning of the eight dhyānas is explained in detail in a separate chapter.

In the dhyāna of the virtuous person, first the number is raised in the question, and later its characteristics are analyzed. "Non-savoring dhyāna" refers to the fundamental pure dhyāna (*śuddhaka-dhyāna*).

The latter four are the fruits of the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). Because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is conjoined with these, they are termed "conjoined" (*sahagata*).
Among all the practices, the initial inquiry first presents the number, then provides the explanation, and finally offers the conclusion. Within the explanation, the first six types are clarified.

Wholesome dhyāna constitutes one category, namely, pure dhyāna (*śuddha-dhyāna*) and untainted dhyāna (*anāsrava-dhyāna*). Unneutral transformation-creation constitutes the second, namely, the fourteen kinds of transformations, as explained extensively in a separate chapter;
this should be discussed in full detail. These two constitute one pair when distinguished by their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

When divided by function, the aspect of calm abiding (*śamatha*) is threefold, while the aspect of insight (*vipaśyanā*) is fourfold. These two constitute another pair when distinguished according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Self-benefit constitutes five [factors], while benefiting others constitutes the sixth. These two are distinguished as a pair according to their application to benefit. Next, the latter seven are explained.

Among these seven, the first three concern the differentiation of what is produced: "producing supernormal powers" refers to the arising of the five *abhijñās*. Regarding "name" and "meaning," both arise from wisdom:
wisdom that can understand the verbal teachings is the condition of "name," while wisdom that can comprehend the meaning of the teachings is the condition of "meaning."

The three—stilling (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are distinguished according to their cultivation. From "present happiness" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*) downward, they are distinguished by way of their essential nature.

The eight worldly truths are called "happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*). Purity that accords with principle is called the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*). This concludes the section on names.
In the *Dhyāna that Eliminates Affliction*, the initial question introduces the enumeration, while the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation.

Here, in the first question of this [section on] future lives, the scriptural authority is introduced, followed by a detailed analysis. Among the nine [topics], the first three concern the distinctions in the karma of transformation.

The bodily action of supernormal powers, the verbal action of teaching in accordance with what is spoken, and the mental action of instruction—because it bestows [benefit] through the movement of the mind, it is called "mental.
Next, there are three phrases concerning the distinctions of transformative benefit: the bodily action that benefits sentient beings who are evil and those in the evil destinies.

Benefiting sentient beings who have lost their eloquence by means of eloquence is the benefit of verbal action (*vākkarman*). Benefiting sentient beings who have lost their mindfulness by means of mindfulness is the transformation of mental action (*manaskarman*).
Below are three phrases concerning the distinctions in transformative activities: by composing non-erroneous treatises, one brings about understanding in those beings being transformed.
The transformation through the benefit of skillful means brings about happiness; the transformation through the cessation of evil and the emission of light brings about the departure from suffering.
Within the context of pure dhyāna, the initial question enumerates the categories, followed by a detailed analysis. Among these ten, the first two are analyzed according to their respective stages.
The mundane pure concentration is termed "mundane. This explains the meaning of the ninth pure dhyāna within the context of mundane pure meditations;
therefore, it is called the "pure-pure dhyāna. In the subsequent phrases, the repetition of "pure" follows this same pattern.
"Neither relishing nor being stained" reveals the aforementioned purity. It is called "not relishing" because it is free from craving and attachment;

it is called "unstained" because it has abandoned other afflictions. "Supramundane purity" refers to untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna. Because it clarifies the meaning of purity within supramundane purity, it is termed "supramundane pure purity.
The subsequent three [categories] are distinguished according to the beginning, middle, and end of cultivation. "Purity of means" (*upāya-śuddhi*)...
The preliminary preparations for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are as follows: "fundamental purity" refers to correctly attaining the essence of dhyāna;

"superior advancement" refers to being able to enter superior states by relying on the aforementioned fundamental stage. The following two lines distinguish between entering and exiting: the power of entering, abiding, and arising constitutes the process of sequential entry.

Initial entry is called "entry. Abiding correctly is called "abiding. Emerging from meditative concentration is called "arising. Because entry and emergence are mastered with ease, they are termed "powers" (*bala*).

To abandon [the state] and then re-enter is "reversing entry. Previously, emerging from concentration was described as "abandoning"; because one returns once more to enter within it, it is called "re-entry.
Because entry and emergence are mastered with ease, they are termed "powers. Below, there are three gates for the analytical classification of the arising of virtues.

The first phrase brings forth supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the latter two produce wisdom (*jñāna*). Within the section on wisdom, the first statement refers to the wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) which is free from all views.

"The severance of the two obstacles" refers to the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), namely, the severance of the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The preceding section has extensively analyzed [the practice]. From here on, the third part concludes with a praise that reveals its excellence. "Immeasurable meditators" concludes the explanation of the breadth of the practice;
the following praises the capacity of that practice. "Attaining great enlightenment" generally reveals the capacity of the practice; based on this, it is further revealed again below.
The Manifestation of the Essentials of Virtuous Brilliance, Having Already Attained and Yet to Be Attained.
*Dichilun Yiji*, Scroll Three (Part Two).
*Dichilun Yiji*, Scroll Four (Part One).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan of Jingying Monastery during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on Wisdom (Hui-pin).

Regarding the Chapter on Wisdom: the preceding section clarified the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because the mind is stilled, wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to attain illumination. Therefore, the Chapter on Wisdom is explained next in detail.
To elucidate this meaning, it is called the "Wisdom Category" (*prajñā-varga*).

Within this category, there is first the question, followed by the explanation, and finally the praise that reveals its excellence. Within the extensive explanation, the nine numbers are first set forth.
Next, the nine names are listed; their meanings are as explained above, while the following provides a detailed analysis and exposition.

Within the section on "nature," there is first the question, then the explanation, and finally the conclusion. In the explanation, the initial portion up to the phrase "according to the Dharma" explains contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

This is the skillful means for entering the object of knowledge through the wisdom of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Ultimate truth is the objective sphere of that which is known; "entering" refers to the understanding that accords with [the name].

That which follows "having entered" (*anupraviṣṭa*) is correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Because it discriminates the right from the wrong, it is called "discerning contemplation" (*pravicaya-vipaśyanā*).
That which takes the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) as its object is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); the former is general, while the latter is specific.

Regarding all [these categories], the question is posed first and the explanation follows later. Within the explanation, there are two sections. First, the division according to stages (*avasthā*) has two parts:

that which is prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is called "mundane" (*laukika*), and that which is above the path of vision is called "supramundane" (*lokottara*). Second, the division according to practice (*caryā*) has three parts.

For each of these two [divisions], the number is stated by restating the headings, followed by the enumeration of the three names. The first of these is the wisdom of ultimate truth (*paramārthajñāna*); the latter two...

Worldly wisdom (*loka-jñāna*) is the skillful means for observing and understanding the reality known within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This constitutes the aforementioned four types of seeking.
By citing the reality that is known, it manifests its capacity for observation; this is true understanding.

Through the accomplishment of the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*) that accords with awakening and discernment, one realizes the reality of the objects of knowledge as they truly are; taking this as awakening, one achieves [it].
Because it relies on initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*), it is called "conforming" (*anupraviṣṭa*). Because it realizes the truth and discerns with clarity, it is termed "discrimination" (*vibhāga*).

Skillfulness in the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and the three aggregates of dharma (*triskandha*) constitutes conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). The first two [aggregates] pertain to one's own practice, while benefiting sentient beings constitutes the wisdom of transforming others within conventional wisdom.
These will be explained extensively below.

In the explanation of the first gate, it is stated that through wordlessness and the realization of non-self, one fully comprehends the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This explains the "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) within the preceding section on names.
This passage is somewhat abbreviated; if it were complete, it should state: "The ultimate truth of the object of knowledge consists of the ineffable dharma of non-self."
"By" (yi) means "to employ" (yòng). Principle transcends words, and names are beyond verbal expression. Truly departing from emotional attachments, one realizes that there are no self or dharmas.
When a Bodhisattva employs this as the true object of knowledge, they awaken to the truth; knowing that what preceded was non-self is called awakening to the True Truth (satya).
Having awakened, one subsequently discerns [the object] within the first state of tranquility (*śamatha*); this explains the preceding term "subsequent discernment" (*anuvicaya*).

The initial phrase "having awakened" restates what precedes to introduce what follows. The portion from "within the first" onwards precisely clarifies the wisdom of subsequent discernment. Within this, there is first *śamatha*.

Next is contemplation, followed by relinquishment. The initial stage, reaching the removal of falsehood, is *śamatha* (calm abiding). The "supreme *prajñā*" and the "first state of stillness" therein constitute the objective domain of *śamatha*.
"Supreme" (*shang*) refers to what precedes; that which can awaken the mind is called supreme *prajñā*, and that which is awakened as true is called the first state of stillness of supreme *prajñā*.
This, then, reiterates the previously awakened True Truth (*satya*) as the objective domain of *śamatha*.
To bind the mindfulness and dwell securely is the very essence of *śamatha* (calm abiding). To depart from delusion and eliminate falsehood is that which is abandoned by *śamatha*.

Internally apprehending the stilling of the mind is called "departing from false conceptualization. The non-arising of delusive objects is called "eliminating the false and deceptive. Entering into equanimity is its *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Because the principle of non-self is uniform, it is called "equality. Since the essence of all phenomena is identical, it is termed the "Great Universal Characteristic" (*mahāsāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

To understand and know this is called "entry" and "contemplation. One who stands apart from both affirmation and denial enters the Middle Way; this is the relinquishing of existence and non-existence.
To harmonize the mind with the single reality is called entering the Middle Way. This concludes the section on the name.

In the first section of the second gate, there is first an explanation and subsequently a praise. Regarding the preceding explanation, it is taught that the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) constitute the objective domain of wisdom (*prajñā*), while the three aggregates (*trikaṇḍa*) are specifically explained.

"Meaningful" refers to what is wholesome (*kuśala*); "meaningless" refers to what is unwholesome (*akuśala*); "neither [meaningful nor meaningless]" and "neither non-meaningful nor non-non-meaningful" refer to indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena.

The inclusion within the eight bases (*aṣṭasthāna*) correctly clarifies the essence of wisdom. It is called "inclusion within the wholesome" because one contemplates the phenomena and enters into their profound nature.

The following verses express praise to manifest its excellence. The phrase "endowed with wisdom" (*prajñā-saṃpanna*) demonstrates the perfection of its cause. "Buddha-wisdom" (*buddhajñāna*) refers to that great, unsurpassed wisdom;

the "multitude of wisdom-equipments" (*prajñā-sambhāra*) refers to the various capacities for the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and so forth, which serve as its causes. "Perfectly complete" (*paripūrṇa*) signifies being fully endowed. "Attaining enlightenment" (*bodhiprāpta*) encompasses the ultimate limit of the fruit.
Regarding the benefit of sentient beings, the eleven [verses] preceding the chapter on morality briefly manifest its [qualities].
Regarding the section on "difficult wisdom," the initial question sets forth the enumeration, which is subsequently analyzed in detail. Among these, the first is difficult because it enters deeply;
the second is difficult because it involves skillful transformation; and the third is difficult because it entails extensive knowledge.
Within all the gates, the initial question sets forth the number, while the subsequent detailed analysis divides them into four: hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization.
The first, hearing, is self-evident. The wisdom of reflection consists of the contemplation of that wisdom. "The Bodhisattva practices below" refers to the wisdom of cultivation.

The cultivation performed by a bodhisattva should be explained according to its characteristics. Following this, cultivation that accords with the removal of obstacles will be explained; the removal of obstacles is realization, and cultivation is that which accords with it.

Regarding "that which is subsumed by the power of reflection," this clarifies cultivation in contrast to what preceded it: because cultivation arises from reflection, it is said to be subsumed by reflection.

The lower realization through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*). This realization, subsumed under the power of cultivation, is elucidated in contrast to the preceding [realization]. It is termed "subsumed under the power of cultivation" because it arises from cultivation.

Regarding the wisdom of the stage of right concentration (*samyaktva-niyāma*), realization is distinguished according to its locus. That which is supramundane and non-retrogressive is called the stage of right concentration. Realization that exhausts the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is called immeasurable wisdom (*apramāṇa-jñāna*).

Regarding virtuous persons, first the number is stated, followed by a detailed analysis. Within the detailed analysis, there are two sections. The first section, consisting of five items, is a classification based on the types of practitioners.
The latter section, also consisting of five items, is a classification according to conditions, causes, and stages. The first five still pertain to hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization;

since realization is divided into two parts, there are five [categories] in total. Hearing and reflection are easily understood. [The remaining categories concern] self-benefit and benefit for others.

This is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). Among the latter two realizations, the wisdom that is non-erroneous regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is the knowledge of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga-jñāna*).

"Phenomena" refers to the general; "abiding in characteristics" refers to the specific. Phenomenal characteristics pertain to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the abiding of phenomena pertains to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Because ultimate truth is immovable, it is called the "abiding of phenomena. Within this, being free from views is termed "non-inverted," and because it eliminates doubt, it is termed "decisive wisdom" (*niścita-prajñā*).
The wisdom that is free from afflictions is the knowledge of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-jñāna*). Among the latter five gates, the first two concern the objects of focus (*ālambana*);
the next pair concerns the causes; and the final two follow the stages [of practice]. Regarding the first two objects of focus, "subtle" refers to the profundity of the sphere;

"entering according to its nature" means penetrating deeply into those very dharmas as they are in their true nature (*dharmatā*). "Pervasive" refers to the breadth of the sphere; "entering according to its nature" means...
The meaning is the same as explained previously. That one’s original attainment of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is the cause of this fault. Regarding the term "co-arising" (*sahaja*):

it refers to that which arises through habituation in the present and co-arises with the retribution; hence it is called "co-arising. In the subsequent section on the stages, the statement that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are all able to receive [the teachings] refers to the wisdom of the *āgama* prior to that stage.
"Dharma" refers to the verbal expression of the teaching; "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the purport of the teaching. One attains the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*).
Regarding the wisdom subsumed by ultimate realization, which is supramundane realized knowledge:

among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the initial inquiry first enumerates the categories and subsequently provides a detailed analysis. This detailed analysis expands upon the preceding six [categories];
