therein, the first four are categorized according to their objects (*viṣaya*), while the latter two are categorized according to their functional capacity (*śakti*). Regarding *kṣaya-jñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) and *anutpāda-jñāna* (knowledge of non-arising), the commentaries offer differing interpretations. According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, there is no... [text fragment ends].

The initial stage of training is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) when it is able to exhaust the causes of existence; it is called the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) when it ensures that future retribution will never again arise.
According to the *Abhidharma*, the "knowledge of exhaustion" refers to the arising of the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*) which is able to exhaust present afflictions;

this knowledge of exhaustion can be attained by those of both sharp and dull faculties. As for the knowledge of non-arising, it is possessed by those of sharp faculties but not by those of dull faculties; it arises in those of sharp faculties who maintain the thought [of its attainment].

That which has already been deluded and will not arise again is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Because those of dull faculties do not dare to guarantee that delusion will not arise, they lack this knowledge of non-arising.
Now, in this context, it should be understood in accordance with the explanation in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

Within the latter seven [types of knowledge], the first three are distinguished according to their essential nature (*svabhāva*), while the latter four gates are distinguished according to their qualities (*guṇa*). Regarding the two knowledges of dharma (*dharma-jñāna*) and inference (*anvaya-jñāna*), the commentaries differ in their explanations. [The *Tattvasiddhi* states:]...

In the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, they are distinguished by way of time: knowing present phenomena is called *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena), while knowing those of the past and future is called *anvayajñāna* (subsequent knowledge).
If one follows the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other such treatises, they are distinguished by way of realm:

knowing phenomena of the desire realm is called *dharmajñāna*, while knowing phenomena of the higher realms is called *anvayajñāna*. These two are untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is tainted (*sāsrava*).
Because it knows all phenomena, it is called "equalizing wisdom" (*samatājñāna*). A detailed explanation of these three is as found in the chapter on the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).

Regarding the latter four [knowledges], "knowledge of supernormal powers" (*abhijñājñāna*) refers to the knowledge of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). "Knowledge of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇajñāna*) refers to the penetration of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), as it knows the characteristics of phenomena.

"Skillful means of the ten powers" (*daśabalopāya*) refers to the causes of the ten powers; they are also called "skillful means" because they can be applied with dexterity. "Possessing the four matters" refers to the four...
The wisdom of fearlessness is fully designated as "endowment.

Within the context of removing affliction, the first four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are the wisdom that initiates teaching; subduing the heterodox and establishing the correct is the wisdom of universal transformation.
Managing one's livelihood and resolving disputes are matters that employ wisdom.
Regarding the happiness of this world and the next, the initial question provides the enumeration, which is later analyzed in detail.

Among these, the first five concern the distinctions of the Dharma, while the latter four concern the distinctions of transformative benefit. These clarify, in general, the effects of ignorance, negligence, and indolence.

Transformation and benefit: those who are ignorant have no understanding; those with the other two [defilements] lack practice; the negligent possess evil; and the indolent lack goodness. All are transformed and made correct.

The following section specifically clarifies these four benefits; together with the preceding ones, there are nine. Following the sequence reveals the order of the latter four types of transformation.
"Showing, bestowing, illuminating, and gladdening" are the characteristics of this sequence. "Showing and bestowing" refers to the initial presentation of the teaching.

It is said: "To show" means to explain and bestow by name. To illuminate and bring joy toward the meaning is what is first called "illumination. Because it explains and interprets so that understanding arises, joy is produced.

Within the section on Pure Wisdom (*viśuddha-prajñā*), there is first the question that sets forth the number, followed by the detailed exposition, and finally the conclusion. Within the detailed exposition, there are five pairs; the first pair is as follows:

Regarding the wisdom of ultimate truth (*tattva-jñāna*), there are two actual meanings presented here as a general summary. Because the principle transcends the delusions of the mundane mind, it is called "actual meaning" (*vastu-artha*).

Below, these are specifically elucidated. Because it transcends appearances and points toward the true, it is said "even unto" (*yāvat*); thus, nature (*svabhāva*) is taken as one, while suchness (*tathatā*) is taken as two.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the distinct gateways of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are termed "nature" (prakṛti). The uniformity of the Dharma-realm is termed "suchness-nature" (tathatā-prakṛti).
These two types are equally designated as the meaning of reality (bhūtārtha). Below are four pairs; these pertain to the wisdom of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

Among them, the first pair distinguishes cause and effect. Regarding the meaning of "flowing," there are two general headings: because the cause is able to receive the fruit, it is called "appropriation" (parigraha).

Proceeding from cause to effect is termed "evolution" (*pravṛtti*). Because cause and effect are divided into two parts, there are two types. The names of the primary cause and its result are listed separately.
Next, there is a pair that distinguishes them according to their objective referents; there are two meanings for "appropriation" (*upādāna*), which are presented here as a general heading.

Because the mental state (*citta*) is able to grasp phenomena (*dharma*), it is called "appropriation" (*parigraha*). "Grasping" (*udgraha*) refers to the reaching out toward objects; because this may be either erroneous or correct, there are two types.
Their names are listed separately as "inverted" (*viparyāsa*) and "non-inverted. Erroneous ideation is called inverted, while correct gnosis (*jñāna*) is non-inverted.
Next, there is a pair concerning the cause, which is presented by way of a general heading: "expedient means" (*upāya*). Because the cause can lead toward the fruit, it is termed "expedient means."

Regarding what should and should not be done, their respective names are listed separately: wholesome dharmas should be practiced, while unwholesome dharmas should not. Below, there is one pair that distinguishes them according to their results.
Finally, there are two [categories] that serve as a general summary; they are called "ultimate" because they refer to the ultimate point in relation to cause and effect.
The defiled and the pure are listed separately by their names: birth-and-death is defiled, and nirvana is pure.
These five kinds and ten kinds of wisdom are subsequently cited and praised. They are called "five kinds" because they follow five pairs of dharmas;
they are ten because they follow ten distinct classifications. Because these ten purities are ultimate, they are called "foremost."

The above constitutes the extensive explanation. From here on is the third section, which summarizes, praises, and reveals its excellence. "Skillfully resolving the unsurpassed" defines the essence of its practice;

"its capacity for practice" below summarizes the power of that practice; "attaining the fruit of Bodhi" concludes the power of the practice; and "relying on this to fulfill" below explains the basis by which it is attained.
From the question "How did you come here from [the land of] Dāna? onwards, this is the third major section, which extensively explains the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
From here on, the fourth section cites scriptural teachings to establish the proof, praising their excellence and exhorting study. This section contains three parts:

first, it clarifies that these six perfections were spoken by the Buddha in order to inspire faith in beings; second, it clarifies that these six perfections were practiced by the Buddha so as to cause sentient beings to rejoice.

Desire. [The Buddha] exhorted [the disciples] to train by praising the excellence [of the practice]. Within the first section, these six points are where the World-Honored One distinguishes [the teachings];

here, "I shall now briefly [explain]" is a general statement establishing commonality through testimony. From "As the Tathāgata has said" onwards, specific statements establish commonality through testimony. The initial teaching on *dāna* (generosity) and so forth establishes commonality through the practice.
From "Self-nature and so forth" onwards, it establishes commonality through the meaning. In the second section, [it concerns] the ascetic practices performed when he was a bodhisattva.
The preceding section generally clarifies the Buddha’s conduct; alternatively, it specifically clarifies the Buddha’s conduct through [the perfections] such as *dāna* (giving) and so forth.

In the third section, this "arising of bodhi" generally praises and reveals its excellence. Following the phrase "Great Pure Dharma," there is a specific praise that reveals its excellence. Within this specific section, there are four phrases: "Great Pure Dharma" refers to the dharma of initiating practice;
"Great Pure Ocean" refers to the dharma of gathering virtues; and "the True Dharma of all sentient beings" [refers to the dharma of maturation].

"Causes" (hetu) refers to the previously mentioned pure dharmas. The conduct and patterns of sentient beings are called "sentient-being dharmas. Because they are the basis for the conduct of sentient beings, they are termed "causes.
Because these dharmas are complete without exception, they are called "all-aspects" (sarvākāra). "Supreme treasures" refers to the aforementioned pure ocean.
Just as that great ocean accumulates and stores a multitude of jewels, these six likewise fully encompass all precious jewels of merit. Thus it is said.

The following section concludes by praising and manifesting its excellence. "Immeasurable virtue and wisdom" praises the breadth of the practice: the first five are termed "virtue" (*guṇa*) and the sixth is termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Because they serve as the causes for *bodhi*, they are called "requisites. "One who attains *bodhi*" praises the efficacy of the practice.
Chapter 154: The Four Means of Integration (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*).

Regarding this chapter on the four means of integration: what has been discussed above constitutes the practice for one’s own benefit; now, one must engage in benefiting others. Within the context of benefiting others, the four means of integration are used to transform sentient beings.
This meaning is explained in detail in the chapter titled "The Four Means of Integration" (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*).

Within this chapter, love-speech (*priyavāditā*) is explained first, followed by beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and finally common purpose (*samānārthatā*); the means of generosity (*dāna*) is omitted here.

If one were to further clarify giving (*dāna*), it would not differ from the previously discussed generosity (*tyāga*); therefore, it is omitted here. Regarding kind speech (*priyavāditā*), the initial question is followed by the explanation.

Within the explanation, there are nine parts: first, the number is stated in general; second, the categories and so forth are listed by name. As for "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), it refers to the essential nature of kind speech.
"Everything" refers to the characteristic of loving speech (*priyavāditā*). To speak with love toward that which is difficult to endure is called "difficult loving speech.
That all loving words are subsumed within this gateway is called the "gateway of everything. Speech uttered from a virtuous mind is called the speech of a good person (*satpuruṣa-vāk*).
Among all conditions, the practice of affectionate speech is called "all-encompassing conduct. Because speech can remove affliction, it is called "removing affliction.
Because speech can produce happiness, it is called "speech that brings happiness in this world and the next. Because the essence of speech is faultless, it is called "pure speech."
The following provides a detailed explanation.
Regarding the nature [of these qualities], there is first the question, then the explanation, and finally the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are five phrases.
First, "delightful" means not using harsh speech. "Truthful" means not using false speech. "In accordance with the Dharma" means not using frivolous speech. "Beneficial in meaning" refers to...
He does not engage in divisive speech. As for "speaking with living beings," this refers to responding to their speech with the four types of discourse.

Within the entirety [of this section], there is first the introduction by way of posing a question and stating the number; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, discourse that accords with worldly conventions;
second, from "having explained all kinds of merits" onwards, the discourse that correctly teaches the Dharma. Within the former, there are three parts: first, consolation...

Question: There are two [sections]: first, the expression of good wishes; second, the praise. Within the first [section], the initial inquiry constitutes the general [framework]. "With a relaxed countenance" and what follows constitute the specific details. Within these specifics, there are four phrases:
first, "with a relaxed countenance" and so forth, which manifest the etiquette of the inquiry. A relaxed countenance is the etiquette of the body;

speaking first is the etiquette of the mouth—these two form one pair. Gazing levelly is the etiquette of the body; maintaining right mindfulness is the etiquette of the mind—these two form another pair. Whenever one intends to inquire, one should first...
1. "Giving rise to the mind of inquiry" means that mindfulness is foremost. 2. Under the phrase "the two questions," the actual expression of consolation is clarified;

the inquiries regarding the road and so forth constitute the questioning, while the exclamation "Welcome! constitutes the consolation. Because one praises the excellence of their arrival, it is called "Welcome. 3.

From "In this way" onwards, the mind of consolation is clarified as being impartial and without partiality. 4. From "In accordance with" onwards, the words of consolation are clarified as being skillful.

It is not clumsy. The characteristics of incantation, aspiration, and praise are clearly manifest and thus knowable. Regarding the statement that within the correct teaching of the Dharma one speaks of a dharma corresponding to a single merit:
this phrase is the general summary. The dharmas of the six perfections can produce merit; they are called "dharmas corresponding to all virtues.

Below, these are specifically elucidated. To speak continuously is termed "constant" (*nitya*); to speak instantaneously is termed "equal" (*sama*). These are the foremost, supreme, and wondrous aspects.
The teaching of the Dharma is supreme. Regarding the term "beneficial," it means that which can benefit sentient beings. Below this, the conclusion is presented, both in general and in detail.

"All these" is the general conclusion; the remainder are the specific conclusions. Two types are enumerated. Following worldly convention, they are correctly explained by designating their distinct names.
Below, the preceding text is cited and contrasted to provide a definitive critique. "Consolation and praise" cites the first [section]. Above, there was also a vow; now...

It is omitted and not explicitly cited. This is a conventional expression that correlates names with their referents; it follows the first citation. Since there are many such passages above, it is based on the subsequent citations.
This is the formal explanatory discourse that correlates names with their referents.
In this difficult passage, first there is the question, then the enumeration, and finally the explanation; the text is clear and may be understood accordingly.
Within all the sections, the initial question presents the enumeration, followed by the detailed exposition. Of the four [sections], the first two concern the methods of instruction.

Next is the instruction (*avavāda*), followed by the transformation (*pariṇāmanā*). Within the preceding instruction, "severing hindrances and directing toward the wholesome" refers to the beginning of the instruction for practicing the five perfections (*pāramitā*).
"Cessation of the mind to treat the fetters" is termed "severing all hindrances. "Conforming to the path of departure" is termed "directing toward the wholesome destination.
The commencement of the practice of the five perfections is termed "the initial application of the method. This teaching is expounded for the purpose of accomplishing these aforementioned virtues.

"To those whose minds are increased by the abandonment of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), one speaks of the Truths" means that this concludes the instruction on contemplating the Four Noble Truths. To exhaust delusions through the contemplation of the Truths is called "the abandonment of all hindrances.
When the contemplation of the Truths becomes increasingly superior, it is called "the advancement of the true mind. One speaks of the Truths in order to bring about this virtue.

"Rebuking the negligent" means admonishing and censuring them so that they may abandon their transgressions. "Opening for those who doubt" means teaching and demonstrating the Dharma so that they may attain understanding.
Regarding the virtuous persons, first the teachings are questioned and raised; next, their names are listed. The first two are the admonitions. Those whose primary cause is to be disciplined—
Because what is taught is not erroneous, it is called "correct" (*samyak*). Because a rule is established due to an offense, it is termed the "Dharma of Discipline as a Cause" (*nidāna-vinaya*).
Regarding "correct emergence," for those who have committed violations against the aforementioned Dharma, one instructs them in repentance so that they may emerge from their karmic obstructions.

Next are the two instructions on "correct reliance," which means explaining the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) as the conditions for giving rise to the Path. Regarding "correct deliverance," it is correct...

It is said that he expounds the Path to enable beings to cross over birth and death. Below, the manifestation of the three wheels of conversion is briefly indicated, and below that, it is explained in detail.
Within the first gate, the location and the causal conditions constitute the "cause" (*hetu*). For example, when the first precept was established at Vaiśālī, this is called the "location.
The incident involving Sūdena’s transgression is called the "causal condition. As for the term "establishing the precepts," this explains [the following].
The method of subduing is to be understood as the second [point]. Regarding the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*) explained in the third section:
ragged robes (*pāṃsukūla*) and so forth are called the four reliances. "Unerring dharma" distinguishes these from the fivefold false dharmas of Devadatta.
As for the "path leading to the destination," nirvāṇa is that which is reached; because the four reliances can reach it, the four reliances are termed the "path leading to the destination. Second...

Among the four gates, that which demonstrates the departure from suffering is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). Within the fifth gate, the three types of demonstration refer to body, speech, and mind.

Regarding all practices, first the teaching is cited in response to a question, followed by its explanation, and finally its conclusion. Among the preceding six [gates], the first two concern prohibitions and permissions.

These are words of instruction. The latter four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are words of transformation. Manifesting all dharmas is the unhindered knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*);

because speech can manifest the Dharma, it is called "manifestation. The remaining phrases are to be understood by this analogy. Manifesting the characteristics of all dharmas is the unhindered knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).

The names and terms appearing in the present life constitute the unimpededness of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). The various delights in explaining the verses of the Dharma constitute the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

Within the latter seven [unimpeded knowledges], one initiates loving speech (*priyavāditā*) in accordance with generosity, beneficial conduct, and collaborative action; the first two lines accord with collaborative action.
One speaks with those who share in the same suffering. "Words of consolation" refers to using speech to comfort sentient beings who are terrified.

"Words that inspire joy" refers to opening the hearts of sentient beings who are distressed by grief and suffering so that they may find joy. Next, there are three phrases concerning giving in accordance [with the recipient].
To allow others to freely use one's requisites and to accept their words in vain refers to the giving of material wealth in accordance with their needs.

Allowing them whatever they require is called "self-indulgence" (*svairī*); providing material things is called "providing requisites" (*pariṣkāra-pradāna*); and personally attending to their service is called "acting on their behalf. Regarding "accepting in vain" and "universally receiving," there are two meanings:

first, from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, because there is no restriction regarding the gathering and benefiting [of beings], it is called "accepting in vain"; this does not discriminate between enemies and kin.

To encompass all of these is called "universal inclusion" (*paryāpanna*). Second, with respect to sentient beings: because they obtain benefit without exerting effort and without cause, it is called "receiving in vain" (*mudhā-graha*);
because they obtain whatever they require, it is termed "universal inclusion. To speak words that grant permission for this is called "loving speech" (*priyavāditā*).
Bestowing security upon those who are terrified is the gift of fearlessness. Being a possessor of the Dharma, one practices the gift of Dharma by teaching in accordance with it.

The two lines below concern practicing in accordance with what is beneficial: awakening the unwholesome by teaching the Dharma oneself, and exhorting those who have the power to request others to teach it.
Its essence is loving speech; therefore, there is nothing further that accords with loving speech.

Within the section on removing affliction, first the number is raised by means of a question, and subsequently its characteristics are explained. The four purities and eight noble [paths] are briefly set forth as headings.

The following provides a detailed explanation. First, the four purities are explained. Herein, it is for the purpose of clarifying the eight kinds of removal of affliction that the four purities of speech are taught.
Why? Because the eight forms of speech cannot be established without being free from the four faults; therefore, they must be clarified. Below, the eight forms of speech are explained.
These eight noble ones are called "noble speech" (*āryavāk*). The distinctions in the meaning of "speech" are as extensive as explained in a separate chapter; this should be discussed in full detail.
Within the exposition on the happiness of this world and other worlds, first the number is stated in response to the question, followed by a detailed analysis. The first five eliminate suffering.

The latter four are endowed with goodness. Among the former three, the first three remove the suffering of material retribution; the next one removes the suffering of karma by causing one to cultivate the practice of precepts;
and the final one removes the suffering of afflictions by causing one to attain right view.
The latter four are endowed with goodness so as to bring about the perfection of ethical discipline, right view, dignified demeanor, and pure livelihood.
Regarding the statement that "twenty kinds [of purity] are as previously explained" within the context of purification:

this refers to the twenty modes of teaching the Dharma elucidated in the *Balagotra-paṭala* (Chapter on Power and Lineage), which consist of fifteen types of conformity and five types of purity. It is these that are being indicated here.

Regarding the practice of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), there is first the question and later the explanation. Within the explanation, first its similarities and differences are distinguished in contrast to the preceding kind words (*priyavāditā*);
subsequently, it is analyzed in detail. Regarding the distinction between their similarities and differences, "like" (*yathā*) refers to the similarity as explained in the section on kind words;

that is, the characteristics of beneficial conduct are like the dharmas explained previously in the section on kind words, hence the term "like. Below, their differences are distinguished. As for these differences, they shall now be explained.

This is a general statement granting permission to speak. Previously, the Dharma was taught directly; now, this Dharma is used to exhort beings to engage in cultivation, and for this reason it is called "different.
This specific meaning shall now be explained. Below, it is specifically revealed: "All loving speech" refers to restating the meanings of the teachings previously spoken in loving speech.
"Benefiting and bringing peace to beings" refers to the meanings of the teachings spoken in that preceding loving speech.
Exhorting beings to undertake cultivation is explained in detail below.

Within the section on its essential nature (*svabhāva*), there is first a question and then an explanation. Loving speech (*priyavāditā*) fully sets forth and restates the previously explained methods of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
The limit of clarity and sharpness regarding how sentient beings should practice according to their respective capacities is as follows:

practicing the Dharma in sequence toward the clearly manifest and sharp Dharma in order to transform sentient beings is called "practice" (*caryā*). Because one encourages them to cultivate according to the sequence of those practices, it is called "sequence of the Dharma" (*dharmānudharma*).
To exhort others toward what they should pursue is called "orientation toward the Dharma. One who abides in compassion clarifies the causes for beneficial conduct;

because they abide in compassion, they are able to transform others out of pity. One whose mind is free from greed removes obstacles to beneficial conduct; with a true heart, they provide genuine benefit without seeking any reward in return.

The characteristics of the practice of exhortation, guidance, and establishment are sharp and clear. Exhortation refers to the beginning: it exhorts one to abandon evil and guides one toward the good.

Instruction is the intermediate stage: it teaches one to depart from evil and bestows upon one wholesome dharmas. Establishment refers to the conclusion: it disciplines one to leave behind transgressions.
Establishing and causing one to abide in the wholesome is called the "lower bond" (*adhaḥ-saṃyojana*).

Regarding all [these bonds], first there is the question and subsequently the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, the division according to persons; second, the division according to time.

Furthermore, the three citations of scripture are presented, followed by the enumeration of the three names, and finally, the detailed analysis. Within the section on the present life, the teaching is first given.

Seeking wealth; subsequently, teaching the Dharma. Within the context of seeking wealth, he exhorts sentient beings toward righteous merit and deeds (*dharma-karma*), and teaches them the means and crafts for acquiring it—this constitutes the activity of obtaining wealth in accordance with the Dharma, which he exhorts them to perform.

Regarding the preservation of wealth once obtained, he teaches how to protect it. As for "increasing," he further teaches how to cause it to flourish and multiply. This concludes the summary of the present section; below is the teaching [on the future].
Regarding the training in the Dharma: it is known that the training in clear knowledge (*vidyā*) is beneficial because it brings about renown and joy.

Through training in worldly dharmas, one presently attains great fame and the benefits of various requisites. Within the preceding section, the former part first taught the pursuit of a profession, while the latter clarified the acquisition of wealth.
In this present section, the former clarifies the benefit of the teaching, while the latter clarifies the teaching itself. The arrangement of the text corresponds to what follows.

In this world, he exhorts the relinquishing of great wealth and teaches the practice of giving (*dāna*). From "non-householder" (*anagārika*) onwards, he teaches the practice of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

This is followed by a summary. The phrase "because it is certain" provides the explanation: because the retribution in a future life is fixed, it is called "future benefit"; because the retribution in the present life is not fixed, it is not called "present.

The section beginning with "exhorting householders" clarifies the benefits of both worlds. "Householders and renunciants" identifies the persons who receive these benefits. [The term] "meditative absorption and supernormal powers" (*dhyāna-abhijñā*)...

The monastics and the laity alike exhorted him accordingly. "Successive detachment from desire" (*anupūrva-vairāgya*) clearly elucidates beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). The gradual relinquishing of the eight dhyānas is called "successive detachment.
This is what is meant by "binding. The following provides a detailed analysis: attaining the bliss of tranquility (*śamatha-sukha*) is the benefit in the present life;
being born in heaven is the benefit for future lives; and *nirvāṇa* encompasses both.

Regarding the initial inquiry among the difficulties, it is explained later. The first is difficult because it is past and lacks a cause; the latter two are difficult because they are present and obstructed.
The former is craving and the latter is view; all these can be understood through their various aspects and as they are manifested in association with virtuous persons.

Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the initial question provides the enumeration, while the subsequent section offers a detailed analysis. Within the first six gates, there is the distinction of those who are gathered through the two methods of "gathering" and "subduing":
those who are virtuous are gathered, while those who are non-virtuous are subdued. The final four gates concern the distinctions in the benefits of transformation and edification.

Transforming those who violate the law by removing obstacles causes them to give rise to faith; transforming those who abide in the middle causes them to enter [the path] and gives rise to understanding.

Abiding in the middle based on the Buddha-dharma is called "abiding in the middle. Having mastered the sūtras and understood the vinaya, one has entered the legal system. Having entered it, one matures others through transformative practice.
Having brought them to maturity, one causes them to be liberated and transformed so that they may attain the fruit.

Regarding the latter seven [categories], the first five gates distinguish according to practice (*caryā*), while the final two gates distinguish according to the Great and Small Vehicles (*mahāyāna* and *hīnayāna*). Within the first five, the first concerns the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

The phrase "protecting and nurturing through material requisites and encouraging them to achieve [the goal]" generally clarifies the wisdom of hearing; that is, one protects and nurtures them with material requisites and subsequently encourages them.

This brings about the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Specifically, "encouraging the abandonment of the Lesser Vehicle" (*hīnayāna*) separately clarifies the meaning of encouragement, while "protecting the Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*) separately elucidates the meaning of guidance.

Next is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Just as in the case of providing nourishment and protection—where the subsequent is categorized according to the preceding—the former [wisdom] protects and nurtures through various requisites, and it is the same within reflection;
therefore, it says "thus. To dwell alone in stillness with a single mind is correct reflection.

The latter three are cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Purifying hindrances is tranquility (*śamatha*); mindfulness is insight (*vipaśyanā*); and cultivation itself is equanimity (*upekṣā*). Because tranquility and insight are practiced together, it is called "cultivation.
In the Mahāyāna, these are divided into two; their distinct characteristics can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the removal of affliction (*vighāta*), the initial question provides a summary, which is later analyzed in detail. That is to say, one transforms [the practitioner] so as to cause them to leave behind the eight enveloping afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
While it is stated in the *Saṃyukta-hṛdaya* that there are ten envelopments, why are only eight mentioned here? A certain master of the treatises (*śāstrin*) says:

The two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are of the nature of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Anger is of the nature of hatred (*dveṣa*), and concealment is of the nature of greed (*lobha*); therefore, they are not discussed here.

Regarding the explanation of the happiness of this world and other worlds, there are four types of bodily action (*kāyakarman*): abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants.
There are four types of verbal karma; when combined with mental karma, they constitute one. Thus, there are nine kinds.
Within the section on purity, first the number is stated in the question, followed by the explanation, and finally the conclusion. In the explanation, internal and external are first distinguished:

external transformation being free from fault is called external purity, and the internal mind being free from defilement is called internal purity. Below, these are extensively elucidated. Five external [factors].
First, the introduction; next, the listing of their names; then, freedom from fault and separation from hindrances; finally, the four methods of instruction and treatment.

"Not following in transmigration" means not following along with the cycle of birth and death within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). Regarding "gradual sequence," one should measure the capacity of those to be transformed and guide them accordingly.

Regarding "all-encompassing," it benefits both ordinary beings and sages alike. Regarding "according to what is appropriate," one bestows the teaching by measuring the suitability according to the size of the vessel.
Next, the detailed analysis. Regarding the first gate, concerning those who engage in mixed evil conduct where good and evil arise together:

those whose previous conduct was evil are made to become good; those who were exclusively evil practice only what is unwholesome and possess no goodness whatsoever—they are called "faultless" because they are caused to leave behind the obstacles of transgression.
The following two gates may be understood accordingly. In the fourth gate, the mention of the "four castes" refers to the three vehicles and the happy realms.

This refers to the four castes (*catur-varṇa*). It continues until the point where "transcending the holy among gods and humans" refers to elevating the ordinary. "According to capacity" (*yathā-śakti*) means according to the capacity of others;

"according to power" (*yathā-bala*) means according to one's own power to bring benefit and peace to living beings. Within the fifth gate, regarding the superior, middling, and inferior goodness according to what is appropriate:

the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) is inferior goodness; the Middle Vehicle (*Madhyamayāna*) is middling goodness; and the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*) is superior goodness—each according to what is suitable for the recipient.
Skillful means for the benefit [of others]. This is called "external purity," which serves as a general conclusion.
Within the latter five [categories], the first restates the preceding section, while the subsequent ones provide a detailed analysis. The first is non-aversion; the second is indefatigability.
The third is freedom from pride; the fourth is non-attachment; the fifth is non-retrogression. Unsurpassed Bodhi is the ultimate state.
Constantly seeking non-retrogression in order to benefit sentient beings is called "inner purity. This summarizes the latter five.
Thus, by externally citing the preceding and internally combining them with the subsequent, they are consolidated into ten.

Regarding the section on "common benefit" (*samānārthatā*), it is first questioned and subsequently explained. Following the preceding pattern, there should be nine categories, ranging from "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) to "purity" (*viśuddhi*);

however, these are not discussed in detail here. How is it known that they exist? As stated in the subsequent text: from "universal giving" (*sarvadāna*) through to "common benefit," and up to the ninth category;
and from "pure giving" (*viśuddhadāna*) through to "common benefit," it is clearly evident that they are fully present.

Why is this summarized? It is because the aforementioned "common benefit" (samārtha) is identical to that of all other practices; it shares the same nature as sentient beings and possesses no distinct dharma apart from them.

This can be understood by analogy with what precedes, and thus cannot be fully detailed; therefore, it is summarized and not discussed at length. Within the text, there are three parts: first, a general clarification of common benefit;
second, "having attained this common [benefit]" and below, a clarification of its common benefit; third, "there being common benefit" and below, a detailed analysis according to the meaning.

Within the first section, the term "this meaning" (*artha*) refers to the meaning of one's own level of qualities (*svabhāga-guṇa*). The term "this goodness" (*kuśala*) refers to the goodness of superior cultivation (*viśeṣa-pratipatti-kuśala*).

This is because the benefits of one's own level of practice have already been accomplished, it is termed "meaning"; and because it accords with the higher stages through superior cultivation, it is described as "goodness."
Regarding the phrase "if equal," it means transforming others so that they achieve practice equal to one's own level.

Regarding the phrase "if superior," it means transforming others so that they likewise attain the excellence of further progress (*viśeṣa-gāmin*). Furthermore, this meaning may also refer to the sense of practicing these first six perfections for oneself.
Regarding the phrase "this goodness," it refers to the aforementioned three types of gathering [of disciples] that benefit others. Regarding the phrase "if [the other] is equal" and so forth:

within the first two types of practice—the stage of self-benefit—one benefits others by making them equal to oneself. If [the other] is superior, one bestows [teachings] upon them during the first two types of superior cultivation;

one benefits others by causing them to practice together with oneself. Because both the stage of self-benefit and the stage of superior progress involve practicing together with others, it is said they are "all the same. This concludes the summary.

In the second section on benefits, there are four distinct parts. First, it says that when a bodhisattva attains this "common benefit" (*samānārthatā*) for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, they become firm and resolute, clearly understanding that all things follow from it.
Second, in the end, they cannot regress, and there is nothing that does not follow from it.

Third, the phrase "Why? serves as an explanation for the first point regarding how all follow; it first poses a question and then provides the resolution. They think: "One who shares my common benefit will certainly be able to..."

I establish peace and happiness for sentient beings by clarifying them so that they give rise to a resolute mind. This is explained below through two methods: first, by way of conformity (*anuloma*); second, by way of reversal (*pratiloma*).
Because those who have received [the teaching] practice it themselves, this is the explanation by way of conformity. It is not the case that it does not descend; rather, it reverses.
Fourth, if one explains it in the same manner as below, there is none among the preceding second [section] that does not follow from it.
In the third section, there are first four headings, followed by a detailed analysis.

Regarding the first heading, "having the same benefit but not revealing it to others," this clarifies the virtue of having the same benefit as that which one has accomplished for oneself. To briefly define its characteristics based on the first stage (*bhūmi*):

the merits accomplished by a bodhisattva in the first stage are called "the same benefit" because they share the same name as those of other beings in the first stage; thus, there is no need to manifest them for oneself.
To manifest the meritorious virtues one has accomplished to those who are similar is called "not showing to others. Second, regarding "showing common benefit to those with different benefits":
this clarifies that following the stage below, one accords with the function of common benefit. The merits of the first stage are not the same as those of the lower stages;

thus, they are "different benefits," yet by appearing in accordance with the lower stages, one manifests them as "common benefits. Third, regarding "showing common benefit to those with common benefit": this refers to gathering sentient beings through commonality.

First, when one begins to practice and acts in accordance with [the Dharma], it is called "sharing benefits" (*sādhāraṇārtha*). When the benefit for others is ultimately accomplished and one gathers beings to share in the same [attainment] as oneself, it is called "demonstrating shared benefits.
In the fourth case, there is neither difference nor demonstration to others; it does not arise in contrast to "shared benefits."
The following provides a detailed explanation. Within the interpretation of the first gate, one first restates the preceding gate: namely, that those of equal virtue abide in the bodhisattva path.
This explanation of the preceding gate includes the point of "common benefit. Regarding the bodhisattvas of equal virtue who conceal their true virtues and do not manifest them:

In the preceding section, it was not shown that [the Buddha] differs from others; since his virtues are identical to his own, he does not further manifest his own virtues to gather and transform them.

In the second section, first the preceding section is restated. Regarding those inferior beings who fear the profound Dharma, this explains how he does not share the same benefit as in the preceding section.
Regarding his contemplation of skillful means and manifestation as being the same as them, this explains the preceding section.

This demonstrates "identical benefit" (*samārtha*). Skillful transformation that accords with others is called "demonstrating identical benefit. For example, when a *caṇḍāla* quickly attains benefit, the Buddha immediately points to the matter at hand and says:
"The Bodhisattva, in order to transform the *caṇḍāla*, assumed the form of a *caṇḍāla* to enable him to attain benefit, cease his afflictions, and become disciplined.
Transforming him so that he achieves goodness is called 'attaining benefit'; transforming him so that he leaves evil behind is called 'ceasing and disciplining.'"
Transforming others so that they sever their afflictions is called "pacifying distress. Transforming them so that they cease unwholesome karma is called "subduing.

In the third section, the preceding section is first restated: for the purpose of subduing those who are agitated, it is explained that within the preceding section there is also "commonality of benefit.
Sentient beings of the lower realms who possess superior roots of goodness capable of entering the path to liberation are termed "agitated"; in order to subdue them, one practices together with them.

Therefore, it is called "common benefit" (*samārtha*). By means of abiding in roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) or superior roots of goodness, common benefit is manifested. This explains "common benefit" within the preceding section.
That which is established by one's own level is called "abiding in roots of goodness"; that which is practiced through further advancement is called "superior roots of goodness."
The inclusion of "acting in accordance with oneself" is termed "demonstrating common benefit. In the fourth section, first the preceding section is restated;

"the mind itself being dissipated" explains the lack of common benefit within the preceding section, while "abandoning the benefit of others" explains that one does not demonstrate it to others within the preceding section either.
This concludes "Affectionate Speech. Second is "Benefiting Others.

From here below is the third section, which summarizes the practices, elucidates their virtues, and demonstrates the benefits of cultivation. This section contains three parts: first, a summary of the characteristics of the practices;

second, an exposition on the cultivation of virtues regarding the three types of practice from "Giving" to "Sharing in Benefit"; and third, [the specific details] from "Giving" to "Sharing in Benefit."
The phrase "cultivating purity to full completion" below indicates the benefits realized through cultivation.
Within the first section, from "generosity" up to "commonality," the preceding practices are cited; since there are nine categories of generosity, it is described as "various."

The same applies to the precepts and so forth. The following summarizes their characteristics: the perfection of the Buddha-dharma through one's own practice is separately categorized as self-benefit;
the accomplishment of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) is separately categorized as benefiting others. This is called the brief summary that concludes the whole.
In the second section, the passage from "from giving" up to "various immeasurable factors of enlightenment" restates the preceding practices;
what follows explains the cultivation of virtue based on these practices. First, three gates are opened; next, they are analyzed in detail; finally, they are summarized again.

Regarding the three types of practitioners who initiate practice and achieve its fulfillment within the previously mentioned opening of the gates; the two types of superior ones who give rise to and cultivate excellence;

and the three types of pure ones who perfect virtuous qualities and attain purity—these shall now be analyzed in detail. It should be understood that "body, speech, and mind" refers to the practitioner.
Since giving and the other [perfections] all arise based on the three types of action, they are all termed "formative activities" (*saṃskāra*).
Regarding the distinction between the two superior types—namely, the sublime and the untainted—it should be understood that the superior ones are briefly indicated here.

The excellence of initiating virtue is called "sublime," while being free from faults and reaching the ultimate limit is described as "untainted. The following will explain these in detail; first, the sublime is explained.
It is the unsurpassed, uncommon, and supreme understanding of the sublime meaning. It is called "unsurpassed" because no other meaning can be added to it;

this explains its supremacy. It is called "uncommon" because others cannot equal it; this explains its sublimity. The terms "arising," "activity," "time," and so forth, manifest these characteristics of supremacy and sublimity.
First, three sections are listed; they may be understood in detail below.

In the explanation of "being unstained," first the number is cited and raised, next it is explained, and finally it is concluded. Regarding "being unstained," the preceding is cited; there are four [points], which raise the number.
In the commentary, the section from "initially" up to "therefore one does not give rise to sorrow or suffering" constitutes the first [stage]:

freedom from the defilement of sorrow and regret. Because one has not yet cultivated exultation (*prāmodya*), one is free from sorrow and suffering; because one has cultivated the joy of self-abandonment, there is no regret.

The section beginning with "not distressing others" constitutes the second: freedom from the defilement of affliction and agitation. "Not distressing others" means not contradicting the benefit of others; it refers to skillfully protecting the minds of sentient beings.
Therefore, one does not afflict others. One is unattached, unmixed, and does not contradict one's own benefit. Being "unattached" means being free from various views;
being "unmixed" means being free from evil conduct and mixed evil karma. Because one is free from all faults when practicing generosity and the other perfections, it is called "untainted."
"Single-minded application" (*ekotībhāva*) and below constitute the third [section], the abandonment of the defilement of laxity and indolence (*kausīdya*). Within this, there are four parts:

first, "single-minded application" manifests the abandonment of the defilement of laxity and indolence; "exertion" (*pragraha*) is termed "single-minded," and because the focused mind is made manifest, it is called "manifestation.

Second, "firmness" (*sthiti*) manifests the abandonment of the defilement of regression. Third, "tranquility" (*vyupaśama*) abandons the defilement of arrogance and haughtiness. Fourth, "certainty" (*niścaya*) abandons doubt.

Regarding the defilement of delusion: because one’s own intention is resolute, it does not depend on others. Not being inferior in giving is its fourth aspect, the abandonment of seeking through differentiation.
Within this, there are three points: first, not seeking future fruits by means of giving and so forth; second, not seeking retribution from others.
Third, not seeking fame, profit, body, or life. The preceding section has provided a detailed explanation; below, these points are restated and concluded. First the restatement, then the conclusion.
Regarding these practices, "pure and accompanied by joy" restates the first [point] above: being free from the defilement of sorrow and regret.

"Not causing disturbance" restates the second: being free from the defilement of agitation. Since this refers back to the first point, it says "not disturbing. As for the term "single-minded devotion":
The phrase "dedicating oneself" (*ekāgra*) restates the third [point], the freedom from the defilement of laxity and indolence, as it was presented at the beginning.

The term "without dependence" (*anāśrita*) restates the fourth [point], the freedom from the defilement of seeking other things. These four [points] recapitulate the preceding sequence from giving to sharing.
The designation "free from defilement" (*asaṃkliṣṭa*) serves as the concluding summary.
Next, the three purities are explained. First, they are briefly set forth: "Blazing" is the first; "Immovable" is the second; and "Swiftly Pure" is the third. This is the summary.
Below, they are extensively elucidated. Regarding the entry into the Stage of the Pure Mind-ground, it is called "Blazing" because it is blazing and immovable.

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, because one cultivates the mind with diligent application without even momentary interruption, it is called "immovable" (*acala*). Because one cultivates this immovability, it is called "blazing" (*jvalana*).
Regarding the explanation of immovability: when a Bodhisattva of pure mind does not intentionally give rise to any wholesome dharmas, it is because their mental cultivation has reached maturity.
It is called "immovable" because it is free from fluctuation. Because it has been cultivated to maturity, it arises spontaneously without depending on deliberate reflection.
The wholesome qualities it encompasses do not decline; because its practice has become firm and stable, it is named "immovable. Regarding these, the first method is as follows:
Next is the analogy; following this is the application. Within the explanation according to the Dharma, that which is attained is the practice of one's own level (*svabhūmi*).

That which is called "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) is the practice of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*). Thus, "not falling back" means being immovable within one's own level, and not falling back in the future means being immovable in superior progress.
The analogy and its application may be understood accordingly.
In the explanation of "Swift Purity" (*kṣipra-viśuddhi*), regarding the abiding in the ultimate stage, it is spoken of in broad terms as "one lifetime of continuous succession.

Within this Swift Purity, attaining the fruit after passing through a birth is termed "one lifetime. If it is the final body at the pinnacle of Swift Purity, one attains Buddhahood immediately upon birth.
Prior to its completion, it is called the "final body. The roots of goodness attained therein are termed "exceedingly pure.
Generally speaking, all ten stages (*bhūmi*) are the most excellent among the pure; reaching the ultimate limit in a single lifetime is called the "final body. This clarifies the state of purity.
There is no further explanation above regarding the meaning of "blissful purity" (*praśrabdhi-viśuddhi*).
What has been explained extensively above constitutes the summary of the names. Third, the summary of the three types of conduct summarizes the preceding bodily, verbal, and mental conduct.

Second, the summary of the two excellences summarizes the preceding sublime, wondrous, and undefiled states. Third, the summary of purity summarizes the preceding blazing, immovability, and blissful purity.
From here below is the third section, which clarifies the benefits of cultivation and accomplishment. This is because one attains *bodhi*;

whereas all preceding sections spoke of attaining the fruit of *bodhi*, this section now makes that explicit. Within this, first, the preceding practices are restated; second, the benefits of cultivation are clarified; and finally, it is summarized.
The passage from "from dāna" to "is the same" reiterates what was previously stated. The section beginning with "all giving" below demonstrates the benefits of cultivation.
However, in the preceding text, all nine gates—from essential nature (*svabhāva*) up to purification—were presented;

here, we address only the latter eight gates to demonstrate the attainment of specific fruits, without discussing essential nature. Why is this so? Because the previous discussion on essential nature comprehensively revealed the fundamental substance of the practice.

Regarding the distinctions in the meaning of the eight types of cultivation that are all equal, if discussed collectively, only one fruit is obtained; however, if discussed according to their specific differences, eight fruits are individually obtained.
Since this treatise discusses the specific fruits, it conceals the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, the intrinsic nature is directly discussed here as the essence of the practice itself.

This is not a matter of distinctions in the performance of practices or the initiation of cultivation; because the characteristics of the resulting fruit are subtle and hidden, they are set aside and not discussed here.
"All" at the beginning refers to practicing fully and without regression; therefore, that which is attained is firm and long-enduring. This adamantine firmness is its *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).
The long endurance of the True Dharma is the Dharmatā-kāya. One knows that the fruit is attained because it performs what is difficult to perform, such as giving what is difficult to give;
and because it encompasses all modes of conduct throughout all births, it is an object of veneration for all sentient beings.
Because the conduct practiced by virtuous persons is purely wholesome, they are supreme among all sentient beings.
Because their every action is always performed with complete perfection, they attain the immeasurable qualities and the primary and secondary marks of a Tathāgata.

Because they eliminate the afflictions of beings, they are not moved by Māra at the time of attaining Buddhahood. This is because they cultivate practices that bring happiness in this world and the next, thereby producing joy for all living beings.
One achieves the immeasurable bliss of meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth, because through pure conduct one is free from all faults.

One thereby attains the Buddha’s four purities (*catur-viśuddhi*), the three ways in which there is nothing to guard against (*trīṇy arakṣyāṇi*), and so on. Among the four purities, that which is called "purity of object" (*ālambana-viśuddhi*) is termed "purity of the objective sphere" (*viṣaya-viśuddhi*) in the *Pratisthāpana-parivarta*.
This concludes the "Section on Lower Fetters," Chapter Seven of the Treatise.
Chapter Sixteen: On Making Offerings and Associating with the Immeasurable.
Regarding the "Chapter on Cultivating the Association with the Immeasurables": the upper section concerns one's own nature, while the lower section concerns the cultivation of superior progress.

Within these two sections, the first, the Chapter on Offerings, explains the preparatory means for practice; the second, the Chapter on Factors of Enlightenment, explains the completion of cultivation and its integration with the Path.
Within this present chapter, three topics are elucidated: first, offerings; second, cultivating the association; and third, the immeasurables. It is for these reasons that the chapter is so titled.
This is titled "The Chapter on Making Offerings and Cultivating Intimacy with the Immeasurable.

The meaning of this chapter is threefold, as fully explained above. Regarding the division of practice, there are two parts: making offerings and cultivating intimacy constitute one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).
Immeasurable benefit for others. Within this, the merit of making offerings is subsumed under "self," while the wisdom of gathering [beings] is subsumed under "practice.
Regarding the preceding section on offerings, it first explains ten types of offerings to the Triple Gem and subsequently clarifies six types of the mind of offering.
Furthermore, within the aforementioned ten, it first clarifies making offerings to the Buddha, next applies this by analogy to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and finally summarizes them.

Regarding the initial inquiry within the section on making offerings to the Buddha, there is first the question and subsequently the explanation. Within the explanation, there is first a general introduction, followed by a listing, and finally a detailed exposition;
this is concluded with a summary below. Among the ten names listed, they are subsumed into five pairs. The first pair clarifies the objects of the offering:

"offering to the body" refers to making offerings to the Buddha’s physical form, while "stūpa" (zhiti) refers to making offerings to sacred shrines. As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, these are places where relics are present.
It is called a *stūpa*. That which lacks *śarīra* (relics) is described as a *caitya*. Now, this is generally referred to as a *caitya*.

The next two pairs clarify the time and place of making offerings, distinguishing between those that are manifest and those that are not. The following two pairs clarify the persons who offer worship.

There is that which pertains to oneself and that which pertains to others. The next two pairs clarify the matters of the mind of offering: "material offering" clarifies the matter of material wealth, while "superior offering" clarifies the mind of offering.
The final two pairs clarify the virtues of the practice of offering: "untainted" means being free from faults at the time of offering;
"the path leading to the destination" means that the offering is capable of reaching the fruit—the unsurpassed bodhi, which is the destination to be reached.

That which serves as the cause for reaching that [state] is called the "path leading to the destination. This path leading to the destination is termed "Dharma-offering" (*dharmapūjā*) in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, and is termed "practice-offering" (*caryāpūjā*) in the *Bhūmi-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Next, this shall be explained in detail. The bodily offerings are as previously understood. Regarding the explanation of *caityas*, the term *stūpa* mentioned therein is synonymous with *tā* (tower/pagoda);
originally it was a single name, but the phonetic transmission has resulted in different forms.
The second pair [of verses] has three distinct sections in the Chinese text: first, clarifying the characteristics of being present before one’s eyes (*pratyakṣa*) or not;
second, clarifying the benefits of making offerings based on these conditions; third, from "having obtained great [merit] through present offerings" onwards, manifesting the distinctions in merit.

Within the first section, there are only two categories: the present and the non-present. In the commentary, there are three parts: first, clarifying the present; second, clarifying the... [non-present].
"Present before one and not present before one": the three types of knowledge that are not present before one are excluded. Seeing the *caitya* of the Buddha is what is meant by "present before one";

this constitutes the first section. In the second section, first the "present before one" is explained; next, the others that are "not present before one" are categorized by analogy with the "present before one"; finally, it concludes the summary.
Within the initial "present before one," regarding those accompanied by aspiration, they vow to always encounter the *caitya* of the Buddha; this is accompanied by joy.
This means that because the mind of those who see, hear, and make offerings corresponds with this [reality], it is called "concomitant" (*saha*). This clarifies what is present before one's eyes.
From the phrase "as one" onwards, by means of what is present, the rest that is not present is categorized. Within this, there are four propositions. First, "as one Tathāgata":
in this way, the dharmas of the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present are categorized by means of the body of the Buddha currently manifest.
1. Not manifest. Second, as with one *caitya*, so it is with all *caitya*-dharmas: by means of the manifest *caitya*, the others that are not manifest are categorized.
These two form a pair. Third, one forms this thought: "Just as I am making offerings to the Tathāgata in his presence," and so on through the past and future;
here, by means of the manifest offering to the Buddha, the others that are not manifest are categorized. Fourth, from "I now offer to the *caitya*... and so forth.
Making offerings to all *caityas* and *stūpas* throughout the ten directions:

because those [offerings] are made directly before the *caitya* types that are present, while others are not present, these two form a pair. This is called "present and non-present," which serves as a general conclusion.
Below this, the third section clarifies the "non-present. Within this, there are two parts: first, a pair concerning the person who makes the offering, which clarifies the non-present. At...
When one does not see a Buddha-caitya face-to-face, this is called "not being present. Second, when facing a Buddha [statue], it is manifested as "not being present.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all offerings are likewise called "not being present"; even if one faces a caitya, it is also called "not being present.
Now, it is said that when a bodhisattva mentally contemplates and makes offerings to a Tathāgata caitya that is not present before them, this constitutes an offering to all Buddhas as one.
All caityas: the first is not manifest; this is called the "lower bond. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the construction of stūpas and so forth—the second—is not manifest;

this is called the "lower bond. Regarding "not manifest in detail," it is called "detailed" because those that arise are numerous. Above, the characteristics of manifestation and non-manifestation have been extensively explained.
Below, the second section explains the benefits of making offerings, which consists of four points. First:
1. Attaining great fruits; 2. encompassing brahmic merit; 3. not falling into the evil destinies; 4. fulfilling the requisites for bodhi.

The first three are mundane benefits, while the last one is supramundane. Among the mundane ones, the first two clarify the attainment of happiness, while the last one clarifies the departure from suffering.

Furthermore, within the first two, the former attains the fruit of happiness, while the latter attains the cause of happiness. Regarding "brahmic merit," it corresponds to the causes for the Brahmā realm of the first dhyāna.
Because it resembles [the merit of Brahmā], it is called "Brahma-merit" (*brahma-puṇya*). From here below is the third section, which clarifies the distinctions among merits.

When the object of offering is manifest but narrow, the merit is merely great; when the object is unmanifest but broad, the merit is even greater. Since both manifest and unmanifest objects are vast and extensive, this merit is the greatest of all.
Because the Buddha-field is supreme, there is no merit in making offerings to the Buddha that is not great.

Next, the offerings for oneself and others will be explained. Within this, first the characteristics of self and other are clarified; subsequently, the distinctions in merit based on self and other are clarified.
However, while the preceding section merely explained self and other, in this current explanation there are three ways of combining and separating them.
First, making offerings oneself is explained; next, making offerings together is explained; finally, making offerings by others is explained.

Regarding the discussion of their relative merits, it says that "making offerings oneself yields great fruit" because when one's own goodness is singular, the fruit obtained is likewise singular and great.

It says that "making offerings by others yields even greater fruit" because by exhorting others, one achieves both self-benefit and benefit for others; thus, the fruit obtained is even greater and more vast.
Regarding "the greatest of the great produced by both oneself and others": because the benefit produced together is vast, the resulting fruit is the greatest of the great.
Since the field of the Buddha is supreme, there is no fruit that is not great.
The explanation of the offerings of wealth consists first of the exposition and subsequently of the conclusion. Within the exposition, there are three parts: first, the offering of requisites;

second, from "incense" downward, the offering of respectful implements; and third, from "inexhaustible" downward, the offering of ornaments. Regarding the first section, clothing, food, and so forth constitute the requisites.
From "having inquired after their health" downward, it clarifies the protocols for the physical and verbal presentation of these gifts. "Inquiring after their health" refers to speech.
The Rituals. Regarding the ritual of the physical approach for welcoming: in the first part of the second section, the initial offering of incense and so forth constitutes the requisites of respect.

From the verses of praise onwards, it further clarifies the rituals for the offering of body and speech. The praise represents the ritual of speech; the prostrations and so forth represent the ritual of the body.

As for the "five-point prostration" (*pañcāṅga-praṇāma*), the two hands, the two feet, and the crown of the head constitute the five points. Performing the prostration expresses respect; circumambulating manifests affection. This concludes the third section.
"Immeasurable" (*akṣaya*) means "many. "Excellent wealth" (*viśiṣṭa-vitta*) means "fine. "Excellent wealth" is the general term, while "maṇi-jewels" and so forth are the specific instances.
In the explanation of the "excellent offerings," first the preceding section is cited; next, the excellence is demonstrated; finally, the conclusion is cited.
Regarding "the Tathāgata," this cites the first [section] on bodily offerings. Regarding "and the *caityas*," this cites the second [section] on offerings to *caityas*.
Regarding offerings of material wealth (*āmiṣa-dakṣiṇā*): if they are numerous or superior, refer back to the seventh [section], "Offerings of Material Wealth";
if they are present, refer back to the third, "Present Offerings"; if they are not present, refer back to the fourth, "Non-present Offerings."

If one performs it oneself, this refers back to the fifth [type of offering], "offering performed by oneself. If another performs it, this refers back to the sixth [type of offering], "offering performed by another.
Below, based on the seventh [type of offering], the excellence of the mind is clarified. There are four kinds of mental excellence: first, pure faith.

First, the mind of faith: it is appropriate to make offerings because the Buddha’s virtues are supreme. Second, the mind of single-minded devotion: the mind is free from laxity or negligence. Third, the mind of understanding:
understanding the ritual procedures for making offerings, and further knowing that the merit of offering to the Buddha is vast and great. Fourth, the mind of dedication: seeking awakening (bodhi).
These four minds constitute the first seven offerings, which are termed "superior offerings. Thus concludes the section below.
Regarding the explanation of being "unstained," first the preceding section is restated; next, based on what was restated, unstainedness is elucidated; finally, it is summarized.
The phrase "with one's own hand" refers back to the fifth [category], making offerings oneself. "To the Tathāgata" refers back to the first, bodily offering.
"And to a caitya" refers back to the second, offering to a caitya. Among the preceding eight sections, these three are briefly cited;
from here on, we shall proceed with them to clarify the absence of defilement. First, we shall clarify the absence of defilement by means of the internal mind.
Next, regarding the requisites for wealth, there are six points within the mind: first, not disparaging others, which clarifies the abandonment of pride and arrogance;
that is, not thinking to oneself, "I alone am capable. Second, non-negligence, which means being free from worldly pleasures such as singing, dancing, and games. Third, non-laziness.

1. Offering with a dedicated mind and diligent effort. 2. Offering with a focused mind and reverence, not treating even the lowliest with contempt; that is, having deep faith and respect for the field of merit that is the Buddha. 3.
Offering with an undistracted mind, single-mindedly making offerings without being moved by worldly affairs. 4. Offering without defilement, remaining free from other afflictions (*kleśa*).
These six types [of offerings] involve an inner mind that is undefiled. They do not concern material wealth, nor do they apply to kings and others who possess faith.
"Defiled": because seeking wealth through flattery and crookedness violates right conduct, it is defiled; because matters such as using yellow arsenic (雌黃) are base and depraved, they are defiled.
Since a bodhisattva is free from these, they are said to be "undefiled. These six types of names are established with reference to the mind.
Next, the explanation proceeds from here up to the "offering of the path. First, there is an extensive analysis; second, a summary and praise. Within the extensive analysis, there are three parts:

first, clarifying the path that leads to the destination through material offerings; second, clarifying the path that leads to the destination through sympathetic joy in the offerings of those who lack material wealth (beginning with the section on "not by one's own power");
and third, clarifying the path that leads to the destination through the offering of practice (beginning with the section on "constancy," etc.). These are the three.
Because all [of these] can lead to Bodhi, they are equally named "Reaching the Path. Within the first section, it first restates the previous offerings:
the term "extraordinary" (viśiṣṭa) restates the eighth [type], the "Superior Offering"; the term "unstained" (asaṃkliṣṭa) restates the ninth, the "Unstained Offering";
the term "material goods" (āmiṣa) restates the seventh, the "Material Offering"; and the phrase "offering to the Tathāgata" restates the preceding [passage].
First is the offering of one’s own body. Regarding the *caitya*, this refers to the second type of offering mentioned previously.
Among the nine preceding categories, these five have been briefly cited; from here on, we shall clarify the paths leading to those destinations. This section contains three parts:

first, attainment through one's own power, which means obtaining wealth through the application of one's own skill and effort to make offerings; second, seeking from others; and third, attainment according to one's wishes. Regarding these...

Within the section on "Wish-fulfilling" (*cintāmaṇi*), there are five distinct points: first, a general explanation of obtaining wealth through wish-fulfillment; second, the transformation of the body into many forms;

third, the extensive performance of offerings based upon those many bodies; fourth, a summary conclusion; and fifth, the clarification that these offerings do not depend upon the appearance of a Buddha.
If one obtains [wealth] according to one's wishes, this is the first section. From "Mastery" (*vaśitā*) onwards is the second section.
For Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), wealth arises from the mind; this is called "mastery" and "obtaining wealth according to one's wishes.

The passage beginning with "Having prostrated to each and every body" constitutes the third section, which contains four parts: (1) reverent worship and offering, consisting of prostration with many bodies; (2) respectful service...
1. Offering of worship: many hands hold various flowers and incense. 2. Offering of loving-kindness:
many bodies praise and extol the Buddha’s virtues and his benefits for sentient beings. 3. Offering of respectful giving: many bodies present superior and exquisite articles of utility.

In the second phrase above, one personally maintains [the offering] to express respect; now, one causes it to be bestowed. This constitutes the difference. The section beginning with "Thus, etc. below is the fourth summary.
The section beginning with "Without waiting for... is the fifth segment. Next, regarding sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), the path leading to the destination is clarified.

Within this, first three ways of acquiring wealth are excluded, followed by the explanation of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). "Not acquired through one's own power" and "not sought from others"—these exclude the aforementioned [methods].
Now, the section beginning with "but toward others" correctly explains sympathetic joy. "Giving to other sentient beings" identifies the persons toward whom one feels joy;
"Jambudvīpa and so forth" identifies the places for which one feels joy; and "the offerings performed with superior, middling, or inferior minds" refers to the nature of the acts performed.

This is a matter of joy. Through the skillful means of pure faith, resolute conviction, and sympathetic rejoicing (*anumodanā*), one comes to know with faith that making offerings possesses great merit.

"Universal rejoicing" (*pariṣanda*) explicitly clarifies sympathetic rejoicing; the following verses praise it to manifest its excellence. To give rise to mental conceptions alone without relying on material things is called "minor skillful means.
Universal rejoicing and reverent compliance is called "great offering," which can accomplish immeasurable merit and assist the path.
This is titled "The Compendium of the Requisites of Enlightenment.
From here on, the third section explains the path to the destination through the practice of worship.

Regarding the statement, "One should cultivate with a mind that is constant, true, and joyful," this briefly cites an exhortation to study so as to ensure constant cultivation; thus it says "constant" (*nitya*), and likewise "true" (*bhūta*).
This is the practice of skillful means. "Equality" refers to the four immeasurables, which constitute the mind intent on the benefit of others; "true wisdom" is the mind intent on one's own benefit.
"That which is delightful" refers to the accomplishment through cultivation and practice. The virtuous mind that benefits both is called "delightful";
a bodhisattva should train in this.
The following provides a detailed exposition. First, the initial section extensively explains "equality with reality" (*tattva-samatā*) and "protection.

Below that, it extensively explains the preceding "delightful" aspect. Within the former, it first extensively explains the "superior mind. Because its initial cultivation is difficult to maintain constantly, it is called "for a short time," continuing until the limit of its manifestation is reached.
Regarding the "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) below, it extensively explains the preceding "true mind. This contains three parts: first, the instruction on observation.
Regarding the phenomena of birth-and-death and nirvana, and defilement and purity: the second teaching involves practicing the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) to incline toward nirvana;

among these, the recollection of the perfections (*pāramitānusmṛti*) corresponds to the recollection of morality (*śīlānusmṛti*) and the recollection of giving (*tyāgānusmṛti*) within the six recollections, with the recollection of the heavens (*devatānusmṛti*) being omitted for brevity.
