The third teaching involves contemplating the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to be able to transcend birth-and-death; herein there are two parts: first, the teaching on preliminary contemplation; second, the illustration of ultimate accomplishment. Within the first section, up to...

For a short time, one practices the skillful means of contemplation through a minor degree of patience regarding the Dharma. It is called "a short time" because the initial practice is difficult to sustain for long. Contemplating the Dharma without breadth is termed "minor patience" (*kṣānti*);

here, "patience" (*kṣānti*) is synonymous with "understanding. The following clarifies that which is accomplished: it refers to the contemplation accomplished by knowing that [reality] is beyond words and so forth.

The true essence transcends speech, hence it is called the "nature beyond words" (*nirabhilāpyatva*). To be in profound accord is termed "suchness" (*tathatā*). To be free from characteristics and unimpeded is designated as...

Liberation. This refers to taking the principle of the Dharma as liberation. To know this is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). It is the mind produced by departing from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
When the grasping mind ceases, it is called "departing from false conceptualization. Because the characteristics of the grasped object are severed, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).

This clarifies that which is to be abandoned. The concentration of the mind upon the Dharma is called "abiding of the mind" (*cittasthiti*). This reveals that which is accomplished. This teaches a brief contemplation; what follows below serves as an illustration.

It is ultimately accomplished. Having attained a slight degree of patience regarding the Dharma, and having already cultivated that patience, one is able to know that the self-nature of phenomena is beyond verbal expression, free from all conceptual constructions, and to abide in a signless mind.
How much more so when there is extensive contemplation; because this extensive contemplation surpasses the former, it is said to be "superior.

Next, the following section extensively explains the aforementioned joyful mind. First, the practice for oneself is clarified; second, the benefit of others is clarified. Within the practice for oneself, one guards the precepts and remains free from transgressions.
The remainder are the gathering of virtue. Calm abiding and insight are the path; because they are the skillfulness of the path, they are called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
The various *pāramitās* constitute its practice. The following clarifies benefiting others: the various virtuous means of gathering beings, namely the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The preceding extensive analysis is termed "conclusion" (*nigamana*). What follows below is the "praise for manifesting excellence" (*praśaṃsā-prakāśana*), which constitutes the conclusion.

From "the foremost" (*agra*) onwards is the praise for manifesting excellence; "foremost," "supreme," "most excellent," and "unsurpassed" are direct praises that manifest its excellence. From "prior to this" (*pūrva etasmāt*) onwards, it manifests excellence by contrasting it with inferior states.

Regarding "this path leading to the destination" (*yena yāty-akṣayam padam*): first, in terms of material wealth and affairs, it clarifies that the path leading to the destination is no different from the previous nine paths.
One must not say that it is superior. Later, when one reaches the stage of the *cittavajra* (mind-vidyā) through sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) and practice, it surpasses the previous nine;
this present section is based on that stage. Therefore, it is said that the previous nine do not apply here. Thus, these ten [stages] conclude the offering to the Buddha.
Just as with the offerings to the Buddha, the subsequent sections describe the methods for offering to the Dharma and the Saṅgha; these three lower sections collectively conclude the preceding part.
The upper portion clarifies the act of making offerings, while the lower portion clarifies the mind of offering. It provides a general summary of the six pure minds generated toward the Tathāgata.

As clarified in the section on the "Concluding Verses," these six types of mind apply universally to offerings made to the Three Jewels; however, because the Tathāgata is mentioned first, he is referred to specifically here. Next, they will be explained individually. The first five are easily understood. Regarding the sixth category, "all worldly and supramundane possessors": 1. Worldly possessors of wealth who have not yet generated the resolve for awakening (bodhicitta). 2. Those who have generated the resolve for awakening but have not yet attained the path of seeing (darśanamārga). 3. Those who have attained the path of seeing but have not yet attained the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). 4. Those who have attained the path of cultivation but have not yet attained the fruit of Arhatship. 5. Those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship but have not yet attained the stage of Pratyekabuddha. 6. Those who have attained the stage of Pratyekabuddha but have not yet attained the stage of Bodhisattva. 7. Those who have attained the stage of Bodhisattva but have not yet attained Buddhahood. 8. Those who have attained Buddhahood but have not yet entered parinirvāṇa. 9. Those who have entered parinirvāṇa. Among these, the first seven are worldly, while the latter two are supramundane. Furthermore, regarding "worldly" and "supramundane": the first seven are worldly, while the latter two are supramundane. Moreover, among the former, the first six are mundane, while the seventh is supramundane. Among the latter two, the one who has not yet entered parinirvāṇa is mundane, while the one who has entered parinirvāṇa is supramundane. Thus, it is said that "all worldly and supramundane possessors" are included. As for "possessors" (*dhanin*), this refers to those who possess the wealth of the Dharma. As for "offerings," there are two kinds: material offerings and the offering of the Dharma. Regarding the "Dharma-offering," there are two kinds: the teaching of the Dharma and the practice of the Dharma. Regarding the "material offering," there are two kinds: the offering of the body and the offering of requisites. Regarding the "offering of the body," there are two kinds: the offering of one's own body and the offering of the bodies of others. Regarding the "offering of requisites," there are two kinds: the offering of internal requisites and the offering of external requisites. Regarding the "internal requisites," there are two kinds: the offering of the sense organs and the offering of the limbs. Regarding the "external requisites," there are two kinds: the offering of clothing and the offering of food. Regarding the "teaching of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the teaching of the Dharma for oneself and the teaching of the Dharma for others. Regarding the "practice of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the practice of the Dharma for oneself and the practice of the Dharma for others. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through speech and the offering of the Dharma through mental application. Regarding the "offering of speech," there are two kinds: the recitation of the Dharma and the preaching of the Dharma. Regarding the "offering of mental application," there are two kinds: the contemplation of the Dharma and the cultivation of the Dharma. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma with form and the offering of the Dharma without form. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma with form," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma as written characters and the offering of the Dharma as vocal sounds. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma without form," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma as mental images and the offering of the Dharma as non-conceptual wisdom. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and the offering of the Dharma for the sake of the Dharma. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma to lead them to liberation and the offering of the Dharma to bring about their benefit. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma for the sake of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma to uphold the teachings and the offering of the Dharma to propagate the teachings. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the three gates of liberation and the offering of the Dharma through the four immeasurables. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the three gates of liberation," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through emptiness and the offering of the Dharma through signlessness. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the four immeasurables," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through loving-kindness and compassion, and the offering of the Dharma through sympathetic joy and equanimity. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the six perfections and the offering of the Dharma through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the six perfections," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through generosity and the offering of the Dharma through ethical discipline. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the four foundations of mindfulness and the offering of the Dharma through the eightfold noble path. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the ten powers and the offering of the Dharma through the four fearlessnesses. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the ten powers," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the power of knowing what is possible and impossible and the offering of the Dharma through the power of knowing the ripening of karma. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the four fearlessnesses," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the fearlessness of realizing all phenomena and the offering of the Dharma through the fearlessness of having exhausted all defilements. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the offering of the Dharma through the great compassion. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the unerring knowledge of the past and the offering of the Dharma through the unerring knowledge of the future. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the great compassion," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the great compassion that saves sentient beings and the offering of the Dharma through the great compassion that purifies the buddha-fields. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the three bodies and the offering of the Dharma through the four wisdoms. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the three bodies," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the dharmakāya and the offering of the Dharma through the sambhogakāya. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the four wisdoms," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the mirror-like wisdom and the offering of the Dharma through the wisdom of equality. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the five eyes and the offering of the Dharma through the six supernatural knowledges. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the five eyes," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the flesh eye and the offering of the Dharma through the divine eye. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the six supernatural knowledges," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the supernatural knowledge of the divine ear and the offering of the Dharma through the supernatural knowledge of the knowledge of others' minds. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the ten stages and the offering of the Dharma through the ten pāramitās. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the ten stages," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the stage of joy and the offering of the Dharma through the stage of the cloud of dharma. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma through the ten pāramitās," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the pāramitā of generosity and the offering of the Dharma through the pāramitā of wisdom. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma," there are two kinds: the offering of the Dharma through the four means of attraction and the offering of the Dharma through the three secrets. Regarding the "offering of the Dharma

This clarifies that the Buddha possesses complete knowledge of all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane. Because his knowledge of these phenomena enables him to serve as a refuge for sentient beings, it is called the "meaning of reliance.
This encourages one to give rise to a vision of the Buddha. By means of these six [points], the difficulty is resolved and his superiority is revealed.

The preceding section has explained the merit subsumed by the practice of making offerings to the vidyā; from here on, we shall explain the wisdom subsumed by the practice of associating with the vidyā.

Within this, first seven topical gates are established for exposition, which will subsequently be analyzed in detail. Of these seven, the first four concern the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), while the latter three concern the meaning of associating with them. Question:
Since this present section is intended to clarify the practice of associating [with the vidyā], why is there a question regarding the spiritual friend?

Indeed. Because it is intended for practitioners to recognize and draw near [to them], and because one wishes to cause people to study this as a means of making friends, it is necessary to inquire about them.

Regarding the first four [categories] mentioned above, the initial inquiry—"How many practices constitute a spiritual friend?"—asks about the essential nature of the virtues and conduct of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

The inquiry—"In how many practices does a spiritual friend provide unimpeded guidance?"—asks about the mental states of a spiritual friend. Furthermore, there are several practices for abiding in a pure mind.

Regarding the locus: I ask about the protocols for a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in gathering and transforming others. The sphere in which worldly beings conceive faith is called the "locus of faith. Now I ask:
how many modes of conduct must a spiritual friend possess to serve as a dwelling place for the pure faith of sentient beings?

How many modes of conduct are required to discipline beings as the duty of a spiritual friend? I ask about the methods by which a spiritual friend provides instruction and transformation; by what means does one gather and transform sentient beings?

Birth serves as the activity for benefiting spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Below, the inquiry concerns "familiarity" (*sevā*): how many types of conduct constitute familiarity? This asks about the ritual of familiarity.
Furthermore, how many types of mental orientations (*saṃjñā*) characterize one who regards them as a spiritual friend? This asks about the mental state of familiarity.

Moreover, how many types of conduct characterize one who is free from such mental orientations? This asks about the faults to be abandoned. Below, these preceding questions are explained in detail in successive order. First, let us clarify this.
Consciousness. Later, the practice of cultivation will be explained.
Within the first section, eight matters are established to provide a general overview of the conduct of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); these will be detailed individually below.

Of these, the first three concern one’s own practice, while the latter five concern the benefit of others. Within the former—concerning one’s own practice—the well-established moral discipline clarifies conduct that is free from faults.

The latter two encompass the accumulation of merit. "Much learning and awakening" clarify that one possesses understanding; "attaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth" demonstrates that one possesses practice.

Meditative concentration refers to the cultivation of wisdom through mundane concentration, as well as other practices of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* that are untainted (*anāsrava*). Within the subsequent section on benefiting others:
The first four are mental actions (*manas-karman*), and the last one is vocal action (*vāk-karman*); their characteristics are manifest and thus easily understood.
In the second section, the first part is general and the latter is specific. Within the initial general section, there are five points that enumerate the categories.

As for the phrase "endowed with all such meritorious qualities," this refers back to what preceded to introduce what follows; being fully equipped with the eight types of knowledge, conduct, and virtues is termed "all virtues."

Possessing good spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Their activities are unimpeded, manifesting these five abilities; based on the aforementioned virtues, by means of these five minds, they are able to act as spiritual friends, providing guidance without obstruction.
In the subsequent detailed exposition, the first is the vow of transformation. Regarding "first desiring to bring peace":
if, in whatever one practices, one does not first desire to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, then one will abandon others and be unwilling to benefit them.
It is called "having obstruction" because, in the practice undertaken, one first gives rise to the aspirational mind with the desire to bring peace to sentient beings;

subsequently, because one is able to benefit them, it attains "non-obstruction. Regarding the next two types of transformative wisdom, that which correctly knows reality without inversion regarding pleasure is its correct wisdom.

If one employs skillful means, this constitutes skillful wisdom (*kauśalyajñāna*). Because it is skillful, it possesses power. If one employs skillful means by speaking in accordance [with the listener], this refers to the general presentation of the subject matter.

From the phrase "skillfully able" (*śaknoti*) onwards, the text correctly clarifies the power of skillfulness. "Able to accord with" (*anulomayati*) means to accord with the production of wholesome states (*kuśala*).
To subdue those who have been born [in evil states] means to discipline them so that they may leave behind evil. Both of these [types of conversion] possess this power.
As for the latter two transformative minds, they do not weary of constant transformation, treating others with impartiality and equality.

In the third section, five matters of the locus of faith are presented collectively as a general heading. It is shown that others rejoice upon hearing [of these], let alone those who see them directly;
this demonstrates the excellence of the faith generated by these five matters. Below, they are explained individually. The first two are worthy of reverence; the latter three are worthy of affection.

Among the preceding [categories], the first concerns clothing that accords with the Dharma; the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*) is listed by name and explained individually below. Regarding "tranquility" (*śānti*):

it means that one’s attire is composed and deliberate, without agitation or movement. "Possessing full deportment" means that the entire body is aligned, clarifying that one is free from other faults.

As stated in the Vinaya: wearing the inner robe in a neat and orderly manner, wearing the three robes in a neat and orderly manner, not tucking up the robes, and not covering the head—these are called being "fully endowed.
The following section clarifies the gravity of the three types of action; "the mind dwelling in peace" means guarding the mind so that it abides in the Dharma.
The actions of body, speech, and mind are neither fickle nor restless, and are free from the faults of violating the Dharma. "Fickleness" refers to the mind; "restlessness" refers to body and speech.
Regarding the latter three [qualities], the first is non-deceitfulness, the next is non-envy, and the last clarifies non-miserliness and non-greed.

Therefore, it is "lovable. Regarding the listing of names without flattery, the explanation below will clarify this. Regarding the listing of names without envy, there are three parts to the explanation below.
First, one does not give rise to a mind of envy toward the fame and profit obtained by others; "others" refers to those who preach the Dharma.

Furthermore, obtaining wealth and profit constitutes benefiting others; one should not be envious of this. Second, one should always humble oneself and encourage others to receive fame and profit for themselves—this is encouraging them to speak of giving fame to others.
If wealth is directed toward oneself, one should encourage it to be given to others, which is benefiting others with profit.
One who is free from flattery and hypocrisy acts with sincerity when giving; because of this sincerity of heart, one is requested to speak without guile.

When giving wealth, one is not deceitful; those whose minds are always joyful will have no subsequent regret. Third, seeing others inferior to oneself, one assists them in generating joy in regard to their fame and profit.

Seeing others preach the Dharma, seeing others attain renown, and seeing others obtain benefit and happiness, one gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) because one desires that they obtain what one has obtained oneself; thus, one manifests deep joy. The Bodhisattva constantly desires...
To bring forth fame and profit for others, he now personally attains [these] in accordance with his original vow; thus, his joy is profound.
In the fifth phrase, "contentment and little accumulation" clarifies his lack of greed, while "being able to relinquish what has been obtained" demonstrates his lack of stinginess.
In the fourth section, five matters for training and guiding sentient beings are first presented in general; they are subsequently explained in detail.

The first three concern instruction (*śikṣā*), the next one concerns admonition (*avavāda*), and the last one concerns transformation (*vinaya*). Within the preceding instruction, there are distinctions between the beginning, middle, and end; therefore, there are three phrases.
"Initial speech" refers to speech that leads and guides one toward the arising of affection and joy. "Speech associated with mindfulness" encourages the arising of a virtuous mind.
"Instructional speech" refers to the teaching of the Dharma based upon the mind. "Admonitory speech" concerns the gains and losses regarding the practice based on what was previously instructed.
Instruction and exhortation serve to bring about the benefit of practice. To "preach the Dharma" means to provide instruction and transformation.

Because [beings] previously lacked faith in and did not cultivate the Dharma, one preaches the Dharma to instruct and transform them so that they will practice it. By this, the five [categories] below are cited to refer to other teachings.

In the fifth section, the four matters that constitute fulfillment are presented collectively as a general heading. Because one is fully equipped with the practice of attending upon [the teacher], they are termed "fulfilled.

Below, these are explained individually. The first clarifies respectful service and making offerings; providing sustenance at all times, whether one is ill or healthy, specifically defines the act of offering.
What follows clarifies the mental state of offering, which is fourfold: first, the mind of affectionate regard, characterized by a desire for close attachment.
2. A mind of reverence: inwardly feeling devotion and veneration. 3. A mind of pure faith: believing in what has been taught. 4. A mind of benefit:
intending to bring about their welfare. 2. Reverent offering and service: at all times paying homage, inquiring after one's well-being, and welcoming them.

3. Reverent offering through giving: bestowing clothing, food, and so forth. 4. Reverent offering through compliance: if one is a dependent, requesting [the teacher] to serve as one’s preceptor. Below...

To act in accordance with what has arisen is bodily action that accords with the Dharma when one acts as prescribed without wavering. To speak according to reality is verbal action that accords [with the Dharma].
These two constitute a pair regarding what one has already done without contradiction. To approach at the appropriate time is bodily attendance;
to inquire by speaking about what ought to be done is verbal consultation. These two constitute a pair regarding what has not yet been done, acting in accordance [with the Dharma].

In the sixth section, the five perceptions regarding listening to the Dharma are first presented as a general summary; below, they are explained individually. The "perception of treasure" (ratnasaṃjñā) lists the name;
"difficult to encounter" explains its meaning. The "perception of the eye" (cakṣuḥsaṃjñā) lists the name; "the cause of innate wisdom" (sahaja-prajñā-hetu) reveals its characteristic.

The wisdom that arises immediately upon cultivation and understanding is termed "innate wisdom" (sahaja-prajñā). Because this innate wisdom-eye is obtained through a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), it is called the "cause."
Because of this cause of wisdom, the perception of the eye arises; this is the perception of the effect arising from within the cause.

The perception of clarity enumerates the names, and the attainment of the co-nascent eye reveals all things. This explains its characteristics: although one already possesses the co-nascent eye of wisdom within oneself.
If there were no one with knowledge to preach the Dharma and provide guidance, one would be unable to see the Dharma.

Because their exposition enables me to see it—just as a lamp illuminates objects—it is called "clarity" (*āloka*). The manifestation of the Dharma is not of a single name; it is designated as "all-aspected" (*sarvākāra*).

What is taught is not false, and thus it is called the "object as it truly is" (*yathārtha-viṣaya*). Furthermore, all of these can manifest both conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as they truly are.

This causes others to behold them. Regarding the first three contemplations of the spiritual friend, one forms the perception of worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*). Regarding the latter two contemplations of the spiritual friend, one forms the perception of the supramundane (*lokottara*).

In the former, one forms the perception of the fruit; in the latter, one forms the perception of the cause. One enumerates their names with the perception of great fruits and benefits. Unsurpassed Bodhi is that great fruit.
To observe the virtuous friend and form this perception of the fruit is, in fact, to give rise to the perception of the fruit within the conditions (*pratyaya*).
The path to *nirvāṇa* explains its characteristics. *Nirvāṇa* is the fruit of cessation; the path is the fruit of the merit of bodhisattva practice.
Because one attains that [fruit] by means of a friend, the "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) is considered its cause. Because it is preeminent among causes, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
One enumerates their names as having the characteristic of being blameless (*anavadya*). Furthermore, one contemplates these friends as being the cause for their own *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*.
Within those causes, the realization of the Dharma that accords with the spirit is called "bliss" (*sukha*); being free from faults and pure, it is described as "blameless."
One contemplates the spiritual friend as being that [object]. The following explains this contemplation: "not attaining the path to nirvana in the present life" excludes the aforementioned fruits;
since nirvana and the path are the aforementioned great fruits, they are termed "not attained in the present" because they have not yet been realized.
Having thus correctly contemplated as it truly is, one regards the spiritual friend as the cause for the perception of joy and the absence of fault within that causal state;

although one does not yet attain the fruit of the path to nirvāṇa in the present, because the spiritual friend brings those causes to fruition, one regards the spiritual friend as the perception of that cause.
The joy of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is the joy of realizing the Dharma within that causal stage.

That which is called "blameless" refers to conduct free from faults within that causal stage. As for what is meant by "cause": the joy of blameless conduct arises from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); therefore, the spiritual friend is designated as its cause.
One who observes according to reality examines the spiritual friend as the cause of that joy of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* and of blamelessness.
In the seventh section, the five points regarding the failure to attend to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) are first presented as a general summary. Next, they are explained individually.
In each and every phrase, the name is listed first, followed by an explanation of its characteristics. The first three [points] are easily understood. Regarding the fourth phrase:
Regarding the phrase "corrupting the flavor," this refers to incorrect terminology. A bodhisattva seeks the meaning and does not cling to words;

therefore, they do not dwell on these [faults] but set them aside while listening to the Dharma. The explanation below is clear. In the fifth phrase, "corrupting beautiful speech" refers to coarse and clumsy diction.

The Bodhisattva seeks the meaning and does not rely on verbal expression; therefore, he does not dwell upon these [verbalizations] but listens with a mind that has turned away from them. The subsequent explanation is clear.

Thus, the five "lower" points conclude the discussion of gain and loss. In these five instances, not dwelling [on verbalization] while diligently upholding the True Dharma concludes the section on gain.

If one of inferior faculties harbors inferior fetters, this is a fault. When one reflects upon the five faults of others and withdraws their mind from listening, it is therefore called "the mind withdrawing from listening due to the faults of others.
Because one withdraws from listening to the Dharma, wisdom declines and diminishes.

The former [immeasurables] benefit oneself; the latter benefit others. Therefore, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are clarified. First there is the question, followed by the explanation. Within the explanation, there are four parts:
first, listing the four names; second, subsuming the four into three; third, subsuming the four into two; and fourth, subsuming the two into one. The listing of the names is self-evident.
The meaning of the four immeasurables is extensive, as found in other chapters; this should be discussed in full detail.
In the second section, first the number three is raised; next, the three names are listed; and finally, they are explained in detail.

Below, their similarities and differences are discussed. “Briefly, there are four, yet [here] there are three” is the raising of the number. “The phenomena of birth have no object” is the listing of the names.

The distinctions of these meanings are as extensive as those in a separate chapter. “Establishing [them] below” is the explanation: first, within the context of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the three objects are extensively analyzed; subsequently, compassion (*karuṇā*) and the others are explained.
Within loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the characteristics of the object-condition consisting of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*) are first clarified.

To "settle" all sentient beings of the three categories—whether they are in suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—is to understand the object-condition of sentient beings. Because the observation of the mind is distinct and specific, it is called "settling.

The three categories of sentient beings are presented as a general heading, while suffering, pleasure, and so forth are enumerated according to their specific distinctions. In other sūtras and śāstras, this is contrasted with the categories of enemies, friends, and neutral parties.
And one cultivates the immeasurables. Why, then, does this [text] speak here in terms of suffering, pleasure, and so forth?

It explains that if these—suffering, pleasure, and so on—are still the cases of enemies, relatives, or neutral persons elsewhere: that which harms oneself is called suffering, and that is one's enemy; that which benefits oneself is called pleasure.

This refers to one's own kin. That which is neither harmful nor beneficial is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant," referring to neutral persons. The desire for their peace and happiness explains the meaning of *maitrī* (loving-kindness).

To form the perception of bestowing happiness upon the three groups of beings is therefore called "cultivating loving-kindness. The passage beginning with "pervading completely" explains the meaning of the "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*).

The initial arising of the mind intent on benefiting others is called "abiding in mental resolve" (*adhimukti-sthiti*). This concludes the section below. Within the *dharmālambana-maitrī* (loving-kindness directed toward phenomena), one gives rise to the Dharma.

Regarding the "perception of numerical categories" (*dharmagaṇanā-saṃjñā*): it is the contemplative understanding of the meaning of the conditions of phenomena through the practice of observing the numerical categories of dharmas. To observe that all arising things are merely the numerical categories of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is called the perception of the numerical categories of dharmas.
One observes that these numerical categories of dharmas are the cause of sentient beings; therefore, one designates the numerical categories of dharmas as the "conduct of sentient beings.

Thus, the practitioner of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) explains the meaning of loving-kindness: they contemplate that within all phenomena there is fundamentally no self or person, yet sentient beings act on their behalf.

They are bound by fetters and are deeply pitiable; therefore, one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Furthermore, to contemplate and preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings is also called the cultivation of loving-kindness.
This is termed the "concluding summary. Within the objectless loving-kindness (*apraṇihita-maitrī*), one abandons deluded views regarding phenomena to understand the meaning of "objectlessness.

Regarding the aforementioned categories of phenomena, not grasping at existence or non-existence is called "abandoning deluded thoughts. Thus, the practitioner who cultivates loving-kindness explains the meaning of loving-kindness by contemplating phenomena.
Emptiness and stillness. Contemplating how all sentient beings are bound by the delusion of existing phenomena, one gives rise to deep compassion;

thus, one arouses a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Furthermore, contemplating that preaching such a Dharma for the sake of living beings is also called the cultivation of loving-kindness—this is termed the "concluding summary.

The latter two [immeasurables] among these are omitted here without explanation, as their meaning regarding "immeasurability" (*apramāṇa*) can be understood from the first. Below, the remaining three are explained, beginning with:

From within loving-kindness (*maitrī*), there arise the types of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) that have no specific object (*anālambana*). These will be explained separately later.

Although the three [types of] objects are the same, because their respective mental formations (*saṃskāra*) differ, they must be discussed individually. However, below, the distinction between the three is made solely with respect to the object of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*).

Regarding suffering sentient beings, this is the object of sentient beings; one cultivates the thought of removing their suffering, correctly resolving upon a compassionate mind, and practices until it is fully perfected. This concludes the section on compassion.
The meaning of "measure" (*pramāṇa*) constitutes the concluding summary below. Regarding sentient beings who experience pleasure, this is the object-condition of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*).

To give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and right understanding toward their pleasure, and to cultivate the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) so that they are fully pervasive—this is the concluding summary below.

These three types [of immeasurables] continue in sequence as the object-condition of sentient beings. Thus, these three types collectively summarize the aforementioned three groups of sentient beings for the purpose of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the objective sphere (*viṣaya*): among these three types [of feelings], this third one—equanimity (*upekṣā*) cultivated by sentient beings—arises first;

therefore, it is singled out for mention. Following that sequence: next, one contemplates suffering as being identical to neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, and subsequently, one contemplates pleasure as being identical to neither-suffering-nor-pleasure;
hence, it is called "sequential. This passage on "arising free from delusion" and so forth clearly explains the mind of equanimity regarding the [feeling of] neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

Regarding suffering, one cultivates the perception of detachment from delusion; regarding that which has already become suffering, one cultivates the perception of detachment from aversion; regarding that which has already become pleasant, one cultivates the perception of detachment from craving.
Cultivating these fully, one explains the meaning of the immeasurables. This is called the "concluding summary.

From here on, the fourth section distinguishes the similarities and differences with respect to non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles. Regarding the "compassion based on sentient beings" shared with non-Buddhists: [the non-Buddhists...]

Furthermore, one practices the four immeasurables based on the four dhyānas of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). However, because they are unable to destroy the perception of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃjñā*), and because the Bodhisattva’s object of focus regarding the characteristics of arising is similar to theirs, it is called "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*).
Regarding the immeasurables that take phenomena as their object (*dharma-ālambana*) and are shared with the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*):

since the two vehicles are also able to contemplate phenomena and destroy the perception of sentient beings, and the Bodhisattva is similar to them in this regard, it is called "shared. The objectless (*anālambana*) [immeasurables] are not shared with the Śrāvakas.

Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas and the non-Buddhists: since the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) is attained only by Bodhisattvas, the four [immeasurables] mentioned above are subsumed into three.
Next, the four are further subsumed into two. As for the statement that "the first three are thoughts of bestowing happiness and the last one is peace":

within the first three types, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) directly bestows happiness, while compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) assist it accordingly; therefore, they are termed "happiness."

The fourth is the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*). It is called "peace" (*śānta*) because it abandons greed, hatred, and delusion, bestowing wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) equally. Furthermore, their characteristics are distinguished as follows:

the first three involve active engagement (*sa-abhisamskāra*), gathering and transforming beings according to their circumstances; because they pacify emotional afflictions, they are called "bliss" (*sukha*). However, because this is not ultimate peace, they are not called "peace.

The last one is characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), gathering and transforming beings through the principle of the Dharma (*dharmatā*); because it eternally severs danger and fear, it is termed the "perception of peace" (*śānta-saṃjñā*).
Regarding the statement "all immeasurables are termed compassion," this subsumes the four into one. Within this, there are three parts: first, the subsumption of the four into one;
second, the cultivation [of compassion] by observing the one hundred and ten sufferings of the realm of sentient beings, which analyzes the objects of focus;

third, the section beginning with "there are four types of practice" which clarifies the distinctions among the practices. In the first section, "all immeasurables are termed compassion" subsumes the specific [immeasurables] into the general.

In summary, "compassion" (karuṇā) refers to pity; pity functions to extract one from suffering. Since all four immeasurable minds (apramāṇa-citta) equally aim to rescue beings from suffering, they are subsumed under and enter into the category of pity.
This is merely stated according to one particular perspective. If one were to unify all practices through the practice of loving-kindness (maitrī), they would all become loving-kindness;
thus, it is said in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* that all practices are entirely for the sake of loving-kindness, extending even to sympathetic joy (muditā).

The examples for the inclusion of the characteristic of relinquishment (*tyāga*) are likewise. This is truly because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) share the same essence and arise through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), mutually supporting one another; this is what is called "compassion" (*karuṇā*).
The term "compassionate" (*kāruṇika*) is used to manifest the person by attributing virtue to them.

From here below is the second section, the analysis of the objects for the cultivation [of compassion]. Within this, first one cultivates the mind of compassion by taking one hundred and ten types of suffering as its object, thereby demonstrating the extensiveness of that compassion.
Subsequently, one cultivates the mind of compassion by taking the eighteen superior great sufferings as its object, thereby manifesting the greatness of that compassion.

In the first part of the middle section, the statement regarding the observation of the one hundred and ten sufferings of the realm of birth serves to clarify the mind of compassion by way of a general heading;

the following sections will explain this in detail. Within the detailed explanation, the one hundred and ten sufferings are first clarified, followed by the manifestation of the cultivation of compassion. Regarding these sufferings, a question is first posed.
Next is the exposition; finally comes the conclusion. What is the question? In the exposition, there are two sets of fifty-five sufferings;
therefore, in total, there are one hundred and ten. How do these two sets differ? As stated in the *Śīla-sūtra*, the first fifty-five [sufferings] contemplate the suffering of sentient beings.

The subsequent fifty-five [types of compassion] involve observing one's own suffering. Therefore, the preceding text states that compassion arises from seeing others suffer or experiencing suffering oneself.
Within the observation of others' suffering, one begins with a single type and gradually increases it up to ten, totaling fifty-five.
The final ten types constitute ten [categories] by themselves; taking the first type as a heading for the subsequent nine, they collectively form twenty.
Taking the first two types as headings for the subsequent eight, they collectively form thirty. Taking the first three types as headings for the subsequent seven...
Including the preceding forty, by taking the first four types as headings for the subsequent six types, they total fifty.
Including the five intermediate types, they combine to form fifty-five types; the latter fifty-five categories can be understood in this same manner.

Within the preceding section, the initial statement that "there is one suffering" subsumes all sufferings into a single category, meaning that all births fall into the suffering of accumulation (*saṃudaya-duḥkha*).

Bringing forth their suffering bodies—suffering that arises through conditions and accumulation is called "the suffering of accumulation" (*saṃudaya-duḥkha*). This explains the preceding meaning without distinction.
Next, two [types of suffering] are explained in further detail, consisting of four propositions therein: first, stating the two numbers; second, listing the two names.

That which arises as suffering from the transformation of the objects of desire—the fundamental basis of craving—is the "suffering of change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). The sensory realms of the five desires can give rise to the mind of desire, serving as the basis for sentient beings' greedy attachment.
That which is called the root of desire consists of affectionate thoughts; the destruction of these things is termed "change. Because this leads to affliction, it is called the suffering of birth.
The retribution of ignorance is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). This suffering does not arise from conceptual discrimination, hence it is called the suffering of retribution.
For what reason is it specifically said to be the retribution of ignorance? Ignorance is the root of all delusions; therefore, it is mentioned specifically.

Furthermore, because the portion of retribution one receives is dull and stupid, it is called "delusion" (*moha*). When extreme suffering touches the body, the expressions "I am suffering! I am suffering! manifest its characteristics.
For what reason is "suffering of conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) not mentioned? It is now established as the second [category].

Because the subtle pervasiveness of the suffering of conditioned existence is subsumed within the previous two, it is briefly not discussed. Third, delusion and sorrow are also called the "two arrows," using a metaphor to illustrate them.

[This is] an error. Because this suffering is profound, it is likened to being struck by an arrow. In the *Dharmapada*, sorrow is described as a "wound from a blade" and folly as "being struck by an arrow.
Sorrow is like a wound from a blade because its objects are broad; folly is likened to being struck by an arrow because the retribution of its suffering is profound.

Thus, that text states: "Nothing surpasses sorrow for inflicting a wound; nothing surpasses folly for striking one with an arrow. This is something no strong man can extract, except through extensive learning (*bahuśruta*)."

[The Buddha] excluded it. He spoke this verse because he praised extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). Regarding the four types of feeling (*vedanā*), there are bodily feelings and mental feelings, which are distinguished according to their basis.

Because suffering resulting from retribution (*vipāka*) depends on the body, it is called "bodily feeling. Because distress (*daurmanasya*) depends on the mind, it is called "mental feeling. Next, three [types of suffering] are taught in addition;

these are still the transformation and disintegration of the three sufferings (*duḥkha*). Next, four [types] are taught in addition: union and separation. Among the eight sufferings, this refers to the suffering of craving (*tṛṣṇā-duḥkha*).
The suffering of separation. What is called the suffering of interruption is the suffering of death. The suffering of continuity is the suffering of birth.

The ultimate suffering is the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*); because all five aggregates prior to attaining the path to ultimate *nirvāṇa* are suffering, it is termed "ultimate suffering.
Next, five more are taught, namely the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). Next, six more are taught. [As for] the former...
Second, regarding the internal [suffering], there is a distinction between cause and effect. Regarding the external [suffering], the latter four are categorized as follows:

the first two form one pair—seeking suffering when it has not yet been obtained, and guarding against suffering when it has already been obtained; the latter two form another pair—dissatisfaction with what has not yet been obtained, and the suffering of change regarding what has already been obtained.

Next, seven types are explained by increasing the count. Among the eight sufferings, five of the "five aggregates of clinging" (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are excluded, and the remaining seven kinds are taught because the five aggregates of clinging constitute the totality [of suffering].
These are excluded. Next, eight are taught in addition; the first seven are as previously understood, with "long-abiding deportment" (*īryāpatha*) as the eighth. Next, nine are taught in addition:
"one's own incompleteness" refers to the non-integrity of one's own limbs and joints; "others' insufficiency" refers to the non-integrity of the limbs and joints of one's retinue;
"incompleteness of kin" refers to the scarcity of relatives; and "incompleteness of freedom from illness" refers to...
Because of the presence of illness, one cannot be complete; because there is no suffering from illness, it is said that "the suffering of being incomplete due to lack of health" does not exist.
Next, ten [types] are explained in increasing order; their characteristics are manifest and thus knowable. Up to this point, one has contemplated the suffering of others and one's own.

Regarding the first category of suffering, there are nine types when general and specific aspects are distinguished. Within the first of these, the suffering of accumulation (*upacaya-duḥkha*), there are further nine distinctions according to differences in meaning. As for the preceding...
Regarding "suffering through others" and "present self-suffering," why are these nine types distinguished based on the former?

The explanation states that because "self-accumulated" is similar to the former, it is called the first suffering, with the remaining nine types following. In reality, within this category of accumulated suffering, the other nine distinctions are opened up;
this initial accumulated suffering constitutes one [category], while there are fifty-four within the remaining nine gates. Therefore...
These constitute fifty-five types of suffering. Next, their names are listed: first, the aggregate of all sufferings as one category;
second, all [sufferings] collectively; third, great sufferings; fourth, all categories [of suffering]; fifth, unwholesome actions; sixth, rebirth;
seventh, not obtaining what one desires; eighth, harm and injury; ninth, continuity; tenth, all modes [of suffering]. Hereafter, the enumeration increases based on these categories.

Explanation: The initial summary may be understood generally; however, I shall explain only the remaining nine points. "All suffering" refers to the second category. The subsequent explanation has two parts:

that which arises from causes is the suffering of retribution (*vipāka-duḥkha*); that which occurs during the process of transformation due to conditions is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

These two correspond in meaning to the three types of suffering mentioned above. "Great suffering" refers to the third category previously mentioned. The subsequent explanation has three parts: [the first is] the long night...
"Profound suffering," "various sufferings," "many sufferings," "uninterrupted suffering," and "heavy suffering"—possessing these constitutes the term "great.

"All gates" reiterates the fourth [point] above; its explanation below has four parts: the three miserable destinies constitute three, and the revolving of the happy destinies is included in the previous statement to make four.
"Evil conduct" reiterates the fifth [point] above; its explanation below has five parts: from the beginning up until one's own person currently acting and returning to oneself...

The suffering of birth resulting from past actions is the first unwholesome conduct of birth. The arising of afflictions through improper reflection is the second, the unwholesome conduct of generating delusion.
The frequent commission of evil deeds by body, speech, and mind, which result in future suffering, constitutes the third, the unwholesome conduct of creating karma.
Including the preceding, there are five. Because one commits evil in the present and returns to create offenses, they are termed "birth."

Regarding "evil conduct": since the very commission of karma constitutes evil conduct, it is divided into three types. Regarding "the suffering of rebirth," this refers back to the sixth [point] above;
the following provides six explanations: first, the instability of one's own person; second, the instability of wife and children; third, the instability of servants and attendants;
fourth, the instability of friends and ministers; fifth, the instability of kinsmen and relatives; sixth, the instability of wealth and property.
"Concentration. "Not following desire" restates the seventh section; the subsequent explanation contains seven [points], whose characteristics are manifest and thus easily understood.
"Contradictory and harmful suffering" restates the eighth section; the subsequent explanation contains eight [points], whose characteristics are manifest and thus easily understood.

"Continued suffering" restates the ninth section; there are nine [points] enumerated, though their names are not listed in detail. This may be because they are identical to the nine [points] mentioned above. "In all aspects."
This refers back to the tenth [section] above; below, there are ten explanations. Among these, the first five reverse the five aforementioned pleasures to constitute the five sufferings.
The latter five types are discussed separately according to their respective meanings. Within the first five, there are five enumerations.

As for those that are contrary to the five types of pleasure mentioned previously, they are explained collectively in contrast to pleasure, as described in the preceding "Chapter on Self-Benefit and Benefit for Others."
Happiness is the opposite of that, which constitutes the five kinds of suffering. Below, happiness is specifically distinguished through its opposites:
"caused by suffering" refers to the reversal of what was previously caused by happiness; "experiencing suffering" refers to the reversal of what was previously experiencing happiness;

"the antidote to happiness" refers to the reversal of using suffering as the antidote for happiness, such that happiness becomes the antidote for suffering; and "not abandoning experience" refers to the reversal of the aforementioned abandonment of experience.

For this reason, one undergoes uninterrupted suffering therein. From "having left the household life" onwards, the former [state] where there was no fault is inverted to become the suffering of fault.
There are four kinds of faultlessness: first, the joy of leaving the household life, which refers to the observance of the precepts; second, the joy of seclusion, which refers to the first dhyāna;

third, the joy of cessation, beginning with the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and fourth, the joy of bodhi, which refers to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). Now...

The term "leaving home" (pravrajyā) refers to the joy of initial renunciation. The term "separation" (viveka) refers to the joy of detachment. The term "quiescence" (upaśama) refers to the joy of cessation.

The term "the joy of awakening" (bodhi-sukha) serves as the antidote to the non-home; it is the inverse of the aforementioned "leaving home. The term "desire realm" (kāmadhātu) is the inverse of the aforementioned "separation.
The conjunction of sensation and perception (vedanā-saṃjñā) is the inverse of the aforementioned "quiescence. The term "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana) is the inverse of the aforementioned "awakening."
This is called the "lower summary. Furthermore, regarding the "five sufferings," they are explained separately according to different meanings; their distinct characteristics can be understood.
These five, together with the preceding fifty, constitute the ten [categories]. This is the third section, the lower summary.
The section following the "One Hundred and Ten Sufferings" clarifies the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*). "Taking that as an object" refers to the initial arising of compassion.
"Cultivating and increasing" refers to the sequence of its development. "Accomplishing and fulfilling" refers to the perfection of the practice of compassion.
Next, the eighteen great sufferings are explained to clarify the greatness of the compassionate mind.

This serves as a general heading for those who give rise to great compassion based on the conditions of those eighteen sufferings. Among the one hundred and ten [sufferings] previously mentioned, one focuses specifically on the most weighty ones.
Therefore, it is said that one gives rise to great compassion toward those [beings] based on the eighteen types of suffering. The following section specifically elucidates this.
How so? This is the inquiry. The list below provides their names. The first nine are the predominant, heavy sufferings among the first fifty-five;
the latter nine are the predominant, heavy sufferings among the latter fifty-five. Thus, there are eighteen. Regarding these within the first fifty-five sufferings:

There are ten distinct categories, beginning with one type and extending up to ten types. Among these ten, the first, fifth, and eleventh do not mention [the suffering of] the realms of existence (*gati*).
The eighth and ninth each mention two sufferings, while the remaining five categories each mention one suffering.

Thus, there are nine kinds. "The retribution of delusion" refers to the suffering of the retribution of delusion within the third [category]; it is singled out because the suffering of retribution is profound and heavy.
"The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)" refers to the gate of the suffering of conditioned existence within the preceding third [category];

it is singled out because the suffering of conditioned existence is deep and vast. "Ultimate suffering" refers to the ultimate suffering within the preceding fourth [category]; it is ultimate because it is long-lasting.
Therefore, these are cited selectively. The suffering of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) from the previous fifth section is not cited at all here.

Regarding "suffering due to causes" (*hetu-duḥkha*), this refers to the initial "suffering due to causes" within the previous sixth section; because this is the fundamental nature of suffering, it is cited selectively.

Regarding "suffering of birth" (*jāti-duḥkha*), this refers to the initial "suffering of birth" within the previous seventh section. Regarding "suffering created by oneself" (*svayaṃ-kṛta-duḥkha*), this refers to the "suffering created by oneself" within the previous eighth section.
"Oppressing others" and "causing those who practice virtue to suffer" are combined into a single phrase;
this is also the "suffering caused by others" mentioned in the eighth section above. "Suffering from bad precepts" refers to the "suffering of incomplete precepts" in the ninth section above.
"Suffering from wrong views" is likewise the "suffering of incomplete views" in the ninth section above. The tenth section is omitted here for brevity.

From here on, among the subsequent fifty-five [sections], the remaining nine types of suffering are clarified. Within this, there are ten gates. Of these ten, the first, sixth, and ninth are not mentioned at all;
the fourth and tenth each mention two types of suffering; and the remaining five gates each mention one type of suffering.

Thus, there are nine kinds [of suffering]. As for "suffering caused by the primary cause" (*mūlahetu-duḥkha*), it is that which arises from the preceding cause, as discussed in the second section above.

The foolish receive suffering as their retribution. As for "great suffering," this refers collectively to the great suffering previously categorized in the third gate; it is now mentioned here in its entirety.
"Suffering of the hells" refers to the suffering of the hells within the fourth gate, "All.

"Suffering arising from the wholesome" likewise refers to the suffering of the wheel of birth and death arising from the wholesome within the fourth gate, "All. "All natures" refers to the fifth [gate].

Among the sufferings of misconduct, there are five kinds of misconduct; these are now collectively termed "suffering of all natures," because the nature of the suffering of afflictions and karma is itself suffering.
The six modes of rebirth from the sixth section previously mentioned are not raised here in brief.

Regarding the suffering of ignorance, it was mentioned in the seventh section under "not obtaining what one desires": the desire to obtain wisdom and the lack of delight in the afflictive suffering of folly arise [from this].
Regarding "the increase of suffering," this refers to the suffering of the increase of afflictions within the eighth section on the suffering of contradiction and harm;

the suffering of continuity mentioned in the ninth section is not briefly cited here. Regarding "the experience of suffering," this refers to the second type of suffering among all types mentioned in the tenth section.
Regarding "the suffering of loathsomeness," this is also the suffering of defilement within that same tenth section.

The preceding section was the second [part], which analyzed cultivation with respect to its objects. From here below, the distinctions among the practices of compassion (*karuṇā*) are explained in detail.

This section contains five parts: first, demonstrating the different varieties of compassionate practice; second, distinguishing them according to their respective locations; third, manifesting the functional power of compassion;
fourth, manifesting its superiority through joy in response to hypothetical questions; and fifth, manifesting [the results] through the possession of four virtues.
Regarding the benefits of its cultivation:

within the first section, there are four enumerations, which will be explained individually below. The first two constitute a pair categorized by the components of cultivation, while the latter two constitute a pair categorized by the benefits of transformation.
As for "arousing compassion toward suffering that is profound, subtle, and difficult to know due to dependent origination":

By taking conditions as objects, it reveals the profundity of compassionate practice. By being nurtured over a long duration, diligently cultivated, and giving rise to awakening, it reveals the origin of the compassionate mind.
Because of long-term cultivation, when one now encounters conditions of suffering, one immediately awakens and brings forth what was previously practiced;
this is called "giving rise to awakening. Among the latter two benefits, the former is able to relinquish pleasure, while the latter is able to undergo suffering.

Regarding the previous section on "Relinquishing Happiness," for those who, according to their awakening, enter into the mind of compassion, this serves as a transition from the preceding to the subsequent. The phrase "In order to...

and so forth correctly explains the ability to relinquish happiness; it means that if one can perform such a grave task as giving up hundreds of thousands of bodies to bring about the cessation of suffering, how much more so can one give up a single body?

By using the heavy to illustrate the light, it is shown that the mind is capable of such action. Below, it clarifies that [the Bodhisattva] undergoes various sufferings on behalf of sentient beings. Since suffering is a phenomenon of retribution, how can it be substituted?
It is precisely because the Bodhisattva remains within suffering to teach and transform them so that they may emerge from suffering that it is said to be "substitution."
Furthermore, one may also undergo external sufferings such as flogging and the like on their behalf.

From here begins the second section: the classification according to location. This classification is twofold: first, the place of pure bliss, which refers to the Stage of Ultimate Perfection (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*) and the Stage of the Tathāgata;
the tenth stage is designated as the Stage of Ultimate Perfection. Second, the place of cultivation and accomplishment, which refers to the stages prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the stages on the grounds (*bhūmi*), when a bodhisattva cultivates compassion therein, they are cultivating all forms of compassion.
This stage of cultivation is that by which one swiftly attains compassion. Regarding this cultivation, the analysis of the objects of focus constitutes the cultivation of all [aspects of] compassion;
the manifestation of its complete perfection constitutes the ability to swiftly attain the manifest function of compassion. This applies from the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward.
In order to purify the stage of compassion (*karuṇā-bhūmi*), it is said that one "swiftly attains" it because the stage previously accomplished prior to this level is not far from it.

"Entering the pure mind" and below indicates the place where this is accomplished. The first part reveals the characteristics of its accomplishment; the phrase "not like... and below distinguishes the superior from the inferior.

Within the former, regarding those for whom one has the perception of extreme intimacy, one abandons the obstruction of distance; as for "loving concern," it is deep within the midst of affectionate intimacy, for there is naturally such intimacy.
It is not necessarily [a matter of] personal affection. A compassionate mother feels deep affection for her child; because a Bodhisattva is likewise, it is called "loving concern.

One who merely wishes to act for another’s sake naturally possesses loving concern, yet has no intention of actually substituting themselves for that person in what must be done. The Bodhisattva is not like this.

There are those who desire to act as a substitute for all [sentient beings] and do not grow weary, yet they possess only the capacity to substitute and cannot do so perpetually. It is not so with the Bodhisattva;

he is always able to do so without weariness. As for one who substitutes for others in undergoing suffering, there may be those who can do so without weariness when it concerns pleasant matters, but they are unable to endure it when it is suffering.
It is not so for the Bodhisattva; they can also take suffering upon themselves. Regarding "mastery," it refers to having the capacity to substitute for others;
because the mind’s effort in substitution requires much deliberation before one is able to do so, it is called "lack of mastery. It is not so for the Bodhisattva;

because their substitution for suffering becomes spontaneous and effortless, it is called "mastery. Within the distinction between the inferior and the superior, this is unlike the Truth of Suffering.

The term "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) distinguishes the Great Vehicle from the Small Vehicle. Within the Small Vehicle, it refers to the beginning of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), occurring immediately after [the path of preparation].

According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is called "uninterrupted" because the contemplation of emptiness during the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is not separated by any interval. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, however...

The eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*) proceed in uninterrupted succession. This is now the same as the *Abhidharma*. By citing the initial uninterrupted [moment] of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it includes by implication everything up to the ultimate stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
hence the use of the term "etc. (*ādi*). Since the Bodhisattva differs from that, it is said to be "not like" that.
In the final section, the distinctions between the Small and Great Vehicles are briefly discussed.
From here on, the third part reveals the capacity of its practice: compassion precedes all action, briefly clarifying that compassion serves as the head of practice.

Because these are performed prior to the actual practice, they are called "preliminary practices" (*pūrvāṅga*). The section on the "One Hundred and Ten [Verses]" below explains in detail how compassion gives rise to various practices.

Within this, the initial statement regarding "cultivating compassion by contemplating one hundred and ten sufferings" reiterates the aforementioned compassion; the subsequent portion clarifies the arising of practice.

Regarding internal and external things, there is nothing small that is not relinquished; based on compassion, one initiates generosity, and there is no ethical discipline (*śīla*) that is not maintained.
One upholds the training in ethical discipline by relying on compassion; there is not a single instance of patience that is not beneficial which one does not cultivate by relying on compassion.

There is not a single form of diligence that is not courageous which one does not practice by relying on compassion. There is not a single meditative concentration that is not correctly attained which one does not cultivate by relying on compassion.
There is not a single wisdom that cannot be entered which does not arise by relying on compassion.
From here below is the fourth section, which praises [compassion] to manifest its excellence. This contains four parts: first, the unique characterization of the person;

second, the emergence from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); third, the vastness of its gathering and benefiting; and fourth, the reason for its excellence as being purely wholesome and faultless.

If someone asks about the Buddha, one should answer that compassion is precisely this [excellence]. If someone asks the Buddha a hypothetical question to provoke a response, it is for the sake of what meaning?

The partial statement asks the Buddha; the Buddha provides the answer to manifest the excellence and certainty [of the teaching]. The response concerning compassion is a provisional answer intended to manifest excellence:
because one possesses compassion, one is constantly able to benefit sentient beings; therefore, one who possesses compassion is precisely a bodhisattva.
From "That one" onwards is the second excellence. As in the preceding text, the four are subsumed into one; thus it says, "That one is as previously explained."
The arising of compassion through transformative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*) is supreme; therefore, it is said that "toward all manifestations, [compassion] is immeasurable.

Question: Previously, the four were subsumed into one. Against what, then, is this "immeasurability toward manifestations" contrasted? Explanation: Although previously the four were subsumed into one, [the distinction remains].
Within this, there is no lack of distinction between the primary and its associates (*sahāya*). Compassion is the primary; the others are termed its associates.

Because the primary is considered in relation to its associates, it is said that [compassion] is immeasurable with respect to all sentient beings. From "having accumulated" onwards is the third excellence:

"gathering immeasurable fruits" refers to the vastness of the maturation (*vipāka*) obtained; "lovely fruits" means they are desirable as virtuous results. "Gathering immeasurable practices" refers to the vastness of the causes established.
Being consistently and purely wholesome, without any fault, is the fourth excellence.

From here below, the fifth [excellence] clarifies the benefits of cultivation. There are four virtues of cultivation which are first presented as a general summary; they will be explained individually below.

The first three [perfections] are for one's own benefit, while the last one is for the benefit of others. Within those for one's own benefit, the first two constitute qualities of self-maintenance (*svabhāva-guṇa*), and the last one is advancement (*viśeṣa*).

The initial statement that "one first attains dwelling in happiness in the present life" refers to the quality of realization (*adhigama-guṇa*); that "immeasurable qualities are fully embraced and increased" refers to the quality of scriptural mastery (*āgama-guṇa*).
The characteristics of the advancement for the benefit of others are manifest and thus easily understood.
Chapter Seventeen: The Factors of Enlightenment (*Bodhipakṣa*).

Regarding the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment: the preceding Chapter on Offerings encompassed the cultivation of skillful means; once that cultivation is perfected, it accords with the Path. The distinctions in the practice of this Path are termed the "Factors of Enlightenment.
To extensively expound upon this meaning is called the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment.
Within this chapter, the essence of the path is first established, followed by an explanation of the text. The essence refers to the ten dharmas, beginning with faith.
However, what is explained here both accords with and differs from the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*. They are said to accord because they both take these ten dharmas as the essence of the path.
There are two types of differences: first, a difference regarding presence or absence; that [sūtra] explains all ten, whereas this [text] only explains...

Sixth: Faith, compassion, loving-kindness, and equanimity are omitted in brief. Why is faith not mentioned? If it is said that it is not different from the "Chapter on Power," where it states that one extensively cultivates faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).

Why are compassion and loving-kindness not mentioned? If it is said that they are not different from the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) discussed previously in the "Chapter on Making Offerings," and are therefore omitted without being discussed.
Why is equanimity (*upekṣā*) not mentioned? It is because it is further stated to be no different from the preceding discussion on giving (*dāna*).
This chapter is therefore not discussed. The preceding chapters did not intend to clarify this faith, compassion, loving-kindness, and equanimity;

if they were to be explained here again, it would be no different from what was already said, and for that reason it is not discussed. Second, because the sequence differs from before, as in the *Dharmabhūmi-sūtra*, where the sequence is:
indefatigability, knowledge of treatises, knowledge of the world, shame and remorse, and firm cultivation. Therein, "firm" is explained in the same manner as it is here.
Immovable. In this present passage, first shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*) are clarified, followed by the immovable.

The remaining qualities—freedom from weariness, knowledge of treatises, and knowledge of the world—are practiced according to the teachings; their sequence is identical to that [in other texts]. Why is it not the same?

In the *Bhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, freedom from weariness, knowledge of treatises, and knowledge of the world are proclaimed as the essential body (*svabhāva*) of practice; therefore, they are explained first. Shame and modesty are firm, as stated.
The preliminary practices for cultivation and protection are therefore explained later. However, this current sequence is of a different kind:
since shame and dread of blame involve the avoidance of faults, they are clarified first. Because one avoids faults, the mind becomes firm and is not moved by external conditions.

Because it is unmoved, the mind is free from weariness and seeks the Dharma without fatigue. Because there is no weariness, one is able to understand the sūtras and śāstras; having understood the sūtras...

Because of this treatise, one skillfully understands the proper timing and rituals; being able to conform to worldly conventions, one is then able to practice according to the Dharma as it has been taught.

Next, the text is explained. Within the section on shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*), there is first a question and then an explanation. In the explanation, the two names are first cited and subsequently listed.
"Self-nature" refers to the essence of shame (*hrī*) and modesty (*apatrāpya*). "Basis" refers to the objects of shame and modesty. Below, their characteristics are explained.

Within the section on self-nature, first shame is analyzed individually, followed by an individual explanation of modesty. Furthermore, from "shame and modesty" onwards, the superior significance of shame and modesty is clarified in general;
this concludes the preceding section. Within the section on the basis, there are four items enumerated, which are subsequently explained in detail.
If one feels shame because they do not establish themselves in accordance with what ought to be done, there arises a sense of shame and remorse for failing to perform what is wholesome.
If one feels shame because they establish themselves in accordance with what ought not to be done, there arises a sense of shame and remorse for performing what is unwholesome.
These two form one pair. As for the third phrase, shame and remorse arise because one conceals the evil deeds one has committed against oneself.
As for the fourth phrase, shame and remorse arise because doubt and regret arise regarding the good deeds one has performed against oneself. These two form another pair.

Regarding the first inquiry within the section on immovability (*āniñjya*), there is first the question and subsequently the explanation. Within the explanation, [the subject] is first introduced, followed by the enumeration of its names.
"Self-nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the essence of immovability; "basis" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) refers to the object of immovability. Below, this is extensively elucidated.

Within the self-nature, first immovability is clarified in relation to conditions (*pratyaya*), and subsequently it is explained in relation to causes (*hetu*). There are four types of relations to conditions: first, the non-... of afflictions (*kleśa*).
1. Immovability amidst movement; 2. Immovability amidst the two types of suffering; 3. Immovability amidst gain and profit; 4. Immovability amidst fear.
Even when encountering these four, one does not waver while correctly practicing wholesome dharmas. Regarding the phrase "self-comfort" within the section on causes below:
