because past practice has now been perfected, one is able to remain immovable. Regarding the phrase "one whose nature is capable of reflection": because one currently reflects upon skillful means, one is able to remain immovable. This is called the concluding summary.
Regarding the section on the bases (*āśraya*), first the number is stated, and below it is explained in detail. Among the five, the first concerns one’s own practice:

because it can swiftly eliminate various sufferings without wavering, it is called "unwavering" (*akampya*). The latter four concern the benefit of others; among these, the first two transform people to leave behind evil.
Regarding sentient beings who create evil and thereby undergo suffering, one transforms them to eliminate their evil conduct. The [last] two transform those who hold heterodox views.

The first two lines transform and eliminate wrong views. The next two lines transform others into goodness by preaching for the great assembly to generate right understanding, which reverses the latter line [of the previous verse];
and by expounding the sublime Dharma so that those who have received the precepts may transform themselves into initiating virtuous conduct, which reverses the former line.

In this section on "The Arising of Practice," it is taught that one should perform virtuous deeds through the transformation of the sublime Dharma; one should receive the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*) as the transformation for cultivating the virtue of tranquility (*śamatha*).

Within the discussion of "Non-Contention," the initial question sets forth the enumeration, which is subsequently analyzed in detail. Of the five points, the first four concern non-contention regarding one's own practice.
The latter one is for the benefit of others. Regarding the first four [of the six perfections], the first two are for self-benefit.

Those whose nature is powerful do not grow weary because their past practice has now been perfected; those who practice repeatedly do not grow weary because their current cultivation has reached maturity. The latter two are for superior progress.
The first [of the two] refers to initial learning; the latter refers to the perfection of cultivation. Within the context of initial learning, it is subsumed under skillful means (*upāya*).

Within the wisdom of cultivation, skillful wisdom (*prajñopāya*) is able to encompass [the practice]; this is called being "subsumed by skillful means. Through the superior cultivation of courageous and vigorous effort, one observes for oneself what precedes and follows to reveal the preceding skillful means.
One observes for oneself that what precedes is inferior and turns away from it with equanimity (*upekṣā*), while observing for oneself that what follows is superior and turns toward it.

One seeks [the goal] by means of this; therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). Because that which is cultivated becomes increasingly superior, it reveals the vigor (*vīrya*) mentioned previously. Regarding the subsequent attainment of the profound and sharp wisdom:
because one has long practiced wisdom and achieved clear vision of the excellent benefits, one is able to remain without weariness.

As for the accomplishment through reflection: because one currently contemplates with clarity and precision, one is able to remain without weariness. Within the lower category of benefiting others, one deeply gives rise to compassion; such is the depth of that compassion. Constantly...
This is because the scope of their compassion and loving-kindness is so vast.

In this treatise, first there is the initial inquiry that gives rise to the discourse, followed by its extensive analysis. Within that analysis, there are four sections: hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization.

"Initial mastery through thorough understanding" refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). This is the beginning of hearing what has been learned from others regarding the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

"Fully grasping and receiving" refers to the subsequent stage of hearing. "Reciting and practicing until mastery" signifies the completion of the wisdom derived from hearing. From the phrase "from others," one proceeds to reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Having heard the meaning from another, one cultivates the skillful means of reflection (*cintā*). One who is skilled at reflecting possesses the very essence of reflection. Following the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*), one cultivates further:
knowing both the phenomena and their meaning, and having already received them, one does not forget as one gives rise to the skillful means of cultivation. Knowledge of phenomena begins with hearing.
Understanding the meaning marks the beginning of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Not forgetting the Dharma brings the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) to completion;

not forgetting the meaning brings the wisdom of reflection to completion. Since cultivation (*bhāvanā*) arises from these, they are mentioned here. The gradual increase of what has not yet been cultivated is precisely cultivation. The culmination of hearing and reflection corresponds to the cause for concluding with cultivation;
because the present wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) arises from the preceding hearing and reflection, it is called "culmination. This is the sequential downward demonstration.
The sequential maturation that leads to entry into the means of realization refers to the gradual progression toward realization through the cultivation of wisdom;
the attainment of a joyful and pure mind is precisely the essence of realization. From this point downward, the passage concludes by praising and manifesting its excellence.

It is known that within this treatise, there is first the question and subsequently the explanation. Within the explanation, there are three parts: first, knowing the world as it is known in the world;

second, seeing the upper seat and the lower seat as they revolve in the world; third, revolving as in the world, followed by a double restatement to conclude. Within the first part, there are again three sections: first, knowing worldly affairs;
second, knowing the meaning of the world, starting from "knowing the origin of the world"; and third, [knowing] the sentient beings and the receptacle-world.

The following pairs are cited to conclude [the section]. Within the preceding middle portion, first there is the knowledge of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), and subsequently the knowledge of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

Regarding the knowledge of sentient beings, first is the general [overview], followed by the specific, and finally the summary. "The Bodhisattva understands beings as they truly are" is the initial general statement.

What follows below constitutes the specific details. Within the specific details, there are two parts: first, knowing the arising and ceasing, the birth and death, of sentient beings—namely, birth and old age;...
To know, as it truly is, that one dies here and is reborn there is the knowledge of passing away (*cyuti*).

To know, as it truly is, the emergence from birth and death is the knowledge of emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*). To know, as it truly is, when the turbidity of sentient beings increases is the knowledge of increase (*vivardhana*).

To know, as it truly is, when one is free from that turbid increase is the knowledge of freedom (*vivarjana*). This refers to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) emerging from below as previously described.

This further clarifies what was previously excluded. First, the number five is raised; next, the five names are listed. The corruption of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*) is suffering. The corruption of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is karma.
The corruption of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) refers to when sentient beings commit evil and people lack virtuous conduct. The remaining two are corruptions of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

Because all of these can turbidly disturb the pure mind, they are called "corruptions" (*kaṣāya*). Below, these are explained in detail. The corruption of lifespan is easy to understand. As for the corruption of sentient beings:
In the first part, it is shown that sentient beings do not recognize kindness and righteousness; in the second part, it is shown that they lack wholesome conduct.

Within this, there are four sections: first, the absence of active wholesome deeds (*kriyā-kuśala*); second, the absence of restraint (*virati-kuśala*), which clarifies the lack of cessation [of unwholesome states]—these two refer to the beginning.

Third, the failure to cultivate giving (*dāna*), which clarifies the absence of active wholesome deeds; fourth, the failure to cultivate the fast (*upavāsa*), which clarifies the absence of restraint—these two refer to the end. Regarding the first section:

By not cultivating principles, it clarifies their lack of understanding; by not performing what ought to be done, it clarifies their lack of practice. Such beings are well-disposed toward what they ought to do.
In the second section, it clarifies that they feel no fear regarding the evil fruits of the future world arising from the evil karma of the present life.
In the third section, "not cultivating giving" means being unable to relinquish wealth; "not performing meritorious deeds" means failing to give rise to other forms of goodness.

In the fourth section, "not cultivating the fast" means not observing the eight precepts of the *aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*; "not upholding the precepts" means not maintaining the remaining precepts of the seven classes of practitioners.
This is called the concluding summary. Within the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the increase of unrighteous greed is the affliction of craving (*rāga*).
The giving of swords, blades, and the like is anger. The giving of such things as swords and blades is its bodily action (*kāyakarman*);

litigation, strife, and discord are its vocal action (*vākkarman*). These illustrate internal anger by means of external manifestations. Deceit (*śāṭhya*) is the defilement of deceit; guile (*māyā*) is the defilement of guile.
Regarding "false speech," this refers to deception manifested through words. "Accepting what is perverse" refers to delusion (*moha*), as well as other evils, namely:

lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), pride (*māna*), and so forth. This is called the "concluding summary. Within the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), "the destruction of the Dharma" refers to the destruction of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

"The disappearance of the Dharma" refers to the disappearance of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpa-dharma*). The mention of the arising of the Semblance Dharma clarifies the preceding destruction of the Dharma.
Because the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is destroyed, the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) gradually arises. Because it resembles the Semblance Dharma, it is called the "Semblance Dharma.

As false dharmas (*mithyādharma*) increasingly arise, it is revealed that the preceding dharma has vanished; thus, because the Semblance Dharma vanishes, false dharmas arise. This is called the "concluding summary" (*adhastāt-nigamana*).

Within the *kalpakaṣāya* (the defilement of the eon), the three internal eons are clarified as constituting the *kalpakaṣāya*. The detailed explanation is as in the sutra. The above concludes the individual [explanations]. This is called... [and so forth].
In summary, this is the knowledge of arising. Regarding the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), knowing it as it truly is—whether in its formation or its destruction—is briefly indicated here;
a detailed exposition is as found in the Sūtras.
Thus far is the first [section]: the knowledge of worldly phenomena. Below this is the second: the knowledge of the meaning of the world. This, then, is the knowledge of...

The knowledge of the world consists of eight aspects therein. Of these, the first seven are the preliminary means for knowing the meaning of the world, while the last one is the direct contemplation that knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Within the preliminary means, the first is the world as the fruit of suffering; the world as its origin is the cause of accumulation.
That which excludes the causes and fruits of the world is called the cessation of the world; that which is free from the antidotes to the world is called the path of the world.

These four are the observations regarding the nature and meaning of the world (*loka*). Next, one observes its arising. "The gratification of the world" (*lokassa assāda*) means that the world can produce accumulation;

"gratification" (*assāda*) is synonymous with craving (*tṛṣṇā*). "The suffering of the world" (*lokassa ādīnava*) means that the world can produce suffering. "The escape from the world" (*lokassa nissaraṇa*) is also called "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) in the sūtras.

This contemplation of the world can give rise to cessation (*nirodha*); "separation" (*viveka*) and "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) are alternative designations for cessation. These three [cessations] are what is produced;

the first seven [contemplations] are the preparatory means for the contemplation of learning (*śaikṣa*), while the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the path itself. This is the meaning of the contemplation of the world.
Regarding the eye and forms, one observes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the world below. Now, one contemplates the ultimate truth by means of eight matters.
These eight matters are: first, name; second, birth; third, lineage; fourth, nutriment; fifth, suffering; sixth, lifespan; seventh, long endurance; [and eighth, the limit of existence].
Regarding the eight limits of lifespan: here, the single section on the limit of lifespan is omitted for brevity.

Concerning the first of the remaining seven types, one contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) by first examining names and subsequently applying this to the other six. Within the examination of names, the designation "person" is established based on the eye, form, and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

"Eye" refers to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*); "form" refers to the objective field of form (*rūpa-āyatana*), which consists of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by the four great elements.

[The author] replies: Because the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the eye are inseparable, they are said to be "co-arisen" (*sahaja*). Question: Since there are six distinct sense organs (*indriya*) and six corresponding objects (*viṣaya*), why is only the eye and its object, form (*rūpa*), mentioned here? Answer: Because it is the first [of the senses], the others may be understood by analogy. Furthermore, one might ask: since the sense organ of the eye and the four great elements that constitute the person are co-existent, those should be cited; likewise, the external object of form and the four great elements that constitute the form are co-existent. [The author] replies: ... [as before]. Because the great elements and the eye are inseparable, they are called "co-arisen. It is not that [the aggregates] are not the person; why then are they mentioned? Although they do not constitute the meaning of "person" in their own right, they are mentioned collectively because [the person] is dependent upon them.
As for the term "puruṣa" (person): *puruṣa* is a specific designation for the "self" (*ātman*) or "individual" (*pudgala*).

What was previously mentioned—the collection of the eye, visible forms, the great elements, and so forth—constitutes the human body and is called the "body of the puruṣa. Based on its governing function, it is designated as a "person. There is no third [category] below this.

Contemplating the principle: first one contemplates that it is substantially non-existent, and subsequently one contemplates that it exists nominally. There is no third [category]. The statement "the notions of self and sentient beings" clarifies the essence of non-self.
This explanation has two meanings. First, regarding the internal and external distinction between the sense faculties and their objects:
the eye-faculty and the four great elements that compose it are combined into one; the color-object and the four great elements that compose it are likewise combined into one. These two—
Apart from these, there is no third entity of a divine self (*pudgala*) that can be called "I," "a sentient being," and so forth; the same applies to the rest.
Therefore, many sūtras extensively investigate the twelve bases (*āyatana*) from both internal and external perspectives to clarify the non-existence of a self or a person.

Second, regarding the distinction between the internal and external: the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) constitutes one [category], and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that compose the eye likewise constitute one. Of these two—
Externally, there is no third statement that "this is I" or "this is a sentient being. Nor is there a third statement that "I see forms with my eyes," up to "I cognize phenomena.
This clarifies the absence of a self-function. Since the substance of a self does not exist, how could there be a third statement such as "I see forms," up to "I cognize phenomena"?
Such a view is logically non-existent; it is merely a conventional designation. To say "this is the Elder" is to observe that only names exist; in reality, [there is nothing].
Because there is no self, it is merely a conventional designation that one says, "this is an elder. "Elder" (sthavira) is still just a specific title for a person.

In this way, by taking what follows as an analogy for what precedes, it clarifies that all such things are non-existent. First, one knows the world; next, one knows its meaning. From here on, both are concluded together.
Regarding "the world of birth" and "the receptacle world," these recapitulate the first section above. "The eightfold contemplation" recapitulates...

The preceding second section provides a general summary in eight lines. "The meaning of the worldly" specifically summarizes the first seven [sections], while "the ultimate meaning" specifically summarizes the eighth.
Therefore, it is called "knowledge" and concludes with this general summary.
The preceding first section was as known in the world. From here below is the second section, which is as it functions in the world;

herein there are four parts: first, acting according to what is appropriate for others; second, acting according to what is appropriate for oneself through the deliberations of body, speech, and mind;

third, "for the sake of others' kin," etc., which clarifies the perfection of transformative virtue in contrast to the first [point]; fourth, "accomplishing the eight kinds of noble speech," etc., which corresponds to the above.
The second section clarifies the purity of one’s own assembly. Within this, there are four parts: first, being able to accord with those who are superior, middling, or inferior;

second, being able to follow virtuous friends among all one’s kin and inferiors; third, being able to follow the poor and beggars among the solitary and lowly; and fourth, being able to follow even those who are distant without becoming dejected by sorrow.
Regarding the first of these sections, there is first the specific treatment and later the general. Within the former, the first is following those who are superior.

Regarding "the Elder of Superior Virtue," this distinguishes the object of compliance; the subsequent passage clarifies that compliance. "Respectful" refers to compliance through the mental action (*manas-karman*);
"welcoming" refers to compliance through the bodily action (*kāya-karman*). "Inquiring after one's well-being" refers to compliance through the verbal action (*vāk-karman*).
Next, regarding "those of middle standing whose years and virtue are equal," this distinguishes the object of compliance; the subsequent passage clarifies that compliance. Correctly...

"Speaking gentle words" refers to compliance through verbal action (*vākkarman*). When the other questions, the Bodhisattva responds with correct speech; when the Bodhisattva questions them, he comforts them with gentle words.
"Not giving rise to pride" refers to compliance through mental action (*manaskarman*); bodily compliance is omitted for brevity.

Next, regarding compliance with those inferior in age or virtue, this distinguishes the objects of compliance. Below, compliance is explained, which consists of three parts: first, compliance through mind and speech.
Second, if one sees that what is sought by others is not contrary [to the Dharma]. Third, not looking down upon those who are inferior or slighting them. Regarding the first section:

encouraging the confession of transgressions accords with the verbal karma (*vākkarman*); encouraging those without virtue and praising those with virtue, while concealing their faults without slighting them, accords with the mental karma (*manaskarman*).
In the second section, seeing those who seek wealth or the Dharma and not turning one's back on them [is described].

He practices impartial giving, neither being biased nor turning his back on this side while giving exclusively to that. He does not frown upon others but receives them with a joyful and harmonious countenance.

In the third section, he does not obstruct others but accords with them through the lack of verbal misconduct; seeing others, he does not treat them with contempt but accords with them through right mental action.
"Earth" refers to the earth-element; "decline" refers to exhaustion and decay. What precedes is specific accordance; what follows is general accordance. If one sees a single...
All people—whether superior, middling, or inferior—raise up those whom they follow. This clarifies "following in accordance" (*anuvartana*), which consists of three parts:

first, following through verbal action (*vākkarman*) by observing their appearance and inquiring first, then praising their virtue; second, following through physical action (*kāyakarman*) as appropriate by bestowing wealth and the Dharma;
and third, following through mental action (*manaskarman*) with a non-deceptive and humble mind, meaning that one does not flatter superiors but respects them with a sincere heart.

One does not speak to a person of equal status with crooked flattery, nor with disrespect or arrogance; failing to give rise to the pride of equality toward such a person is called "not being self-important.
One does not give rise to great pride by claiming oneself to be superior to them, which is called "not being self-exalting. One does not speak to an inferior person with excessive haughtiness;
failing to disregard the age of an inferior person and treating them with contempt is called "not being self-aggrandizing. One does not [reckon]...
Though one’s virtue is superior, one does not deceive others by making one’s reputation high; nor does one boast of being unique. "Boasting" (*jing*) is synonymous with arrogance (*māna*).
Because the signs of arrogance manifest outwardly, it is called "boasting of uniqueness. Above, [the text] followed the superior, middling, and inferior types of persons.

Below this, secondly, it follows those who are intimate and kind. Regarding all such kinsmen and friends, it specifies the object of compliance; below, it clarifies the manner of compliance: providing everything by means of wealth.
Regarding "following along": if one has already brought down the three karmas, one follows along by acting as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to transform others and lead them toward goodness.

One remains free from all enmity and does not harbor resentment or ill will. From here below is the third section, "following along with the poor and beggars. Those who are destitute and without refuge are specifically identified as the objects of this following;
one acts as their protector and support, clearly demonstrating this compliance. From here below is the fourth section, "following along with those who are distant," which is not [to be done] by...

When sentient beings are afflicted by sorrow and suffering, one should comply with them through physical action (*kāyakarman*). When the causal conditions for such affliction are minor, one should comply through verbal action (*vākkarman*).

First, one abstains from frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*); subsequently, one abstains from harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). When causal conditions arise, engaging in playful laughter in accordance with the Dharma is not frivolous speech.

If others harbor doubts or resentment toward the Bodhisattva due to certain causes and conditions, or if causes and conditions for the arising of sorrow and distress in other sentient beings occur, one should comply with them through playful words.

Because one engages in play with them, it is called "playful. To proclaim worldly matters in accordance with the Dharma and to remove their doubts and distress is called "in accordance with the Dharma.

Because one does not engage in idle chatter, there is no "non-Dharma. Because one does not describe others by means of playful speech regarding their forms or names, it clearly demonstrates the avoidance of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
That one does not speak [of such things] even toward those who are intimate demonstrates the gravity of this fault; ultimately, one does nothing for the sake of others [that would cause such harm].

Regarding the subordination of one's mental karma, herein, first, it clarifies not deprecating others oneself; if one is treated with contempt by another, one does not become angry even when troubled by them.

Thus far was the first section, acting in accordance with what is appropriate for others. Below follows the second section, acting in accordance with what is appropriate for oneself, through the actions of body, speech, and mind.

Acting after deliberation means performing tasks with careful scrutiny; because one acts after first reflecting, there are no faults or transgressions. The section beginning with "free from the fourteen bases" concerns the excellence of wholesome action.

Within this, the first part clarifies the conduct of householders, while the section beginning with "always possessing a sense of shame" clarifies the conduct of those who have left the household life.

Among the practices for householders, one first abandons wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*). The subsequent section on "happiness in the present life" clarifies the abandonment of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).

Within the abandonment of wrong action, observing the force of this textual passage, it appears as though the abandonment of the fourteen stains (*caturdaśamala*) is first set forth; that is, from "concealing" (*pracchādana*) onwards, each is specifically identified and refuted.

According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is not so. That text speaks of being free from fourteen types of defiled karma, being free from concealing the six directions, being free from the four evil friends, and embracing the four virtuous friends—each of which is distinct. What are these fourteen defilements from which one is free?
As it is said therein: one is free from the karma of the four fetters, namely killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech;

one does not commit various evil deeds in the four circumstances, namely through greed for wealth, delusion, fear, or anger; and one does not give rise to evil karma based on these. One is also free from the six ways of wasting wealth:
first, indulgence in alcohol; second, gambling; third, profligacy; fourth, infatuation with music and dance; fifth, [evil]...
They obtain friends. Sixth is indolence. Among those six, each has six faults; they cannot be discussed in detail.
These are the fourteen directions from which one should withdraw, as stated in that sutra:

In the city of Rājagṛha, there was the son of an elder named Sujāta, who had for generations handed down the tradition of constantly worshipping the six directions at dawn, so that the deities of those directions would always...
While attending to his household affairs, he encountered the Buddha and inquired whether such a teaching existed. The Buddha replied, "It exists, though it is not the same as yours.
[The son asked,] "What are its characteristics? [The Buddha said: "Parents are the eastern direction; teachers and elders are the southern direction; wife and children are the western direction;
relatives and friends are the northern direction; servants and laborers are the downward direction; and śramaṇas of high virtue are the upward direction."

As stated in that sutra, there are five matters for each of the six directions as they relate to oneself, and five matters for oneself as they relate to each of the six directions; these cannot be discussed in detail here.
Regarding the avoidance of the four evil friends, it is as stated in that sutra: one should recognize four types of enemies who appear like friends. First, the friend who subdues through fear;

he subdues you out of fear, yet has no genuine intention of friendship. Second, the friend of pleasant speech; his words are compliant, but his intentions are contrary. Third, the friend of... [reverence].
The compliant friend: although one respects and complies with them in heart, they do not offer any admonition or restraint regarding the good or evil deeds one performs.
Fourth is the evil friend: they associate in evil matters, such as drinking alcohol together, gambling, indulgence in lust, or engaging in singing and dancing, as described in that sutra.
Within each of these categories, there are again four sub-types, which cannot be detailed exhaustively here. As for those who embrace the four kinds of virtuous friends, it is as follows:
That sutra states that there are four kinds of relatives who are worthy of being relied upon: first, the friend who restrains one from what is improper, restraining one from evil deeds;

second, the compassionate friend, who feels pity for one in times of suffering; third, the friend who benefits others, who shares joy with one; and fourth, the friend who acts in concert, who practices virtuous deeds together with one.
As stated in that sutra, each of these further contains four [subdivisions], which cannot be discussed in full detail. One should infer this from that [text] to verify the present case.
Here, it should be said that one is free from the fourteen defiled actions, free from concealing the six directions, and free from the four evil friends while embracing the four virtuous friends.

Regarding those items that ought to be reversed, I have not seen them in that sutra; namely, "concealing" and so forth are used to clarify the preceding fourteen [defilements]. Therefore, [the claim that they are] erroneous is [unfounded].
[This is] the ear[-root]. As extensively revealed by the *Sūtra* (sūtra), it refers to the *Śāṇakavāsin-sūtra* within the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

Below, in the section on "Right Livelihood" (*samyagājīva*), it first clarifies that a bodhisattva is fully endowed with material resources (*bhoga*). Belonging to the category of wealth, these things can produce happiness in the present and simultaneously benefit others;

therefore, they are termed the "meaning of happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhārtha*). Having no lack of what is required is called being "endowed with wealth. Next, it clarifies the bodhi-... [text continues].

This explains the source by which wealth and resources are acquired: through diligent effort at the time of acquisition and through guarding them once obtained, one thus attains an abundance of those riches.

The following clarifies that when a bodhisattva seeks [wealth], they act in accordance with the Dharma and remain far removed from wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). They seek it through various crafts in a lawful manner;

they are free from wrong livelihood by being without crookedness or illusion, and so forth. Their bodies are not crooked or sycophantic, their minds are not deceptive or illusory, and their speech is not fraudulent.

Deceit. The preceding section clarifies the conduct of the householder; the following clarifies that of the renunciant. "Having shame and remorse, one is without fault" clarifies the absence of grave transgressions:
"shame and remorse" refer to the mind, while "without fault" refers to body and speech. "Possessing dignified deportment" clarifies the avoidance of minor offenses:
"possessing deportment" refers to body and speech, while "grave caution" refers to the inner mind.
From here below is the third section, which, corresponding to the first part above, clarifies the perfection of transformative virtue as appropriate for others. This section contains three parts:

first, clarifying the accomplishment of trustworthy conduct and freedom from greed; second, the skillfulness in decisively resolving matters concerning speech and body; third, governing and transforming through the Dharma, starting from "If one is a king... and so forth.
Within the first part, it concerns not encroaching upon what has been entrusted by others due to intimacy, nor failing to repay debts.

To possess trustworthiness is *śraddhā* (faith). To distribute wealth without partiality is *dharma* (righteousness). If one acts with truthfulness, according to reality, and provides the proper price, this is *alobha* (non-greed).
In the second section, there are four distinct phrases: first, speech; second, body; third, speech; and fourth, body.
Settling worldly affairs and discerning matters with promptness and precision constitutes the first phrase, which is the skillfulness of vocal action (*vākkarman*). This clarifies the terminology.

Because it is thorough, it is called "discernment" (*pratibhāna*). Because the words necessarily accord with principle, they are called "correct. Because what is resolved is swift and sharp, it is named "expeditious faculty" (*tīkṣṇendriya*).

All of these constitute the second phrase, the skillfulness of bodily action (*kāyakarma-kausalya*). Being able to answer according to the question constitutes the third phrase, which again clarifies the skillfulness of speech (*vāk-kauśalya*).
Performing the correct task constitutes the fourth phrase, which again clarifies the skillfulness of body (*kāya-kauśalya*). Within the third section:
The first section clarifies how he governed the common people as king according to the Dharma; the section on "evil precepts" below explains how he instructed them in the Way through the Vinaya.

The eight items following this constitute the fourth section. This corresponds to the second [section] above, which clarifies his own purity of conduct; here, the purity of speech is briefly explained.
The formation of the eight [categories] summarizes them collectively;
the details below can be understood accordingly. The first [section] is as known in the world; the second is as it evolves in the world. The following section concludes both together.

"Forming such things as they are known in the world" reiterates the first section above to clarify *lokajñā* (knowledge of the world). "As it evolves in the world" reiterates the second section above to clarify *lokacaryā* (conduct in the world).
"This is called knowing the world" is the summary.

From here below, the sixth section clarifies "acting according to what has been taught," which consists of eleven gates: first, the clarification of the four reliances; second, the four unhindered knowledges.

1. The three types of enlightenment (*bodhi*); 2. The four types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*); 3. The factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*); 4. The contemplation of the truths (*satya-vipaśyanā*); 5. Calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*);
6. Skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); 7. Dharanis; 8. The various vows (*praṇidhāna*); 9. The various samādhis; and the eleventh section clarifies the *udāna*.
Since the Dharma is the foundation of practice, the Dharma is elucidated first. Since understanding arises based on the Dharma, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are elucidated second.

Since practice is initiated based on understanding, the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are elucidated third. Since the path is perfected through the maturation of practice, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are elucidated fourth.
Since one enters the truths by means of the path, the contemplation of the truths (*satyadarśana*) is elucidated fifth. When this contemplation of the truths has become thoroughly matured—

Because quiescence and illumination are unimpeded, the sixth point clarifies śamatha and vipaśyanā. Because the dual cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā is skillful, the seventh point clarifies skillful means (*upāya*).
Because of this skillful cultivation, one attains the dhāraṇī of all dharmas; thus, the eighth point clarifies dhāraṇī.
By the power of dhāraṇī, one is further able to seek higher advancement; thus, the ninth point clarifies the aspirational mind (*praṇidhāna-citta*).
Because the mind can abide in the Dharma through the power of aspiration and seeking, the three samādhis are explained next in succession.
Because the mind abides in the Dharma, one perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*) of phenomena; therefore, the eleventh section explains *udāna*.

Within the text concerning the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), there are three distinct sections: first, the definition of their characteristics; second, how they are established, wherein the subsequent section on unimpededness (*apratigha*) reveals the perfection of the reliances;
and third, the complete mastery of the Great Teacher’s wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), which demonstrates his virtues by way of the person.

Within the first section, there is first the question, then the explanation, and finally the conclusion. How is the question posed? In the explanation, one should first clarify the meaning of the four reliances before proceeding.
Explanation of the Text. The meaning is as discussed in a separate chapter. Within the text, the first section clarifies reliance upon the meaning (*artha*);

the second, reliance upon the Dharma (*dharma*); the third, reliance upon sutras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha-sūtra*); and the fourth, reliance upon wisdom (*jñāna*). The first two clarify the sequence for encompassing the teachings:

since meaning can bring about practice, one relies upon it first. "Meaning" refers to principle (*li*). Since meaning is manifested through verbal expression, one next relies upon the Dharma. "Dharma" refers to the teaching (*śāsana*).

The latter two clarify the sequence for initiating cultivation: because one cultivates correct understanding based on the aforementioned teachings, the third follows by relying on sūtras of definitive meaning;
because one cultivates wisdom and practice based on the preceding principles and meanings, the fourth clarifies reliance upon wisdom.

Regarding the practice of listening to the Dharma for its meaning rather than for its flavor, this has been briefly indicated above; it will now be cited and explained below. "For the sake of the meaning" cites what was stated previously;
"if one hears" and following explains it. If one hears worldly teachings that are not skillful means, this clarifies that while they possess meaning, they lack skillful flavor.
A Bodhisattva also listens to them; this clarifies the reliance on the person, as even those teachings that are not skillful means constitute their flavor.

The Bodhisattva also listens. How is it that he does not rely [on the letter]? The commentary explains that regarding the scriptural teaching on "not relying on the flavor," this means the Bodhisattva does not rely on meaningless flavors;
it does not mean that he never relies on flavor at all. Next, the reliance on the Dharma is explained, which is divided into two sections.

First, clarifying reliance on the Dharma and not on the person; second, restating this to demonstrate its realization. Within the first section, from the beginning up to "knowing that which one should rely upon" constitutes reliance on the Dharma.

Knowing the distinction between light and darkness, and right and wrong, is general understanding. Knowing that which one should rely upon is the discernment of what is correct and the rejection of what is erroneous.
Correctly knowing the basis of reliance means not relying on status—high or low—which is non-reliance on the person. This, then, is non-reliance on the four kinds of greatness.

Regarding the Dharma spoken by others: it is not merely that one must abandon ordinary people; furthermore, among those who are human, the Bodhisattva does not rely on those who speak what is not the Dharma.
This does not mean that one never relies on humans at all. The four types of great persons are: first, one who knows the Dharma;
second, one who knows much of the Dharma; third, the Saṃgha; and fourth, the Buddha. If someone says, "The Dharma I speak is the supreme," [the Bodhisattva] does not rely upon them.
When a person of wisdom speaks, one should neither accept it immediately nor disparage it. One should examine it against the Tripitaka;

if it accords with them, it should be accepted, but if it does not, it should be discarded. Some may say, "The Dharma I speak was heard from such-and-such two or three venerable elders," or they may say it was heard from the Sangha, or from the Buddha.
It should be examined as previously described. Now, this teaching does not rely on [the authority of] those above.

Sitting is the act of a single person; it does not mean that because many people recognize [the Buddha], he becomes many. Whether it be the Buddha or the Saṃgha, these are included within the previously mentioned four.
One should not rely exclusively on such descriptions of these individuals. This is shown by the subsequent citation of the text. Such is the wording of the citation.

Relying on what ought to be cited from the preceding section on relying on the Dharma: "not relying on persons" cites not relying on persons; "unwavering regarding the truth" reveals that one attains [realization] by relying on the Dharma as stated in the preceding text.
"Being able to know for oneself without depending on others" reveals that one attains it without depending on the four types of persons mentioned previously.

Within the section on relying on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the former clarifies reliance on the definitive, while the latter clarifies not relying on the non-definitive (*neyārtha*). Now, in this [passage]:

The explanation provided concerns the distinction between the clear understanding of the wise and the lack of clarity in the ignorant. What is spoken by those of correct wisdom each reveals its respective significance; this is termed "clear understanding.

When the ignorant mind grasps the specific characteristics of the Dharma-gates, they are mutually contradictory; all such instances constitute "lack of clarity. Within the aforementioned section on clear understanding, there are two distinct points:

first, clarifying that one relies upon what is clearly understood and not upon what is not; second, restating [the principle] to demonstrate the attainment [of that understanding]. Regarding the first of these sections:

The Tathāgata’s profound faith is pure; he single-mindedly believes and accepts what the Tathāgata has taught. Relying on those teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), he correctly clarifies his reliance upon them.
Because he takes up the Dharma with deep faith and his words are without concealment, it is called "definitive. It is not that which is non-definitive; one does not rely on the non-definitive.
By abandoning delusion and slander, it is called "not non-definitive. The following section reiterates this to demonstrate attainment: "Relying on the sūtras of definitive meaning... is thus.

This restates what was previously mentioned. That the laws and regulations are not destroyed indicates that [the teaching] has been correctly attained; because the interpretation of the Dharma does not deviate, it cannot be destroyed. Below, the failure to understand is clarified.
This section is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the lack of understanding; second, restating this to reveal the error.

Within the first part, "failing to understand the sutras" is stated as a general heading. The phrase "taught through various gateways" indicates that there should be questions regarding the characteristics of such a lack of understanding.
The Tathāgata’s teachings vary according to different gateways and are thus called "various explanations. To fail to understand them due to doubt is called "lack of certainty.

Because of this lack of certainty, there arise many questions regarding the principle; therefore, it is said that [the teaching] "should exist" [as a definitive point]. The following section cites and reveals the fault:

"to treat a sūtra of definitive meaning as uncertain" is the citation of the preceding point, while "the Dharma and Vinaya would be subject to subversion" is the revelation of the fault. This refers to the mutual contradiction of holding differing views.

Therefore, it can be destroyed. Regarding the principle of relying on wisdom (*jñāna*) and not on consciousness (*vijñāna*), first its characteristics are explained, and subsequently its attainment is demonstrated.

Within the first section, attaining and cultivating firm wisdom is what constitutes relying on wisdom; this means that a bodhisattva relies upon their own wisdom to apprehend all phenomena and does not rely on the wisdom of others.
It clarifies that one does not rely on consciousness by specifying that one does not rely on the dharma and its meaning as apprehended through hearing and reflection.

The two minds of hearing and reflection do not fully comprehend the Dharma; because they are subsumed under perception (*saṃjñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), they are termed "consciousness. The subsequent passage cites this to demonstrate its attainment:

knowing through the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) rather than through hearing and reflection is the citation of what preceded. Not giving rise to slander when hearing profound meanings is the demonstration of its attainment.
This concludes the explanation of the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*). Thus it is summarized.

The preceding section has explained the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*). In this way, the subsequent section establishes the absence of hindrance (*apratighāta*) in relation to what follows, thereby demonstrating the fulfillment of the reliances.

This "establishing in such a manner" refers back to the previously mentioned practice of the reliances; the explanation of the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) serves to clarify their meaning, while the reference to the subsequent absence of hindrance demonstrates the fulfillment of the former.
The latter four are called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because the knowledge of the dharmas they involve is vast and manifold; this does not apply to compassion and the others.
Those four immeasurables manifest the meaning of the accomplishment of these four reliances. This is because, within the context of relying on wisdom, the latter four are distinguished.
Thus, by means of that, this is manifested and established.

From here below is the third section, which clarifies the virtues through the person, demonstrating that these four reliances are what the Buddha has fully realized and what the Bodhisattvas have understood.
The initial section on the preliminary skillful means clarifies that these four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) are fully realized and perfected by the Buddha.

It enumerates the four reliances known to the Buddha, encompassing everything known through the Great Teacher’s wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the Great Teachers of the world.

Because the Master’s virtue is perfectly complete, it is said that he is "fully endowed. Since the Dharma of the four reliances is that which the Buddha has realized, it is called "the four reliances known by the Great Master.
The "skillful means of equality" clarifies that the Buddha has reached ultimate realization; to exhaustively realize its true nature is termed "equality."
Furthermore, "knowing equally" is also termed "equanimity" (samatā). Skillfully knowing according to characteristics is called "expedient means" (upāya).
That a bodhisattva is thoroughly proficient in these refers to the bodhisattva’s understanding of the aforementioned four reliances (pratisaraṇa).

From here below is the second section, which clarifies the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). First, the question is posed; second, the explanation follows. Within the explanation, there are three parts: first, defining their characteristics;
second, clarifying the vastness of what is known through these analytical knowledges; and third, clarifying how these four encompass all-encompassing wisdom.

Regarding the first part, one should first provide a detailed explanation of the meaning of the four analytical knowledges; the meaning is as discussed in a separate chapter. In the text, it first says: "Regarding the dharmas and their phrases..."

One who possesses the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) knows that all teachings are the unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). One knows the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are;

knowing the meanings of the two truths—their specific and general characteristics—is the unimpededness regarding meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*). One who possesses the wisdom of cultivation knows the names of all phenomena; this is the unimpededness regarding names and terminology (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).
One who possesses the wisdom of cultivation knows the various distinctions among all types; this is the knowledge of the various differences within expressions.
To discern according to the inclinations of beings' minds is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

These four, categorized according to their respective meanings within the aforementioned basis of wisdom, are therefore all said to be known by the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*). Thus, the following section clarifies the vast scope of what is known by these four unimpeded knowledges.
These unimpeded knowledges are collectively designated as the five immeasurables (*pañca-apramāṇa*); among these five, they are distinguished by their specific modes of cognition.
Immeasurable. Skillful knowledge of this is called *upāya* (expedient means). This will be explained in detail below. "Aggregates" (*skandha*) refers to the five aggregates.

"Elements" (*dhātu*) refers to the eighteen elements. "Bases" (*āyatana*) refers to the twelve bases. The twelve links of dependent origination are called *pratītyasamutpāda*. The principles of cause and effect, right and wrong, are called "the possible and the impossible" (*sthānāsthāna*).
One possesses skillful knowledge regarding all five of these. Below this, the four types of unhindered knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) are clarified.
This encompasses all wisdom exhaustively. The first [section] follows the sequence; the latter reverses it. That which can awaken oneself to all phenomena is the equipment for self-benefit;

that which is manifested for others is the equipment for benefiting others. This is the preceding sequential explanation; below, it is explained by way of reversal. Apart from this, there is no one else who can awaken themselves;
outside of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there is no dharma for self-benefit, let alone any other manifestation that constitutes a dharma for benefiting others.

From here below is the third section, which clarifies the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). First, there is the question; second, the explanation. Within the explanation, first [the subject] is raised, then two names are listed, followed by a reference to what was previously stated, and finally, the relative superiority and inferiority are distinguished.
Record of the Meaning of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*,
Volume Four (Part One) / Record of the Meaning of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, Volume Five (Part Two).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan of Jingying Temple during the Sui Dynasty.

The preceding section was the fourth, which extensively analyzed their characteristics. From here on is the fifth section, which clarifies the limits of the factors of cultivation for each stage (*vihāra*).
This section contains two parts: first, explaining the distinctions in the accomplishments of the various stages;

second, explaining the limits of the factors of cultivation for each stage, wherein successive superior qualities are absent in the preceding grounds. This is the first part. In the previous twelve stages, the qualities of practice gradually increase.

This is called "successive progression" (*krama*). Because later virtues surpass those preceding them, they are termed "superior qualities" (*uttara-guṇa*). What precedes does not reach what follows; thus, the former stages do not exist [in the latter].

Each of these [stages] is followed by a second stage. Within this, the initial statement regarding "each of those abidings" means that for those of middling or superior faculties, many achieve [the goal] over hundreds of thousands of millions of eons; those of dull faculties are not counted.

Regarding the classification of the twelve stages of excellence within the lineage (*gotra*), the Bodhisattva universally encompasses all the merits of the various stages within each individual stage.
Nevertheless, prior to the lineage, there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties, resulting in the speed or slowness of their accomplishment.
From the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward, those of equal faculties achieve [the goal] regardless of whether it takes long or short;

therefore, when entering the spiritual lineage from the twelve abodes of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), those of middling and superior faculties often achieve accomplishment within each individual abode over hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas*.
Because those with dull faculties are slow and late, they are not included in this count.

All those who abide therein must necessarily pass through the twelve stages of abiding—from the lower [levels] up to the *dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma) stage—within the context of the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) to define the limits of their attainment. Within this, there are two parts.

First, the delimitation of the factors for cultivation in the various stages (*vihāra*); second, the two types of *kalpas*, clarifying whether there is an excess or lack thereof in the magnitude of the *kalpas*.
Regarding the first section: all those stages are collectively indicated as requiring three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
*Asaṃkhyeya* is a foreign term; here it is translated as "incalculable. A *kalpa* is a specific division of time.

[The term] "named" [is used]; the following sections distinguish them individually. First, regarding the *asaṃkhyeya* of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), this clarifies the place from which one emerges.

From "attaining joy" (*pramuditā*) onwards, it clarifies the places to which one arrives. "Attaining joy" marks the beginning of what is reached; the five practices of superior progress mark the end of what is reached.

In the second stage, one maintains ethical discipline (*śīla*); in the third stage, one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*); in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one cultivates and practices wisdom (*prajñā*). Within wisdom, there is...

Three. This encompasses the previous five [stages]. The second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa refers to the period from the Joyful Abode (pramuditā-vihāra) onwards, up to the point where the "opening" (vivarana) emerges;
this is the stage of attainment. The "non-opening" (avivarana) refers to the destination reached below that.

The commencement of reaching the state of non-opening is manifested by the name of the assembly of Bodhisattvas with Resolutely Pure Minds (niyata-śuddha-citta-bodhisattva-pariṣad). In the section on the lower stages, this "non-opening" is designated as "resolute" (niyata).
Therefore, they are now brought together here; this is precisely that "Stage of Certainty" (*niyata-bhūmi*). It is the ultimate destination reached through certain and superior progress.

That "Abiding in Non-obstruction" (*anāvaraṇa-vihāra*) is named "Certainty and Superiority. It is the place from which one emerges after passing beyond the "Unmanifested Abiding" (*anabhisamskāra-vihāra*) during the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
It is the place where one arrives at the station of the supreme abode. Within the second section, the first part clarifies...
Kalpas have both large and small dimensions. The subsequent section clarifies that among the various stages (*vihāra*), there are those that are surpassed and those that are not.

The preceding section clarifies that within a kalpa there are two types, providing their enumeration; in full, there should be three—namely, small, medium, and large—but here, referring only to the two extremes, it mentions just two.

Below, their names are listed: "One day, etc., an immeasurable number is called a *saṃkhyeya*. This means that when the number of days is immeasurable, it is termed a *saṃkhyeya*. [The same applies to] months.
The categories of years and seasons are likewise thus. The divisions such as spring, autumn, and summer are called "seasons" (*ṛtu*).

Within these, there should be intermediate eons (*antarakalpa*) of immeasurable duration called *asaṃkhyeya*, such as the Bhadrakalpa and others. Therefore, the text below states: "A bodhisattva’s diligence can turn back an intermediate eon, but cannot turn back a great [eon].

How much time is designated as an intermediate eon? As Nāgārjuna says: four... [four *kalpas*]... [four *kalpas*]... [four *kalpas*]. (Note: The original text appears to contain a repetitive or abbreviated enumeration.)

Suppose a city one thousand *li* square were filled with mustard seeds, leveled smooth with a wooden board. If one seed were removed every hundred years, the kalpa would not yet have ended when those mustard seeds were exhausted.

Furthermore, suppose there were a stone four thousand *li* in size; if a celestial robe weighing six *zhu* were used to brush it once every hundred years, the stone would be worn away before the kalpa had ended.

The kalpas are still not exhausted. Counting these immeasurable numbers is called a *saṃkhyeya*. However, among these, the *antarakalpa* (intermediate kalpa) is frequently discussed in the *Sūtras* and *Śāstras*;

because its characteristics are manifest and easy to understand, it is omitted here without further discussion. Regarding the second type, the immeasurable number called a *saṃkhyeya* that constitutes a *mahākalpa* (great kalpa):
according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, from the initial fire-kalpa until the final wind-kalpa, the total combined duration of sixty-four kalpas is termed one great kalpa.

Regarding the sixty-four kalpas: there are seven sets of seven fire-kalpas (*tejo-kalpa*), one set of seven water-kalpas (*ap-kalpa*), and one wind-kalpa (*vāyu-kalpa*). Thus, in total, there are sixty-four.

Alternatively, it may be that the number of intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*) reaching the *asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable) constitutes a great kalpa (*mahā-kalpa*). This interpretation is excellent and accords with the *Saṃgrahaṇī-śāstra*.

However, as the specific characteristics of these phenomena are difficult to discern, they should not be hastily determined. One should count these great kalpas until they reach the state of the *asaṃkhyeya*.
The measure is called a *mahāsāṃkhyeya*.

The following clarifies that among the various stages (*vihāra*), there are those with transgressions and those without. Within this, there are two parts: first, contrasting the "great" with the "small" to clarify transgression and non-transgression;

second, contrasting the "great" with the "middle" to clarify transformation and non-transformation. Regarding the first section, the number of years constituting a *sāṃkhyeya* is as previously stated.

Regarding the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas: because the number of years passed by the Bodhisattva is short [in comparison], when the first *asaṃkhyeya* is completed upon reaching the stage of *pramuditā*, he has already passed through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
it does not stop at merely these three, which is why it says "passed. As for the latter three *asaṃkhyeyas*, there is no such thing as "passing" them;
this expression is somewhat obscure. If one were to speak fully, it should be said that during those subsequent great kalpas of the three *asaṃkhyeyas*, there is no [such passing].

Regarding "exceeding": among the two preceding kalpas, the great kalpa (mahākalpa) follows; that subsequent great kalpa consists of three asaṃkhyeyas. Among all the stages (vihāras), none can exceed this;

they do not even exceed three, so how could they exceed more? Below, by means of the great kalpa, it is contrasted with the intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa) to clarify what is transformable and what is untransformable.
As for the statement that "superior diligence can transform the intermediate kalpa but cannot transform the great [kalpa]," it refers to the diligent practice.
It is called "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) because it transforms a long duration of time into a short one. For instance, a period such as the Bhadrakalpa is not exceedingly long;
therefore, superior diligence (*adhimātra-vīrya*) is capable of transforming it. However, a great eon (*mahākalpa*) is so protracted that even superior diligence cannot transform it.
What kind of diligence can transform an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*)? As stated in the sūtras, Śākyamuni transcended nine [intermediate] kalpas and twelve...

Regarding the *kalpas* and so forth: why is it said that he transcended nine [kalpas] yet speaks of twelve? Śākyamuni, in the past, first cultivated the various *pāramitās* throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Subsequently, during one hundred kalpas, he cultivated the karma for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Only then did he attain Buddhahood. Because he exerted diligent effort during those three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, he transcended three kalpas.
Within the period of the hundred kalpas, at the very beginning, he encountered Buddha Puṣya and praised him single-mindedly for seven days. Furthermore...

They transcend nine *kalpas*. Therefore, it is said that they transcend nine *kalpas* based on the latter [of the three] explanations; including the first two, it is said that they transcend twelve. In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, it is said that this is real;

in the teachings of the Mahāyāna, it is said that this is a transformation (*nirmāṇa*). Regarding their actual practice, from the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward, the faculties and practices are equalized such that there is no transcending of *kalpas*;
rather, they are established according to whether the faculties of sentient beings have matured early or late.
There is a sequence of before and after.
From here, the sixth section clarifies the distinctions regarding the abandonment of obstacles in the various stages (*vihāra*).

The statement that "the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*) which defile the twelve stages are severed" serves as a general heading; what follows below provides a detailed exposition.

First, the limits of abandonment regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) are clarified. The statement that "the afflictions of those three abodes (*vihāra*) are abandoned" is a general clarification of the points at which the afflictions are severed.
Here, the Joyful (*pramuditā*), the Immaculate (*vimalā*), and the Supreme (*parama*) are designated as the three abodes; in all these abodes, [the afflictions] are abandoned.
These three constitute the limits of the scope [of this discussion], and thus they are mentioned specifically. Below, they are explained individually.
Regarding the statement that "in the Joyful Abode (*pramuditā-vihāra*), among the predominant afflictions of the miserable realms (*apāya*), none are active at all":

within the delusions of the four abodes, the middle and upper grades are capable of producing evil karma and receiving retribution in the miserable realms; therefore, these are termed "afflictions of the miserable realms. Upon reaching the Joyful Abode...

"At that time, everything is exhausted. Regarding the statement, "There is no further development; the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) purifies the defilements of affliction so that they do not function at all," this means that upon reaching the eighth stage (bhūmi), the lower grades of the four abidings (catvāra āśrayāḥ) no longer function. This is because the greed of attachment to the Buddha is exhausted at this point.

Regarding the statement, "Abiding in the supreme state, one severs the obstacles of the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of all afflictions and enters the state of a Tathāgata," this refers to the [severance of] the four abidings.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Below, the limits of abandonment regarding the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are clarified. First, the characteristics of the obstructions are analyzed; subsequently, the points of abandonment are explained. Within the analysis of the obstructions, there are three parts:

the enumeration, the specific designations such as "skin" and so forth, and [the analogy]. The essence of the Dharma-body possesses skin, flesh, and bone. That which precedes the stages (*bhūmi*) is like the skin.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, the *dharmakāya* is like skin; from the eighth stage upward, the *dharmakāya* is like bone.

Within the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), there are coarse, medium, and subtle levels. The coarse grade of ignorance, residing in the skin and acting as an affliction, is called the "skin-obstruction" (*tvag-āvaraṇa*).
Medium-grade ignorance resides in the skin and is called the "skin-obstruction"; subtle-grade ignorance resides in the bone and is called the "bone-obstruction.
One may also say that these obstructions are like the skin and bone, obstructing the substance of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

The following clarifies the locus of severance. Within this, first, the coarse [explanation] briefly clarifies the locus of severance by means of three stages; subsequently, it is discussed in detail. Regarding the coarse [explanation], there is first a specific distinction:
joy severs the skin, non-attachment severs the flesh, and the Tathāgata severs the bone. Question:

Previously, within the context of the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it was stated that from the eighth stage upward, one merely severs habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Why, now in the context of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), is the term "habitual tendency" not mentioned?

The commentary states that the most subtle state of the four abodes is "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*); only when ignorance becomes subtle does it truly constitute the "ground" (*bhūmi*), and thus it is not discussed as a habitual tendency.

Furthermore, it is asked: if the habitual tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*) are exhausted throughout the ten grounds, why is it that the most subtle obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are only severed upon reaching Buddhahood?
The coarse afflictions of the four abodes are easily severed and are exhausted first; ignorance, the root, is difficult to sever and is eliminated last. Therefore, these cases are not analogous.
Herein concludes the discussion. Regarding the remaining abodes, following the lower stages, one proceeds according to the subtle reality.
To speak according to actual reality, the remaining seed-natures and so forth are gradually severed in succession, such that each stage becomes a true and sublime practice.
From here below, the seventh section clarifies the distinctions regarding the purification of the thirteen stages of abiding (*vihāra*). Thus, these thirteen are summarized by eleven purifications;

they are specifically detailed below as there should be thirteen. Because the wisdom-practice (*prajñā-caryā*) is identical in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, they are combined into a single "purification of vision" (*darśana-viśuddhi*);
thus, there are eleven. The twelfth stage corresponds to the one who possesses all-knowledge in every respect (*sarvākāra-sarvajña*).
It follows the Buddha’s wisdom. The remainder is easily understood.

From here on, the eighth section clarifies the distinctions encompassed by the thirteen abodes. Regarding the inclusion of the eight dharmas in the previous "Chapter on Merits," this serves as a transition from the preceding to the subsequent.
By stating that these are included within the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*, it establishes the locus of their exposition. These thirteen inclusions are explained according to their respective locations.

Because they are cultivated and perfected within the thirteen abodes, these eight are subsumed under the thirteen; this will be explained in detail below. Regarding the first and second, those in whom faith arises:

"faith" refers to the stages of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). As for the statement that those in the stage of practice through understanding attain hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*): [End of excerpt]

It is said that hearing and reflection pertain solely to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*); however, in reality, they pervade all stages. Here, because we are addressing the qualities of practice accomplished through supramundane cultivation, it is stated that hearing and reflection belong to the stage of practice through understanding.
As for the statement that "the third dwelling attains the pure mind," this refers to the beginning of the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Those who have attained non-retrogressive faith achieve the name of "one who has gained a pure mind. Regarding those who are beginners: practicing the conduct of the second stage (*bhūmi*) while at the completion of the first stage is called being a beginner.

From the fourth stage up to the stage where wisdom is extensively cultivated through intermittent and signless practice—referring to the stages from the second stage up to the seventh—the conduct gradually expands.
These are subsumed under the wisdom of cultivation during the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth [stages].
Regarding the fulfillment of the fruit of cultivation: all practices and virtues from the eighth stage onward, arising from prior cultivation, are subsumed under "cultivation.
When the retribution of these practices has reached full maturity, it is termed the "fulfillment of the fruit of cultivation. The Tathāgata’s transcendence is the eighth of these.
From here on, the ninth section uses the great to categorize the small. The stages of the śrāvaka’s dwelling in the Dharma also consist of twelve, which are presented as a general outline.
Just as with the bodhisattva, the great is used to categorize the small; these will be explained individually below. First, regarding the "śrāvaka lineage stage":
That which is called "Heat," "Summit," and "Patience" is termed "contemplation of the truths. Attaining the portion of the noble ones is termed the "nature of a śrāvaka.

Regarding the second stage—entering the correct path without yet transcending the sequence for attaining realization—the Sūtra on the Precepts describes this as the "Supreme Mundane Dharma," which is termed "entering the correct path but not yet attaining realization.

Being in causal connection with the principle of the truths through that Patience regarding Suffering is termed "entering the correct path. This constitutes the continuity of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The stage where the sequence has not yet been severed is called "not having transcended the sequence. Not yet having attained the noble path is called "not having realized the fruit.

Progressing toward the noble state is called "abiding in the preparatory means" (*upāyavihāra*). The third, the abiding of transcending the sequence and realizing the fruit, is described in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* as the mind of "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhakṣānti*) and so forth.
The abandonment of the mind through conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) is called "transcending the sequence. To presently obtain the Noble Path is called "attaining realization and abiding.

Regarding the attainment of the indestructible purity (*aveccappasāda*) and the subsequent transition to the higher, untainted precepts and the exhaustion of outflows: this refers to the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, who is called "one of indestructible purity" because they have accomplished the four kinds of indestructible purity.
There are differing explanations regarding the meaning of "indestructible purity" in the treatises; according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it consists of accomplishing the four types of faith.
Faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, together with faith in the precepts, are called the four purities (*catur-viśuddhi*).

According to the Abhidharma, the first three are faith—faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—and the last one is the precept; these are collectively explained as the four indestructible purities (*catvāri avetyaprasādāni*). Thus, that treatise states:
The first three [kinds of purity] are purity of mind; the last one is the purity of the four great elements.

Once that stream-enterer has attained these four purities, if they have not yet relied upon noble ethical discipline (*ārya-śīla*) to advance toward the abandonment and cultivation of the afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), they are said to be "not yet possessing noble ethical discipline. When they subsequently eliminate the outflows (*āsrava*) and rely upon superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), they attain the higher stages.

Regarding the arising and abiding of the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*): this refers to the candidate for the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* who, relying on the aforementioned noble ethical discipline (*ārya-śīla*), advances in the cultivation of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is called the arising and abiding of the training in higher mind. Among the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the first five are coarse impurities.
If one restrains the mind and abides in its objects, one is able to become detached from them; therefore, it is called "mind" (*manas*).

As for those who have attained the wisdom of the True Truths (*satyābhisamaya*) through the sixth, seventh, and eighth [consciousnesses]—namely, the candidate for the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, and the candidate for the fruit of *anāgāmin*—these three types of persons are collectively termed "abiding in wisdom" (*prajñāvihārin*).
This is because, among the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the latter four grades are subtle and difficult to perceive.
Only through wise observation can it be severed; therefore, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*). The three stages that follow are those of the candidate for Arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*).

Regarding the statement, "observing birth, one dwells in the skillful means of the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*)," this refers to the practice of antidotes from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Observing the arising [of suffering] from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness and generating a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*) is termed "observation."
Birth. Attaining the higher dhyāna-samādhis and becoming detached from the characteristics of lower faults is called the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).

Gradually arising and ascending is called the abiding in skillful means (*upāya-vihāra*). Ultimate signlessness refers to the attainment of the extinction concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by a body-witness *anāgāmin*.

Among the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*), this extinction concentration is the most extreme in its detachment from signs; therefore, it is called the ultimate signless samādhi. This is the awakening of liberation.

The "abode" refers to the practice that serves as the antidote to the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Only untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is capable of counteracting the afflictions of that stage;
therefore, it is called the "Abode of the Awakening of Liberation. As for the phrase "the abode of all kinds of Arhats," this refers to the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
Although there are many types of Arhats, they are subsumed collectively into one category, termed the "abode of all kinds of Arhats."
Treatise, Volume Ten.
Chapter One: The Chapter on Birth (*Janma-varga*).

Regarding the first chapter, "The Abode of Birth through the Ultimate Means" (*atyanta-upāya-sthāna-janma-varga*), of the three abodes (*tri-dhāraṇī*), the first two have already been completed. From here...

The third section below clarifies that which is accomplished. Because the practices and virtues differ, they constitute the ultimate sustenance (*atyantadhāraṇa*). That which is the pinnacle among these three is called "sustaining the ultimate" (*atyantadhāraṇa*).

The explained sustenance of the Dharma serves as the foundation for practice and is thus termed the "stage of skillful means" (*upāyasthāna*). Alternatively, this may be called the "stage of skillful means" because it refers to the virtues of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
The preceding section clarifies self-benefit; the following clarifies the benefit of others. This marks the beginning of benefiting others: [the stage of] receiving [the precepts].
Because it arises in accordance with phenomena, it is called "Arising" (*jāti*). A detailed exposition of the meaning of arising is termed the "Chapter on Arising.
Within this section, there are five distinct sub-chapters; as this chapter initiates the sequence, it is designated as the "First. This chapter consists of four parts.
First is the general heading with a brief eulogy; second, the enumeration of their names; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion.
Within the first section, the general heading, there are five parts, beginning with the citation of the number. The phrase "all abodes and all practices" praises the vastness of their conduct.
This birth is omnipresent throughout the twelve stages (*dvādaśa-vihāra*), fully encompassing and exhausting all modes of conduct in those births; thus it is called "all stages and all conducts.
