Regarding the phrase "blameless and blissful for all births," this praises the efficacy of his conduct:
performing wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) to benefit sentient beings is termed "blameless," while bringing pure fruits to benefit things is termed "blissful."
Next, their names are listed. These five types of birth are each fully present within every stage (*bhūmi*).

When distinguished according to their characteristics, the first three occur prior to the stages, while the latter two occur within the stages. This is because within each of the bodhisattva’s dwellings (*vihāra*), all twelve qualities of the dwellings are fully encompassed;
therefore, these five births occur wherever they may be: three constantly occur prior to the stages, and two constantly occur within the stages.

Because a Bodhisattva’s taking of birth can eliminate afflictions, it is called "the cessation of suffering. Because they take on forms identical to those of sentient beings to gather them in and lead them away from evil, it is called "birth according to their kind" (*yathā-jāti*).
For Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), the experience of the eight types of excellence through their own virtuous karma is called "excellent birth" (*viśiṣṭa-janman*).
The superior retributions of the ten kings from the first bhūmi upward are called "superior births.
Bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way in their final body; this is called the "final birth."

The following explains their characteristics. Within the resolution of the cessation of suffering, the first [section] concerns the cessation of manifest suffering. Through the arising of right view, one is taught to sever the causes of evil, thereby ceasing subsequent suffering.

Within the cessation of manifest suffering, the mastery of the power of aspiration constitutes the cessation of the causes of suffering. The section below correctly effects the cessation of suffering.

The first part clarifies how the Bodhisattva is able to alleviate the suffering of sentient beings during the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. The section beginning with "having bound" (*bandhana*) and following clarifies how he is able to alleviate the suffering of sentient beings at other times.

Within the alleviation of subsequent suffering, the arising of wrong views and evil conduct is what is being addressed; the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*) is the cause for taking birth through mastery;
"being born in those celestial realms" precisely clarifies the act of birth; and "severing those wrong [views]" and so forth clarifies the benefits derived from that birth.
The above has explained the quantity of births; this is termed the "concluding summary.

Regarding the explanation of "according to type," the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*) is the cause for acting according to type, while the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) is termed "mastery" (*vaśitā*).
Among the various beings such as devas, nāgas, and ghosts, they are born according to their respective types. Their mutual affliction is the result of their past actions.
This mutual affliction entails suffering; their wrong views and evil conduct constitute the causes of evil. Thus, they are all born therein, arising according to their respective types.
To act as their guide is to benefit them according to their respective capacities. To act as their leader is to lead them into the correct path.

To transform those former non-Buddhists is to cause them to abandon false views and unwholesome conduct. "That which they do" below clarifies that the aforementioned deities and others do not cause mutual affliction.
"Those who act [wrongly] and do not cultivate [the path]" refers to the bodhisattva’s transformation through bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

Furthermore, "those with inferior speech" refers to transformation through verbal action (*vākkarman*). Having thus explained below the extent of those born [in this state], this is termed the concluding summary.
Regarding "birth through excellence" (*viśeṣotpatti*): birth by nature refers to the actual essence of birth as discussed in the formal treatises.

For Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), taking birth through their own mundane natural wholesome karma in accordance with sentient beings is called "birth by nature. Their superiority over the lifespan and other qualities of the world manifests the excellence of their birth.
As for the benefit of self and others, it was previously explained in detail. From "In this way" onwards, there is the discussion of the number of births; this is called the concluding summary.
Within the context of superior birth, the section from "pure mind" up to "the highest dwelling" defines the limits of taking birth.

The section beginning with "in whatever lower realm one takes birth" clearly explains the actual birth. The section beginning with "not having transcended" reiterates these points as a conclusion. Within the final birth, there is the supreme bodhisattva.
The limits of birth; the birth that disciplines karma; and the causes for birth through the requisites for awakening—these constitute the practice of benefiting others.
The birth among the kṣatriyas and so forth clearly illustrates the mode of birth itself. Attaining awakening and so forth refers to what arises from such birth.
This is called the "Lower Bonds.
Having already discussed the lower bonds in the past, this section praises and reveals their excellence.
Section Two: The Chapter on Compendium (Saṃgraha-varga).

Regarding the "Chapter on Gathering" (Saṃgrahavastu): in the preceding chapter, it was explained that birth occurs in accordance with sentient beings and that they are gathered and transformed through causes; thus, it is called "gathering.
Because this meaning is extensively analyzed here, it is termed the "Chapter on Gathering."
Within this chapter, the first part clarifies the gathering of practices (*caryā-saṃgraha*), and the latter part clarifies the gathering of time (*kāla-saṃgraha*). There are twelve difficulties;

the bodhisattva cultivates and refines these so as not to regress amidst them. Within the former [section], there are four parts: first, a general introduction praising its excellence; second, listing their names; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion.
Regarding the first general section, the phrase "all abodes and all practices" praises the vastness of his conduct.

This encompasses everything present throughout the twelve abodes, comprehensively including all practices for gathering and benefiting sentient beings; thus it is called "all abodes and all practices."
Regarding "equally gathering and generating [beings]," this praises the capacity of their practice. There are six enumerations;
next, their names are listed. Of these six, the first three are distinguished according to their practice, while the latter three are distinguished according to time.

Because they gather sentient beings equally through the provision of all means of happiness, it is called "simultaneous gathering" (*tun she*). Gathering beings while abiding in a position of honor is called "superior gathering" (*zengshang she*).

Gathering by means of material wealth and the Dharma is called "taking-in gathering" (*qu she*). Those with dull faculties who ripen slowly are called "long-term gathering" (*jiu she*). Those with middling faculties who ripen soon are called "not long-term gathering" (*bujiu she*).
Those with superior faculties who ripen in the present and reach the culmination of benefit are called "final gathering" (*hou she*).
Next, this is explained in detail. Regarding the "sudden inclusion" (*tun-she*): conceiving all sentient beings as one's own parents is the sudden aspect of those to be converted;
providing all forms of happiness and the requisites for happiness is the sudden aspect of the means of conversion. This concludes the section.
Regarding the increase of understanding, the first [of the three] serves as a householder; the second, as a king; and the third, as a father.
Within the former category of being a master, the first includes parents and other venerable ones who exhort one toward virtue;

it consists of the benefit of the wholesome Dharma and the benefit of joy through timely offerings, knowing gratitude, and repaying kindness. Next, it includes wives, children, and other dependents, which comprises five [aspects].
1. Regarding compassionate care; 2. regarding instruction in what should be done; 3. regarding forbearance toward transgressions; 4. regarding treatment for illness; 5.
regarding exhortation to virtue according to one's ability. As for the subsumption of slaves, servants, and other laborers, there are four distinct points within the category of kings:
1. governing the people with rectitude; 2. bestowing wealth and the Dharma; 3. guarding the borders so as not to invade; 4. transforming them to cultivate goodness.
In his conduct toward his father, he is impartial toward others, let alone toward his own kin; thus his inner mind is without bias.

His speech is always gentle and humble, and his words are compliant. His speech is always soft and mild, meaning he does not engage in harsh speech. It is truthful and not false, meaning he does not engage in lying.
He abstains from all killing, so that his body causes no harm or affliction.

Within the section on "Understanding and Grasping" (*parigraha*), there is first a general heading that subsumes the two conditions; next, the specific details; and finally, the conclusion. Within the specific details, the first gate concerns the grasping of material wealth (*āmiṣa-parigraha*).

The second concerns the grasping of the Dharma (*dharma-parigraha*). There are four aspects to this grasping of the Dharma: first, the general clarification of the grasping of the Dharma by benefiting others through the teaching of the correct meaning;

second, the specific clarification of the grasping of the Dharma starting from "uprooting evil" and below; third, the summary of the grasping of the Dharma starting from "in this way" and below; and fourth, [the concluding summary].

Inclusion. The fourth section, "Not All," clarifies the method of inclusion. The first part may be understood as a general overview. Within the second part, the specific details, the initial section includes those of inferior capacity;
from "equal" onwards, it includes those of middling and superior capacities. Regarding the inclusion of those of inferior and middling capacity, there are three distinctions:

first, clarifying their transformation through teaching; second, from "if they commit an offense" onwards, clarifying their instruction and admonition; third, from "at times" onwards, clarifying their guidance and instruction.

Within the preceding section on conversion, there are five distinctions. First, it clarifies the conversion of sentient beings with wrong views; by uprooting evil and false views, it correctly elucidates the conversion of those who hold such views.

Below, it clarifies the ritual of conversion: "Gathering with an impartial mind" means not being biased toward any person. "Not being stingy regarding the Dharma" means not being parsimonious with the teachings.
"Not making a 'teacher's fist'" means having no physical indolence. "Not harboring a low opinion of others" means having no ulterior motives.
2. "Those who delight in cultivation" clarifies his teaching of sentient beings who delight in goodness; they cultivate with ceaseless joy for the sake of increasing merit. 3.

"Those who have not yet understood" clarifies his teaching of sentient beings who seek understanding; he causes those who do not understand to awaken it, and causes those who already understand it to increase it.
4. "Resolving doubts" clarifies his teaching of sentient beings who are mired in uncertainty. 5. "Causing remorse to awaken" clarifies... [the following].

Regarding the transformation and exhortation of sentient beings who repent their non-virtue: "Repentance" means causing them to awaken; "explaining the meaning according to the occasion" refers to the transformation through verbal action (*vākkarman*).

Because one causes them to know that the mind of repentance has the fault of destroying non-virtue, it is called "causing them to awaken. Transforming them so that they become upright by explaining the meaning constitutes the transformation through verbal action.

Sharing in their suffering and joy constitutes the transformation through physical action (*kāyakarman*). The absence of increase or decrease in the mind constitutes the transformation through mental action (*manaskarman*). Within these instructions, there are those who commit transgressions.

The transgressor is identified by what they are subject to. Below, the characteristics of being "included" (*saṃgṛhīta*) are clarified. With an impartial mind, one instructs and admonishes them; through the mental action (*manas-karman*), one is not biased.

Through verbal expression, one offers both reprimand and praise as appropriate counsel. From physical actions such as tending to their illnesses downward, one follows and accords with them. Within the context of instruction:

first, regarding those of inferior mindfulness and inferior diligence, one should not give rise to thoughts of contempt, nor neglect their initial goodness. One should act according to what is suitable and measure the situation accordingly.
Bestowing the Dharma refers to the five perfections and so forth. "According to the occasion" and below means providing timely instruction;

being able to endure weariness and affliction means teaching the cultivation of *śamatha* when it is time for stillness, and teaching *pragraha* (arousing) when it is time for arousal, and so on. What has come above subsumes what follows; what follows subsumes the middle and the superior.
Regarding equals and superiors, the specific categories subsumed are indicated. Below, the characteristics of subsumption are clarified: one practices superior offerings by means of material wealth.

To follow in accordance with [the goal]. One cultivates compassion and gathers others through the Dharma. It is asked: "Since these [beings] are either equal to or superior to oneself, how can one gather them through the Dharma?
The explanation states: Although they may be equal or superior in other respects, because there are areas in which they fall short, they can be gathered.
Within this, there are four aspects: first, internal compassionate mindfulness; second, being personally free from agitation and accomplishing the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
1. Causing them to practice together. 2. Following along with body and speech: a serene countenance is the body; speaking first is the speech. 3.
Cultivating wholesome deeds oneself without negligence so as to cause others to practice together. The above constitutes the second section, which specifically clarifies gathering through the Dharma.
3. "By means of such as these" and below is the conclusion of the explanation. 4. "Not taking everything" and below clarifies the ritual for gathering: one does not take everything.
It avoids excessive grasping; it does not fail to grasp, thereby avoiding deficiency; it does not act impulsively, thereby avoiding inopportune timing.
This is called "taking up and gathering. This concludes the third section.
The final three [sections] may be understood accordingly. This is called the sixth sub-section, the fourth part: the concluding praise that reveals its excellence.
The six points above clearly explain the inclusion of practices (*caryā-saṃgraha*). Below, it explains how to cultivate and refine oneself so as not to regress when facing difficulties.

Within this, first the twelve kinds of difficulties are presented; below, nine refinements for not regressing amidst difficulties are explained. First there is the detailed exposition, followed by the conclusion.

Regarding the phrase "not considering lightness or gravity as a skillful means," this corresponds to the first difficulty mentioned above: namely, observing the superior or inferior faculties and natures of sentient beings as a skillful means for gathering and transforming them.

It is not merely that one observes the gravity of a present transgression as a skillful means; rather, it may be that one practices compassion by examining others, which corresponds to the sixth [category] before.
Because one has skillfully examined those to be converted, one conceives compassionate thoughts for their benefit.

Or, it may be that one employs courageous skillful means as a creator of conditions, which corresponds to the eighth [category] before. By virtue of the power of courageous skillful means, one acts for the sake of all sentient beings.
Because they create the conditions for birth and death within saṃsāra in order to teach and transform others; and because they know the faults of saṃsāra yet do not abandon it.
Furthermore, through the power of courageous skillful means, they create supramundane conditions for all sentient beings while remaining within saṃsāra.
Therefore, one does not abandon it. Alternatively, cultivating the right aspiration corresponds to the ninth [stage].

Because of cultivating this aspiration, although one has not yet attained a pure mind, one does not lose right mindfulness at the time of death. Alternatively, pure faith corresponds to the tenth [stage].

Because of pure faith, although one has not yet attained a pure mind, when beings whom one holds most dear and precious come to beg, one bestows gifts upon them. Alternatively, one focuses exclusively on contemplation.

Observing without weariness corresponds to the fifth [attribute]. Because of such contemplation, even though one may be born among the gods or humans who are prone to negligence, the inner mind remains fundamentally free from negligence at all times. Or, being gentle corresponds to the second [attribute].

Because of gentleness, one employs skillful means to liberate beings from suffering, protecting oneself from afflictions and not giving rise to anger or resentment. Or, at times, one practices equanimity.
At times, when diligence is applied toward the seventh and eleventh [factors], it is not termed "equanimity" (upekṣā), but is termed "diligence" (vīrya).
Because of these two, regarding that seventh factor, whether one teaches or abandons the limbs and joints that are impaired by delusion and deceit, [it is through diligence].

By means of these two [methods] as well, regarding the eleventh variety of mental resolve—whether acting or relinquishing—and by means of skillful means (*upāya*), one compares this with the preceding fourth and the twelfth [categories].
Because of such skillful means, in that third case, although the material goods are few, one gives them to those who ask for much, after having measured what is appropriate.
By means of skillful means as well, in that fourth case, even though one possesses only a single body...

For those who have many desires, he engages in the same activities as them as appropriate. Furthermore, by means of skillful means, even though he is the twelfth [type of person] who is not heedless, he does not sever the afflictions of sentient beings, nor does he abandon their greed, anger, and so forth.
Thus concludes the capacity for cultivation.
Regarding the third chapter, the "Chapter on the Grounds" (*Bhūmi-varga*):

as for the term "Grounds," it refers to the fact that the preceding section clarified the accomplishment of the virtues of gathering and transforming sentient beings; because these [virtues] are capable of giving rise to [the grounds], they are so named.
It serves as the ground (*bhūmi*). Because it extensively elucidates the practice of the grounds, it is called the "Ground Chapter" (*Bhūmi-paṭala*).
This chapter has five sections: first, citing the preceding stages (*vihāra*) to clarify the grounds; second, a brief classification according to persons; third, listing their names;

fourth, a brief exposition of their characteristics; and fifth, a detailed explanation. As above, the thirteen [stages] are sequentially arranged into seven [grounds]; this constitutes the first section.

Furthermore, the sixth is the second section of the Bodhisattva’s single vision of the common ground (*sādhāraṇa-bhūmi*). From the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) up to the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-gamana*), these names are listed in the third [section].
The fourth, the stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), is briefly explained as being below the stage of spiritual lineage.

The first four are easy to understand. Regarding the statement that "that which is unmanifested is called 'determined' (*niyata*)," this refers to the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). Among the three types of determination, this is the first determination.
The eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are collectively termed "definitive. The eighth stage is the first definitiveness.
That which is called "unimpeded" is termed "definitive practice," meaning that in the ninth stage, based on the preceding, it further increases and is thus named definitive practice.

That which is called "the supreme Tathāgata" is termed "ultimate," because in the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), one reaches the final fulfillment within the path of learning; therefore, one is identical to the Tathāgata as being ultimate.

This concludes [the section on] the fruit. This has been discussed merely from the perspective of a single door; if other doors were considered, the causes and fruits would be distinguished separately and could not be categorized as a single type.

From here below, the fifth section extensively explains their characteristics. As for what the Tathāgata later stated—citing the fruit to point toward what follows—the subsequent portion only explains the cause.

Regarding the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) within the cause, it has already been fully analyzed above and need not be discussed again. Now, this section only explains the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*).

Above, within the section on "Practice through Understanding" (*adhimukticaryā*), there is first the initial inquiry regarding its arousal, second the explanation, and third the conclusion. "How does one enter the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*) and become free from [defilements]?
is the initial inquiry. Within the explanation, there are three parts: first, clarifying practice (*caryā*); second, clarifying vows (*praṇidhāna*); and third, clarifying both vows and practice.

One is able to sever the evil destinies and enter the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Within the preceding section, the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) has been presented in general;
hereafter, they will be explained in detail. First, altruism is clarified; second, self-benefit is clarified. There are four aspects to altruism.
First, one cultivates compassion toward those who suffer. Second, for the sake of sentient beings dwelling long in the evil realms, one studies for the sake of awakening (*bodhi*).

Third, one is capable of enduring [hardships] to act as the cause for removing the suffering of beings. Fourth, regarding the vow to take upon oneself all karma that leads beings to the three evil realms:

since the fruit of karma must be experienced by oneself, how can it be taken over? This has been explained above. Within this state, the Bodhisattva manifests through transformation (*nirmāṇa*) so that...
Because one emerges [from suffering], it is called "receiving in turn. This aforementioned benefiting of others is the ultimate cultivation of all virtues, which constitutes self-benefit.
What has preceded clarifies the practice; the correct aspiration is the second aspiration. Below this, the third section clarifies the intermediate aspirations.
The statement that one can sever the miserable realms through mundane virtues reiterates the preceding practice. The term "correct aspiration" reiterates the preceding aspiration.
Furthermore, the "defilement by afflictions in the evil realms" refers to the cessation of the body received [in those realms], which is the cessation of the evil fruit.
The "transformation of the body in the evil realms" refers to the non-performance of evil karma, which is the cessation of the evil cause. This is called the "lower fetter."

The latter part of the "Chapter on Previous Abodes" clarifies the essence of the various stages (*bhūmi*) beginning from the first stage. The "Chapter on Previous Abodes" explained the ten dharmas, such as faith and so forth, by citing what preceded to initiate what follows.
Here, regarding the purity of this stage, it cites what was previously taught; it points to the specific locations and discusses them starting from the beginning.
This initial purity of the stages (*bhūmi*) means that within this supramundane state, all stages are purified; therefore, the subsequent text speaks of "purifying all stages.
The following explains its characteristics, which is presented in three parts: first, opening the three gates; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the three gates:

the first is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), which clarifies the capacity for remediation through the perspective of cultivation. The second and third are the objects of treatment (*vipakṣa*), which are distinguished according to their constituent factors.

This clarifies that which is to be remedied. There are three [sections] in sequence, clarifying how these ten aspects arise through mutual causality. Next, the following provides an explanation. "How does one apply the remedy?
is the formal inquiry regarding the first gate; below, its characteristics are analyzed. Heedlessness and non-acceptance constitute the opposing obstacles to the Bodhi of faith;
this is because, due to heedlessness and the failure to accept the precepts, one delights in and clings to the mundane world, rendering one incapable of contemplation.
Regarding the benefits of enlightenment (*bodhi*), because one does not perceive such benefit, one is unable to have faith and joy; thus, one violates right faith.
From this point downward, the obstacles are presented in reverse order to demonstrate their remedies. The [meaning of] the next three [sections] can be understood accordingly.

Within the fifth gate, "seeking many requisites" is established as an obstacle in contrast to "tirelessness," because seeking gain and offerings from sentient beings hinders the cultivation of the path leading out [of suffering], and thus violates tirelessness.
The rest may be understood as before. Within the second section, these ten types of counteractive factors are briefly subsumed into two general categories and presented by their names.
All of them are fundamentally the mind and are collectively termed "skillful means. Among them, they are further distinguished: the first three are the minds of the skillful means of practice;

because one has not yet formally engaged with the objects of focus, they are called "purity of mind. The latter seven involve formal engagement with objects; because they constitute actual cultivation, they are [termed differently].
This is called "purification through skillful means. The following section on the analysis [of the stages] can be understood. How is the third [stage] questioned in sequence?

The subsequent explanation can be understood. Thus, these ten practices purify all stages; taken together, they conclude [the discussion]. Because these ten kinds constitute the essence of the ten stages, they universally purify all [stages].
Chapter Four: On Practice (*Caryā-varga*). Regarding this chapter on practice:

According to the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra*, diligence (*vīrya*) is categorized separately and is not included within the [other] three [trainings]. Each may be definitively established according to its respective meaning:
"meditation" (*dhyāna*) refers to the mind; the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) is the training in concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, it refers to the fact that for all dharmas, there are lineages that can be transmitted and lineages that cannot. That which can be transmitted is called "possible"; that which cannot be transmitted is called "impossible. Furthermore, it refers to the fact that for all dharmas, there are transmissions that can be passed on and transmissions that cannot. That which can be passed on is called "possible"; that which cannot be passed on is called "impossible. Furthermore, it refers to the fact that for all dharmas, there are inheritances that can be received and inheritances that cannot. That which can be received is called "possible"; that which cannot be received is called "impossible. Furthermore, it refers to the fact that for all dharmas, there are acquisitions that can be gained and acquisitions that cannot. That which can be gained is called "possible"; that which cannot be gained is called "impossible. Furthermore, it refers to the fact that for all dharmas, there are possessions that can be held and possessions that cannot. That which can be held is called "possible"; that which cannot be held is called "impossible. Furthermore, it refers to the fact that for all dharmas, there are enjoyments that can be experienced and enjoyments that cannot. That which can be experienced is called "possible"; that which cannot be experienced is called "impossible. Furthermore, it refers to the fact that for all dharm
The correspondence between cause and effect is termed "possible" (*sthāna*); the contradiction between cause and effect is termed "impossible" (*asthāna*).

Although this power comprehends all things, it is preeminent within the context of teaching through the knowledge of cause and effect; therefore, it is specifically described as "wisdom" (*jñāna*) because it illuminates this [distinction].

The meaning of "power" (*bala*) is as explained below. First, it is called power because of its capacity (*karmanya*), for it is able to benefit sentient beings. Second, it is called power because of its intensity (*prabalatva*), for its own virtues are so firm that even Māra cannot destroy them.
Regarding "the power of one's own karma": this refers to one's own karma within the context of the causes and effects of good and evil.

It is termed "one's own" (*sva*) to distinguish it from extrinsic causes such as *prakṛti* (primordial matter) or Īśvara (the Lord). Nevertheless, within this power, one fully understands both afflictions (*kleśa*) and suffering (*duḥkha*).
The four dharmas beginning with pleasure (*sukha*) have the meaning of "feeling" (*vedanā*). Because karma is predominant, they are referred to simply as "the power of karma.
Regarding "the power of right reception (*samāpatti*) through dhyāna, vimokṣa, and samādhi": *dhyāna* refers to the four dhyānas; *vimokṣa* refers to the eight liberations;

"samādhi" refers to the three samādhis; and all others are collectively termed "right reception. Because one is able to enter and know these dhyānas and so forth, they are called "powers. [This applies to] the faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding "faculties" (*bala*): faith, diligence, mindfulness, and so forth, having been cultivated through past practice, are now perfected; because they are able to produce [wholesome states], they are called "roots" (*indriya*).
Among these roots, their combination or separation is not fixed. When combined, they are one; when divided, they become two—namely, the sharp and the dull.

Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* says: "The limit of dull faculties is exemplified by Śreṇika; the limit of sharp faculties is exemplified by the Buddhas. It is for this reason that the "middling faculty" is taught.
Because they are infinite, they are not mentioned; alternatively, they may be classified into three types—namely, weak, medium, and superior—as explained in the subsequent text.

However, among the faculties (*indriya*), one that universally knows all faculties, such as those of good and evil, is intended here; because one wishes to rely on the faculty of goodness to transform and bestow the Path, it is specifically discussed.

"Diverse inclinations" (*nānādhimukti*) is also termed the power of desire (*chanda-bala*) and is also termed aspiration (*prārthanā*); it is so named because it knows the objects of a being's faith and understanding.

The power of understanding (*adhimukti-bala*). Knowing and understanding gives rise to desire, which is called the power of desire (*chanda-bala*). Because the mind of desire seeks after [its object], it is termed aspiration (*prārthanā*). Regarding the various elements (*dhātu*):

they are also called the power of nature (*prakṛti-bala*) and the power of latent tendencies (*anuśaya-bala*). Because habitual desires do not change, they are termed "nature" (*prakṛti*). The differentiation of natures is called "elements" (*dhātu*).

When a bad nature follows a person, it is designated as a "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*). To know these is called "power. Regarding the path leading to the destination (*yathāgata-mārga*): suffering and pleasure...
The term "reaching" (*gati*) refers to the destination reached. Because wholesome and unwholesome causes are able to reach those destinations, they are called the "path to reaching" (*gati-mārga*).

Since it knows both the destination and the path, it is named the power of the knowledge of the path to reaching (*gati-mārga-jñāna-bala*). What is the difference between what is known by this power and [the power of] the possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*)?
As explained in the treatise: the former, the power of the possible and impossible, knows cause and effect in a general sense; now, this [power] knows them specifically. This is the cause.

One is able to reach that fruit and discern specifically that this fruit arises from that cause. Regarding the power of past lives (*pūrvajanma-bala*): "past" (*pūrva*) means what has ceased and gone;
"life" (*janman*) refers to the continuity [of existence]. This power comprehensively knows eight matters and six modes within past lives. "Life" follows after these.

Based on what follows, it is declared that [the power of] knowing past lives is partial. As for the power of birth and death, it is also called the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) in the sūtras.
If one speaks of the divine eye according to its primary designation, "heaven" (*deva*) refers to the dhyānas; because the eye is obtained by relying upon the dhyānas, it is called the "divine eye."

The mastery of the illuminating function of this divine eye is called the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurbala*). Regarding the "knowledge of birth and death" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), the designation is established based on the latter [aspect].
Following what the eye perceives regarding present sentient beings, knowing that they will die here and be born there in the future is called the knowledge of birth and death.

In reality, this power knows the eight kinds of future matters and so forth; however, because one wishes to cause people to know the past and thereby engender revulsion, it is called "birth-and-death.

Regarding the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*), there are two interpretations: first, it is named according to its capacity; the noble wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that can exhaust all outflows is called the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Second, it is established as a designation based on its object; [it refers to] the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles.

The extinction of this [ignorance] is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Knowing this exhaustion is called a power (*bala*). The following relies on the *Bala-sūtra* to analyze and explain its characteristics.
The phrase "as in the *Daśabala-sūtra*" is a general reference; all sūtras that speak of the ten powers are collectively termed the *Daśabala-sūtra*.
Alternatively, it may refer to a specific text, which will be explained extensively below. Within the initial explanation of the powers, the sūtra states:
There are ten phrases: first, the Tathāgata; second, the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*); third, knowing them as they truly are; fourth, these are powers;
fifth, their accomplishment; sixth, their excellence; seventh, their security; eighth, self-knowledge; ninth, the ability to turn the Brahma-wheel; and tenth, the ability to roar the lion’s roar.
Now, this author of the treatise first explains them in accordance with the sequence of these ten phrases, beginning from "self-security" [and continuing] downward.
This is an analysis according to the meaning. The initial statement that "what is spoken does not contradict the *tathatā*" explains the *Tathāgata*.

This is a case of employing words to manifest internal virtue; because one realizes *tathatā* through wisdom, the speech uttered does not contradict it. Since wisdom is difficult to manifest directly, it is manifested by means of words.
Therefore, the final summary is provided. The term *tathāgata* is a word of the Central Land (Sanskrit); it is called "Tathāgata" [in Chinese]. Regarding the second phrase, "pure and impure":
this explains that the distinction between pure and impure fruits depends upon their respective causes. This is termed "the appropriate place" (*sthāna*).
The fruit of pleasure is called "pure," while the fruit of suffering is "impure. Purity depends on virtuous causes, and impurity depends on non-virtuous ones; each relies upon its own distinct cause.

Because there are four principles [regarding these], they are termed "possible" (*sthāna*). That which contradicts the causes for the differentiation between pure and impure fruits is termed "impossible" (*asthāna*).

As it is said: that pleasant fruit arises from an evil cause, or that suffering is obtained through virtue—because these contradict the true nature of cause and effect, they are termed "contradictory.

To state such things is called "impossible" (*asthāna*). Having explained the third phrase by way of excluding overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the term "one who knows according to reality" (*yathābhūta-jña*) is briefly explained as knowing according to reality within the Sūtra. One who possesses overweening pride does not truly know the Dharma.

To falsely claim knowledge for oneself is not called "knowing as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Because the Buddha is free from pride, his knowing in accordance with the Dharma and reality is called "knowing as it truly is.

In the Hīnayāna teachings, ten types of knowledge are proclaimed as the essence of the powers (*bala*); here in the Mahāyāna, it is taught that the power has "knowledge as it truly is" as its essence.
As previously stated, the subsequent passage explains the departure from pride; its characteristics are manifest and thus easily understood. From "capable" (*samartha*) onwards...
The fourth phrase is explained as follows: "Capable of benefiting sentient beings in every way" refers to power in terms of the capacity for altruism.
"Victorious in abandoning all Māras and adversaries" refers to power in terms of the strength of self-benefit. This concludes the section.

The fifth phrase, "cultivation and inclusion," explains that the essence of the power of cultivation and inclusion is accomplished; the power of mastery according to one's desire is also accomplished.
This is termed the conclusion of the name. The sixth phrase, "nirvāṇa as supreme," explains that this is termed the fulfillment of the fruit.

The eighth noble [truth] is explained as "peace" (*śānta*), which clarifies the perfection of the cause; this corresponds to the seventh phrase. To "know for oneself what has been attained" explains the eighth phrase.
In relation to the final two phrases, the preceding [terms]—nirvāṇa and the eightfold path—are designated as "that which is known by oneself."
The passage beginning with "By means of compassion" explains the ninth phrase.
"To extensively expound for others with a compassionate mind is called 'turning'"—this explains the term "turning. Why is this asked?
That is, why is that which is turned called the "Brahma-wheel"? The following explains its characteristics: "Brahma" is named for purity. There are two kinds of purity: first, self-purity.
The second is purifying others. From the beginning up to "pure, cool, and true" refers to self-purification.

Because the causes and effects of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) involve manifold afflictions and disturbances, they are called "various. "Pure and quiescent extinction" means the cessation of the cause; "pure, cool, and true" means the disappearance of the fruit.
From "the first turning" onwards is the purification of others. This concludes the section on names. It is called "attaining the supreme above and below."
This explains the tenth phrase: "attaining the Dharma proclaimed by the supreme teaching. The true Dharma heard from past Buddhas is called the "supreme teaching.

To encompass the virtues of the unsurpassed teacher who proclaims it is called "encompassing the Great Master. To have well-accumulated the virtues of the teacher is what is meant by "encompassing the Great Master."
This explains the "correct lion's roar" attained by oneself. It is the roar of power that destroys those of other paths;
it is the roar of a mind that is not intimidated by others. It is the roar of victory, supreme and unsurpassed, over all treatises.
This clarifies that all the Buddha’s discourses are the most excellent and unsurpassed among all paths. It is the roar spoken for the sake of the fourfold assembly, which reveals its benefits.

This is called the "lower fetters. The first section above, which explains based on the sūtra, is now complete. From here on is the second section, the analytical classification according to the meaning. This contains two parts:

first, the analysis by way of the two gates of "establishing oneself" and "establishing others. Briefly stated, the first eight phrases concern establishing oneself. [The subsequent part concerns] establishing others... [briefly stated].
The latter two phrases refer to that. "Both self and others are at peace" is a double conclusion of the preceding virtues.

"Developing, revealing, instructing, and explaining" concludes the characteristics of the teaching; it clarifies how the Buddha, within the *Daśabala-sūtra*, develops and reveals these two merits, instructing sentient beings and proclaiming them for the sake of the multitude.
These two attainments of meaning are analyzed through two gates. This is a brief explanation.

"Attaining the meaning" refers to the first eight phrases. It is called "attaining the meaning" because it brings about one's own supreme benefit. "Attaining the means" refers to the final two phrases.
Because of turning the Brahma-wheel and because of the lion’s roar, it causes other sentient beings to attain wisdom and attainment;
since it serves as the means for others to obtain these, it is called "attaining the means. This is the general heading; below, its characteristics are explained. [This applies to] humans and devas.
That which was sought is all obtained by me. This general explanation of the latter two [turnings]—enabling others to attain wisdom—is termed the "concluding summary.

As with the recovery from illness, the subsequent specific explanation of the latter two—enabling others to attain cessation—is as follows: the former turning of the Brahma-wheel enables those who practice through craving to eliminate craving and attain cessation;
the latter lion’s roar enables those who practice through views to eliminate views and attain cessation. Within the turning of the Brahma-wheel, it is like the case of illness.

"Attaining the removal of affliction and finding peace means that one's own ailments are exhausted. By citing the exhaustion of one's own [ailments], it clarifies the ability to exhaust those of others;
furthermore, one treats others so that they may achieve cessation. This is called the 'concluding summary.

Within the Lion’s Roar, causing false and heterodox teachers to obtain various remedies so that their illnesses are cured, and causing the Six Teachers and others to all obtain correct treatment so that they perceive their ailments and they vanish—this is called..."

The lower section: Regarding the explanation of the power of karma (*karmabala*), first the scriptural text is interpreted, and subsequently it is cited to provide a summary. Within the sutra, these are explained in sequence through seven gates: (1) knowing the karma of the three periods of time;
(2) distinguishing the divisions of conduct to know bodily karma and so forth; (3) furthermore, there are four [points] below to know the four types of dharma-reception (*dharmopādāna*).
First, they are known; next, they are explained; finally, they are summarized. Within the knowledge [of these], the first is general; [it concerns] the present and the future...

The coming of suffering and pleasure is explained in both general and specific terms as the four types of feeling (*vedanā*). The arising of wholesome and unwholesome feelings is explained as the four dharmas. Below, their characteristics are defined;

here, the first gate is briefly presented, while the remaining three refer back to what precedes, and can thus be understood from that. Next, the conclusion is stated: "This is called the skillful means regarding the bases (*sthāna-upāya*).
Here, the retributions of suffering and pleasure are designated as the "bases," while the states of stability and instability are termed "skillful means. If there are four... [the assembly...]
1. By "sentient beings," one knows those who initiate karma. 2. By "non-sentient beings," one knows the objective sphere of karma;

since this sphere encompasses both the sentient and the non-sentient, it is referred to here simply as "non-sentient" due to brevity in the text. This is called "sentient beings," concluding the preceding point regarding those who, being sentient, initiate karma.
[The text] is abbreviated and does not conclude the subsequent point regarding the category of non-sentient beings as the objective sphere. 6. That which is well-performed is...
The "cause" (*hetu*) refers to clearly understanding the causes of karma. This text is inverted and moreover incomplete;
it should correctly state "the roots of merit performed," or, to be complete, "the roots of merit performed and the unwholesome deeds performed"—this is called the cause.
The seventh section, "the desirable and undesirable," clarifies the results of karma below: pleasant results are desirable, while painful results are undesirable. "Calamity" (*āpad*) is precisely...
It is not that suffering is unloved; rather, merit is precisely that which is desirable and pleasant. The following summarizes and concludes this:
"At all times" refers back to the first point, the karma of the three periods of time; "all actions" refers back to the second point, the actions of body, speech, and mind.
"Everywhere" refers back to the third of the four dharmas of reception. "All phenomena" refers back to the fourth, namely those that are of the category of sentient beings.
"All objects" refers back to the fifth, which takes that which is not of the category of sentient beings as its object.
"All causes" refers back to what was previously stated regarding the sixth [topic], the actions performed by the roots of goodness.

"All calamities and blessings" refers back to the seventh [topic], the fruits of calamity and blessing—whether beloved or unloved. "In this way, the Tathāgata fully knows all" is the summary that concludes the knowledge [of these matters].

Regarding the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*), the term "meditative absorption and liberation" (*dhyāna-vimokṣa*) is explained by means of the four dhyānas and eight liberations. Following the section on dhyāna, there is now the section on the Buddha’s power of clarity (*vidyā-bala*).
Within this, there are two parts: first, it clarifies that the Tathāgata’s mastery over entering and emerging from self-attained meditative concentrations is called the power of concentration;
second, it further explains that causing others to attain concentration is also called the power of concentration. Within the first part, there are four sections; the first is a brief exposition.

Explanation: One who possesses mastery over the mind regarding dhyāna and liberation possesses mastery over the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). That which accomplishes each respective function of concentration is called "mastery of application.

This is the concluding summary. Second, citing scriptural authority to establish this proof: as the World-Honored One’s realization through the correct reception of *samādhi* proves the Tathāgata’s mastery over the essence of concentration;
likewise, his manifestation of light during that correct reception, illuminating down to the Brahma realm, proves the Tathāgata’s mastery over the application of concentration.

In the *Āgama* sūtras, it is said that at times the Tathāgata, in order to transform the Brahmā assembly, would go to that celestial realm, emitting supreme light from his body and proclaiming the wondrous Dharma with his mouth.
When the various Brahmās saw the light and heard what was being taught, they did not perceive his physical form; therefore, this passage is cited here.
Third, following the meaning of "by this principle" and below, the conclusion of this meaning is established based on what was cited there: by means of this Tathāgata-samādhi.

While dwelling in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), he emits light and preaches the Dharma with the wondrous voice of Brahmā, causing the assembly of Brahmās to hear only his voice without seeing his form.
When the Tathāgata enters the *samādhi* that is common to the world, he is able to swiftly accomplish the entry into that which is common to the world.

The *samādhi* that resembles what is not common to the world is the essential body of the Buddha’s concentration (*dhyāna*). That which is entered is the name of the worldly pure concentration; it is called "common."

The world [of this samādhi] is exquisite and surpasses that of the mundane; therefore, it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). Because that which enters [into it] resembles worldly concentration (*dhyāna*), it is named the "Image-like Samādhi" (*pratibimba-samādhi*).
It is capable of swiftly accomplishing the function of the Buddha’s concentration. Fourth, regarding "at the level of dhyāna," this reiterates the present point to conclude the previous discussion.
This reiterates the text to explain it, thereby establishing the power of concentration as described in the *Daśabala-sūtra*. At the level of dhyāna...
"Liberation of mind" refers to mastery over the essence of concentration mentioned in the first section;

"attaining mastery at will" refers to mastery over the function of concentration mentioned in the first section. Possessing these two kinds [of mastery], the sutras speak of the powers of dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and so forth.
The preceding section was the first, clarifying what the Buddha himself attained. From here on is the second, clarifying how he enables others to attain it; this contains three parts.
First, it clarifies that sentient beings, despite possessing the two types of afflictions regarding the various *dhyānas* and so forth, are unable to attain meditative concentration.

First, because they have not yet cultivated [the path], the afflictive hindrances prevent them from practicing. Second, even if they have already attained [a state], the fetters of their own stage prevent them from exerting diligence.

The second section, "The Tathāgata," below, clarifies how the Buddha’s skillful transformation enables beings to attain dhyāna. First, it clarifies the Tathāgata’s skillful transformation through the three karmas; subsequently, it clarifies the benefits of this transformation.

Initially, "employing various conventional words" refers to transformation through the karma of speech (*vākkarman*); because the sounds and voices differ according to the respective categories of beings, they are termed "various.
"According to their forms and appearances" refers to transformation through the karma of body (*kāyakarman*); that is to say, according to sentient beings—
The manifestation of different physical forms constitutes the "manifesting body" (*nirmāṇakāya*). Adapting to what is appropriate refers to the transformation of mental karma (*manas-karma*).

To observe the nature and mind of sentient beings and measure what is suitable for them is termed "adapting to what is appropriate. The following clarifies the benefit of this transformation: causing others to attain goodness corresponds to the first [of the three bodies].
For those who have not yet practiced, it causes them to attain dhyāna; because that which is attained is not of a single kind, it is called "dhyāna and so forth.
For those whose cultivation of wisdom is complete, it corresponds to the second [category] mentioned previously. For those who have already attained it, it causes them to advance further.

Regarding the term "freedom from affliction," it refers to transforming the first category mentioned previously by causing them to attain dhyāna, thereby becoming free from afflictions. Regarding the term "purity," it refers to transforming the second category mentioned previously by causing them to reach fulfillment.
This is ultimate purity. Third, "if one attains" serves as a summary to conclude [the preceding]. To say "if one attains" refers to the second point within the first section:
having already attained [a state] that contradicts further progress (*viśeṣagamana*). To say "if one does not attain" refers to the first point within the first section:
not yet having cultivated [it], such that it is not attained. To say "if it is inferior" refers to the second section: causing the attainment of dhyāna. To say "if it is superior" [refers to...]
This refers to the fulfillment of wisdom through cultivation within the second [stage]. The phrase "all according to reality" below summarizes the knowledge.

Regarding the faculties and powers, those who have previously attained the superior stage of "warmth" (ūṣmagata) in faith and so forth—namely, the five faculties of faith and the rest—are established based on the preceding meditative concentration.

Because it introduces the subsequent stage by referring back to the preceding one, it is called "toward completion" (*xiàngchéng*). Regarding the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, in the previous enumeration of names they were merely described as "sharp" or "dull";
now it is stated that there are three levels, and [this stage] is the highest among the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stages.

Within the power of understanding (*prajñā*), the causes of desire consist of generating faith through others and knowing through one's own reflection. Within the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), the superior degree of desire consists of knowing the essence of desire.
This is termed the "inferior fetter. It is called the "power of understanding" because it functions as a fetter at the initial stage.
Within the category of the power of nature (*dharmatā-bala*), the various natures are first indicated in their entirety; they are subsequently explained in detail.

Among these are the pure natures of the three vehicles and the defiled natures such as greed, which were not enumerated among the eighty-four thousand [teachings] mentioned in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

In the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates are elucidated; here, those should be translated as the eighty-four thousand natures of affliction (*kleśa*). Below, this is summarized.

Regarding the path leading to the destination: first, one approaches the path leading to the destination by means of the clarity of pure dharmas; furthermore, various aspects are discussed from the perspective of defilement.

These various factors are individually opposed, yet they are collectively presented as a general heading, which is subsequently explained in detail. To give rise to divergent views is for the mind to enter into opposition.

They are constantly engaged in mutual strife and their words are contradictory. For example, as the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) below cite persons to refute [the teaching], so the *Sūryasthānasūtra* (Time-Sūtra) extensively clarifies it by citing scriptures.
There must, therefore, be a separate *Sūryasthānasūtra* in foreign lands; the *Mānavīya-sūryasthāna-sūtra* currently transmitted here does not explain this meaning.
Within the power of past lives (*pūrvajanma-bala*), the initial knowledge of how sentient beings establish various names through conventional designations (*saṃketa*) serves as the general heading.
Among the eight matters and six types of conduct, this is presented by taking the first; therefore, only "names" are mentioned.

This refers to the past, which is further elucidated in detail. Within this detailed exposition, there are four parts: first, the past is cited as the thematic gateway consisting of the eight matters and six types of conduct.
He and the self as the subject are explained separately as eight matters; their mutual commonality is termed "conduct" (*saṃskāra*).
Thus concludes the summary. Second, to distinguish their characteristics: the phrase "eight kinds" reiterates the first section above, while the following portion distinguishes those characteristics.
This is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, the *Dharmaskandha-sūtra*. There are three points of difference: first, differences in presence or absence;

that which exists in the former is absent here. Second, differences in division or combination; here, "long-term abiding" and "limit of lifespan" are treated separately, whereas in the former they are combined and termed "life-span.
Third, differences in sequence; in the present text, the fifth [topic], suffering and pleasure, is [treated differently].
It is the eighth [category]. The others are all similar. "Name" refers to such as the past [figure] Mahājanaka and so forth.
"Birth" refers to being born into one of the four castes, such as the Kṣatriya and so forth. "Lineage" refers to such as the Zhang or Wang clans and so forth.
Food, drink, suffering, and pleasure are clearly manifest and thus knowable. The latter three types concern the distinctions within lifespan. Regarding "long-lived," this refers to lifespan.
"Extremely few" means that those called "long-lived" reach middle age; they are described as long-lived in contrast to youths.
Those said to have a "limited lifespan" are youths who die prematurely. The six types of practitioners refer back to the second section, where their characteristics are explained below.

"Worldly designations and names" refers to the aforementioned names. "Kṣatriyas and so forth, in terms of appearance" refers to the aforementioned birth. The forms of the Kṣatriyas and others are thus described.
It is called "form" (*rūpa*). Furthermore, form may be distinguished by the four castes, as when people in the world speak of various distinctions of form, and so forth.
"Parents" refers to the locus of one's lineage. "Food and drink" are the same as previously mentioned. Regarding "good and evil":
while the preceding eight matters were explained in terms of their results as suffering and pleasure, here they are explained in terms of their causal conduct as good and evil. Good...
This is because [the Buddha] manifested his shared practice with those who delight in evil and so forth. Regarding "life span," this refers to the three lifespans of the beginning, middle, and end.

Third, the eight types of matters clarify the eight and six [categories], which apply universally to both self and others. Fourth, from "He spoke thus" onwards, he extensively clarifies his own realization based on those six matters:
first the individual analysis, and finally the conclusion. As for these names of "I," they are as the Buddha himself said regarding the past Mahānāma.
These are my names and so forth. The following four [categories] may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the subsequent life-span: "if young" refers to the limit of one's lifespan; "if middle-aged" refers to dwelling for a long time.
The term "long-lived" (*dīrghāyus*) refers to longevity. Thus concludes the preceding section.
Now, regarding the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), I shall provide a detailed explanation following the sequence of the text in the *Daśabala-sūtra*.

In the sūtra, it first clarifies how the divine eye surpasses that of ordinary humans, and subsequently clarifies what is seen by it; I shall now explain both in full. All meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) are termed "divine abodes" (*devasthāna*).

Among the three abodes, the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments are collectively termed the "abode of devas" (*devasthāna*). Regarding the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*) obtained by relying on these dhyānas:

it is designated as the "divine eye" because the name is established based on its fundamental support. That which is called "exceedingly pure" (*praśuddha*) refers to the fulfillment of the pure fruit;

while the divine eyes of other persons are merely termed "pure," the Tathāgata’s divine eye is so pure that it is called "fulfilled. It is called "exceeding" because it is fulfilled, and thus it is known to surpass that of ordinary humans.
The following explains what is seen. There are two types of what is seen: first, seeing the beautiful or ugly colors at the time of death;
second, giving rise to wrong views regarding the precepts and seeing the retribution of suffering or pleasure resulting from performing good or evil deeds.

Regarding the first section, "when sentient beings are at the point of death," this explains the phrase "seeing the time of birth and death" in the sutra. It refers precisely to the moment of death when life is severed for a single kṣaṇa. However—
The gradual deterioration of the faculties while life has not yet been severed is called the time of approaching death; these collectively comprise what is known as the time of death.
Seeing the signs of the deterioration of the faculties during this period refers to the "beautiful colors" and "ugly colors" mentioned in the sūtra.

This vision pertains to the intermediate state (antarābhava) following death. Within the category of ugly colors, the two types of darkness are divided into two based on their degree of intensity, as follows:

These are the types that ride upon the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This clarifies that this intermediate state resembles a shadow, like black darkness or black wool. Below, its categories are set forth:
it is like the extreme evil color of nocturnal darkness, or the light and evil color of black wool; therefore, they are categorized as "inferior.
Within the category of beautiful colors, the two types—white and pure—are further divided into superior and inferior. Such are the types that ride upon [the intermediate state].

The meaning of birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is the same as explained previously. Below, its categories are set forth: for example, the light of the bright moon is of an exceedingly beautiful color, while the cloth from Vārāṇasī is of a subtle, beautiful color;
therefore, this is termed the "conclusion of the lower."
In the section on observing the creation of karma and the reception of its retribution, one first observes the creation of evil and the reception of its evil retribution.
This contrasts with the aforementioned observation of the reception of retribution for good. Within the category of evil, there are three aspects: first, the observation of the creation of evil;

second, the formation of lower views through various wrong views and unwholesome actions, which serve as the cause; third, the attainment of the fruit through the completion of the causes of lower views within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Regarding the first of these:

"Arising from unwholesome discipline is called unwholesome discipline of body, speech, and mind" means that when a person of right view gives rise to violations of the prohibitions through body, speech, and mind, this is termed the unwholesomeness of unwholesome discipline of body, speech, and mind; such a person’s conduct is ruined, though their view is not.

Therefore, they are simply called "unwholesome discipline" (duḥśīla) with respect to the body and so forth. As for the various types of false and inferior views that constitute unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind:
when someone, due to false views, gives rise to bodily and other such karmas, these are called unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind arising from false views.

The second section from hereon below shows that what was previously performed can serve as a cause for what follows. Within this, the first point shows that karma of body, speech, and so forth, arising from wrong views, can serve as a cause for what follows;
the latter point shows that karma of body, speech, and so forth, consisting of immoral conduct, can serve as a cause for what follows.
Within each of these two, there are three phrases: first, the accomplishment of views; second, views as the cause; and third, the conclusion.
Regarding the initial accomplishment of views within the preceding section on evil views, there is both a general and a specific accomplishment.

The various false views and evil deeds constitute the general explanation of accomplishment. The following provides the specific exposition: slandering the noble ones is termed false view, which specifically clarifies the accomplishment of views.
They slander and cling to false causes and false effects; based on this, they perform all manner of wrong actions.

This specifically clarifies how the evil conduct of body and so forth arises from wrong views. Having performed these wrong actions, they experience pleasure in the present, taking their inferior views as the cause.

Regarding those who experience happiness in the present life but suffering in the future: there are some who hold wrong views and do not believe in cause and effect, acting recklessly and committing evil;
therefore, they experience happiness now but will suffer in the future. Regarding those who experience suffering in the present life and suffering in the future:

there are some who hold wrong views and seek liberation by tormenting their bodies; therefore, they experience suffering now and will also suffer in the future. This is called "binding that wrong karma through wrong causes."

This refers to the meaning of being a cause. In the context of the inferior precepts of misconduct below, various evil views are established; their establishment constitutes birth within the evil realms, which is seen as the cause.
By citing birth in the evil realms, the meaning of its causality is made manifest. "That which is called the cause" concludes that the meaning of these inferior precepts is to serve as the cause.

From here below is the third [section], which shows how suffering retribution is received from evil causes. Within this, there are four statements. First, regarding "the dissolution of the body and the separation of name-and-form":
the four aggregates (skandhas) are called "name" (nāma), and the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is called "form" (rūpa). The separation of these two parts is termed "the dissolution of the body."

Second, the explanation of the end of life. That which exhausts the factors of birth is called the "factor of birth" because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) prevents the disintegration of form and mind and acts as the cause for birth;
when these factors of birth are exhausted, it is termed the "end of life. Third, the explanation of rebirth in evil destinies.

Here, birth is not explained in detail, but only the evil destinies are interpreted. Unrighteous and unwholesome conduct is termed "evil"; because they are the cause of evil, they are so named. [Regarding the suffering experienced... no...
Regarding the term "evil destinies" (*durgati*): the two retributions of ghosts and animals are called evil destinies because they are destinations toward which one goes due to evil [karma].

The fourth explanation concerns falling into *naraka*. "Falling" (*patana*) refers to descending; "turning one's back on compassion" (*karuṇā-pṛṣṭhībhūta*) explains the nature of that fall. Because it is the lowest point, one tumbles headlong into it; thus it is called "falling.

Because one is separated from all noble ones (*ārya*) and sages, it is called "turning one's back on compassion," and so forth. Because it is supremely loathsome, it is called *naraka*; this is the hell into which one falls.
This is the locus. Because it is predominant within the miserable realms (*apāya*), it is discussed separately.

Below, regarding the wholesome (*kuśala*), that which is contrary to the above is termed the "pure portion" (*śukla-bhāga*); this refers to the wholesome cause. Below, the attainment of the fruit is clarified.
Those who are born through the practice of wholesome deeds are called those of "fortunate rebirths," which refers to the human realm. Those whose experience is naturally so are called "gods.
Because they are superior among fortunate rebirths, they are discussed separately.
Within the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-bala*), only one’s own exhaustion is clarified; the knowledge of others is not discussed. This section contains three parts:

first, the clarification of the destruction of the outflows; second, the antidotes for the destruction of the outflows, explained below; third, the virtues of the destruction of the outflows, explained below regarding the attainment of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).

Regarding the first: "all outflows without remainder" refers to the disappearance of the arising afflictions (*kleśa*); "the severing of all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)" refers to the total exhaustion of both the active and latent dispositions. The second [part] concerns the antidotes.

The term "counteractive" (*pratipakṣa*) mentioned in the middle serves as a general heading, which is then specifically elucidated below. First, the absence of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) is explained; following the phrase "the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*), its liberation (*vimukti*) is clarified.
Within the preceding section on the absence of hindrances, "outflow-free mind" (*anāsrava-citta*) refers to the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) that counteracts the preceding outflows.

"Outflow-free wisdom" (*anāsrava-jñāna*) refers to the untainted insight (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that remedies the preceding latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). The transformation of the name [from "mind" to "wisdom"] reveals the superior nature of the insight.

The preceding untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) among the three trainings. The preceding untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) among the three trainings.

In the passage concerning "lower liberation" (*adho-vimukti*), the statement that the exhaustion of outflows is called "liberation of mind" (*ceto-vimukti*) and "liberation by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*) is a brief enumeration of their names.
The culmination of the aforementioned higher mind, which transcends all burdens, is called liberation of mind. The aforementioned higher...

Wisdom that ultimately emerges from the burdens of existence is called "liberation through wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*). One who attains liberation of mind and wisdom based on vision and cultivation attains the state of liberation.
Because one abandons delusions and removes burdens by relying on these two paths, one attains the two types of liberation. This is termed "subsequent existence" (*punarbhava*) as a general summary.

These two liberations are so named because they are accomplished externally by means of obstacles; hence, they are called "subsequent existence. From here below is the third [section]: the virtue of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-guṇa*).

In the first part of the middle section, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are clarified. From "according to reality" (*yathābhūtam*) downward, the attainment of the four knowledges (*catasraḥ prajñāḥ*) is clarified. "According to reality" means knowing for oneself that one has realized the four knowledges and can explain them to others;
it is expressed by resorting to words to manifest [this realization]. Therefore, the phrase "knowing for oneself" (*svayam viditvā*) at the beginning summarizes this self-knowledge.

From "birth is exhausted" (*kṣīṇā me jātiḥ*) downward, it demonstrates how what was previously known for oneself is manifested through words for the sake of others. "Birth is exhausted and the holy life is established" refers to the former two knowledges. Thus it is explained in detail.

Regarding this, there are four aspects explained in detail: "Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; and there is no further existence hereafter. What is the distinction between these four? The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"Birth has been exhausted" is the knowledge of the cessation of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*). "The holy life has been established" is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

"What was to be done has been accomplished" is the knowledge of the realization of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). "There is no further existence hereafter" is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).

"Wisdom. This refers to realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*), not merely the wisdom that contemplates objects in a general sense. How can there be four [aspects] when the mind of realization is of a single flavor?
Although its essence is of one flavor, its meanings are distinguished as four. What are their characteristics?

According to the Lesser Vehicle, when the mind of an Adept (*aśaikṣa*) arises, it correctly contemplates the principle of the Truths (*satya*) without mental discrimination, such as "my births are exhausted" or "the holy life is established," and so forth. However, this noble...

Wisdom is able to exhaustively collect all causes; this is explained as "my births have been exhausted. When this noble wisdom has perfected the practice of the path, it is explained as "the holy life has been established.
When cessation is realized to its ultimate extent, it is explained as "what was to be done has been accomplished.
Being able to sever future suffering, it is explained as "not receiving further existence. Thereafter, one emerges from meditative absorption and abides in the state of having a mind.
Taking as its object that which was previously attained, it then reflects to itself: "My births are ended," and so forth, up to the fourth [fruit]: "I shall not undergo further existence.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, when the Buddha’s wisdom first arises, it correctly illuminates reality (*tathatā*) and is likewise without conceptualization (*avikalpa*).

Statements such as "my births are ended" merely follow from the distinctions in meaning; apart from these four aspects, they are identical to what preceded them. However, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of suchness continues perpetually without interruption.

[Interval. This is not the same as the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) emerging from meditative absorption with discursive thought regarding what they have personally attained; rather, it is for the sake of manifesting to sentient beings what they themselves have realized, saying:

"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (brahmacarya) is established," and so forth. Question: What is the difference between these four [knowledges] and the two knowledges of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and non-arising (anutpādajñāna)?

In the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna, it is taught that among these four, "birth has already been exhausted" constitutes the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), while "not receiving a future existence" [constitutes the knowledge of non-arising].

Regarding the knowledge of the non-arising of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-anutpāda-jñāna*), the Abhidharma does not hold this view. As for "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*): it directly perceives the exhaustion of the causes and effects of birth and death.
As for "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*): it definitively guarantees that the causes and effects of future birth and death will never arise again.

Within that knowledge of exhaustion, there are four types of knowledge; within the knowledge of non-arising, there are likewise four types of knowledge, as Nāgārjuna has explained. If one observes directly...
To discern that "my births have been exhausted" up to "this is the fourth [knowledge]: there will be no further existence"—this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
To say, "birth is exhausted and will not arise again; the holy life has been established and need not be practiced further; what was to be done has been accomplished and will never again be undone;
there is no further existence and it will not be experienced again"—this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Such are the four knowledges.
Above, the Master of the Treatise has provided an explanation based on the sūtras. From here on, the Master sets forth his own interpretation.
First, he cites the number seven; next, he lists their names; finally, he explains them in detail. "Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) clarifies the essential nature of power.
"Discrimination" (*vibhāga*) refers to the differentiation of their characteristics. "Unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) means not being common to others. "Equal" (*samatā*) means that all Buddhas are equal.
The term "creator" (*kāraka*) clarifies the power and efficacy; the term "succession" (*anukrama*) clarifies the arising of the causes for transformative activity;
and the term "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) clarifies the limits of that power. These will be explained extensively below. Within the explanation of the first section, two positions are first presented:

some say that its nature consists of the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), while others say its nature is wisdom (*jñāna*). Below, the authoritative teachings are cited to distinguish between what is correct and incorrect; once the characteristics are clearly revealed, they can be understood.

Within the second section, there are three parts: first, citing the heading to state the number; second, defining their characteristics; and third, the temporal classification, which refers to the distinctions among the three periods of time.

Regarding the past, future, and present, these are explained as entering into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) to clarify their characteristics. Within the ten powers (*daśabala*), the power of knowledge of past lives pertains to the past, and the power of the divine eye pertains to the future.
