With the exception of the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*), the remaining powers pertain to all three periods of time. As for the power of the exhaustion of outflows:
The power of realizing the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-bala*) through one's own direct realization is termed the "present knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.

The exhaustion of that which is to be known does not belong to the three times; however, according to conventional usage regarding persons, it may be said to pervade the three times. Entering into omniscience (*sarvajña*) accords with foreign terminology;

according to this [system], one should say "entering into all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā-praveśa*). "Entering" means "understanding. Thus, the Buddha’s omniscient understanding of the three times is established.
"Dharma" is named "universal entry" (*sarvatraga*). "Various distinctions" refers to the differentiation according to dharmas.

The phrase "all conditioned phenomena enter into all aspects through their specific and general characteristics" explains and reveals their characteristics. The Ten Powers (*daśabala*) have knowledge of both the conditioned and the unconditioned;

here, for the time being, we speak only of the conditioned. Within the conditioned, the distinctions such as cause and effect are called "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*), while [the characteristics of] impermanence and suffering [are general characteristics].

The emptiness of all phenomena is collectively termed their "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Among the ten powers (*daśabala*), the first—the power regarding what is possible and what is impossible—is the most broad and general, as it involves knowledge of both the self-characteristic and the common characteristic.

From the seventh power up to the [eighth], the power of knowing the path, there is knowledge of both the self-characteristic and the common characteristic. Knowing impurity and so forth is knowledge of the self-characteristic;

knowing the dharma of non-self is knowledge of the common characteristic. Within the tenth power, the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*), one knows both the self-characteristic and the common characteristic.

[The first power] is common. Seeing that there is that which removes darkness, one knows its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); realizing emptiness and exhausting the outflows (*āsrava*), one knows its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Because the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows knows only the specific characteristic and does not know emptiness, the remaining seven powers know only their own specific characteristics.

To understand and know all such phenomena in every respect is therefore called "entering into all aspects" (*sarvākāra*). The conceptual distinctions of sentient beings vary according to the individual.
Furthermore, the phrase "entering all realms of birth for the sake of all benefit" clarifies its characteristics. All ten powers take all sentient beings as their object;
regarding these sentient beings, they understand all skillful means for their benefit. Therefore, it is called "entering all benefit.
Thus concludes the section below. The unique qualities (*āveṇika*) and the corresponding characteristics can be understood through this clarification.
The phrase "one who performs actions" (kāraka) refers to the fifth section; below, its characteristics are explained. "Possible and impossible" (sthānāsthāna) cites the essence of its power.
"One who knows the true cause and effect in this way" explains the characteristics of that power. It is called "true" because one knows the correct cause and effect.

To subdue disputes regarding cause and effect, one clarifies their functioning. Those such as the śramaṇas are people who deviate from reason; though they seek [the truth], they do not find it and instead give rise to many divergent attachments.
They dispute cause and effect: some say that a virtuous cause can obtain a pleasant fruit, while others say it results in suffering.
The same applies to unwholesome [actions]. Because one knows the correct causes and effects through this first power, one is able to subdue them.

The "power of knowledge regarding one's own karma" (karmasvaka-jñānabala) sets forth the essence of that power: knowing, in accordance with reality, that the results one experiences are the very actions one has performed oneself; this defines its characteristic.

One knows that what one has done is not without cause; that this karma receives its fruit is not without result. To subdue those who disparage the merit of giving, he clarifies the performance of deeds.
Various śramaṇas dispute over giving, disagreeing on whether it possesses merit or lacks merit—this is called "disputing the merit of giving.
It is precisely because the power of karma reveals that giving possesses merit that he is able to subdue them; in principle, he thoroughly subdues them all.
Regarding all the debates concerning the merits and demerits of actions performed, there are many who dispute the nature of giving; therefore, this is stated specifically.
The powers of dhyāna and liberation present the essence of those powers, omitting a detailed analysis of their characteristics. Below, the activities are clarified:

the three types of manifestation constitute the activity of taming, instructing, and correctly transforming others. "Subduing" refers to the activity of crushing heterodoxy through antidotes. [This applies to] various śramaṇas and others.
Some say that asceticism is the correct antidote; others say that prostration is the correct antidote.
All such [positions] are termed "antidotes. Because these conflicting disputations can be correctly transformed, they are able to subdue this dispute regarding antidotes.
Regarding the powers of the faculties (*indriya-bala*), their essential nature is presented; regarding the various births and so forth, their characteristics are explained;

as is appropriate below, their functions are clarified. Regarding the power of diverse understandings (*nānādhimukti-bala*), their essential nature is presented; regarding the various births and so forth, their characteristics are explained.

"Teaching the cultivation of purity" clarifies its function. "The power of various realms" cites the essence of that power. "Regarding the arising of all births" distinguishes the characteristics of that power.
"According to their faculties" clarifies its function; since the nature must depend on the faculties and desires to be established, it is "according to the faculties.
Since the mind relies on the nature to receive the Dharma, it is "according to the desires. [This applies to] each respective gateway of liberation (*pāramitā*).
This explains the benefit of the teaching.

Regarding the power of the path that leads to the destination (*yāna-pratipatti-bala*), the first section identifies its essential nature; the next clarifies its activity; and the final section restates and summarizes it.

The "power of the path leading to the destination" constitutes the first section. The phrase "for the sake of sentient beings" refers to its activity. Within this, there are two parts: first, by means of the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*);...

The instruction on the phenomena of things (*vastudharma*) is explained in full detail as in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*. Second, regarding the instruction on the principles of lower reasoning (*nyāyadharma*):

herein, the initial section clarifies the instruction for bodhisattvas; from the passage "one should reflect in this way" [regarding] the Śrāvaka vehicle onwards, it concurrently teaches the śrāvakas.

Within the section "Teaching Bodhisattvas," there are three distinct parts: first, the inquiry that initiates the discourse; second, the detailed explanation in response to the question, beginning with the "perfection of samādhi";
and third, the conclusion and praise following the explanation of the name. Regarding the initial inquiry, it asks: "How does the Tathāgata teach those who are beginners?

Here, "beginners" refers to bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi), who have not yet attained self-realization and thus rely on the provisional instruction of a teacher. This is how he teaches them.
What [is this]? In the second explanation, first the ritual of the teaching is clarified; from "for those who are without deceit" onwards, the persons to be taught are clarified;
from "uttering these words" onwards, the words of the instruction are clarified; and from "all such as this, once known" onwards, the benefit of the instruction is clarified.

Regarding the stabilization of the mind through the requisites for samādhi within the aforementioned ritual of the teaching: one must first cause it to abide by means of those eleven requisites for concentration.
Having first cultivated the mind, one then instructs them in those principles and dharmas. The eleven factors for concentration (*samādhi-sambhāra*) are as explained in the *Tattvasiddhi*:

(1) pure observance of the precepts; (2) obtaining virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); (3) guarding the sense-gates; (4) moderation in eating; (5) diminishing sleep; (6) possessing wholesome states of mind (*kuśala-vitarka*);
(7) possessing faith and resolve; and (8) possessing the factors of practice, namely: faith, lack of deceit, little illness, and diligence.
1. Endowment with wisdom; 2. possessing the nine bases of liberation (*navavimokṣasthāna*), namely:

the Buddha preaching the Dharma for them, monks reciting the sūtras well and preaching the Dharma for others, and contemplating alone in stillness while skillfully grasping the signs of meditative concentration; 3. being without hindrance, meaning the elimination and departure from the three obstacles;
4. non-attachment, meaning the relinquishing of a mind of clinging.
Regarding those among the instructed who are said to be "without guile": being upright and abandoning delusion is what is meant by "being without guile.

Within the words of the instruction, he first teaches the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Following the passage on "seeing with the eyes," he teaches the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Thus, through the method of dismantling the self, he concludes both at the end of the path of means. Regarding the emptiness of persons, he first teaches the contemplation of the present; he does not [teach it] regarding the future.
The instruction concerns contemplating the future; the past is omitted for brevity. Within the present, there is first a general overview, followed by a detailed analysis, and finally a summary.

"You should dwell alone and contemplate the names established [for these aggregates]"—this is a general exhortation to practice contemplation. All sentient beings seek out names and grasp at them as a self.

Therefore, the teaching on the names is intended to bring about the knowledge of non-self (*anātman*). Furthermore, among the eight objects, the names come first; since this is stated from the perspective of the beginning, the teaching focuses on the names.
The remaining [objects] are omitted and not discussed here. The eight objects of observation are as explained previously in the "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa-paṭala*).
This is called the distinct teaching (biejiao) of contemplation. First, it teaches that [the self] is truly non-existent; later, it teaches that [phenomena] are conventionally existent.

Thus, the statement that the six internal and external bases (āyatana) are all non-existent refers to the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya). Among the twelve bases, the six sense faculties are termed "internal."
The six sense objects are called "external. That which is indicated by those names—such as "self" and "sentient beings"—is entirely non-existent both internally, externally, and in between.

Furthermore, there is no self-nature (svabhāva) outside of phenomena (dharma), nor are there any phenomena outside of self-nature. Therefore, it is said that self-nature is also non-existent. This teaching is truly non-existent;
it is merely a name, a teaching for the purpose of contemplation regarding provisional existence. Existence is but a name and a conceptualization.
Because it is a designation based on causes and conditions, it is not substantially existent. Thus, the following summarizes the reflection:
observing the future, since the "I" does not exist in the present, it will likewise not exist in the future; therefore, one does not give rise to the notion of a person regarding the future.

Regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*), one first contemplates the emptiness of the eye, subsequently applying this analogy to other phenomena. Within the contemplation of the eye, one first contemplates the present, followed by the past, and finally the future.

Within the present, there are three parts: first, contemplating the emptiness of the essence of the eye; second, from the words "In this way" (*evam*) onwards, contemplating the emptiness of the causes and conditions upon which the eye depends to establish the emptiness of the eye;
third, from the words "For what reason? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) onwards, contemplating the emptiness of the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
It establishes the emptiness of the eye. Within the first section, there are two distinct points: first, contemplating the conventional existence; second, contemplating the ultimate non-existence.
Regarding the present eye, applying the designation "eye" and the conceptualization of "eye" is the contemplation of conventional existence.

That there is merely a designation based on names and concepts, and that it does not exist as a reality, is the contemplation of ultimate non-existence, which follows from the phrase "one should contemplate for oneself. One should contemplate for oneself that even one's own eye...
The essence of the eye cannot be apprehended as non-existent; how much less so can that which is designated by names and signs be called "the eye"?
Within the conditions of the eye, the eye itself is also absent. In the second section, such designations of names and concepts are entirely devoid of causes and conditions and are empty.
Since these designations of names and concepts are utterly without reality, it is established that the eye is empty. These designations of names and concepts are...
The eye is that which relies [upon its basis]. Since the basis itself does not exist, how could the nature of the eye exist? In the first part of the third section, the question "For what reason?

is raised to transition from the preceding to the subsequent argument: "The eye is able to produce consciousness; for what reason do you say it does not exist? The explanation below has two parts: first, observing the emptiness of consciousness;

second, establishing the emptiness of that consciousness by means of the emptiness of the eye, thereby using the emptiness of consciousness to manifest the prior emptiness of the eye. Within the former [section], there are two statements. First:

In the beginning and middle [of this analysis], it is not that the eye does not actually exist when observed; rather, the two types of observation—conventional and nominal—are what are called "the eye.

When one observes that which is designated by the mental construct (*saṃjñā*) of "eye" and gives rise to the cognition of "eye," this is observing its actual non-existence. What is termed "eye-cognition" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) refers to the act of discerning;

because the essence of eye-cognition is empty, it is not produced by names and so forth. It is only through conventional linguistic expression that eye-cognition arises, and thus one observes its conventional existence. It is merely names that arise.
Because it is a cognition, it is not real. Below, the emptiness of consciousness is established by means of the emptiness of the eye.
That which cannot be heard or known as the nature of that eye is observed to be non-existent in reality. This passage is insufficient; if it were complete, it should state:

"That which cannot be heard or known as the nature of that eye, yet gives rise to the cognition of an eye—this is observed to exist conventionally when the cognition arises with respect to names and things. However, regarding the eye alone...
The perception of the eye arises based on the causal conditions of the designation "eye"; therefore, it is not real. Thus far, we have examined the present;
henceforth, we shall examine the past. Since the present eye mentioned above exists only as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) and lacks any fixed reality, the same applies to the future.
It is merely a name and so forth; one cannot perceive the future. Thus far, we have examined...

The eye. The subsequent categories are analogous to other dharmas. First, one uses the eye-faculty as an analogy to reveal the other dharmas; subsequently, one uses present dharmas as an analogy for those of the past and future.
As previously stated, "like the eye" refers to what was observed above. In the same way, from "the ear" onwards, one correctly applies the analogy to other dharmas:

the ear, nose, tongue, and body analogously reveal the dharmas of form, while [the faculties of] seeing and so forth analogously reveal the dharmas of mind. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing constitute the distracted mind.
Furthermore, visual consciousness is called "seeing"; auditory consciousness is called "hearing"; olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses are termed "awareness" (*vitarka*);
and mental consciousness is termed "cognition" (*vijñapti*). "Seeking" refers to the initial stage of cultivation, while "attainment" refers to its final perfection.

Within that seeking, the coarse aspect of the mind is termed "awareness," and the subtle aspect is termed "examination" (*vicāra*). In this manner, all such categories illustrate those phenomena that are neither form nor mind.

[The ellipsis] etc. These [terms] refer to phenomena (*dharma*). From the category of the eye up to the future, and regarding the three periods of time from the present category up to the future—because it transcends [the present] to cite what is yet to come, it says "up to" (*yāvat*).
First, one contemplates the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); next, one contemplates the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Below, these two are concluded together:
thus, the means for destroying the self is subsumed under the preceding contemplation of the emptiness of persons, up to the means for destroying phenomena.
This concludes the section on the emptiness of phenomena following the summary of the fetters. You should dwell alone until this third point, which clarifies the words of instruction.

From here below is the fourth point, which clarifies the benefits of the instruction. Thus, "one who observes all these well" serves as a transition that summarizes what precedes and introduces what follows.
The following clarifies its benefits. There are two kinds of benefits: first, that which is abandoned; second, that which is attained.
From the beginning up to "there is nothing to be grasped" refers to what is abandoned. The phrase "all notions of phenomena and notions of the future" refers to the mind that has abandoned these.

To discuss the mind in terms of phenomena is called the "perception of phenomena" (*dharmasaṃjñā*). To discuss the mind in terms of time is called the "perception of the future. Because it is raised by way of what follows, it is specifically termed "the future.
Furthermore, since the future is precisely that which is to be loathed, it is singled out for mention. All that is false and deceptive refers to the characteristics of what is to be abandoned;
because discursive thought is not true, it is called "false and deceptive. "Without perception and without thought" means being free from the aforementioned mind.
It is called "non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñā*) because one has severed all conceptualizations of phenomena. It is called "non-thought" (*acitta*) because one is free from future conceptualizations.
What is termed "signlessness" (*animitta*) refers to being free from all preceding false signs. The phrase "not grasping at any object" summarizes this state of liberation.
The following clarifies that which is attained. There are two types of attainment: first, the cause; second, the fruit. Within the cause, there are four [factors].

First, one attains the lineage of the wisdom-samādhi: the cause of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is called the nature of wisdom, and the cause of the Tathāgata’s concentration is called the nature of samādhi.
Second, one attains the five perfections. Third, one attains the eight dhyānas. Fourth, one attains the bodhisattva’s immeasurable samādhis.
The section beginning with "gradually" (*jianshi*) below concerns the attainment of the fruit;
the preceding portion has completed the explanation. The section beginning with "this is called" (*shi ming*) explains the conclusion and the eulogy; this refers to the conclusion.
The section beginning with "the Tathāgatas of the past for those of initial practice" (*guoqu rulai wei chuye*) below is the eulogy of excellence.

From the beginning, how has the teaching for those at the initial stage been clarified? It explains the instruction for bodhisattvas, while the lower section on the Śrāvaka Vehicle also concurrently transforms those of the Small Vehicle.
When śrāvakas contemplate this principle of selflessness, they swiftly attain the six supernormal powers and the four types of unhindered wisdom.
The preceding section explains the activities performed. All of these are now summarized and concluded at the end.

"The power of recollecting past lives" (jātismara-bala) identifies the essential nature of that power; "observing past lives" distinguishes its characteristics; and the following section clarifies its activities.
To speak of the cultivation of goodness and the abandonment of evil, as well as of weariness with [the mundane], purity, and self-mastery, constitutes the correct transformation of karma.

To have faith and joy in goodness is called a "pure mind"; to feel weary of and detached from evil is called a "mind of weariness. One preaches the Dharma to subdue sentient beings so that these two minds may arise:
subduing them through the mind of weariness to cause them to leave evil behind, and preaching to the pure mind to cause goodness to arise.
"Subduing the theory of permanence" refers to the activity of crushing heterodox views. Because one knows that effects arise from causes, one subdues the theory of permanence.

"The power of knowledge regarding birth and death" cites the essence of this power but does not briefly explain its characteristics. "Explaining to sentient beings" below clarifies the activity of transforming others.

"The power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows" cites the essence of this power but does not briefly explain its characteristics. "Subduing doubt and hesitation" below clarifies its functional activity.
Regarding the term "sequential," this refers to the sixth section, where its characteristics are subsequently explained. Initially, upon attaining *bodhi*, one suddenly acquires the ten powers;

thus, the essence of the powers is sudden. When the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) arises, it is attained all at once. As for the subsequent [attainment], the functional application of the powers is gradual.
The preceding section has generally explained the sequence of manifestation; hereafter, it will be specifically revealed. Within this specific exposition, there are three parts:

first, the sequence of manifesting transformation based on worldly knowledge; second, the sequence of manifesting transformation based on the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*);

and third, the sequence of manifesting transformation based on the Tathāgata’s knowledge that thoroughly penetrates the *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination. Regarding the first of these sections, one first employs the first power.

Knowing the causes and effects of the world. Regarding the power of discerning what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*) within the causal categories of the *āveṇika* (unshared) Buddha-dharmas:
this clarifies the dharma of incomparable perfect enlightenment.

Within this dharma of incomparable perfect enlightenment, in order to know the causal categories of worldly dharmas, one observes the causal categories of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by means of the first power; this power is the general [foundation].

The remaining nine powers below follow this sequence to gather and transform sentient beings. First, by means of the power of karma, one knows the karma of the desire realm to gather and transform sentient beings.
For the sake of the mundane, one subsequently uses the power of meditative concentration to know the karma of the higher realms to gather and transform sentient beings.

And for the sake of leading forth from the world: desiring to enable sentient beings to attain transcendence, [the Buddha] uses the remaining seven powers to lead them forth and gather them through transformation.

By the power of faculties, inclinations, and dispositions, he knows the mental capacities of beings. By the power of the destination and the path, he gathers and causes their minds to abide. Through the powers of recollecting past lives and the divine eye, he transforms them so they may leave behind the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Finally, by the power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, he brings them to ultimate completion. Within the second gate, he first employs the first power.

He knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Based on this sequence, he employs the remaining nine powers to gather and transform sentient beings. First, by means of the power of karma (*karmabala*), he knows the activities of householders to gather and transform them;
next, by means of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhibala*), he contemplates the activities of those who have left the household life to gather and transform them.

The subsequent remaining seven powers, their modes of emergence from the path, and their further characteristics are the same as before. Within the third gate, one first uses the first power to contemplate the dharma-realm of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the *dharmadhātu* of the Buddha-dharmas, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, share a single essential nature while mutually conditioning and assembling;
this is called "dependent origination. That these distinct gates are each different is called the "dharma-realm. The first power is thus understood. Below are the remaining nine...
By means of these powers, he gathers and transforms sentient beings according to this sequence. First, by the power of karma, he contemplates the karmic fruits of the world.

Next, relying on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he manifests the three wheels to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to abandon worldly evils and practice worldly virtues.
Finally, the remaining seven powers provide benefit for those seeking the path, following the same sequence as before.
Regarding the "distinctions," this refers to the seventh section, which is first cited, then explained, and finally concluded. The first power is easily understood.
Within the second power, one knows the distinction between the characteristics of what is wholesome and unwholesome, what is desirable and undesirable, and what is performed and not experienced;

from here on, the differences are distinguished in contrast to what follows. Furthermore, within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*), one thoroughly understands that while this is karma, that is not, and yet both are the power of karma.

This is called the "lower fetters. Within the third power (*bala*), one knows the threefold manifestation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*), distinguishing their respective characteristics.

Furthermore, from this point downward, the differences are explained in contrast to what follows. Among the five faculties (*indriya*), the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is termed "pure" (*viśuddha*).

Because "purity" is cited as representative of the other four faculties, it is said to be "purity and so forth" (*viśuddhādi*). This continues until one knows that those five faculties are co-arisen and associated with a concentrated mind (*samāhitacitta*).

This is also the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is called the "concluding summary. Within the fourth power, knowing the dull and other faculties is called the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*);
this is the analysis of its specific characteristics. Below this, it proceeds to distinguish [it] from what follows. Aspiration is desire (*chanda*).

Even knowing that the arising of the faculties produces that aspiration and desire is also called the power of the faculties. Within the fifth power, from the beginning up to "attaining the understanding of nirvāṇa in the Mahāyāna," [is explained].

One should analyze their characteristics. To know these various aspirations is termed the power of understanding (*adhimukti-bala*); this serves as a general heading. Understanding has six aspects, which will be explained below in detail:
the analysis of whether they emerge or do not emerge from abiding; and the analysis of whether they are distant or proximate, pure or impure, and superior or inferior.

The distinctions between the present life and the future are categorized as great and small; furthermore, below this, the differences are explained in relation to what follows, both generally and specifically.
Generally speaking, the power of understanding (*jñāna-bala*)—which includes the various types of metaphors arising from knowledge and comprehension—is its general designation.

Specifically, the diversity of natures is like worldly seeds, such as the differences between rice, beans, and so forth; these are called "seed-metaphors. This extends to the way knowledge and comprehension bring those various natures to fruition.

The analogy of the seed is likewise an explanation of the power of understanding (*adhimukti-bala*). There are four types of differentiation; for instance, the "nature-seed" (*prakṛti-bīja*) is what is specifically termed the power of understanding.
The natures of the realms (*dhātu-prakṛti*) of the three vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) differ from one another, and thus they are explained as being of four kinds.

These four natures of the realms are like worldly seeds, in that their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are each distinct. Therefore, they are described as being "like nature-seeds. This differentiates the aforementioned power of understanding.
Because the four elements that are accomplished are the seeds of their own nature (*dharmatā*), they are called the power of understanding (*adhimukti-bala*).

Within the sixth power, first knowing the various seeds of conceptual differentiation is called the power of the elements (*dhātu-bala*); this refers to the differentiation of their actual characteristics. Knowing the various natures and differentiating these natures—just as one differentiates worldly seeds—is called the power of the elements.
The following sections contrast this with what follows to clarify the distinction. Regarding those who possess the nature for *nirvāṇa*:
This is the destination reached. What is called the "path-trace" (*mārga-pada*) is that which is able to reach the Path. This path-trace arises based on the aforementioned realms;

therefore, it is called the "path-trace conforming to the realms. Furthermore, knowing the Nirvana to be reached by the realms, as well as knowing the path-traces that arise in conformity with the realms, is also termed the "power of the realms.
Within the seventh power, one knows the various natures and purities of all paths.

The "path leading to the destination" (*yātikara-mārga*) should be distinguished according to its characteristics. "The path of all modes" (*sarvākāra-mārga*) is the general category; "distress and purification" (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*) are the specific distinctions.
From this point downward, the differences are explained in contrast to what follows. Within the past, all causes for rebirth in various destinies constitute the path leading to the destination.
Therefore, even the knowledge of the causes for all destinies within past lives is also subsumed under the power of knowing the path leading to various destinations (*yatrāgati-jñāna-bala*).
Within the eighth power, the knowledge of the six aspects of the past is termed the "distinguishing of the specific characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*) of past lives.

The six types of concomitant activities are termed the "six modes of expression. One also knows eight matters, though they are not mentioned here in brief. The following section contrasts these with what follows to clarify their distinctions.
Up to the point of knowing the past lives of those sentient beings as they proceed toward future births and deaths—this is still termed "knowledge of past lives" (*pūrvanivāsa*).
Within the ninth power, the knowledge of future births and deaths is the "power of death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), which should be distinguished by its specific characteristics.

From the passage below, the differences are explained in contrast to what follows: namely, knowing that within the future lives of sentient beings, [the state] persists until the attainment of the ultimate [enlightenment], even up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

The exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is one's own welfare; it is still called the ninth power regarding birth and death. Within the tenth power, there is no further distinction to be made regarding its specific characteristics.

To know the ultimate meaning and to know that others have attained the exhaustion of outflows in the present life—just as one has oneself attained the exhaustion of outflows—these ten [powers] are thus summarized as a conclusion.

Within the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), there are three distinct textual sections. First, the citation and reference to the sūtra; the meaning of the four fearlessnesses is explained extensively in a separate chapter.

Second, a brief explanation of how the Tathāgata is fearless because he has realized this for himself. Third, an extensive analytical explanation beginning from the section on "the cognitive obscurations" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Within this extensive section, there are five parts: first, clarifying the equipment of fearlessness; second, clarifying fearlessness [beginning with] "The Tathāgata... and so forth.

[The characteristics of fearlessness are: First, the characteristic; second, the liberation from the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the awakening to all phenomena, which is not shared with the śrāvakas—this is the possession of the fearlessness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*);

third, the liberation from the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which is shared with the śrāvakas; fourth, the section beginning with "self-settled" explains the virtue of fearlessness; fifth, the section beginning with "awakening to the equality of all phenomena" explains the function of fearlessness.

Within the first section, the liberation from the cognitive hindrances and the awakening to all phenomena that is not shared with the śrāvakas constitute the equipment of the fearlessness of omniscience. The liberation from the afflictive hindrances is shared with the śrāvakas.

The first is the equipment for the fearlessness of having exhausted the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*). The second is the equipment for the fearlessness of teaching the path leading out of suffering (*mārga-nairyāṇika-vaiśāradya*).
The third is the equipment for the fearlessness of teaching the factors that obstruct the path (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*). These four kinds constitute the equipment for fearlessness.
Because one has no fear toward others at such times, they are also called "objects" (*viṣaya*), as they are what is illuminated and known by the wisdom of fearlessness.
Therefore, within the second characteristic, the Tathāgata possesses the characteristic of fearless wisdom that knows this as it truly is.
To slander this by claiming he does not know it is impossible; because such a thing is impossible, he attains fearlessness, which is the characteristic of the fearless mind.

Within the third essence, there are two distinct meanings: first, the essence of wisdom; second, the essence of mind. Having internally illuminated and known these, he is fully endowed with the four [fearlessnesses].

Virtue is the essence of his wisdom (*jñāna*). Not being intimidated by difficult conditions is the essence of his mind (*citta*). Now, it is said that not being intimidated is the essence of the mind;
the section below on "not doubting" is the essence of wisdom. Because he clearly and thoroughly understands that he himself possesses the four qualities of a teacher, he does not doubt.
Within the fourth quality, "establishing oneself and establishing others" serves as the general heading; the details below can be understood accordingly. Fifth is the function (*vṛtti*).
In the middle [section], the first wisdom specifically transforms bodhisattvas, because bodhisattvas practice and study all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
The second specifically transforms those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), because they seek quiescence (*śama*). The latter two transform both.
Regarding the transformation of both, within the category of bodhisattvas, the two collections (*piṭaka*) are distinguished and divided; their characteristics are manifest and thus easily understood.
Within the three applications of mindfulness, the first cites and points to the sūtra. Next is the general explanation: "Dharma" refers to the sūtras; "Vinaya" refers to the precepts.
The Tathāgata constantly maintains mindfulness of my Dharma and my Vinaya as being the most honored and supreme among all other dharmas; thus he is called the Great Master of Dharma.
Because one constantly practices equanimity toward both what is received and what is not received, there is no suffering or affliction; thus, it is said here that one "is not troubled.
This mentions only one side for emphasis. Below, this is explained in detail: first the number three is cited, next the three names are listed, and finally it is summarized.

Regarding these three groups, to have neither increase nor decrease means: to feel no joy toward the correct, no affliction toward the false, and no deluded indifference toward that which is neither false nor correct.

Regarding the three things that need no guarding (*trīṇy arakṣāṇi*), first, the initial section cites the sutra. It briefly states that all concealments are completely severed, thereby demonstrating the three things that need no guarding and correctly defining their characteristics.
From the passage beginning with "The Arhat," the superiority [of the Buddha] is revealed by contrast. Within this, there are four parts:

first, it generally explains that because the remaining faults of the Arhat are not yet exhausted, he must maintain protection; this refers to neutral (*avyākṛta*) offenses and lapses of body and speech (*duṣkṛta*) which cannot [otherwise] be restrained.

Because it is a result, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta). When one's actions violate the Dharma, it is termed a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); at times, this may also arise from forgetfulness or a lapse in mental action (*manas-karman*).
Second, it is clarified that because the Tathāgata is entirely devoid [of such faults], there is no need for protection;

being entirely devoid [of them], he has no unwholesome states. Being entirely real, he possesses only what is wholesome. Third, it is specifically clarified that because the three types of action (*tri-karman*) of an Arhat may still have faults, they must be guarded.
Guarding against [faults]: at times, during debate, one fears falling into a position of defeat due to verbal errors; at times, one feels displeasure due to physical errors;
and at times, one succumbs to indolence due to mental errors. Therefore, one guards oneself. It is explained that the Tathāgata is entirely free from all such things.
"Great Compassion" refers back to the aforementioned state of not forgetting the Dharma; herein, the Tathāgata’s deeds are constantly and continuously recollected in their entirety.
This is the general heading; what follows is the specific exposition. "All that is done" refers to the actions of the body.

"All that is spoken" refers to the speech of the mouth. "All skillful means" refers to that which is known by the mind. To say that one "never forgets these matters at all times" is the summary of non-forgetfulness.

Regarding the elimination of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), first the preceding section is cited, followed by an explanation of its characteristics. The passage "The Tathāgata’s movements and stillness are free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions" correctly defines these characteristics.
The section beginning with "All arhats... uses contrast to clarify this point. Finally, the section beginning with "Therefore... provides the conclusion.

Within "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), the phrase "all modes" (*sarvākāra*) excellently summarizes the preceding section. The subsequent explanation has three parts: first, a general exposition; second, a specific exposition; and third, a concluding summary.
Knowing the meaning and its benefits, etc., constitutes the general exposition. Knowing the meaning is wholesome (*kuśala*); not knowing the meaning is unwholesome (*akuśala*).

That which is neither meaningful nor meaningless is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Next, this is specifically elucidated: knowing the evil and the indeterminate is termed "all-aspected" (*sarvākāra*);
knowing the wholesome is termed "sublime" (*praṇīta*). The following summarizes these points collectively as the "sublime wisdom of all aspects" (*sarvākārapraṇītajñāna*).
The extensive explanation above concludes with this second summary of the one hundred and forty dharmas.

From here below, the third section clarifies the locus where the qualities of all Buddhas are ultimately perfected. First, it clarifies the locus where the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) are fully perfected;

next, it clarifies the locus where the remaining qualities are ultimately perfected; finally, it provides a summary. The passage stating that "all primary and secondary marks are obtained in the final body" clarifies the locus where the primary and secondary marks are achieved.
The section beginning with "excellent purity" (*praśānta*) and following clarifies the locus where the remaining Buddha-qualities are accomplished.

Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the locus of fulfillment; second, clarifying the characteristics of fulfillment. That the dharmas of the "quickness and purity" category are fulfilled only beneath the Bodhi tree refers to the locus of fulfillment.
As for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), they are easily accomplished; therefore, at the time of the final birth, they are already complete from the very moment of conception.

The remaining virtues are difficult to accomplish; thus, they are fulfilled only when one attains Bodhi beneath the Bodhi tree. The Bodhisattva, in his final birth, cultivates the thirty minor marks of excellence (*anuvyañjana*) to manifest the signs of perfection.

Within this process, he first cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Next, he attains the Samādhi of the Various Marks Free from Obstructions (*vividha-lakṣaṇa-vighna-vinirmukta-samādhi*), and subsequently realizes the Buddha-way.

This is the stage of the second *citta-viśuddhi* (purity of mind), occurring at the time of attaining the "Luminosity" (*prabhāsvara*). When compared to the preceding Vajra-like [Samādhi], it represents a further advancement.

The arising of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is designated as the second mind. One suddenly attains the ten powers (*daśabala*) up to the sublime wisdom (*jñāna*), thereby illuminating what has been attained.
The following section praises these attainments to manifest their excellence: "Swift, pure, and unsurpassed" refers to the excellence of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*).

"Unobstructed with respect to the knowable" refers to the excellence of the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*). "Swift, pure, and free from defilement" manifests the aforementioned virtue of abandonment. "Equanimous awakening" manifests the aforementioned virtue of wisdom.
All that precedes is summarized by way of conclusion.
Regarding the question, "What is the distinction of the ultimate Tathāgata?"—this fourth section clarifies that the cause differs from the fruit. First, the inquiry is raised:
since the preceding text treats the supreme Tathāgatas as being unified into a single ground (*eka-bhūmi*), it is necessary to distinguish their differences; therefore, this [section] is composed.
Question: Next, the meaning is clarified through metaphors. There are five distinct metaphors, followed by a summary below.
Above, one establishes one's own virtue; below, one establishes the benefit of others. Within this, there is first a general statement, then a detailed exposition, and finally a conclusion.
The ten directions of activity are briefly explained as nine matters; this constitutes the initial general statement.
Within the *āveṇika-dharmas* (unshared qualities), there are eleven distinct categories. Excluding the four purities (*pariśuddhi*), the remaining ten categories are condensed into nine:

the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*vyañjana*) are combined into one, while the other eight each constitute a single category; thus, there are nine. For what reason are the four purities excluded?
This is because the four purities are inherently pure by virtue of one's own qualities; since they do not manifest as benefiting others, delusion is not discussed in relation to them.

Furthermore, among the four purities, the first—purity of body—is subsumed under the marks and signs of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), while the latter three purities are encompassed by the remaining qualities; therefore, they are not discussed separately.
What is the distinction? First, the inquiry is raised; below, this is explained in detail. The first [mark] and the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) arise together to produce a single faith.

The second [section], which eliminates doubt and gives rise to the ten powers (*daśabala*), produces understanding in sentient beings. In the third section, within the context of the activities, the ten powers of the Buddha are used to give a general overview of all meanings;
that is to say, based upon the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) and all functional applications of meaning are brought forth.

Next, these are explained individually. By manifesting knowledge and vision through hearing, one demonstrates that one possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). By answering all questions, one reveals that one’s outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*).
By subduing all heterodox arguments, one clarifies one’s actual capability. By proclaiming the obstacles to the path and establishing the True Dharma, one clarifies one’s actual capability.
By teaching the path to the exhaustion of suffering, one gives rise to the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); this serves as the general conclusion. This is the fourth matter.

If the Tathāgata’s wisdom within abides or does not abide according to those who are to be tamed and are free from all afflictions, the Buddha’s impartial wisdom tames those sentient beings—whether they abide in wholesome dharmas or do not abide in wholesome dharmas—and does not give rise to affliction toward those who do not abide in the wholesome.
For this purpose, the three foundations of mindfulness are established. As stated in the fifth matter, it is as previously described.
Regarding the statement "arising non-protection because of acting in such a manner":
it refers to the arising of non-protection due to the complete severance of all concealments regarding everything that has been done, as described above; this is to be understood as the sixth point.

Regarding the seventh matter, "arising non-forgetfulness toward all births and all actions" means that one does not forget any of the deeds performed through the three types of action (body, speech, and mind). Regarding the eighth matter, [concerning] the Tathāgata...
"Practice that accords with suchness without remainder" means that because the conduct of the three karmas accords with principle, all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are severed.

Regarding the ninth matter, "neither meaningful nor meaningless, but entirely detached," it means that through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one is completely detached from both the unwholesome and the indeterminate.
"The meaning and benefit become manifest" refers to the sublime wisdom that discriminates wholesome dharmas to transform sentient beings.
It is for this reason that he gives rise to various sublime wisdoms. The following summarizes these points.

From the explanation of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) up to this point constitutes the second section, the extensive explanation of the Buddha-dharmas. From here on, the third section concludes and establishes all the aforementioned meanings.
However, at the beginning of this chapter, the Tathāgata’s abodes and the uncommon Buddha-dharmas of the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*) were cited as the introductory theme.
Now, in this conclusion, the establishment of the abodes and the uncommon Buddha-dharmas is summarized, while the ultimate stage is not. This is merely a matter of the text’s phrasing.
This is the "Tathāgata-abiding" within the "Chapter on Abiding in Bonds. This is called the tenth establishment among the ten establishments.
It will be explained and clarified below. Why is this asked? Regarding the phrase "establishing all matters for benefiting sentient beings based on what is learned through training":
"training" refers to the practice of learning, and "what is learned" refers to the dharmas of training. Because one accomplishes virtue by relying upon these, it is called an "establishment."
If one considers it from the perspective of self-benefit, the qualities of the fruit are established; hence it is called "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*).

Now, from the perspective of benefiting others, the one hundred and forty dharmas are able to establish nine kinds of activities for the benefit of sentient beings; thus they are named "establishment.

Therefore, the conclusion below states that because self-benefit and benefiting others are not like those of the Two Vehicles, they are called "unshared" (*āveṇika*). This concludes the meaning of the "unshared" [qualities] discussed in the preceding chapter on Unsurpassed Bodhi.

This sentence provides a general summary, which is then explained in detail below. Great Compassion, non-forgetfulness, and the Wisdom of the Exhaustion of Habitual Tendencies are called "unshared" (*āveṇika*) because they are entirely absent in the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, all other [qualities] are called "unshared" because they are not fully possessed by them.
From above, how is it that the third, the "Extensive Explanation of Bringing Forth" (*āhṛta-vistara-vyākhyā*), is named? From here below, the fourth [section] concludes the explanation.
There are five distinct names: first, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*; second, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-mātṛkā*;
third, the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha*; fourth, the *Abhedyapradarśana*; and fifth, the *Asaṅga-jñānamūla*. Among these five, the first four should be considered as the causes.

[The text] concludes. The latter name [of the section] is established by way of the fruit. Regarding the first four [names], the first is established by way of the intended meaning (*artha*), the second by way of the expression (*vyañjana*), the third by way of the intended meaning, and the fourth by way of the expression.
Within the conclusion of the first name, it is shown here that the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*) and its fruit are clarified by way of the expression to reveal the intended meaning.
Among the ten dharmas taught in this treatise, the first nine constitute the path of training, and the last one constitutes the fruit of training.

The fruit (*phala*). This treatise elucidates this meaning. Because it is the locus where all paths of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*) and the fruits of the path of training are truly taught, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*).
To summarize the essential point: "all paths of training" specifically refers back to the preceding [discussion of] training;

"and the fruits of the path of training" specifically refers back to the preceding [discussion of] fruits; and "all that is real" collectively refers back to the preceding two, clarifying that both of these two kinds are real.

Because it possesses virtue, it is called "the Real. This refers to the locus where the path of training and so forth are explained; thus, from the perspective of what is expressed (*vācya*), it is named the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Second, within the second [name], it is called the *Bodhisattvapitaka* to distinguish it from the Great [Vehicle] and the Small [Vehicle]. Third, within the third [name], it is called the *Mahāyāna-mātṛkā* to distinguish it from the Sūtras and the Śāstras.
Regarding the third name, the *Mahāyāna*: all that is taught in this treatise pertains to the stages of the Mahāyāna based upon the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Therefore, it is called "included within the Mahāyāna. Fourth, regarding the title "The Manifestation of the Indestructible":

this refers to the manifestation of the Dharma that does not contradict [reality], hence it is called "the manifestation of the indestructible. Fifth, regarding the title "The Root of Unobstructed Wisdom":
the Buddha’s wisdom is that unobstructed wisdom; since this treatise explains what can serve as its cause, it is called the "root."
If there are devas, humans, or asuras, this concludes the third section on the propagation [of the teaching]. This scripture has two parts: first, the exhortation to study; second, the entrustment.
Now, this section contains only the exhortation to study for propagation. Within it, the beginning clarifies that those who propagate the teaching attain great merit.
The phrase "Why is this? introduces the question-and-answer explanation. The phrase "Therefore" provides the conclusion.

Within the first section, it is explained that seven types of persons attain great merit: first, those who have faith; second, those who understand; third, those who listen; fourth, those who practice; fifth, those who explain it for others;
sixth, those who transcribe it; and seventh, those who make offerings. These are the merits attained by these seven types of persons.
It is no different from the merit of being instructed by the Buddha himself within that Bodhisattva-piṭaka regarding the practices for beginners.

In which Bodhisattva-piṭaka does the Buddha reveal and manifest this? It is in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Who are those beginners? They are the bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*).
What dharma is revealed? It is the dharma of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). In what way is it no different from that [instruction]? [Because it is identical in its qualities.]
That sutra states: "Just as all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā) gathers all merits, so too is it with the Chapter on the Gateways of All-encompassing Wisdom Merits.
If anyone hears this, their merit shall likewise be such. This clarifies that the gathering of virtues within the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless.
The merit of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages is equal to that of a Buddha. Anyone who hears it possesses merit equal to the dharmas of those stages, and may likewise be equal to a Buddha.
Because the merits such as faith herein are identical to those [of the Buddha], it is said that there is no difference.

Regarding the question posed below in the commentary: why is this asked? Since this treatise (*śāstra*) is not the direct scripture (*sūtra*), for what reason do the merits such as faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) arising toward it equal those [merits] derived from the extensive and boundless [scriptures]? The subsequent explanation has two parts.

First, it clarifies that because this treatise reveals the Dharma and Vinaya to cause people to initiate practice, faith, understanding, and so forth, attain great merit. "Revealing the Dharma" means the gathering of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
The Vinaya reveals the departure from unwholesome dharmas. Now, "receiving and upholding many" refers to the arising of one's own practice through the contemplation of the *dharmānudharma*.
"Causing many to receive and uphold" gives rise to the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "Causing many to contemplate" gives rise to the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

The "phrases of the *dharmānudharma*" give rise to the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). "Gradually increasing and expanding" gives rise to benefiting others. These two [points] do not arise in those of inferior capacity; this treatise clarifies them.
Because it is able to cause the True Dharma to flow forth and endure for a long time without perishing, those who possess faith, understanding, and so forth attain great merit.

Regarding the phrase "the semblance-dharma does not arise when the True Dharma exists, nor when the Dharma has been extinguished": this means that during the period of the True Dharma, the semblance-dharma does not arise; it refers to the time when the Dharma has been extinguished.

That which resembles the Dharma but is not authentic is called the semblance-dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*). Since this treatise fully proclaims the True Dharma, the semblance-dharma does not arise during the period of the True Dharma.

Regarding the Dharma: it causes that True Dharma (*saddharma*) to possess the characteristic of extinction; yet, it is that which can cause the true meaning of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) to blaze forth—meaning that during the period of the Semblance Dharma, it can cause the true meaning of the True Dharma to blaze forth.
Although the flow of the True Dharma does not cease even during the Semblance period, it is therefore said that "the true meaning of the Semblance Dharma blazes forth.
Regarding its ability to cause the True Dharma never to perish: this refers to its ability to cause the True Dharma [to endure] during the period of the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*).
The Dharma does not perish. Although it exists during the period of the Final Age (*paścimakāla*), because the transmission of the True Dharma remains unchanged, it does not perish. Question:

If this [Dharma] can cause the True Dharma to remain constantly without perishing throughout the periods of the True, Semblance, and Final Ages, how can there be a Semblance Dharma period and a Final Age?

Answer: There is a reason for this. Because the Dharma follows the people, there are the Semblance and Final Ages. If one sets aside the people and discusses the Dharma alone, the True Dharma is eternally present.
It is extinguished.
Therefore, it concludes below. This is because this treatise reveals the Dharma and Vinaya, causing many sentient beings to give rise to the three types of wisdom;
furthermore, because this treatise can cause the True Dharma to never perish, it is said that the merits of understanding, listening, and so forth are boundless.
